PREFACE

->To the<-
# READER.

Kind Reader, you have here some **Fortuita** <note>The title *Fortuita* translates to "Chance Remarks" or "Random Thoughts," suggesting a collection of miscellaneous philological observations rather than a systematic treatise.</note>, which, just as they were born by chance, were poured out rather than produced with much labor and care. But I have experienced such malicious fortune even in these pages that, had it not been for the expectations of my friends and several other reasons, I would have been the first to discard them like a failed birth. So much has everything been disfigured by printing errors <note>original: "erratis typographicis"</note>, and these often so massive, that I myself can sometimes hardly grasp what I wrote. It also happened that, since I had intended to oversee the printing <term>editioni</term> <note>This refers to the "edition" process, where an author would ideally visit the printing house to check proofs as they were pulled from the press.</note> in person, I left some matters for a final review. Subsequently, because of a change in plans <note>original: "altiore consilio," literally "higher counsel," implying a more important decision or external circumstance forced his departure</note>, these were not arranged or corrected in my usual manner, and they will now fall into the hands of the spiteful as well as frien-

<summary>In this preface, Jacob Tollius apologizes to the reader for the numerous typographical errors in the text, explaining that he was unable to supervise the printing process as intended.</summary>

<keywords>Jacob Tollius, Fortuita, printing errors, preface, publishing history, 17th century, proofreading, philology</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues Jacob Tollius's address to the reader. Having complained about general printing errors on the previous page, he specifically highlights the difficulty of correcting Greek text. He then transitions into a defense of his central, controversial thesis: that ancient Greek myths are actually secret allegories for the secrets of alchemy.</meta>

# PREFACE.

...of friends. I have indeed attempted, as far as was possible, to point out some errors; but I encountered so many in the Greek passages that despair held me back from marking them all. Therefore, I ask this one thing: before you pass judgment, please look at the index of errors <note>original: "erratorum indicem," the errata list common in early books to correct mistakes made during the manual typesetting process</note>. 

As for the subject matter itself, it does not escape me how unexpected, how incredible, and even foolish my opinion regarding the **Greek myths** <note>original: "Græcorum fabulis"</note> will seem to those who believe the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Lapis Philosophicus</term> <note>The legendary "Great Work" of alchemy, a substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and providing the "elixir of life."</note> to be a mere figment of the imagination and something that never existed in the natural world. 

Let them enjoy their disbelief for all I care; I envy no one that perspective. I would wish, however, for them to refute the harmony <note>original: "concentum," a term suggesting a musical or mathematical concord</note> that I demonstrate among the various myths of different nations. Let them produce for me just one myth of any repute from among them all, which—along with all the others, or with that of the **Stone**...

<summary>Tollius continues his apology for printing errors, specifically in the Greek text, and introduces his theory that ancient myths are alchemical allegories, challenging skeptics to disprove the "harmony" he finds between different cultures' legends.</summary>

...the nature of the **Stone** <term>Lapis</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical "Great Work."</note> does not marvelously agree. I *explain*, or rather show, the nomenclature of almost all the Gods in **Alchemy** <term>Chemia</term> <note>In the 17th century, the terms for chemistry and alchemy were often used interchangeably, though here Tollius specifically refers to the "hermetic art" of transmutation.</note>; I present the origin and cause of their attributes, and I point out many more things besides, which are left to be unraveled by one's own intellect. 

Many other myths could have been added: such as that famous story of **Augeas** <note>In Greek myth, Hercules's fifth labor was to clean the stables of King Augeas, which had not been washed in thirty years, by diverting two rivers.</note>, in which the etymology could be observed, along with the Sun or Neptune as his father, and the dung of the herds, purged in a single day—*that is, in a single fusion*—in a crucible by **Hercules**—*that is, by a saline fire* <term>igne salino</term>; and this was done by turning in the rivers. *For the matter must flow*, so that the impure **sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur." # PREFACE.

<meta>Ink bleed-through from reverse page visible throughout.</meta>

...and the **many-named matter** <note>original Greek: μυριώνυμος ὕλη (*murionymos hyle*). This refers to the *materia prima* or "first matter" of alchemy, which philosophers claimed could be found everywhere and was thus given thousands of different names to conceal its true identity.</note> had crossed the sea. I could, I say, have brought forward and treated many more things of that kind, had I not feared the boredom of my readers, or had the constraints of time not called me back.

But these things will be abundantly sufficient and satisfying to those by whom *Basil Valentine* <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemical figure, now believed to be a pseudonym for the publisher Johann Thölde. He is famous for his foundational work on the medicinal and chemical properties of metals.</note> has been read with care, whose *Triumphal Chariot of Antimony* <note>One of the most famous texts in the history of chemistry, describing the extraction of medicinal "essences" from the mineral antimony.</note> no one, so far as I have been able to notice until now, has truly understood. I shall explain that work, God willing, in a commentary on the *Diseases of the Chemical Man*. For everything taught there concerns remedies for the **Philosophical Man** <note>In alchemical philosophy, this represents the perfected human state or the spiritual "body" that the alchemist seeks to heal and transform, rather than just the physical body.</note>; and hence it seems to me not at all surprising if that common, literal preparation <term>vulgaris præparatio</term> <note>The "vulgar" or literal reading of alchemical recipes often involved toxic substances; the author warns that without the secret "philosophical" key, these recipes are deadly.</note> is more pestilential than healthful for the race of mortals. 

If you profit anything from these matters in the meantime, most kind Reader, I shall rejoice; if not, I would wish you to consider that not all things are written for all people—nor indeed are they understood by all. Farewell.

Regarding this inscription, a man of most profound learning and infinite reading has commented thus: *The reason why JANUS was sometimes called PATULCIUS (the Opener), as found in the works of Ovid, and sometimes CLUSIUS (the Closer), is obvious: it refers to the doors of his temple being opened or closed depending on the time <note>Janus’s temple doors were famously open during war and closed during peace.</note>. Why JUNO is called PATULCIA, however, is not so clear. Perhaps only Fabatius, the chief initiate <note>original: *ἀρχιμύστης* (*archimystes*); a high priest or someone initiated into the highest level of sacred mysteries.</note> of this rite (for we know of no one else who has even named her), would have used the term. We must, therefore, conjecture and try to see if we can bring some light to this obscure and unmentioned matter. Since it has just been said that Juno is the assistant of women in labor <note>original: *puerperarum*; women giving birth.</note>, and that she fosters, protects, and facilitates successful births; and especially by accelerating and making the labor easier...*

...the loosening, opening, unlocking, and opening <note>original: *patura*; a rare Latin noun for the act of opening.</note> of the passages, channels, and the closure of the womb is necessary, they believed that this was also provided for and cared for by *Juno*. <sig>A 3</sig>

although it acts visibly. (Hence Nature, to the same Onomacritus, is described as *wrapping her silent footstep with her ankles* <note>original Greek: *Apsophon astragalois podon ichnos eilyousa*</note>.) *For there is a **Volatile Spirit**, which performs its duty within bodies; it has its place and seat in the Divine will.* The ancients called this volatile Spirit, both male and female, **JANUS** and **JANA**—not, as the learned think more skillfully than truly, from *Javan* the son of Japheth, or from *Yayin* <note>original Hebrew: *Jajin*</note>, which signifies wine in Hebrew (as if Janus were actually Noah); nor from the Aeolic *Zan* <note>original Greek: *ζὰν*</note>, from which *Zanos* or *Janus* comes. Rather, it comes from "going" <note>Latin: *eundo*</note>, as Cicero rightly notes; hence even the feet are dedicated to **Diana**, no differently than to **Mercury**. This etymology also occurs in the Greek language, where both **Apollo** and **Diana** are called *Ieios* <note>original Greek: *ἰήϊ@*, an epithet often linked to "sending" or "going"</note>; and *Ioppara* is linked to "going" <note>original Greek: *ienai*</note>, as is *Pheraia* from *Phereaz* in Hesychius <note>Hesychius of Alexandria, a 5th-century grammarian and lexicographer</note>; **Ceres** is called *Epipola* and *Egytho* by the same author, from a known origin. Likewise, **Rhea** received her name from "flowing" <note>original Greek: *rhein*</note>, just as **AVENTINA** was named by the Latins from "arrival" <note>Latin: *adventu*</note>.

In these matters, one must look at the fiction of the myth devised to express the **nature of things**, rather than the true historical record. And thus the name was given to **Venus**, not from the *Benoth* <note>Referring to *Succoth Benoth*, a Babylonian deity mentioned in the Bible, sometimes associated with Venus</note> of the Hebrews or Phoenicians, but from "coming" <note>Latin: *veniendo*</note>; no differently than the month of **April** is named from "opening" <note>Latin: *aperiendo*</note>, and **Proserpina** from "creeping forth" <note>Latin: *proserpendo*</note>. For she is the one who opens the year, whether we take it as the common and natural year, or the **Chemical and secret** year, just like Janus himself.

### CHAPTER II.
#### *The Number Five explained.*

<margin>Verse 1391.</margin>Taking up Lycophron’s *Cassandra* <note>A notoriously difficult and "dark" 3rd-century BC poem</note> to reread during the night hours—for I thought the "darkness" of both the poem and the night complemented each other beautifully—I noticed that two most learned men stumbled over a single small word, missing its elegance. Thus Lycophron writes:

> And the peninsula of him who, long ago,
> Was utterly hated by the Goddess Curitis <note>A title for Juno/Hera</note>,
> The father of the all-shaping, vixen-like harlot,
> Who with her daily earnings
> Wandered to feed the sharp hunger of her father,
> The "Burner" <note>Aithon, a name for Erysichthon, referring to his "burning" hunger</note> who devoured strange limbs.
<note>original Greek: *Kai chersonēson tē palai lēktēriau / Thea Kyrita pampan estygēmenō / Tēs pantomorphou bassaras lampouridos / Tokēos, hēt’ alphaishi tais kath’ hēmeran / Boskein alēthainesken akmaian patros / O’thneia gastrizontos Aithōnos pleura.*</note>

That is, as Canterus <note>Willem Canter, a 16th-century classical scholar</note> translates it:

> *And the coastal peninsula of him who once*
> *Was wholly hated by the Goddess Curitis,*
> *The father of the all-shaped little fox-prostitute,*
> *Who by her daily gains*
> *Nourished the immense hunger of her parent,*
> *The "Burner" devouring foreign extremities.*

**Mestra** (or as others call her, **Metra**), the daughter of **Erysichthon**, is called "all-shaped" <note>original Greek: *pantomorphos*, referring to her ability to change shape</note> here. However, in the written manuscripts, the word is read as "gate-shaped" <note>original Greek: *pylomorphos*</note>, a title not un... <note>The text breaks off, leading into the next page's discussion of this word's "pleasantness" or "suitability."</note>

<meta>This page continues the philological and alchemical analysis of the number "five." It picks up from the previous page's discussion of a specific word used by the poet Lycophron, debating whether it means "all-shaped" or "five-shaped."</meta>

<page-num>7</page-num>
<header>MISCELLANY.</header>
<sig>A 4</sig>

...understood, and therefore was corrected (or perhaps corrupted) by Canter <note>Willem Canter (1542–1575), a Dutch scholar</note>, whom Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch classical scholar</note> has wrongly followed here. I suspect that Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), one of the greatest scholars of the Renaissance</note> saw the truth of the matter, because his translation calls it not *all-formed*, but *many-formed*: which is the correct and proper interpretation of this word <note>original Greek: *pentamorphos*</note>; and this very word should be substituted in place of the other. For the Greeks were accustomed to denote either a number or a great magnitude of body by adding the little word **five** <note>original Greek: *pente*</note>, not unlike their use of the word **nine** <note>original Greek: *ennea*</note>.

<margin>
Hesychius on *enneanegharos* <note>A word meaning "nine times old"</note>.
</margin>

Thus, in the *Greek Anthology*, a certain old woman of extreme longevity is called **Hecuba of the Five-Crows** <note>original Greek: *Pentakorōnē Hekabē*</note>; that is, one who lived longer than many generations of crows. So too in the same book, a man of extreme beggary, poorer even than Irus <note>The beggar in Homer’s Odyssey</note>, is called **five-times-poor** <note>original Greek: *pentepenichros*</note>. Likewise, regarding the "tenth waves" <note>The largest waves in a series</note>, the term **five-wave** <note>original Greek: *pentakymias*</note> is used in that same *Florilegium* <note>A collection of literary excerpts</note>.

<margin>

Old
women.
</margin>

Searching for the origin of this meaning of increasing and amplifying in this word, I find that this number pertains most especially to us and to **our art** <note>A common euphemism for Alchemy</note>: and that the myth, like many others, came forth from the **Chemical workshop**. For **Erysichthon** tearing and rending the earth is **Acid**, which devours all things; to whom his daughter **Metra**—namely, the **vital soul**—supplies daily nourishment; without which

<margin>
Ovid,
Book VIII

Therefore, regarding what concerns and pertains to our "Great Work" <note>The *Opus*, or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>, there were **five folds** <note>original Greek: *ptyches pente*</note> in the Homeric shield of Achilles, which Heraclides Ponticus <note>A Greek philosopher and astronomer</note> interprets as the five celestial zones. Furthermore, to these five elements correspond as many senses: touch to earth, taste to water, hearing to air, smell to fire (because scent or exhalation proceeds from heat), and sight to ether and light. We shall speak elsewhere of softness and hardness, of sweetness, of musical harmony and song, of sweet scents, and finally of sight, the eyes, and the variety of colors—all of which occur in our work and will be illustrated by many examples. ### C H A P T E R III.

->*A Comparison of Petronius with Virgil.*<-

I am accustomed sometimes, when there is more ample leisure, to compare the best writers of both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note> with one another, so that, having weighed their virtues and vices, I may exercise and sharpen my judgment, and at the same time temper the severity of my studies with honorable pleasure. Nor indeed could the sinister opinion of those men ever deter me from this so healthy and elegant practice—nor will it be able to—who judge all things, whether good or bad, provided they are of a great name...

[...of the] name was the author, they mark it with a white line <note>an ancient Greek and Roman idiom meaning to mark something with approval or as a "good day," though here Tollius implies his critics are being overly formal or restrictive</note>, nor do they allow any of the freedom of this age's judgment regarding the <term>ancient writers</term> <note>original: *veteres scriptores*</note>, even if those judgments are as far as possible from the malice of rebuking or fault-finding. For I have many, and very noble, defenders of my opinion to set against them; the weight of arguments is present; and, even if those were absent, <term>reason</term> <note>original: *ratio*</note> itself stands and fights for our side, which allows each person their own free <term>judgment</term> <note>original: *judicium*</note>, since writers themselves have subjected themselves and their writings to the judgment of readers.

But, as in every debate, so in this discussion, emotions ought to be absent: nor is there less sinning in literary matters through ill-advised love than through hatred, envy, arrogance, pride, or <term>petulance</term> <note>original: *petulantia*; here meaning a rude or childishly aggressive attitude</note> and <term>impudence</term> <note>original: *procacitas*; a bold or shameless disregard for others</note>. And indeed, my mind is so far removed from hatred and envy regarding the <term>scholarship</term> <note>original: *eruditio*</note> and virtues of the deceased and the ancients (who are known to me without any injury), that I willingly acknowledge and venerate the brilliant gifts of character even in living enemies. As for the suspicion of arrogance or haughtiness, I will not throw it back at the authors of insults—even if I perhaps could—nor will I refute it because it is baseless. I see no reason why I should deprive myself of this pleasure, or allow myself to be deprived of it by others: especially since the judgments of the **youth** entrusted to us are best formed and refined in this way; and many errors are encountered, from which even those with the most consummate **learning** <note>original: *eruditio*; deep, scholarly knowledge.</note> and most celebrated fame are scarcely immune. I hardly think it worth the effort to bring forth arguments to defend myself, or examples to follow; but I would gladly obtain this from those who attack my opinion, if I ask what is fair: that they prefer to use solid arguments when examining my judgment, and to convict me of error, rather than so purely and unfairly condemning me of ignorance and a barrenness of the **liberal arts** <note>original: *bonarum artium*; literally "the good arts," referring to the humanities and classical education.</note> without a hearing; and while exercising the same judgment on others, not so much to carp at my approach as to command a selection of writers according to their own whim. > *Now the tenth harvest was besieging the sorrowful Phrygians* <note>The Trojans.</note> *amidst wavering fears, and the reliability of the prophet Calchas’s word hung in doubt with dark fear.* <note>original: "Jam decuma moestos inter ancipites metus / Phrygas obsidebat messis, & vatis fides / Calchantis atro dubia pendebat metu."</note>

This is a <term>Cacozelon</term> <note>From the Greek *kakozēlia*, meaning a "perverse imitation" or an affected, distasteful style that tries too hard to be poetic.</note>, this phrase: *the tenth harvest was besieging*. For while "harvest" might be used to represent a "year"—a usage for which Virgil is rightly praised when he used the word *aristae* <note>Literally "ears of grain."</note>—it can be endured, even lauded. But to say that a *harvest* is "besieging" a city cannot be tolerated, because it is contrary to nature. Furthermore, Petronius sins against the laws of elegance by repeating the small word *fear* (*metus*) after such a short interval. And why he calls this fear "dark" (*atrum*), I do not see. Is it because, in Horace’s writing, "dark Care sits behind the horseman," <note>A reference to Horace, *Odes* 3.1, suggesting that no one can escape their anxieties.</note> that he thought men actually become dark-colored with fear? I have always thought that fearful men turn pale and bloodless. But perhaps here "dark" is used for "sad," or "fear" for "care." Come, let us grant him this; but then:

> *When, as the Delian* <note>Apollo, who was born on the island of Delos.</note> *prophesied, the felled peaks of Mount Ida are dragged down:* <note>original: "Quum Delio profante cæsi vertices / Idæ trahuntur:"</note>

Who would concede to such "swollen" language? Are the trees themselves the "peaks" of the mountains just because they grow upon the peaks? Which of the ancient poets ever spoke this way? Who has ever seen "peaks being dragged," even in a dream? Certainly Ennius spoke differently:

> *Would that in the peak of Pelion the fir timbers, hewn down, had never fallen to the earth!* <note>Tollius quotes the famous opening of Ennius’s *Medea Exul* to show a more natural way of describing the felling of trees for timber.</note>

Our author continues:

> *And the timbers, split into a mass, fall—timbers which were to shape the threatening horse.* <note>original: "Scissaque in molem cadunt / Robora, minacem quæ figurarent equum."</note>

There is nothing sane in these lines. For what are "timbers split into a mass"? First, how thin and weak is the word "split" (*scissa*) when joined with these grandiloquent and sonorous words like "mass" (*molem*), "timbers" (*robora*), and "fall" (*cadunt*)? Furthermore, how do they fall...

> *Now the tenth harvest was besieging the mournful Phrygians <note>Trojans.</note> amid wavering fears, and the credibility of the seer Calchas <note>The Greek prophet.</note> hung in doubt through dark dread.* <note>original: "Jam decuma moestos inter ancipites metus / Phrygas obsidebat messis, & vatis fides / Calchantis atro dubia pendebat metu." That is a poor affectation <term>cacozelon: a stylistic fault where a writer tries too hard to be clever or grand, resulting in something strained or absurd</term>, to say "the tenth harvest was besieging." For while using "harvest" <note>original: "messis"</note> to mean "year"—a usage for which Virgil was even praised for using the word "ears of grain" <note>original: "aristarum"</note>—can be tolerated, or even lauded; yet to say that a *harvest* "besieges" a city cannot be tolerated, because it is contrary to nature. Furthermore, Petronius offends the laws of elegance by repeating the little word "fear" <note>original: "metus"</note> after such a short interval. Why he calls this fear "dark" <note>original: "atrum"</note>, I do not see. Is it because in Horace’s poetry "dark Care" <note>original: "atra cura"</note> sits behind the horseman, and so he thought that men also turned dark-colored from fear? I, for my part, have always thought they turned pale and bloodless. But perhaps here "dark" is used for "sad," or "fear" for "care." We shall move on—but truly:

> *When, at the Delian's <note>Apollo's.</note> prophecy, the felled peaks of Ida <note>A mountain near Troy.</note> are dragged away:* <note>original: "Quum Delio profante cæsi vertices / Idæ trahuntur:"</note>

Who would grant him this bombastic language? Are the trees themselves the "peaks" of the mountains, simply because they grow upon the peaks? Which of the ancient poets ever spoke this way? Who ever saw mountain peaks "dragged away," even in a dream? Ennius certainly wrote otherwise:

> *Would that the fir timber, cut on the peak of Pelion, had never fallen to the ground!* <note>original: "Utinam ne in vertice Peliaco / Abiegna cæsa cecidisset ad terram trabes!" A famous line from the tragedy *Medea Exul* by the early Roman poet Ennius.</note>

Our author <note>Petronius.</note> continues:

> *And the oaks, split into a mass, fall, which were to shape the threatening horse.* <note>original: "Scissaque in molem cadunt / Robora, minacem quæ figurarent equum."</note>

There is nothing sound in these lines. For what are "oaks split into a mass"? First, how weak is the word "split" <note>original: "scissa"</note> when joined with these grand and sonorous words like "mass," "oaks," and "fall"? Then, how do they fall

->### RANDOM THOUGHTS.<-
<sig>B 2</sig>

...do they become oak beams <note>original: "robora"</note> only after they have been split into a great mass? But he <note>Petronius.</note> wished to rival Virgil, who said—though somewhat more precisely—

> *And they weave the ribs with sawn fir.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 2.16. Tollius is pointing out that Virgil specifies "fir" whereas Petronius uses the more generic "oak."</note>

It was Virgil who supplied the idea of the "mass" and the "oak" when he wrote of Calchas: <note>The Greek prophet who advised the construction of the horse.</note>

> *Calchas ordered them to raise a huge mass*
> *With woven oak-beams, and lead it up to heaven.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 2.185-186.</note>

Finally, *which might shape a threatening horse.* Certainly that huge horse was threatening, destined to be a great ruin for Priam's empire and the Phrygians <note>Trojans.</note>. Indeed, it was already breathing these threats from its very nostrils, just as follows:

> *While the captive youth murmurs within,*
> *the oaken mass breathes with a fear not its own.* <note>original: "Roborea moles fpirat alieno metu." This line from Petronius suggests the horse itself "breathes" because of the terrified soldiers hidden inside.</note>

Oh, how beautifully these things agree! How elegantly this oaken mass, like a mountain, has been shaped, giving birth to these "elegances" for us! For even mountains sometimes go into labor—lest anyone think me a liar—but they do not give birth to threateningly shaped horses, but to ridiculous mice. <note>A reference to Horace's famous line: "The mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse will be born" (Ars Poetica, 139), used to describe works that promise much but deliver little.</note>

> *A huge enclosure is opened, and hidden caves*
> *Which might contain the camp.* <note>original: "Aperitur ingens cloftrum, & obducti fpecus / Qui caftra caperent." Petronius implies the horse is large enough to hold an entire army camp.</note>

In Virgil’s work, *Sinon releases the bars* <note>The Greek spy who tricked the Trojans.</note>, but he does so to let out the enclosed soldiers. Petronius, however, made this enclosure "huge" because Virgil had attributed "huge caverns" to the horse; and indeed it had to be huge to hold "the whole camp," whereas in Virgil those huge caverns held only the "bodies of selected men." What shall we say then? Does he not surpass Virgil himself <note>original: "τῷ τῆς ἐννοίας ταύτης μεγέθει" — "in the greatness of this conception"</note>? I would say so without hesitation—but only in the way the frog in Aesop’s fable tried to surpass the ox. <note>Referring to the fable where a frog puffs itself up until it bursts trying to be as big as an ox.</note> But as for *hidden* <note>original: "obducti"</note>—that is, closed off by segments of planks—how can these *caves* contain a whole camp? How could an angry...

<meta>catchword: courage</meta>

...is courage hidden? I confess I do not see this, however much this enclosure might be open. For shadows are drawn over my eyes. Or just as the hall of Lucilius <note>A reference to the Roman satirist Lucilius, though the specific "hall" image likely refers to a theatrical curtain or a proverbial obscurity.</note> is covered and uncovered, so too here are "covering" and "opening" synonyms? So I think. Therefore, let us not stir up this Camarina <note>A reference to a Sicilian marsh that, when drained against an oracle's advice, caused a plague; it is a proverb meaning "do not touch a settled but troublesome matter."</note> any further: for the whole Augean stable <note>One of the labors of Hercules; a metaphor for a massive, filthy, and seemingly impossible task of cleaning.</note> still remains to be thoroughly cleansed.

---

> — *To this place, by a ten-year battle,*
> *Angered courage is hidden. The Greeks crowd the heavy*
> *Recesses of the horse, and they lie hidden within the offering.*

Not even in a ten-year battle could anyone prove that these lines are anything but rotten and foolish. Yet someone will say, *the heavy recesses of the horse* are fitting. Quite right, because they are huge: or rather heavy and loaded with the Greeks, who, lest they be seen, *lie hidden in the offering* <note>original: "in voto." The Trojan Horse was presented as a religious offering or "vow."</note>. What then? Since the "offering" is put in place of a "won horse" <note>original: "equo potivo."</note>, does this <term>pedantic concept <note>original Greek: "χολασικὴ νόησις." Tollius is mocking the overly-contrived or overly-intellectualized logic of the poem.</note></term> elude us? No more than the following lines do.

> *O fatherland! We believed a thousand ships were driven away,*
> *And the soil free from war: this the title carved*
> *On the beast, and Sinon—composed for his fate—*
> *Confirmed it, a lie powerful enough for our destruction.*

O divine poet <note>Virgil.</note>, how slow your Aeneas was to exclaim so late:

> *O fatherland, O Ilium, home of the gods, and walls of the*
> *Dardanids renowned in war!* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 2.241-242.</note>

when the fatal machine was already scaling the walls. But this man of ours <note>The author of the poem in Petronius.</note>, before

> *Now the crowd, free from the gates and lacking war,*
> *Hurried to the offerings,*

already knew, all too early indeed, what title had been carved on the beast. And from this was born that hasty and festive exclamation: the sublimity of which...

<header>CHANCE REMARKS.</header>
<sig>B 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Now—</meta>

...at least the little word *only* wonderfully raises and sustains the argument: yet a lie is much more powerful for harm. What? Shall the destruction of Troy be called a *loss*?

> May such losses happen to my enemies. <note>original: "Hostibus eveniant talia damna meis." A line from Ovid, used here to suggest that calling the fall of a city a mere "loss" is an absurd understatement.</note>

I would certainly and gladly do without such a "loss."

> Now the crowd, free from the gates and lacking war,
> Hastens to their vows. Their cheeks flow with weeping,
> And the joy of a trembling mind holds those tears
> Which fear had driven away.

Now the crowd was free from the gates, because just a moment ago the *soil* <note>original: "solum." Tollius is punning on the poet's use of "solum," which can mean "only" or "ground/soil."</note> was free from war. And *the Trojans hasten to their vows*. Conversely, the Greeks *lie hidden in the vow*. <note>original: "in voto." The Trojan Horse was presented as a religious offering or "vow" to the gods.</note>

> To such an extent a sweet tongue pours forth large draughts
> from great fountains out of its own rich heart. <note>A quote (originally from Lucretius) used here ironically to describe the "overflowing" and overly-wordy style of the poem.</note>

Who would now deny that Petronius is copious and eloquent? Who would say a pumice stone lacks water? <note>A sarcastic proverb; a pumice stone is notoriously dry, implying Petronius is the opposite of eloquent.</note> Who would deny that Virgil is arid and dry? For what Virgil says simply, and in a single line:

> Therefore all of Troy releases itself from its long grief, <note>original: "Ergo omnis longo solvit se Teucria luctu." From Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 2, line 26.</note>

see how much more ornately our poet [Petronius] does it, how charmingly, how gracefully, in two little verses! Furthermore, who would not admire this elegant sentiment:

> And the joy of a trembling mind holds those tears,
> Which fear had driven away!

How can a trembling mind have what fear drove away? <note>Tollius is pointing out the logical contradiction: if fear is gone, the mind should no longer be "trembling" or "fearful."</note> And how is the mind "trembling" when the Trojans were already free from war? But of course, that embellishment was not to be neglected—the one born from the opposition of contraries: *joy* and *tears*, *having* and *driving away*, *fear* and *gladness*. Oh, what cleverness! This is how one reaches the very peak of sublimity: by being playful in a serious matter.

> *And now, consecrated to Neptune,* <note>original: "Neptuno sacer." Tollius is about to argue about the grammar of this phrase.</note>
> *with his hair loose, Laocoon fills*
> *the whole crowd with his shouting.*

This happens, you see, before a single word has been spoken about the sight of the horse itself, or about the plan and debate for bringing it into the city. Some critic here might read *of Neptune’s priest* <note>original: "Neptuni sacer."</note> instead of *to Neptune*, just as in Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD).</note> one finds *Valerianus, consecrated to Christ* <note>original: "Christi Valeriane sacer."</note> instead of *to Valeriano*—a correction made by the former Prince of our critics, the most illustrious and noble Heinsius, <note>Nicolaas Heinsius the Elder (1620–1681), a famous Dutch classical scholar known for his editions of Latin poets.</note> if it were even worth the effort to be so foolish. But it is enough to listen to the foolish Petronius, for whom Priam and all the Trojan princes pouring out with their citizens are merely a *crowd* <note>original: "vulgus." Tollius finds it insulting to call royalty a "rabble" or "crowd."</note>, because in Virgil, after the differing opinions of two leaders:

> *The uncertain crowd is split into opposing factions.* <note>original: "Scinditur incertum studia in contraria vulgus." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 2, line 39.</note>

How very fine. Yet Virgil makes them be addressed by the more honorable name of *citizens*, a term which embraces everyone collectively—the great nobles as much as the rest of the common people.

***

> *Soon, with his spear-point drawn back,* <note>original: "reducta cuspide."</note>
> *he marked the belly. But the fates stayed his hand;*
> *the blow rebounded, and added credibility to the trickery.*

What is this, *with the spear-point drawn back*? Truly a grand word, using *point* for the whole *spear*. But what does *drawn back* mean? Does it mean driven backward so it could be hurled with greater force? I confess I have been ignorant of this phrase until now; therefore, I shall "mark" it down, just as Laocoon *marked the belly* with that spear-point. I do not think—if the poets who affirm such a thing will grant me peace—that he was a priest of Neptune, but rather a *censor* <note>A pun on the Roman office of "Censor," who was responsible for public morality and "censoring" or inspecting people. Tollius is joking that Laocoon was "inspecting" the horse's belly for faults.</note> of the Trojan people. So opportunely did he both chastise the crowd and, with a censor’s eye, probe the horse’s belly.

...disgraced with a mark of infamy. Bah! How worthless compared to this is that Virgilian Laocoon, who with such great effort
> *hurled a massive spear with mighty strength*
> *into the side, and into the belly of the beast curved with joints.* <note>original: "Validis ingentem viribus hastam / In latus, inque feri curvam compagibus alvum / Contorsit." A famous passage from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book 2, lines 50–52.</note>

When this fellow [in Petronius], so easily and with no trouble at all, after he had filled the whole crowd with his shouting, marked the belly with his drawn-back spear-point! Oh, what a brave and vigorous man, worthy of having the Fates themselves stay his hands! For had it not been for the Fates, even with such a small impulse, he would have pinned the horse itself with his spear-point like a trophy to the Scaean Gate <note>The main gate of the city of Troy.</note>, denying and blocking any exit for the Greeks from then on. One is inclined to lament here:
> *O Troy, O Fatherland, O Pergamum, O Priam, you have perished in your old age,* <note>Tollius is mockingly imitating the style of a tragic lamentation.</note>

because you lacked a Laocoon like the one in Petronius! And what of this? For now I seem to hear a massive blow, sounding like rolling thunder, *which recoils and lends credit to the ruse.* <note>The "ruse" refers to the wooden horse. Tollius is mocking how the sound effects in Petronius's poetry are supposedly so realistic.</note> So many deep-sounding vowels—if it please the gods—fill and ring through my ears:
> *The hollow cavities rang out, and the caverns gave a groan.* <note>original: "Insonuere cavæ, gemitumque dedere cavernæ." Virgil, Aeneid 2.53.</note>

Yet again, however, *he strengthens his weak hand*,
> *and probes the high sides with a double-axe.*

He attributes a *weak* hand to Laocoon, to whom Virgil had given *mighty* strength. How excellent. <note>Tollius is being sarcastic.</note> But of course, it was of no use against the Fates: hence both Virgil’s *spear* and Petronius’s *point* are changed into a *double-axe*, with which *he probes the high sides*, as if perhaps Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* <note>A reference to Ovid’s famous poem of transformations.</note> might pour out from there: *where joys probe the silent heart.* <note>original: "quo ipsum tacitum pertentent gaudia pectus." Tollius is making a pun on the word "pertentat" (to probe or pervade). He is mocking Petronius for using a word more often associated with the way "joy" or "fear" moves through a person's heart rather than an axe hitting wood.</note> Because of that probing—

->JACOBI TOLLII<-

> The captive youth roar within, and while they murmur,
> The oaken mass breathes with a foreign fear.
<note>original: "Fremit / Captiva pubes intus, & dum murmurat, / Roborea moles spirat alieno metu." From Petronius, Satyricon 89.</note>

<margin>Within</margin> He says "within," and truly so, for they were hidden in the horse; you, the reader, had to be informed of this. We have already said something above regarding this "oaken mass" <note>The wooden Trojan Horse.</note>. But as for his claim that it "breathes with a foreign fear," I remember reading something similar regarding the bull of Phalaris <note>A legendary ancient Greek torture device: a hollow bronze bull in which victims were burned alive; their screams were meant to sound like the bull's bellowing through a system of pipes.</note>, which represented the groans of those shut inside by its own lowing; I do not recall such a thing being said of the Trojan horse. We shall grant this, then, to Petronius’s horse, which undoubtedly had pipes led from the belly into the mouth through the neck, from where that breath of the fearful men was emitted. But behold new cleverness, if the previous examples were not enough:

> The captured youth went along, while they were capturing Troy,
> And they were prolonging the whole war with a new fraud.
<note>original: "Ibat juventus capta, dum Trojam capit. / Bellumque totum fraude ducebat nova." A play on the words *capta* (captured) and *capit* (captures).</note>

Does he, therefore, who narrates the destruction of his fatherland, have the leisure to play with the repetition of words? But how the youth "prolonged the whole war with a new fraud," I would like someone to explain. Or is it like the hour "is led with charming deceits" in Propertius? <note>Referring to Propertius, Elegies 1.15.24. Tollius is questioning the logic of the Greek soldiers "leading" or "drawing out" the war while inside the horse.</note> Or is it clear that **a pedantic thought, through excessive affectation, ends in frigidity?** <note>original: "ἢ δῆλον, ὡς χολασικὴ νόησις ὑπὸ περιεργίας λήγει εἰς ψυχρότητα?" Tollius uses Greek to deliver a sharp rhetorical blow, calling the poetry "chilly" or "spiritless" due to over-thinking.</note>

> Behold other monsters. Where high Tenedos repels the sea
> With its ridge, the swollen narrows rise up;
> And the split wave leaps back, smaller than the calm.
<note>original: "Ecce alia monstra. Celsa qua Tenedos mare / Dorso repellit, tumida consurgunt freta; / Undaque resultat scissa tranquillo minor." This describes the approach of the sea serpents.</note>

"Behold other monsters," he says, because Virgil wrote, *Behold, the hands of a youth* <note>Aeneid 2.57.</note>, and then, *Here another greater thing happens to the wretched...* <note>Aeneid 2.199.</note> But where are the first monsters? The horse was a "horrendous monster, shapeless, huge, like a mountain." Now "the swollen narrows rise up," because of the two snakes, of course. These are corrupt judgments: when they strive for "lofty" <term>celsa</term> descriptions, they slip down into the "swollen" <term>tumida</term>. Hence "the wave leaps back, and that split, and indeed smaller than the calm." What that is supposed to mean, I do not know, and even without consulting the prince of critics... <note>Tollius is mocking the physics of Petronius’s description, suggesting the imagery of a wave being "smaller than the calm" is nonsensical.</note>

# ->FORTUNA<-

<sig>B 5</sig>

...-ceive <note>The conclusion of a word from the previous page, likely *accipe* ("receive/hear") or *percipe* ("perceive").</note>, I think this was presented to us by the writers in place of the **sea**. For Virgil said that the snakes came from Tenedos through the "calm deep," an image which Petronius has attempted to rival:

> *Just as the sound of oars in the silent night*
> *Is carried from afar, when fleets press the sea,*
> *And the struck marble groans beneath the weight of fir,*
<note>original: "Qualis silenti nocte remorum sonus / Longe refertur, quum premunt classes mare, / Pulsumque marmor abiete imposita gemit." Petronius uses "marble" (*marmor*) as a poetic term for the sea's surface and "fir" (*abiete*) for the wood of the ships or oars.</note>

I, however, had expected a far greater noise from those "swollen straits." But he says the sound *is carried from afar*, and perhaps I am a bit hard of hearing. Virgil speaks more simply: *a sound arises from the foaming brine*. Quite right. But how large did Petronius imagine those snakes to be, that he compared them to not just one fleet in terms of noise—especially when he says the *struck marble groans beneath the weight of fir*? Furthermore, to what end is this comparison employed now, when only a little later he is finally going to speak of the sound of their tails? Doubtless it was so that we might look back. At what, I ask?

> *We look back: the snakes with twin coils bear*
> *The waves toward the rocks.*
<note>original: "Respicimus: angues orbibus geminis ferunt / Ad saxa fluctus."</note>

Which of the two are "bearing"—the waves, or the snakes? The phrasing is certainly ambiguous. If they are being "borne" by the waves, they are exceedingly sluggish compared to those snakes of Virgil, who:

> *With immense coils lean upon the sea, and head together toward the shores.*
<note>Tollius quotes Virgil’s Aeneid (2.204-205) to show the superior drama of Virgil's description of the sea serpents.</note>

But if the snakes themselves "bear" the waves—that is, if they are propelling the water toward the shore—why did he describe them as having "twin" coils rather than "immense" ones?

> *Their swollen chests,*
> *Like high ships, drive foam from their sides.*
> *The tails make a sound.*
<note>original: "Tumida quorum pectora, / Rates ut altae, lateribus spumas agunt. / Dant caudae sonitum."</note>

Earlier, the straits had been "swollen" by the snakes; now it is their chests that are "swollen." And no wonder, since they are "like high ships."

...high. <note>original: *alta*. This completes a thought from the previous page regarding the height of the waves or the snakes.</note> Virgil *was content with breasts raised among the waves*, because this seemed sufficient for describing snakes of about ten or twelve feet; but our author [Petronius] presents us with whales instead of snakes. <note>Greek: Ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν οἰδεῖν ὑπεραίρειν βούλεται τὰ ὕψη — "But that swelling [style] wishes to surpass the heights."</note>

---

-> The manes are free from the sea <-
-> *They match the eyes: a lightning-like radiance* <-
-> *Inflames the surface, and the waves tremble with hissing.* <-
<note>original: "Libera ponto jubæ / Consentiunt luminibus: fulmineum jubar / Incendit æquor, sibilisque undæ tremunt."</note>

*The manes [crests] are free from the sea*, just as he previously said *youth free from the gates*, and *soil free from war*, with a marvelous variety and abundance of language. *They match the eyes*. Excellent. For *in harmony, small things grow* <note>original: "Concordia res parvæ crescunt," a Roman proverb suggesting that unity creates strength or, in this case, a combined visual effect.</note>. From this united brightness, that *lightning-like radiance inflames the surface*. But this is nothing compared to: *the waves tremble with hissing*. Most beautiful! Since in Virgil *the spear stood trembling*, how much must we imagine the Trojans trembled when they heard those hisses at which the very waves would tremble! Therefore:

> *Our minds were stunned. Sacred with fillets they stood,*
> *And in Phrygian attire, the twin pledges born*
> *To Laocoon, whom suddenly the shimmering snakes*
> *Bind by their backs.*
<note>original: "Stupuere mentes. Infulis stabant sacri / Phrygioque cultu, gemina nati pignora / Lacoonte, quos repente tergoribus ligant / Angues corusci." Tollius is quoting Petronius's version of the Laocoon myth.</note>

*Sacred with fillets*, what is this? For whoever interprets *sacred* here to mean "priests," surely he is "holding a sieve under a he-goat while another milks it" <note>A Latin proverb, *hirco supponit cribrum*, used to describe an absurd or impossible situation; Tollius is mocking the interpretation.</note>. But where did he learn that Laocoon’s sons wore priestly fillets? Why not also give them *sleeves on their tunics*, and *ribbons on their miters*? <note>Tollius is referencing Virgil's *Aeneid* (9.616), where such clothing is described as effeminate or overly ornate.</note> Regarding this *Phrygian attire*, if Petronius had not informed us, none of us would have even thought of it: so dull are the hearts we carry. For those *twin pledges of Laocoon* <note>A poetic way of saying "two sons."</note>, born of Laocoon, could have stood by their father distinguished by their native dress, or even the garb and finery of the Goths or Indians. Oh, what elegance! But nonetheless, those [snakes] suddenly, before they had obviously ap- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword *pu-* (likely *appulerant*, meaning "approached the shore").</note>

May the earth lie heavy upon you, Virgil <note>A playful reversal of the common Roman funerary prayer "May the earth lie light upon you" (Sit tibi terra levis). Oh, brave boys, educated in the very school of Socrates or Zeno! <note>Socrates and Zeno were symbols of Stoic endurance and the mastery of fear.</note> It is no wonder, then, if the parent runs so diligently to protect their lives.

---

> *Behold, the parent adds his own death to that of his children,*
> *A weak helper.*

The meter of the poem did not allow for "funerals" in the plural. <note>original: *Funera*. Tollius notes that the Latin grammar uses the singular "death" or "funeral" to encompass both children.</note> Therefore, the funeral of the two was one, just as soon there will be *one death*. But behold, though too late, the *weak helper* runs up: he who himself was in need of a helper, so that these things might be a little more sublime. For Virgil is more subdued when he says, *afterwards he himself approaches as a helper*. <note>Virgil, Aeneid 2.216: "post ipsum auxilio subeuntem." Tollius finds Virgil's phrasing less dramatic than Petronius's.</note> Therefore:

> *They invade the man,*
> *Already fed on death, and drag his limbs to the ground.*

Thus the ox falls upon the ground. <note>Tollius likely compares the falling Laocoon to a sacrificial bull, a common motif in this scene.</note> But in Virgil, Laocoon struggles for some time with the snakes and proves himself a man; this he does not do here, since the snakes invade him when they are *already fed on death*. Here, Petronius offers us pure "pigeon’s milk" <note>original: *lac gallinaceum*. A Roman proverb for something exceptionally rare, delicious, or perfect.</note>; by contrast, Virgil offers us vinegar when he says:

# JACOBI TOLLII

...it, and *feeds upon their wretched limbs with its bite?* <note>original: "miseros morsu depascitur artus" — a quote from Virgil's Aeneid (2.215), describing the serpents eating Laocoon's sons.</note> Truly, 
<margin>Nothing is drier than a man with dropsy.</margin> <note>original: "οὐδὲν ξηρότερον ὑδρωπικοῦ" — a Greek proverb suggesting that the more one has, the more one wants; here it likely refers to Tollius's thirst for more poetic detail.</note>
> *The priest lies as a victim among the altars,*
> *and strikes the ground. Thus, with the sacred rites profaned,*
> *Troy, about to perish, first lost its gods.*

These things are described vividly and cleverly enough. For a matter so pleasant cannot be concluded without a touch of wit. But who are these "lost gods"? Who profaned those sacred rites? Was it the snakes, or was it Laocoon? I believe the fault lay with the Trojans, and it was because of such a great crime that the angry gods abandoned Troy. For what could be imagined more monstrous than a priest lying as a victim among the altars on the shore—where, in reality, no altars were? <note>Tollius is pointing out a logical inconsistency or "poetic license" in the description of the scene.</note> Yet, without this detail, the imitation of Virgil would not proceed, for in his work: *All the gods departed from their shrines and left the altars.* <note>original: "Excessere omnes adytis, arisque relictis Dii" — Virgil, Aeneid 2.351.</note>

> *Already full Phoebe had brought forth her white beam,*
> *leading the smaller stars with her radiant torch.*
<note>Phoebe is a poetic name for the Moon.</note>

Meanwhile, as those snakes slaughter Laocoon like a sacrificial victim, the Trojans did nothing: the horse was not yet led into the city, nor was there any rushing to temples or to feasts. Petronius dismissed all these events as nothing, not even thinking them worth mentioning. Instead, with marvelous brevity, he ensures that *full Phoebe might lead the smaller stars with her radiant torch* at the very same time when, in Virgil’s account:

---

> <margin>Night rushes from the Ocean</margin> <note>original: "ruit Oceano nox" — Virgil, Aeneid 2.250.</note>
> *Enveloping both the earth and the sky in a vast shadow,*

and also when the Argive <note>Greek</note> phalanx approached the city *through the friendly silence of the moon.* <note>original: "per amica silentia lunae" — Virgil, Aeneid 2.255.</note> But these contradictions are of no importance. Truly, it was more worthwhile for the stars to be led in a dance, a feat the moon could not have accomplished without her radiant torch; for without that light, they might perhaps have stumbled in the darkness. <note>Tollius is being sarcastic here, mocking Petronius's use of a bright, "dancing" moon during a scene that Virgil famously rendered in dark, silent shadows.</note>

### CASUAL OBSERVATIONS.

> When among the sons of Priam, <note>The Trojans.</note> buried in night and wine,
> The Greeks loosen the enclosures and pour out the men.

Using "night" as a substitute for "sleep" is an elegant and quite timely trope, <note>A trope is a figurative use of a word.</note> especially since the full moon had already brought forth its white radiance; though, truly, I did not know that those who are "buried" could be surrounded by such great light. <note>Tollius is mockingly pointing out a contradiction: the poet says it is dark like "night," yet mentions a bright full moon.</note> Moreover, where do these Greeks come from who "loosen the enclosures"? Virgil had given this task to Sinon; <note>In the Aeneid, Sinon is the Greek spy who convinces the Trojans to bring the horse inside and later lets the soldiers out.</note> and thus the leaders, having been sent out:

---

> They kill the guards, and with the gates standing open, 
> they receive all their allies.
<note>original: "Cædunt vigiles, portisque patentibus omnes Accipiunt socios" — Virgil, Aeneid 2.266.</note>

But someone will say, "This is a trope," or perhaps a change in number. <note>A grammatical shift from singular to plural.</note> I acknowledge the poet's talent, but even more so his judgment. Then he writes, *the Greeks pour out the men*, because in Virgil: *The horse, standing high in the middle of the walls, pours forth the armed men.* <note>original: "Arduus armatos mediis in mœnibus astans Fundit equus" — Virgil, Aeneid 2.242.</note> What a learned imitator! These lines that follow, however, are clearly a "child of Jove's brain": <note>original: "Jovis cerebrum" — a reference to the goddess Athena springing fully formed from the head of Zeus; used here to mean something remarkably clever or perhaps suspiciously over-wrought.</note>

> The leaders test themselves in their arms, just as
> the horse of Thessaly, released from the heavy yoke, 
> is accustomed to shake its neck and high mane for a gallop. 
> They handle their swords again, they move the shields with their hands; 
> and they take up war.

How inept Virgil is compared to Petronius! Virgil did not even think of these things and neglected such a festive comparison. For it is quite believable that the knees of men who had hidden in the horse for so long would have been numbed from sitting, and their arms stiffened from the cold. Therefore, the author rightly and deservedly removes that sluggishness with this brandishing of arms and rotation of shields. I can hardly grasp his sublime meanings, nor even his elegances of speech. For what does it mean here "to take up war"? <note>original: "bellum sumere"</note> Was there a solid peace beforehand? <note>Tollius is mocking the phrasing; since the Greeks and Trojans were already at war, he finds the phrase "taking up war" redundant.</note>

<summary>Tollius continues his satirical critique of Petronius’s poetry, mocking the logic of the Greek soldiers performing "calisthenics" after exiting the Trojan Horse and contrasting it with Virgil's more serious tone.</summary>

> — Here, another cuts down those heavy with wine, 
> and extends their slumbers into the finality of death.
<note>original: "Hic graves alius mero Obtruncat, & continuat in mortem ultimam Somnos" — Petronius, Satyricon 89.</note>

The sons of Priam <note>The Trojans.</note> were already "buried in wine" just a little while before; but wine is also said to "bury" memory. However, when Petronius indeed *extends their slumbers into the finality of death*, he seems to me quite witty, since he manages to joke amidst the death of others. What? Was Virgil then so slow of wit that he could not think up such clever turns of phrase either here or in Book 9 of the *Aeneid*? Obviously [not]. But Petronius is wonderfully <term>inventive</term> <note>original: ἐπινοητικός (epinoētikos) — meaning creative, imaginative, or quick-witted.</note>. And thus immediately:

> — Another lights torches from the altars
> and invokes the sacred objects of Troy against the Trojans.

...with bended knee, and a long, composed speech. For who could do it better? Splendidly, then, our schoolman—or rather (lest I do him some injustice, and to appease those men who do not take this critique of mine so badly as they laugh sweetly over it at their little drinking parties) the prince of schoolmen, the love and delight of the learned, has finished this tragic song of his, and sealed his clever poem with a most clever little maxim. Let us hear Virgil, by contrast:

> — Broken by war and repelled by the fates, 
> the leaders of the Greeks, now that so many years were gliding by, 
> build a horse the size of a mountain by the divine art of Pallas <note>The goddess Athena.</note>, 
> and weave its ribs with sawn fir. 
> They pretend it is a votive offering for their return; that rumor spreads. 
> Here, having cast lots for their bodies, they secretly shut 
> chosen men into the dark side: and deep within the caverns...
<note>original: Virgil, Aeneid 2.13–19.</note>

# FORTUITOUS REMARKS.
## C 4
<meta>catchword: tem-</meta>

> — ...huge [caverns], and they fill the belly with armed soldiers.
> We thought they had departed and sought Mycenae with the wind.
> Therefore all Teucria <note>A poetic name for Troy, derived from its first king, Teucer.</note> released itself from its long grief.
> The gates are opened: it is a joy to go and see the Greek camps,
> the deserted places, and the abandoned shore.
> There, first before everyone, with a great crowd accompanying him,
> Laocoon, burning with haste, runs down from the top of the citadel:
> And from afar he cries: "O wretched citizens, what so great madness is this?
> Do you believe the enemy has sailed away? Or do you think any [gifts of the Greeks lack trickery?]" etc.
> Having spoken thus, with mighty strength he hurled a huge spear
> into the side and into the beast's belly, curved with its joints.
> It stood there trembling, and the belly having been struck...
<note>These lines are excerpted from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 2, describing the Trojans' discovery of the Wooden Horse and Laocoon's warning.</note>

*Broken by war.* <note>original: "Fracti bello"</note> This is a modest but effective and common <term>metaphor</term> <note>original: "tralatio" — a figure of speech where a word is applied to an object or action to which it is not literally applicable.</note>. *And repelled by the fates.* <note>original: "fatisque repulsi"</note> This phrase is of the same quality.

*Leaders of the Greeks.* <note>original: "Ductores Danaum"</note> This is correctly phrased, for the forming of plans belongs to the Leaders. *Now that so many years were gliding by;* <note>original: "tot jam labentibus annis"</note> there is nothing bombastic here, nor is it lowly.

*Like a mountain.* <note>original: "Instar montis"</note> This is an <term>hyperbole</term>, yet its "coldness" <note>In classical rhetoric, "coldness" (frigus) refers to a stylistic failure where a metaphor feels forced, silly, or fails to move the reader.</note> is removed because the horse is made "by the divine art of Pallas." Nothing but the grand and immense befits the Gods.

*And they interweave the ribs with cut fir.* <note>original: "Sectaque intexunt abiete costas"</note> These details are drawn from the nature of things itself.

*They feign a vow for their return, etc.* <note>original: "Votum pro reditu simulant"</note> These lines are not overblown, and the narrative is consistent with real life.

*Bodies of men,* <note>original: "Corpora virum"</note> a very common <term>periphrasis</term> <note>A roundabout way of speaking; using more words than necessary to express an idea.</note>.

*To the blind side.* <note>original: "Cæco lateri"</note> That is to say, the "hidden" or obscure side. This is an unpretentious metaphor.

*Huge caverns.* <note>original: "Cavernas ingentes"</note> Because the horse was "like a mountain."

*Armed soldiery.* <note>original: "Armato milite"</note> Virgil does not say the "whole camp" emerged, as Petronius does. The use of the singular noun here is extremely apt for achieving a truly grand style of speech.

The following lines have nothing affected or "cold" about them. *All Teucria.* <note>original: "Omnis Teucria"</note> This is used just as Herodotus <margin>Herodotus</margin> uses the Greek word for "the whole" <note>original: ὅλην (holēn)</note>. *Long grief.* <note>original: "longo luctu"</note> That adjective is a wonderful addition to the concept of sorrow.

<summary>Jacobus Tollius provides a line-by-line stylistic analysis of Virgil's description of the Trojan Horse, praising Virgil for his restraint, use of appropriate metaphors, and "grand style" in contrast to the more "swollen" poetry of Petronius.</summary>

## C 4
<meta>catchword: Per-</meta>

...expresses a long duration of time. Furthermore, the verse itself aids this delay through its slowness, because it consists of nothing but <term>spondees</term> <note>A metrical foot in poetry consisting of two long syllables (— —), which slows the pace of the line to create a solemn, heavy, or slow-moving effect.</note>.

*The gates are opened.* <note>original: "Panduntur portæ"</note> The action seems to be happening right now because of the use of the present tense verb.

*It is a joy to go.* <note>original: "Juvat ire"</note> The very pleasure that everyone felt from this liberation <note>Referring to the Trojans' belief that the Greeks had finally left.</note> is shown by this word.

*Burning.* <note>original: "Ardens"</note> From this, the ardor of Laocoön's spirit—wishing to restrain the citizens' error, which was joined with such great danger—shines forth in a wonderful way.

*Mighty, etc.* <note>original: "Validis, &c."</note> These words assist one another and increase the overall effect.

# RANDOM OBSERVATIONS
## C
<meta>catchword: Headbands</meta>

> *Drenched in gore on his headbands, and with black poison:* <note>original: "Perfusus sanie vittas, atroque veneno"</note>
> *At the same time, he lifts horrendous cries to the stars.* <note>original: "Clamores simul horrendos ad sidera tollit"</note>
> *The Greeks shut within the womb, and the pine-wood bolts*
> *Sinon stealthily loosens. The horse, opened up,*
> *Restores them to the air, and they joyfully bring themselves out from the hollow wood.*
> *They invade the city buried in sleep and wine.*
> *The sentries are slain; and they welcome all their allies*
> *Through the open gates.*

*The hollows rang.* <note>original: "Insonuere cavæ"</note> There is nothing "swollen" or overblown here <note>Tollius refers to Virgil's restraint; the description is effective without being bombastically dramatic.</note>.

*Laocoön, chosen.* <note>original: "Laocoon ductus"</note> These lines are certainly elegant and polished, yet possess great gravity.

*Behold.* <note>original: "Ecce"</note> This is used opportunely. For here the listener had to be roused to give full attention to the novelty of the event.

*With immense coils.* <note>original: "Immensis orbibus"</note> For later he will say that the snakes rose above Laocoön with their necks and heads. And for that reason, too, the narrator shudders as he recounts it.

*And the crests.* <note>original: "Jubæque"</note> These details are taken from truth itself: there is nothing over-inflated in these descriptions.

*A sound is made.* <note>original: "Fit sonitus"</note> But notice that the magnitude of the sound is not yet expressed <note>Tollius suggests Virgil builds tension by withholding the full scale of the noise until the climax.</note>.

*And burning eyes.* <note>original: "Ardentesque oculos"</note> They could not be depicted more truly or elegantly.

*We fled bloodless from the sight.* <note>original: "Diffugimus visu exsangues"</note> The sheer monstrosity of these omens deserved such a reaction.

*In a steady line.* <note>original: "Agmine certo"</note> This phrase shows that the attack did not happen by chance, but by the divine will of the gods.

*Small [children].* <note>original: "Parva"</note> This adjective is added to evoke pity. Here, however, there are no "trifles" or unnecessary flourishes, as one often finds in Petronius <note>Gaius Petronius Arbiter, a Roman novelist whose style Tollius views as less disciplined than Virgil’s.</note>.

*They bind him in huge coils. (Previously: 'with immense coils').* <note>original: "Spiris ligant ingentibus. supra immensis orbibus"</note> These descriptions are meant to strike terror. The coils had to be truly vast to embrace his waist twice, surround his high neck twice, and still tower over him with their heads.

*He at once.* <note>original: "Ille simul"</note> That word "at once" is repeated to indicate the speed of the overwhelming disaster. For this reason, the speech is <term>asyndeton</term> <note>A rhetorical device where conjunctions like "and" are omitted to create a sense of rapid, breathless action.</note>.

<summary>Tollius provides a line-by-line commentary on the Laocoön episode from Virgil’s Aeneid, praising the poet’s ability to balance terror with technical restraint and "natural" description. He specifically highlights Virgil's use of pacing and word choice to convey divine intervention and overwhelming speed.</summary>
<keywords>Virgil, Aeneid, Laocoön, Sinon, literary criticism, rhetoric, asyndeton, Petronius, poetic meter, Trojan Horse</keywords>

# JACOBUS TOLLIUS

*Headbands* <note>original: "Vittas"</note>. These are mentioned to evoke pity, as his priesthood was of no help to him. *At the same time, horrendous cries* <note>original: "Clamores simul horrendos"</note>. For this face of death is truly horrendous; and that word *horrendous* remarkably expresses the cruelty of the abominable evil and the anguish of the struggling—though in vain—Laocoön. *Shut in the womb* <note>original: "Inclusos utero"</note>. These following things are narrated simply and with gravity; there is nothing here for the sake of showing off academic polish, and no clever wordplay.

One cannot say much about every individual detail, because all of them are excellent, and they easily reveal the exact judgment of that most perfected poet and the prince of all Latins <note>Virgil was often called the "Prince of Poets" in the Latin tradition.</note>.

Someone might perhaps ask what my opinion is regarding that other poem by Petronius <note>Petronius Arbiter, a Roman courtier during the reign of Nero, included a long poem about the Civil War in his novel, the *Satyricon*.</note>, in which he described the civil war of Caesar and Pompey. Although there are many things that might deter me from expressing it freely, I will not be burdened to allow it, for the sake of our studious youth. In my judgment, therefore, this poem is plainly "declamatory" <note>By "declamatory," Tollius suggests the work is more like a rhetorical exercise or a performance piece rather than genuine, inspired poetry.</note>, and it is as far removed from the greatness of Lucan <note>Lucan (39–65 AD) was the author of *Pharsalia*, the definitive Roman epic on the Civil War between Caesar and Pompey.</note>—whom it disparages through figures of speech—as a little flame stirred up from stubble is from the heat and splendor of the sun, or as rushing streams are distant from the Euphrates or the Nile. Let the whole poem be examined; let its individual parts be picked apart; everything will be found empty, loose, and rotten. And if anything in it seems to taste of some greatness, that very thing is derived from the imitation of others. The invention is certainly silly and scholastic; and while he accuses Lucan of failing to use the intervention of the Gods or the fabled "torment of sentiments" <note>original: "sententiarum tormentum"</note> to plunge the free spirit into his work, he himself...

### CHAPTER IV.

#### *Sophocles’ judgment in imitating Herodotus examined.*

I have decided to divide this little work; and to mix critical desserts among the physical and chemical dishes, of which I have already given a taste in the preceding chapters, if by some chance I might be able to:

---
->*To overcome the various distastes of the meal,*<-
->*Of one who touches each thing poorly with a haughty tooth.*<-
---
<note>Tollius is quoting Horace, *Satires* 2.8.76-77, comparing a picky reader to a guest at a banquet who finds fault with every dish. He intends to vary his subject matter between alchemy ("Chemical dishes") and literary analysis ("Critical desserts") to keep the reader interested.</note>

A noble story exists in Herodotus which seemed worthy to me to compare with a certain other fictional one from the tragedies of Sophocles, and to examine the judgment of this poet more accurately in it. Intaphernes was one of those seven most noble Persians who had conspired for the ruin and slaughter of the magi brothers <note>The "Magi" were Zoroastrian priests; Tollius refers to the historical coup where Darius the Great and six co-conspirators overthrew a usurper (the Pseudo-Smerdis) to reclaim the Persian throne.</note>. Having committed a foul crime in the palace, he was thrown into chains by King Darius and was destined for death along with his whole family and relatives. 

But his wife, by coming constantly to the palace gates, weeping and lamenting, moved Darius so far that he gave her the choice of saving one single life out of all her kin. 

**And she, having deliberated, answered these things: "If the king gives me the life of one, I choose my brother from among them all."** <note>original Greek: Ἡ δὲ βουλευσαμένη ὑπεκρίνατο τάδε. Εἰ μὲν δή μοι διδοῖ βασιλεὺς ἑνὸς ψυχήν, αἱρέομαι ἐκ πάντων τὸν ἀδελφεόν.</note> 

When the king, filled with wonder, asked the reason for preferring a brother over a husband and children—who ought to seem closer and dearer to her—she replied: 

**"O King, another husband might be mine, if a god willed it, and other children, if I should lose these. But with my father and mother no longer living, another brother could by no means [be born]..."** <note>original Greek: ὦ βασιλεῦ, ἀνὴρ μέν μοι ἂν ἄλλος γένοιτο, εἰ δαίμων ἐθέλοι, καὶ τέκνα ἄλλα, εἰ ταῦτα ἀποβάλοιμι. # FORTUITA.

"...might happen in [this] way; using this judgment, I chose these things." <note>Tollius is quoting the original Greek: *τρόπῳ γένοιτο· ταύτῃ τῇ γνώμῃ χρεομένη ἐξέλεξα ταῦτα*. He suggests the text should instead read "I chose *this one*" (the brother) rather than "these things."</note> It is said that Darius both approved of her reasoning and, being delighted by the act, granted the life of the woman’s eldest son as well; the others, as he had decreed, he ordered to be put to death.

Sophocles, the tragic poet—whose merits are far beyond any praise I could give—was a contemporary of Herodotus, or perhaps slightly younger. (For he was born around the 73rd Olympiad, while Herodotus flourished in the 77th Olympiad.) <note>The Olympiads were four-year periods used by the Greeks for dating; the 73rd Olympiad began around 488 BCE, and the 77th around 472 BCE. Tollius is establishing that these two great writers lived at the same time and likely influenced one another.</note> Certainly, after Herodotus, Sophocles produced the play *Antigone*, in which this same sentiment occurs. 

However, it seems necessary to first set out the plot of the play, so that the whole matter may be better understood. Creon, King of the Thebans, after the brothers Eteocles and Polynices had perished by wounding one another, had ordered that Polynices be cast out unburied. He established the death penalty for anyone who should bury him. Antigone, having ignored the law, attempted to commit her brother’s corpse to the earth. Caught in that attempt and condemned to be shut up alive in a cave, or a subterranean cavern, she laments her calamity with these words:

> ——— But now, Polynices, for dressing 
> Your body, I win such rewards as these. 
> Yet I honored you rightly in the eyes of the wise. 
> For never, had I been a mother of children, 
> Nor if a husband had died and were rotting away, 
> Would I have taken this task upon myself against the will of the citizens. 
> By what law do I say this? 
> If a husband died, there could be another, 
> And a child from another man, if I lost the first; 
> But with mother and father hidden in Hades, 
> No brother could ever bloom for me again.
<note>This is a famous and controversial passage from Sophocles' *Antigone* (lines 900–912). Antigone argues that while husbands and children are replaceable, a brother is not, because her parents are dead and cannot conceive another.</note>

> "And yet, because I honored you by such a law, 
> in Creon's eyes I seemed to be committing a crime." 
> <note>original Greek: Τοιῷδε μέντοι σ’ ἐκπροτιμήσασ’ ἐγὼ / Νόμῳ, Κρέοντι ταῦτ’ ἔδοξ’ ἁμαρτάνειν. These lines are from Sophocles' *Antigone*, 904-905.</note>

She says that she would have preferred her brother, Polynices, over a husband and children, had she had them; because with her parents dead, she could not hope for another brother. Just as, conversely, there would be hope for another husband if the first were lost, or for other children from another father, if "anything human" <note>The Latin phrase *aliqvid humani* is a common euphemism for death.</note> had happened to them. 

I do not know with what judgment Sophocles wrote these things. For the reasoning of the wife of **Intaphernes** is far different. She, having the opportunity to save a living brother and snatch him from death, chose to do so over either her spouse or her son. But since Polynices had already gone to that place from which they say no one returns, how could this choice have helped Antigone? For she was not able to recall a dead brother back to life so that she might enjoy his company longer, as in the example of the wife of Intaphernes. 

Moreover, among the dead, this choice—besides being unnecessary—would also have been unjust. For a wife owes more to a deceased husband than to a brother; indeed, she owes even more to her own children, because they are "blood of her blood," and a husband is "of one soul" <note>original: *ὁμόψυχος* (*homopsychos*), meaning like-minded or sharing a soul.</note>, or rather "one soul" <note>original: *ψυχὴ μία* (*psyche mia*).</note>, whereas a brother is only "of the same blood" <note>original: *ὁμαίμων* (*homaimon*).</note>. 

Furthermore, if a debate were started concerning <term>duties</term> <note>original: *officiis*. This refers to the Stoic and Ciceronian concept of moral obligations.</note>, to those considering exactly what is owed by a wife to her spouse, the wife of Intaphernes might even seem to have sinned and strayed from her duty. For he who desires to carry out his duty rightly ought to look not at what is most pleasing or delightful to himself, but at what he is bound to provide to another. Now indeed, no one would deny that the duty of a good wife is to "leave father and mother and cling to her husband" <note>Tollius is referencing the biblical command from Genesis 2:24, applying Christian morality to evaluate the classical Greek figures.</note>: how much more so should she place a brother after him?

He further argues from a moral standpoint that a wife's primary duty is to her husband and children, not her siblings.</summary>

**Texena** spoke excellently to her husband **Agathocles** <note>Texena was the wife of Agathocles, the tyrant of Syracuse; when he was dying and facing a coup, she remained loyal despite the danger.</note>: *That by marrying him, she had entered into a partnership not only of prosperity, but of every kind of fortune; and she would not be unwilling to purchase with the danger of her own life the privilege of receiving her husband's final breaths.* What must we imagine this woman would have done if it had been permitted to ransom her husband's life? The story of **Alcestis** <note>Alcestis famously offered to die in place of her husband, Admetus.</note> is a fable chanted in the theaters; but the virtue of **Porcia**, wife of **Brutus**, of **Calpurnia**, wife of **Antistius**, and of **Arria**, wife of **Paetus**, is celebrated in true histories. Even the loyalty of **Herodias** <note>The wife of Herod Antipas; though often portrayed as wicked in the Bible, Tollius notes her loyalty in following her husband into exile in Gaul.</note> is praiseworthy—though in a wicked woman—for she was the companion in exile to the husband for whom she had been the cause of calamity. By these and many other examples of this kind, it can easily be proved that the primary duties of loyalty and love are owed by a wife to her husband rather than to a brother—contrary to the poor judgment made by the wife of **Intaphernes** and King **Darius**.

### CHAPTER V.
#### *The Altar of Amphiaraus Explained Alchemically.*

<margin>
In the *Attica*. <note>Refers to Pausanias's *Description of Greece*, Book 1 (Attica), Chapter 34.</note>

I promised in the second chapter a fuller exposition of the **Altar of Amphiaraus**. Therefore, I shall now fulfill my pledge. **Pausanias** <note>A Greek traveler and geographer of the 2nd century AD.</note> describes it in these words:

> The altar provides five parts. The first is for **Hercules**, **Zeus**, and **Apollo the Healer**; the second is reserved for heroes and the wives of heroes; the third is for **Hestia**, **Hermes**, **Amphiaraus**, and the children of **Amphilochus**. **Alcmaeon**, however, because of his deed against **Eriphyle**, holds no honor either in the section of Amphiaraus or in that of Amphilochus. The fourth part of the altar belongs to **Aphrodite**, **Panacea**, and also to **Iaso**, **Hygeia**, and **Athena the Healer**. The fifth is dedicated to the **Nymphs**, **Pan**, and the rivers **Achelous** and **Cephisus**.
> <note>original Greek: Παρέχεται δὲ ὁ βωμὸς μέρη έ. τὸ μὲν Ἡρακλέους, καὶ Διὸς, καὶ Ἀπόλλωνός ἐστι Παιῶνος: τὸ δὲ ἥρωσι καὶ ἡρώων ἀνεῖται γυναιξί· τρίτον δὲ Ἑστίας καὶ Ἑρμοῦ, καὶ Ἀμφιαράου, καὶ τῶν παίδων Ἀμφιλόχου. Ἀλκμαίων δὲ, διὰ τὸ ἐς Ἐριφύλην ἔργον οὔτε ἐν Ἀμφιαράου τινὰ, ὁμοίως οὐδὲ παρὰ τῷ Ἀμφιλόχῳ τιμὴν ἔχει. Τετάρτη δέ ἐστι τοῦ βωμοῦ μοῖρα Ἀφροδίτης, καὶ Πανακείας, ἔτι δὲ Ἰασοῦς, καὶ Ὑγείας, καὶ Ἀθηνᾶς Παιωνίας. Πέμπτη δὲ πεποίηται Νύμφαις, καὶ Πανὶ, καὶ ποταμοῖς Ἀχελώῳ, καὶ Κηφισῷ.</note>
