So then Hyginus says of them: *Amphiaraus, son of Oïcles and Hypermestra (daughter of Thestius), was an augur. He knew that if he went to attack Thebes, he would not return. Therefore he hid himself, with the knowledge of his wife Eriphyle, daughter of Talaus. Adrastus, however, to track him down, made a golden necklace of gems and gave it as a gift to his sister Eriphyle; she, greedy for the gift, betrayed her husband. Amphiaraus instructed his son Alcmaeon to exact punishment from his mother after his death. After he was swallowed by the earth at Thebes, Alcmaeon, mindful of his father’s command, killed his mother Eriphyle, whom the furies later tormented.* No one, as far as I know, has yet seen, even in a dream, what this fable intends or signifies. For the history of the Theban war, of which this is a part, contains a remarkable secret of nature: it is a mere series and sequence of natural operations, observed by the wise in the creation of the Chemical **Universe** <note>original Greek: τοῦ παντὸς (*tou pantos*), meaning "the all" or "the whole."</note> and hidden under those fictitious names. Indeed, almost all mythological history contains nothing else. <margin>Origen, Book VII, *Against Celsus*.</margin> *For as many things as were more mystical and more worthy of contemplation, and belonging to a theory beyond the hearing of the common people, these they declared through riddles and so-called dark sayings; so that those who do not shirk labor, but undertake every toil for the sake of virtue and truth, might find them upon examination, and having found them, as reason dictates, might put them to use.* <note>Tollius quotes the Greek Church Father Origen to support the idea that ancient myths were intentionally encrypted with deep scientific or philosophical truths.</note> We shall demonstrate this throughout. Amphiaraus is told to have been a priest of Phoebus, or Apollo. **Amphiaraus** <note>original Greek: ἀμφὶ ἀραιὸς (*amphi araios*)</note>, "rare on all sides," is a subtle, thin, and weak **volatile spirit** <term>spiritus volatilis; in alchemy, this refers to a substance that easily evaporates or escapes the fire</term>. He knew that if he went to attack Thebes—that is, the **fixed salt** <term>sal fixum; the stable, non-evaporating residue of a chemical process</term>, the **Philosophic earth** <term>terra Philosophica; the purified material base of the Great Work</term>—he would not return from there, but would be swallowed alive by the opening earth. For where a **volatile acid** <term>Acidum volatile</term> attacks a **fixed alkali** <term>Alcali fixum</term>, it is absorbed by the same: which can be seen daily when vinegar is poured onto chalk or chalky substances. Hyginus writes of them as follows: *“Amphiaraus, the son of Oicles and Hypermnestra (daughter of Thestius), was a seer. He knew that if he went to the siege of Thebes, he would not return. Rightly, therefore, the beginning on this altar is drawn from the number of the underworld because, as we will teach elsewhere, night preceded day in the creation, and our fire lies hidden in the middle. He is also the **Common God** <margin>Livy; Servius on *Aeneid* VIII, 272; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* Book 5, chapter 21.</margin>, because he shares his power with Jupiter and Apollo (or the Sun). From himself, he pours out that force—active and moving all things—which is warm and spirited: hence in his rites, there were once **drinking cups** <note>Latin: *scyphi*</note>, and wine was poured from them as a libation. ...the cup is his attribute, just as the wine-jar <note>Latin: *cantharus*</note> belongs to Father Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus/Dionysus.</note>. Indeed, the ancient sculptors did not without reason depict Hercules with a cup, and sometimes stumbling and drunk: not only because this hero is said to have been a heavy drinker, but also because there is an ancient story that Hercules crossed immense seas in a cup as if in a ship, using the winds. Hercules is the saline fire in the preparation of the **Philosophers' Stone**, and the ship is the **Spirit**, or the wind, which carries him in its womb <note>This is a direct reference to the *Emerald Tablet*, a foundational alchemical text: "The wind carried it in its belly."</note>, so that he may cross the Philosophical Sea.

...and Troy and Oechalia: *how he endured a thousand hard labors under King Eurystheus, by the decrees of unjust Juno. You, unconquered one, slew the cloud-born ones of two forms,* <note>The Centaurs, born of Ixion and a cloud.</note> *Hylaeus and Pholus, with your hand; you slew the Cretan monsters and the vast lion beneath the Nemean rock. No sights terrified you, not even* **Typhoeus** *himself, towering and bearing arms; nor did the Lernaean serpent with its swarm of heads surround you as if you lacked the power of reason.* <note>Original Latin: Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.288-300. This passage recounts the Labors of Hercules.</note>

A whole commentary could be written on these verses if there were leisure for it. I will, however, touch upon a few points as if in passing. If I were inclined to play with words, I would seek the etymology of Hercules from a Hebrew source. I would say that Hercules was named as if *Harki kehelah* <margin>Onomacritus in the Hymns.</margin> — "the pursuer of the congregation," *one who pursued the savage tribes* <note>Original Greek: ἀνήμεϱα φῦλα διώξαντα</note>; or perhaps *Harki El* — "the strong God, the pursuer," *the cloud-gatherer, swelling with mighty labors* <note>Original Greek: νεφεληϱέγετα, βϱύοντα ἄθλοισι κϱαταιοῖς</note>, as the most learned Henricus Hulsius, my closest colleague, immediately suggested to me following my first proposed etymology. 

Or perhaps it is *Hara gal asch* — "the genital vessel of fire." For *Gal* signifies a hollow and round vessel, like the cup attributed to Hercules, as we have already seen. It could also be derived from *Harak el asch* — "the cataract of God’s fire"; or from *Har col* — "the mountain of the universe," so that in the name of Hercules the **Chemical Mountain** <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the Great Work or the furnace.</note> is noted, just as a similar end was found in the etymology of Thebes. 

But, to finally put an end to these trifles, I would prefer simply to follow the Greeks here, who wish Hercules to be named as if *Hera's glory* <note>Original Greek: Ἥϱας κλέος (*Hēras kleos*). This is the traditional etymology of the name Hercules.</note>. For he himself is the unique glory of the **Philosophical Earth**, the balsam lying hidden within it, and the immortal fire. Though the Greeks interpret it differently <margin>Diodorus Siculus, book 5.</margin>, as if he obtained all his fame through Juno. Phornutus...

...accustomed to give forth; likewise, on the ninth day, Deucalion reached Parnassus: and in the ninth year, Achilles was sent to Lycomedes. And these remarks regarding Hercules and those verses of Virgil shall suffice. Does someone desire a geometric figure? I shall give the triangle Δ. From this comes the three-headed monster once placed under the feet of Apollo, following the example of the three-headed Cerberus defeated by Hercules. I will also add the Pythagorean scheme <note>The Tetractys: four dots arranged in a triangle.</note>, so that the perfection of Apollo may be revealed by the triangular ten-fold arrangement of the same sect <note>The complete Tetractys: ten dots arranged in a triangle.</note>. Hercules, therefore, represents the straight horizontal line, which is composed of four points and denotes the united strength of the **four elements**. Jupiter, carried on the wings of an eagle and armed with the three-forked lightning bolt—a symbol of the three volatile spirits of **Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt**—ascends into heaven: and from here, *The great months begin their course*. <note>A famous line from Virgil’s Eclogue 4, often interpreted by alchemists as the timing of the Great Work.</note> Apollo, joining the three seasons of winter, spring, and summer, completes the work at the beginning of the tenth month, and brings the **Chemical Man** forth into the divine shores of light. <note>Original Latin: "Incipe parve puer risu cognoscere matrem. Matri longa decem tulerunt fastidia menses." These lines are from Virgil’s fourth Eclogue, often interpreted by alchemists as a prophecy of the "Stone" being born after a specific period of gestation.</note>

However, so that these months—which are called "Philosophical" because they must be understood in a philosophical sense—may be rightly understood, it must be noted that three spans of time are generally named in this work of ours: the Year, the Month, and the Day. The Year is the solar cycle, in which four seasons, or <margin>Vitruvius, Book 9, ch. 4. Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel, Book 15, ch. 54. Heraclides Ponticus in Homeric Allegories. Numm. Hesychius. Maximus Tyrius, Dissertation 20. Vitruvius, Book 4, ch. 8. Servius on Eclogue 6, 22.</margin> <gloss>hours</gloss> <note>Original Greek: "ὥραι" (horai). In this context, it refers to the four seasons: Winter, Spring, Summer, and the start of Autumn.</note>, are observed: Winter, Spring, Summer, and the beginning of Autumn. The Month completes the lunar course, in which there are four weeks; and Philosophically, according to the ratio of the course of Venus in the heavens, there are forty days. Furthermore, the Day contains both darkness and light. There is one principle, one time, and one labor for all of them. Just as the solar year is completed in twelve months, so also the Jovian <note>Pertaining to the planet or god Jupiter.</note> year is completed in twelve solar years.

Now, Jupiter is—so that we do not neglect things delayed for a little while—an ethereal male spirit, a *fiery essence*, *ether*, a *pure nature of fire*, <note>Original Greek: "πυρώδης οὐσία, αἰθὴρ, πυρὸς εἰλικρινὴς φύσις"</note> and, as the ancients said, *the lightest*. <note>Original Greek: "κουφοτάτη" (kouphotate), meaning the most buoyant or least heavy element.</note> For this reason, he loves high places, and the summits of mountains are consecrated to him; hence he is called *Olympian*, *Idaean*, *of the heights*, and *upon the peak*. <note>Original Greek: "ἀκραῖος" (akraios) and "ἐπάκριος" (epakrios).</note> Likewise, he is called *lofty*, *because he is high up*, according to the testimony of Hesychius. <note>Original Greek: "καρδαῖος, διὰ τὸ ὑψηλὸς εἶναι" (kardaios, dia to hypselos einai).</note> For that reason, it was customary to build the highest altars to Jupiter, while low ones were made for Vesta, the Earth, and the Sea. You will see more concerning mountains below. Because he is truly fiery, the color red belongs to the God; and *among the gentiles, the chariots of Jupiter were painted vermilion*. <note>The Latin "miniatæ" refers to minium, a bright red lead pigment.</note> He is the soul itself, the *nature* of the WORLD, and the life of Man (whence the Greeks call him *Zeus*, *from life*, <note>Original Greek: "ζεὺς, ἀπὸ τῆς ζωῆς". A common ancient etymological play connecting Zeus with "zoe" (life).</note> as some Grammarians maintain). Nor was a beard given to him without reason, just as to Aesculapius, because it is a sign of virility. Basilius Valentinus <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, supposedly a Benedictine monk. His "Twelve Keys" are foundational to alchemical literature.</note> also attributes a quite long beard to his "Old Man," because it is a symbol of the rays of male fire <margin>Concerning the rays of the [Maradii]</margin>; therefore, look closely at whatever Jupiter has irradiated.

## D 2

<margin>Heraclitus, *Homeric Allegories*.</margin> An altar was placed in the middle of a spacious temple, in which a perpetual fire would keep watch: not unlike the altar sacred to the Syrian Goddess <note>likely Atargatis</note> in the middle of a lake, glowing with fires, of which we shall speak later. Therefore, the third part of the Altar was rightly assigned to Mercury, which is the middle part among five. For Mercury also, as the Grammarians maintain, was called by the Latins *Medicurrius* <note>original: "Medicurrius," a folk etymology suggesting "middle-runner"</note>, because he always runs between heaven and the underworld. He is the messenger of gods and men, the **mediating reason** <note>original: μεσίτης λόγος</note>, **being a mediator** <note>original: μεσιτὴς ὢν</note> like the circle of the horizon, which joins light with darkness, day with night, the things above with those below, heat with cold, and fire with water. He is the bond of our sulfur and salt, making white things from black, and black from white; the judge of death and life, which is why Hygieia <note>Goddess of health</note> is joined to him, as the presiding spirit of wakefulness and sleep. He is the inventor of the three voices—the high, the middle, and the low—and of their harmony; as well as the three-stringed lyre, which he later gave as a gift to Apollo.

**It is concerning Mercury** that Plutarch says: **he changes himself into water when condensed, and into fire when dissolved, because of his affinity and kinship to both, yielding softly and receiving the opposite extremes** <note>original: μεταβάλλειν αὐτὸν εἰς ὕδωρ συνιστάμενον, εἰς δὲ πῦρ διακρινόμενον, δι’ οἰκειότητα πρὸς ἀμφότερα, καὶ συγγένειαν, μαλακῶς ἐνδιδόναι, καὶ δεχομένην τὰς ἐναντίας ἀκρότητας</note>. Plato also has much to say about him where he treats the analogy of the four elements; hence the **number four** <note>original: τετράς (tetrad)</note> is sacred to this same Mercury, and he himself is called **four-angled** <note>original: τετράγωνος (square)</note>, and is said to have been born on the fourth day of the month. In the Chemical WORLD, he is simultaneously **god** <note>original: θεὸς</note>, **matter** <note>original: ὕλη</note>, **form** <note>original: εἶδος</note>, and **result** <note>original: ἀποτέλεσμα</note>. *For by these natures, from which ALL things consist, passing to and fro, upward and downward, the conjunction of the parts of the WORLD is maintained.* **This is** what Hermes says in the *Emerald Tablet*: *Let the superior things become as the inferior, and the inferior as the superior.* Hence Mercury himself is called "Common," and **male-female** <note>original: ἀρσενόθηλυς (androgynous)</note>.

Someone might ask: what business do **Amphiaraus** and his son **Amphilochus** have with the gods who preside over medicine? We have learned from **Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> that they were seers who passed down the art of prophesying through dreams. But, besides the fact that a medical remedy is often sought from the gods through sleep <margin>Pliny, Natural History, Book 30, Chapter 1.</margin>, both divination and medicine are parts of the ancient **Magic**. Regarding this, **Pliny** says: *No one doubts that Magic was first born from medicine, and that it crept in under the guise of health as something higher and more sacred than medicine. Thus, to its most enticing and desirable promises, it added the strength of religion, toward which the human race is most blind. And so that it might succeed in this as well, it mixed in the Mathematical arts <note>original: "artes Mathematicas," here referring specifically to Astrology</note>, for there is no one who is not eager to know his own future, believing that such things are most truly sought from the heavens.* These same arts are joined in both **Apollo** and **Isis**; of whom I shall say more elsewhere, when there is leisure.

We touched on the fourth part of the altar briefly above when we discussed the number five. Therefore, we must say here what could not conveniently be said there. That goddess who first presents herself, **Minerva Paeonia** <note>Minerva "the Healer," from the Greek "Paean"</note>, we have dealt with in this very chapter as far as the subject required. **Venus**, whom I showed above was surnamed *Physica* <note>original: "Phyficam," meaning "The Natural" or "relating to the forces of Nature"</note> on an ancient stone, is likewise a medical goddess; this is very easy to prove from the writings of the love-poets alone. Hence so many vows were made to her, and so many fulfilled. There is the well-known story from **Petronius** about **Quartilla** seeking a remedy for a quartan fever. 

But in our work <note>likely referring to the "Great Work" of Alchemy</note>, there is another remedy of Venus. For she <margin>Aelian, On the Nature of Animals, Book 10, final chapter.</margin> penetrates, matures, and cooks all things by her heat—or her most volatile heavenly **sulfur**—in such a way that she transmutes even imperfect metals into perfect ones. This is the origin of the perpetual fire in her temple at Mount Eryx. However, as to what diseases she might cure in these matters, no one [ma...]

**Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, though likely a pseudonym for later authors, famous for his works on antimony and the "Twelve Keys" of alchemy</note> teaches this better: **Panacea** <note>The "all-healer," personified as a goddess and sought by alchemists as a universal medicine</note> occupies the middle place; there is no name more frequently invoked in our art than hers. She is imagined as the daughter of **Aesculapius** <note>The god of medicine</note>, relieving all diseases whatsoever. Fittingly indeed is she joined closely to **Venus**, since in the poet Virgil's work, when Venus is about to provide medicine for her wounded son Aeneas:

> She sprinkles the healing juices
> Of Ambrosia, and the fragrant Panacea.

Where the epithet "fragrant," if nothing else, sufficiently proves what Panacea is, and what its power and efficacy are. **Basil Valentine**, dealing with **Venus** in the passage indicated above, commands her spirit to be joined with the spirit of **Mars** and **Mercury**, and to be purged of all impurity, so that once all corrosive sharpness has been wiped away, they become sweet and fragrant. Once this is done, an incomparable medicine is prepared, by which—once fermented by the splendor of the sun—the **transmutation of metals** occurs. The words of **Servius** <note>A 4th-century commentator on the works of Virgil</note> are most worthy of consideration: "*Panacea is a kind of herb; however, it should be known that Lucretius everywhere calls panacea 'salt'; hence we can also understand salt in this place. For IT DRIVES AWAY ALL PAIN.*" But it is better to understand it as an herb, because Virgil calls it "fragrant." Others say the panacea is a medicine composed of several herbs, which works for every wound. **Hercules** is said to have provided this herb to the Thessalians against the power of poisons. He [Servius] said many things in few words, which he himself did not even understand. He who has knowledge of the **salt of Mars** <term>Alchemical iron sulfate or a specific purified essence of iron</term> will also understand these things, with the same Basil Valentine going before and leading the way with a torch. 

There remains the fifth part [of the altar], dedicated to the **Nymphs**, **Pan**, **Achelous**, and **Cephisus** <note>Greek deities associated with wild nature, rivers, and springs</note>. In these things so many occurrences reveal the nature of our work, that I hardly know...

<margin>
Theocritus, *Idyll* XVII.
Philo, *On the Life of Moses*.
</margin>

...what I should recount first, since there are ten thousand things to say. <note>original Greek: Τί πρῶτον καταλέξω, ἐπεὶ πάρα μυρία εἰπῆν.</note> For

# JACOBUS TOLLIUS
<note>Header: The Works of Jacobus Tollius</note>

G 2

If <note>original: "fi", likely "Si" (If)</note> I look at the number itself, ALL things are contained within the quaternary <note>the number four</note>. **Cardinal Perronius** <note>Jacques Davy de Perron (1556–1618), a French cardinal and diplomat</note> used to judge those minds as hopeless which occupied themselves in investigating the **quadrature of the circle**, **perpetual motion**, and the **Philosopher’s Stone**. I will not deny—if this is as true as a leaf of the **Sibyl** <note>prophetic writings of the ancient Greek prophetesses</note> or an oracle of **Apollo**—that my own mind is the most hopeless of all, for I not only profess to seek these three things, but I also believe I have found them. 

But perhaps I understand them a little differently than Perronius was accustomed to. In our circle, I have already partially shown the higher quaternary when I touched upon the **four seasons** of the year and the **four weeks** <note>likely referring to the four phases of the moon</note>. To complete its quadrature in a few words: it is composed of those **four elements**, the **four quarters of the sky**, and just as many **winds**; it likewise embraces **four qualities** <note>heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note> and **centers**. When these are properly treated by an easy method from an undigested and raw mass <note>a reference to the "Prima Materia" or original chaos</note> with the help of external fire, they complete a most perfect circle, so that nothing is lacking and nothing is redundant. 

We have already encountered the **square Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium tetragonum"</note>, the inventor of four arts: we have also found that our **Apollo** discovered just as many arts. In addition, **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> affirms that all musical harmonies are contained in the **tetrad** <note>the number four</note>; which we showed above to be the foundation of the **decade** <note>the number ten</note>, <term>the measure of justice and equality</term> <note>original Greek: μέτρον δικαιοσύνης καὶ ἰσότητος</note>, in which is the first solid, the generator and the generated: for which reason it was also once called the **WORLD** <note>original: "MUNDUS"</note>, since it indeed encompassed ALL things. For a clearer explanation of what has been said, I will add a table which **Cornelius Gemma** <note>1535–1578, a Belgian physician and astronomer</note>—a philosopher and mathematician of great renown while he lived—supplied to us in his work *Cyclognomica* <note>The "Cyclognomica" attempted to synthesize all knowledge into a universal system</note>.

<margin>
Nicomachus, *Theology of Arithmetic*.
</margin>
If I consider the nature of number itself, ALL things are contained within the quaternary <note>the number four, which Tollius views as the blueprint of creation</note>. Cardinal Perron <note>Jacques Davy Duperron (1556–1618), a French cardinal and diplomat</note> used to judge those minds as hopeless which were occupied with investigating the squaring of the circle, perpetual motion, and the Philosopher’s Stone. I will not deny that, if his judgment is as true as a leaf of the Sibyl <note>an ancient prophetess whose written oracles were easily scattered by the wind</note> or an oracle of Apollo, mine is the most hopeless mind of all; for I not only profess to seek these three mysteries, but I believe I have actually found them. 

However, I perhaps understand these terms a little differently than Perron did. In our "circle," I have already partially demonstrated the Superior Quaternary <note>the higher spiritual or celestial order of four</note>. I touched upon this when discussing the four seasons of the year and the four weeks. To explain its "squaring" <note>the "squaring of the circle" here refers to an alchemical process of balancing opposites</note> in a few words: it is composed of the four elements, the four quarters of heaven, and just as many winds; it likewise embraces four qualities and centers. When these are properly treated by a simple method, starting from a raw and undigested mass and using the aid of external fire, they complete a most perfect circle, such that nothing is lacking and nothing is in excess. 

We have already encountered Mercury as "four-fold" <note>original: *tetragonum*</note>, the inventor of four arts; we also found that our Apollo discovered the same number of arts. Furthermore, Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used numbers to explain the Bible</note> affirms that all musical harmonies are contained within the tetrad <note>the number four</note>. We showed above that this number is the foundation of the decad <note>the number ten; in Pythagorean thought, 1+2+3+4=10</note>, "a measure of justice and equality" <note>original Greek: μέτρον δικαιοσύνης καὶ ἰσότητος</note>, containing the first solid, both generating and generated. For this reason, it was also once called the WORLD <note>original: *MUNDUS*, implying an ordered system</note>, since it encompassed ALL things. To provide a clearer explanation of what has been said, I will add a table provided to us by Cornelius Gemma—a distinguished Philosopher and Mathematician during his lifetime—in his work *Cyclognomica* <note>a 1575 work by Gemma attempting to link all knowledge into a single "circular" system</note>.

<margin>
Horace, Book 1, Ode 10. Scholiast on Homer's *Iliad*, Book 1. Philo, *On the Creation of the World* and *Life of Moses*. Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, Book 1. Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, Book 1.
</margin>

Furthermore, on this part of the altar, I detect an octave harmony <note>original: "Symphoniam *διὰ πασῶν*" (dia pason); the fundamental musical interval of an octave</note> based on a ratio of three parts water to one part fire: just as the proportion once used in the tempering of wine. > There were three ambiguous mothers for Jason:
> Rhoeo, and Alcimede, along with Polymele.
> Of these, Rhoeo was of the Staphyli <note>The "Grapes"</note>, while the others were the children of Autolycus.

Of these, **Rhoeo** is of Mercury <term>mercurialis<gloss>relating to the "mercury" principle in alchemy, representing the volatile, fluid, or spiritual essence of matter</gloss></term>, **Alcimede** is of salt <term>salinus<gloss>relating to the "salt" principle, representing the body, stability, or the solid result of a chemical process</gloss></term>, and **Polymele** is the sulfurous feminine spirit <term>sulphureus spiritus<gloss>relating to "sulfur," the active, combustible, and soul-like principle in the alchemical "Tria Prima"</gloss></term>. In Staphylus [the Grape], I recognize the philosophical wine <term>vinum philosophicum<gloss>a metaphorical "solvent" or the perfected essence of the alchemical work</gloss></term>; and in Autolycus, I hesitate whether to recognize the "whole" or the author of light, the sun Lycabas <note>original: "Lycabonta folem"; Lycabas is an ancient name for the year or the sun's path</note>; yet I lean toward this opinion. The last is **Hygia** [Health], the goal of medicine, called **Salus** by the Latins; whom the Pythagoreans used to pray for as a blessing upon one another, as we indicated above. Her name or epithet was even attached to Minerva, as we shall teach later. And there exists an elegant hymn to her by Onomacritus, in which, among other things, he addresses her thus:

> For from you, the dwellings of mortal men perish not.
> Every house flourishes with great joy because of you,
> and the arts abound; the WORLD <note>original Greek: "KOSMOS"</note> desires you, O Queen.

That is, as I translated while writing these things:

### CHAPTER VI.

### **THE CHANGE OF THE NAME OF PASSIENUS** *indicated in the works of Seneca.*

In Book 5 of the *Controversies* <note>A collection of rhetorical exercises and anecdotes compiled by Seneca the Elder</note>, Seneca mentions a certain schoolteacher with a notable eulogy, which should be observed by those who, while engaged in the study of literature, tear apart the reputation of others in their writings. Thus he writes concerning Otheus <note>The text says "Oseo," likely referring to the orator Otheus mentioned by Seneca the Elder</note>: *Was he himself far from eloquence? He was born to brand insults upon the characters of all. There was no one on whom he did not impress something that they could not escape.* Against the crooked and perverse habit of such a man, like an antidote to poison, <margin>In the *Ibis* <note>A poem by Ovid written as a curse against an unnamed enemy</note></margin> there occurs the noble integrity of Ovid, who, although provoked, nevertheless held back his hand from this "itch" <note>Meaning the urge to use writing to defame others</note>. For thus he says of himself:

> *Up to this time, now that twice five lustra have been completed by me,*
> <note>A "lustrum" is a five-year period; "twice five" indicates Ovid was fifty years old</note>
> *every song of my muse has been unarmed;*
> *And there exists not one letter of Naso <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, the poet's full name</note> that could be read,*
> *blood-stained, in so many thousands of my writings.*

And certainly, if anything is foreign to all humanity, it is to immediately insult the labors of those who either desire to benefit the public or serve their own fame, when perhaps one or two errors are discovered, and to drag their talent or character through the mouths of men: when, on the contrary, for those things which have been well [produced] by them, as...

And for those things that have been usefully discovered and handed down, thanks must be given; that will to deserve well of the public and that honorable desire for a good reputation should be welcomed with kisses and decorated with every ornament of praise. By this, others may be stirred to imitation of the example, and the authors themselves may strive to improve or even surpass themselves. So it follows that even if everything else was skillfully arranged, these fault-finders <note>original: "vitilitigatoribus"</note> and unrefined "Oscans" <note>The Oscans were an ancient Italian people, but in this context, the term is used as a slur for someone crude, vulgar, or unlearned</note> would find themselves furthest from wisdom through their blasphemies and accusations. <margin>Against</margin>
But it was not my intention now to give advice to others, though I had proposed to myself to cast this passage of Seneca into this chapter <note>Jacobus Tollius is explaining his editorial choice to include this specific philological debate here</note>: therefore, I shall get to the point. Immediately following in the same author <note>Seneca the Elder, in his *Controversies*</note>: *He [Otheus] gave Passienus an obscene name by changing his first syllable into Greek.* This passage has exercised many men of great name; some of whom think this **Oscan** person was called *Sassienus* instead of *Shyssienum*; another *Paschaenus*; someone else *Ohasianum*; another again *Paschienum*, and another *Crassienum*, or even *Grassienum*. To me, however, that disgraceful change of the name *Passienus* does not seem so far-fetched; indeed, it is close at hand with a slight restoration of this passage. I read it first as: *changed into a Greek sound* <note>original Latin: "in Graecum mutata sonum"</note>. For that word <term>sonum<gloss>sound</gloss></term> seems to have fallen out of the text. Then, I believe Otheus said *Phassienum* instead of *Passienus*; in the same sense that Mamurra was called a *White Dove of Dione* <note>Dione is a name for Venus; the phrase implies effeminacy or being a "kept man"</note> by Catullus, or, as Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius, a famous Dutch scholar</note> and others before him preferred to correct it (as Erasmus advised in his *Adages*), *Adoneus* or *Aidoneus*, with the same meaning. For <term>phassae<gloss>wood pigeons</gloss></term> were anciently under the protection of Venus, just like doves. The words of Artemidorus are perfectly suited to this: *Wood pigeons and doves signify women.*

<margin>The Interpretation of Dreams, Book II, chapter 20.</margin>

...ring-doves <note>original Greek: "φαίσσαι" (phaissai)</note> are entirely like harlots, while doves <note>original Greek: "περιστεραὶ" (peristerai)</note> are sometimes well-behaved and like mistresses of the house. <margin>Hexaemeron</margin>
These things are remarkably illustrated by a proverb that appears in the letters of the Greeks, where Mormia [writing] to Chremes says, among other things: *But having freed a flute-girl with whom he happened to be in love, and having draped her in the robe of a bride, they say he brought home a wood-pigeon instead of a domestic dove.* <note>original Greek: "αὐλητρίδα δὲ λυσάμενος... φάσσαν ἀντὶ περιστερᾶς"</note> This was taken from Plato, who used it in the *Theaetetus*. > Gifts are prepared for my Venus: for I myself have noted
> The place where the sky-high wood-pigeons have built their nest:

to whom the other, no less naughty, offers golden apples in return. Therefore, *Shassienus* <note>Tollius suggests this was the "obscene name" created by a Greek pun on Passienus</note> is an **androgynous** <note>original Greek: "ἀνδρόγυνος" (man-woman)</note> person in the Oscan style; or *Sathicus* <note>Likely a reference to the Greek "sathos," a slang term for the male member</note>. Hence, among the Dream-Interpreters, wood-pigeons signify women. 

<margin>In the Dream-Interpreters</margin>
Achmet <note>A famous medieval author of a work on the interpretation of dreams</note> says: *If a woman sees that a dove, a turtle-dove, or a wood-pigeon has come and sat upon her head, and she is pregnant, she will give birth to a daughter.* It might seem strange, yet it is not, why those birds signify women rather than men; or even those men who grieve that they were born as men. For female lust:

> *Is sharper than ours, and possesses more madness.*

Moreover, these birds are very "hot" and very lustful. Hence their flesh is also very dry. 

<margin>On Diet, Book II, chapter 17</margin>
Hippocrates says: *Therefore, the driest meat is that of the wood-pigeon, second is the dove, third the partridge, the rooster, and the turtle-dove; the moistest is the goose.* <note>In ancient medicine, "dry" and "hot" were qualities associated with high metabolic or sexual energy</note> Whence, as it is in Herodotus, a sacrifice was made to Isis with a goose. 

<margin>Book II. On Rhea.</margin>
Since, therefore, there is such great heat in doves, they were not without reason sacred to Venus, as we have seen; they were also a symbol of fire, or of the ethereal air, according to the testimony of Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher who wrote on Greek mythology</note>; where the word "air" <note>original Greek: "ἀὴρ"</note> seems to be taken by Velareus for "ether" <note>original Greek: "αἰθὴρ"</note>.

### CHAPTER VII.
### FLORUS & CICERO examined in several places.

<margin>Book II, chapter VI.</margin>
I formerly restored this passage of Florus <note>A 2nd-century Roman historian</note> concerning Hannibal in my notes to Ausonius: *He dared to follow through Lucania under the leadership of Sempronius Gracchus, and to press the back of the falling man: although this man [shame] fought with a slave's hand.* <note>Tollius suggests adding "shame" (pudor) to the text to explain why the general was hesitant to fight with a "slave's hand," referring to the use of freed slaves in the army</note> *For up to this point so many evils had driven them: but having been gifted with Liberty, they made themselves Romans by their valor.* 

I will now bring forward a similar passage from Cicero, from the fourth *Catilinarian* [oration], so that I may bring help to this one as well. *It is worth the effort*, he says, *Conscript Fathers, to recognize the devotion of the freedmen, who, having obtained the right of citizenship through their good fortune, judge this to be truly their fatherland; which certain men born here, and born in the highest rank, [consider] not their fatherland, but a city...*

<margin>Chapter VIII.</margin>

judged them to be enemies. A manuscript <term>codex|A handwritten book, rather than a printed one</term> in our library—not a very ancient one, to be sure, but transcribed from a source of the highest quality (if there is any room for conjecture)—held this reading: *Who, having attained the fortune of this city by their own virtue, judge this to be truly their homeland now.* <note>original Latin: "Qui sua virtute fortunam hujus civitatis consecuti hanc vere jam suam patriam esse judicant."</note> From this, I carve out the following: *who, by their own virtue and fortune, having attained the right of this city, judge this to be truly their homeland now.* <note>Tollius is suggesting the addition of "& fortuna jus" to clarify that they won the "rights" of citizenship.</note> The little word *now* <note>original: *jam*</note> seems to me to contain a singular power, indicating that moment when freedmen <note>Former slaves who had been granted citizenship</note>, having obtained the rights of the city, no longer looked upon Rome as a foreign city, but as their own homeland. Soon after, the same book has: *whom indeed those born here, and born in the highest place, not their country etc.* <note>original: "quam quidem nati hic, & loco nati summo, non patriam &c."</note> This contains a much more vehement and cutting emphasis due to the transposition of words. Not much different is another passage from Florus: <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus, a Roman historian who wrote a summary of Roman history</note> *Who then would wonder that with these customs, by the virtue of the soldiers, the Roman People were victorious?* These words lie flat and are listless.

<margin>Book I, Chapter XVIII.</margin>
You will bring them to life if you correct it thus: *with these customs of the leaders, and this virtue of the soldiers, the Roman People were victorious.* Anyone who compares what came before would contend, by any wager, that it was either written this way originally or ought to have been. However, since other "blemishes" <note>original: *naevi*; literally 'moles' or 'birthmarks,' used here to mean errors in a text</note> presented themselves by chance while I was looking at Cicero, I shall remove these as well by this same effort.

<margin>Chapter VI.</margin>
In the *Second Catilinarian*, <note>One of the four famous speeches by Cicero against the conspirator Catiline</note> the phrase *he grew quiet* <note>original: *vox quievit*</note> is missing in that same manuscript. From this, a suspicion arose in me that the passage should be read: *For clearly the man, timid and very modest, could not bear the voice of the consul. As soon as he was ordered to go into exile, he obeyed, he went.* Now, the word *quievit* (he grew quiet), which follows *paruit* (he obeyed) in the common editions, cannot be tolerated here. For Catiline did not "grow quiet"; instead, he immediately betook himself to the camp of Mallius <note>Gaius Mallius, a centurion and fellow conspirator who was raising an army for Catiline in Etruria</note>. The word *paruit* (he obeyed) might also seem misplaced, were it not that it corresponds to the preceding word *permodestus* (very modest), just as *ivit* (he went) must be referred back to *timidus* (timid).

Otherwise, the speech will be quite clever and elegant if it is read as: *as soon as he was ordered to go into exile, he went.* <note>original Latin: "simul atque ire in exsilium jussus est, ivit."</note> Moreover, what Cicero says here regarding his own command <margin>Chapter 5</margin> appears in the *First Catilinarian*; however, in that passage, the same old book is richer by a single small word. For while the common editions <term>vulgati codices|The standard printed versions of a text available at the time</term> present it as: *Since these things are so, Catiline, continue as you began; depart at last from the city: the gates are open; set out,* <note>original: "Quæ cum ita sint, Catilina, perge quo cœpisti, egredere aliquando ex urbe: patent portæ; proficiscere"</note> in that manuscript it is read as: *continue as you began, go out, depart.* <note>original: "perge quo cœpisti, exi, egredere"</note> Yet, that word *go out* <note>original: "exi"</note> seems to be an interpretation <note>A clarifying note by a scribe</note> of the following word, and it likely crept from the margin into the main text, especially since in Chapter 8 one reads: *Depart from the city, Catiline: free the Republic from fear: into exile, if you are waiting for this word, set out.* <note>original: "Egredi ex urbe Catilina: libera remp. metu: in exsilium, si hanc vocem exspectas, proficiscere."</note> Nevertheless, that word possesses much bitterness and authority. But I change nothing. I am more pleased by the fact that in the final sentence of that same first speech, instead of the common reading *all enemies of good men*, the same book reads *men who are enemies of good men*. I will add the entire passage just as I found it in the manuscript:

->Then you, Jupiter, who were established by Romulus under the same auspices as this city: whom we truly name the Stayer <term>Stator|A title for Jupiter meaning "the one who stops" or "the stabilizer," referring to his role in preventing the Roman army from fleeing in battle</term> of this city and empire: you will ward off this man and his associates from your altars and other temples, from the roofs and walls of the city, and from the lives and fortunes of all citizens. And these men, enemies of good people, foes of the fatherland, plunderers of Italy, joined together by a pact of crimes and an unspeakable alliance—you will visit them, both living and dead, with eternal punishments.<-

In this context, the word *all* <note>original: "omnes"</note> simply cannot be sustained, since he is dealing only with the associates of Catiline.

### C H A P T E R VIII.

### LUCILIUS corrected, and some Natural-Chemical matters concerning Hair. <note>original: "Physico-Chimica"</note>

Lucilius was once considered a charming and witty poet, and above all, a learned one. Delighted by his sophistication—although only a few fragments of his writings remain—I am accustomed to re-reading them from time to time when I have leisure, or when my mind, exhausted by more serious studies, asks to be refreshed and restored by this poetic pleasantness. Recently, therefore, while turning over the pages <margin>Book 17</margin> of this writer, I happened by chance upon a most elegant passage where, from several examples of women once beloved by the gods, he seems to want to conclude—as if by induction—that no woman has ever been so beautiful that some defect was not added by nature to mar an otherwise most perfect form.

> *Do you then think,* he says, *that she of the beautiful braids <note>Greek: καλλιπλέκαμον</note> and beautiful ankles <note>Greek: καλλίσφυρον</note>*
> *Was not permitted to have her belly and even her groin touched by her breasts?* <note>This refers to sagging breasts as a physical flaw</note>
> *That the wife <note>Greek: ἄκοιτιν</note> of Amphitruo, Alcmena, was knock-kneed or splay-footed,*
> *And others (finally, I am unwilling to name Leda herself,*
> *See for yourself, and choose any two-syllable word,*
> *The daughter of Tyndareus <note>Greek: Τυράνυε θυγατέρειαν</note>) had some notable thing,*
> *A wart, or a mole, or at last a single protruding,*
> *Colored tooth.*

That this passage has been thus corrected and punctuated, I shall easily prove to those for whom Criticism is not a stepmother. <note>A Latin idiom meaning those who are naturally gifted in the art of textual analysis and philology</note> In the first verse, the epithet that occurs, taken from the beauty of the hair, signifies something more than praise of form, or or-
<meta>catchword: na-</meta>

<summary>Tollius provides a corrected reading of a fragment by the satirist Lucilius, arguing that even the most beautiful mythological women possessed physical flaws. He uses this as a jumping-off point to discuss the "physico-chemical" properties of hair.</summary>

<header>FORTUITOUS OBSERVATIONS.</header>

...contains an ornament <note>original: "ornamentum"</note> of the head. I learned this from the hymns of Onomacritus <note>A legendary 6th-century BCE poet and priest of Athens</note>. For he also attributed this epithet to Hygieia, the goddess of health—whom we mentioned in Chapter IV. Now, a lovely thickness of hair is not only a distinguished ornament of the human head, especially in women, but also no small proof of firm and sound physical health. Hence among the ancient Greeks, it was the custom to grow out the hair as a sign of strength and bravery.

<margin>Hymn to Diana.</margin>
<margin>In Iliad, Book 2.</margin>
The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator</note> on Homer says: *In ancient times, the Greeks grew their hair long for the sake of valor and manliness; the story goes that Theseus was the first to cut his front locks and dedicate them to Apollo at Delos.* <note>original Greek: "Τῶν ἑλλήνων τὸ παλαιὸν ἆρε τῆς ἕνεκα καὶ ἀνδρείας κομώτων τὰς κεφαλὰς, λόγος πρῶτον Θηβέα ἀποκειράμενον τὴν ἔμπροσθίαν κόμην εἰς Δῆλον ἀναθεῖναι τῷ Ἀπόλλωνί."</note> We shall soon see the reason for this rite instituted by Theseus. And by Ovid, Tragedy—which is a more masculine and robust form of poetry—is described as having:

<margin>Book III of *Amores*, elegy 1.</margin>
> *A head thick with hair* <note>original: "Densum cæsarie caput"</note>

On the other hand, the shedding of hair is a significant sign of damaged health. Thus, in Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, it is said regarding chronic diseases that *hair falls from the head.* <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς αἱ τρίχες ῥέουσι."</note> Likewise in his *Aphorisms*: *If hair falls from the head, it is a fatal sign.* <note>original Greek: "ἢν αἱ τρίχες ἀπὸ τῆς κεφαλῆς ῥέωσι, θανατῶδες."</note> Serenus Sammonicus <note>A 2nd-century Roman physician and poet</note> writes:

<margin>On Internal Affections, chapter 50, Section v, 11.</margin>
> *Hair, driven out by a hidden disease, falls out,*
> *If it is washed too rarely; or if the power of a swallowed poison,*
> *Or the potent salamander—unyielding to any flames—*
> *Has cast down the head's chief honor by its touch.* <note>In antiquity, it was believed that the touch of a salamander caused hair loss.</note>

...it brings deformity, and was also once a sign of servitude. Thus Aethra, the mother of Theseus, who was abducted into captivity by the Tyndaridae <note>The Tyndaridae are Castor and Pollux, the twin brothers of Helen of Troy.</note>, was depicted with her hair shorn to the skin, according to the witness of Pausanias. Therefore, setting these aside, we shall turn back to the medical consideration of hair.

Artemidorus reports that it was a custom to shave the hair when someone had recovered from a difficult <margin>Book 1, chapter 33, *Onirocritica*.</margin> illness: **To dream of being shaved clearly signifies a shipwreck for those at sea, and for those who are sick, it signifies coming to the greatest danger, yet not dying. Ναυαγήσαντες μὲν γὰρ, καὶ ἐκ μεγάλης σωθέντες νόσου ξυρῶνται οἱ ἄνθρωποι, οὐ μὴν οἱ ἀποθανόντες.*</note> This was because they believed they were, as it were, redeeming their life with their hair, if they dedicated it to the gods by a vow (of which more shortly); or because it is very healthy for recovering their original density after an illness, as the remnants of the disease are "exhaled" and new hair grows in the place of that which fell out.

...brings deformity; it was also once a sign of servitude. Likewise, on the other hand, it would be easy to gather the praises of girls for the density of their hair from Achilles Tatius, Aristaenetus, and other writers of that sort, if it were worth the effort.

Therefore, neglecting these points, we shall turn our attention back to the medical consideration of hair. Artemidorus reports <margin>Book 1, chapter 33, *The Interpretation of Dreams*.</margin> that it was a custom to shave the hair when someone had recovered from a difficult illness. <term>To dream of being shaved signifies a shipwreck for those at sea, and for the sick, it signifies reaching the ultimate danger, but not death. For men who have suffered shipwreck and those saved from a great illness shave themselves, but those who have died do not.</term> <note>original Greek: Ξυρᾶσθαι δὲ δοκεῖν τοῖς πλέουσι μὲν διαῤῥήδην ναυάγιον σημαίνει, τοῖς δὲ νοσοῦσιν εἰς ἔσχατον ἐλάσαι κίνδυνον, πλὴν οὐκ ἀποθανεῖν. Ναυαγήσαντες μὲν γὰρ, καὶ ἐκ μεγάλης σωθέντες νόσου ξυρῶνται οἱ ἀποθανόντες.</note> This was because they considered that they were, as it were, redeeming their lives with their hair, if they dedicated it to the gods after making a vow (which I will discuss shortly); or perhaps because it is very healthy for recovering their former thickness after a disease, as the residues of the illness are exhaled and new hair grows in the place of that which fell out.

As for the vows, an example exists in Pausanias; <margin>In the *Description of Greece: Corinth*, page 54.</margin> a statue of <term>Hygia</term> <note>Hygia is the Greek goddess of health and cleanliness.</note> is mentioned, which could scarcely be recognized. <term>It was so completely covered by the hair of women, which they had shorn for the goddess, and by strips of Babylonian clothing.</term> <note>original Greek: Οὕτω περιεῖχον αὐτὸ κόμαι τε γυναικῶν, αἳ ἐκείροντο τῇ θεῷ, καὶ ἐσθῆτος Βαβυλωνίας τελαμῶνες.</note> These were, without doubt, women restored from ill health to prosperity; and therefore they offered their tresses to the <term>fair-haired Hygia</term>. Indeed, that vows were made to the goddesses who preside over hair even when it was lost to disease is established by an ancient inscription; <margin>Gruter, page 1067.</margin> in which *Tullia Superiana* [offered] to *Minerva the Mindful* for the rest- <note>The catchword "ſtitu-" suggests the word "restitutis," meaning "restored [hair]."</note>

->*Yet higher than those others*<-
->*Is the goddess herself, and she towers above them all by her neck.*<-

<margin>Pausanias in Phocica, page 355.</margin> Since this had been observed by Praxiteles <note>A famous Greek sculptor of the 4th century BCE known for his lifelike statues</note>, he made a statue of Diana at Anticyra that surpassed the height of even the tallest woman. Pseudo-Didymus <note>A name used for an anonymous commentator on Homer whose work was historically attributed to the scholar Didymus</note> commented on those lines of Homer: *for the goddess is a nurturer of the young <term>kourotrophos: a Greek epithet for deities who protect and nourish children and the young of all species</term> just like her brother Apollo.* <note>original Greek: κουροτρόφος γὰρ ἡ θεὸς τῷ ἀδελφῷ Ἀπόλλωνι.</note> Here the little word *equally* or *similarly* <note>original Greek: ὁμοίως or ὁμῶς</note> seems to have dropped out after "goddess."

And I have read in Diodorus Siculus <note>A 1st-century BCE historian</note> that the care of infants and the foods required for that age pertained to Diana, and for that reason she held that name. Indeed, my little emendation is confirmed by those words of Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher from the 1st century CE</note>: <margin>On the Nature of the Gods, regarding Apollo and Diana.</margin> *Suitably they also introduced a brother for them, since they are similar to each other and moved by a like motion, and have a similar power over all things, and nurture the things upon the earth in like manner.* <note>original Greek: Οἰκείως δὲ καὶ ἀδελφὸς... τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.</note> For so these words are to be read from the old manuscript, instead of the commonly printed "they introduce to him." <meta>This page continues the argument from page 74 regarding the celestial influences on growth and physical stature. It specifically contrasts the roles of the Sun and the Moon, suggesting that while the Sun provides vital spirit, it is the Moon’s moisture that allows for physical expansion and the "tallness" previously attributed to Diana.</meta>

<page-num>75</page-num>
<header>CHANCE OBSERVATIONS</header>
<note>original: FORTUITA. This header likely refers to a collection of miscellaneous scholarly notes or "happenstances."</note>

...should they be governed? Indeed, bodies are nourished by the heat of one <note>the Sun</note>, the lands are loosened, excessive humors <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) were believed in ancient medicine to control health and temperament</note> are compressed, and the gloom of winter, which binds all things, is broken; while by the effective and penetrating warmth of the other <note>the Moon</note>, the ripeness of the crops is irrigated. Does not human fertility respond to her course? Antyllus, as quoted in Stobaeus, says: <margin>page 550.</margin> *The sun, according to its own power, warms bodies, but the moon rather moistens them.* <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν ἥλιος κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ δύναμιν θερμαίνει τὰ σώματα, ἡ δὲ σελήνη μᾶλλον ὑγραίνει.</note> The Sun was held to be the author of spirit, heat, and light—the father of human life and the <term>daimon: a guardian spirit or guiding divinity assigned to a person at birth</term> of the newborn. To the Moon, however, was attributed the protection of bodies, which is why she was also called <term>Tyche: the Greek goddess of fortune or chance</term>, because physical bodies are open and subject to the shifts of chance. Macrobius writes more on this matter in the *Saturnalia*. <margin>book 1, chapter 19.</margin>

Rightly, therefore, physical growth is attributed to the Moon (or Diana). For the Sun, although it nourishes the body insofar as it supplies life, does not make it tall; rather, it contracts the body because of its heat and dryness. In contrast, the Moon, with her coldness and moisture, expands bodies. *Moisture is the vehicle of nourishment,* <note>original Greek: ὑγρασία δὲ τροφῆς ὄχημα</note> as Hippocrates says. Hence Herodorus of Heraclea, as cited in the eleventh book of Athenaeus, is said to have once written: <margin>On Nourishment, chapter 12, book 2.</margin> *that the women of the moon are egg-layers, and those born there are fifteen times larger than we are.* <note>original Greek: τὰς σεληνίτιδας γυναῖκας ὠοτοκεῖν, καὶ τοὺς ἐκεῖ γεγεννημένους πεντεκαιδεκαπλασίονας ἡμῶν εἶναι.</note>

But setting aside that fable—in which, however, I see something that might prove women are "egg-bearing" <note>An early biological intuition regarding human ova</note>—it is the specific property of the Moon to increase the innate moisture in any growing body, by which that body rises into a greater mass. <margin>book 11.</margin> Apuleius says to Isis (or the Moon): *Nurturing the joyful seeds with moist fires.* <note>original Latin: Udis ignibus nutriens læta semina.</note> <margin>Melesiacs. In the Crypt.</margin> Plutarch writes in *The Syrian Goddess*: *Some consider her Aphrodite, others Hera, and others the cause and nature that provided the origins and seeds of all things from moisture, and who showed the beginning of all good things to men.* <note>original Greek: Οἱ μὲν Ἀφροδίτην... Plutarch's authorship of 'The Syrian Goddess' is now disputed; it is often attributed to Lucian.</note> <margin>On Isis</margin> The mathematicians mentioned by the same Plutarch <note>In his work 'On Isis and Osiris'</note> say the same regarding Typhon and Osiris.

It cites various classical authors to link the Moon’s moistening power to the physical stature of living things and even the legendary size of lunar inhabitants.</summary>

...they thought the world was solar, and Osiris lunar, <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἡ μὲν σελήνη γόνιμον τὸ φῶς καὶ ὑγροποιὸν ἔχουσα εὐμενὴς καὶ χρηστὴ ζώων, καὶ φυτῶν ἐστὶ βλαστήσει. ὁ δὲ ἥλιος ἀκράτῳ πῦρ κεκληρωκὼς θάλπει τε, καὶ κλυαίνει τὰ φυόμενα.</note> *because the moon, possessing a light that is fertile and moistening, is benevolent and beneficial for the growth of animals and plants; but the sun, having been allotted unmixed fire, both warms and parches what is growing.* Indeed, I prefer to read the Greek there as "unmixed fire" <note>original: ἀκράτῳ πῦρ</note> rather than "pure fire" <note>original: ἀκηράτῳ πυρὶ</note>, as it is commonly published. An example of this [lunar influence] is found in oysters and some other animals. **Lucilius** says:

> The Moon nourishes oysters, and fills the sea-urchins,
> Adds fibers to mice, and increases the herd.

The influence of the Moon tends more toward the appearance of the body; that of the Sun toward life or the soul; Mercury toward the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*, here meaning the vital breath or intermediary substance</note> or the link between the two; and Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus toward quality and temperament.

<margin>Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book 2, chapter 6.</margin>

Furthermore, *what else,* says Seneca, *brings forth the fruits and the weak corn, raises the green trees, stretches them into branches, or drives them upward* (for I prefer to read "drives upward" <note>original: *exigit*</note> from the manuscript rather than "raises" <note>original: *erigit*</note>) *than the tension and unity of the spirit?* Therefore, when the Sun casts its rays onto the Moon, and those same rays, reflected by the smooth body of the Moon, encounter the dark and cold night air, a certain moist and warm tempering of the air occurs. This air, when breathed in by animals and perceived by plants, nourishes all things and provides growth—and indeed, provides great height to bodies of a moister temperament. ### CHAPTER X.

->*Several passages in Florus restored.*<-

I have decided to clear Florus <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus, a Roman historian who wrote a sketch of Roman history</note> of several errors in these *Chance Matters* <note>original: "Fortuitis." This refers to the title of Tollius's own work, "Fortuita," where he shares "chance" or "accidental" discoveries in literature</note>, so that I might provide a prelude to a more elegant edition of his work. His words in Book II, Chapter XII are: *“For when the Roman People, with Marcius Philippus as consul, had entered that province and carefully scouted the approaches, he advanced through the Astrude <note>Usually identified as the Ascuris marsh in Thessaly</note> marsh and across harsh and treacherous hills—places which seemed impassable even to birds—and terrified the king, who was resting easy and fearing no such thing, with a sudden outbreak of war.”* 

The scholar Heinsius <note>Nicolaas Heinsius the Elder, a famous Dutch classical scholar</note> seemed to have successfully emended the first part of this for himself using the historian Livy. However, instead of "for" [*nam*], and "beyond the Ascuris marsh through steep and out-of-the-way hills," he reads it differently; yet I believe that "harsh and treacherous hills" [*acerbos dubiosque tumulos*] can be defended. Indeed, if anyone reads Livy, they would admit those hills were exceedingly "harsh and dangerous." They are called "harsh hills" just as one might say a "harsh wound" or a "harsh blow." They are "treacherous" [*dubii*] in the same sense as the "mountain treacherous to climb" mentioned in Propertius <note>An Augustan-era elegiac poet</note>, and the "places treacherous for footing" in Sallust <note>A major Roman historian</note> when discussing a similar matter. But in the following section, I read: *Those [parts], which to the birds also seemed impassable*—namely, Macedonia.

<margin>Book I of the Histories</margin>
Sallust must also be corrected in this way: *“All Gaul on this side of the Rhine, and between our sea and the ocean, was thoroughly subdued, except where it was impassable due to marshes.”* For this, the common reading is "which was impassable from the marshes." The words "Those [parts], which" [*Illa, quæ*] are in the ablative case, with the word "part" or "way" being understood. So, a little further on in Florus: *“Macedonia was caught through other ways, when he [the general] had crept in by one route while threatening another.”* There is a similar error occurring in Book II, Chapter VIII; where, regarding Antiochus <note>Antiochus the Great, King of the Seleucid Empire</note>, you might read "lest he should not seem to act as a leader in some kind of way" [*aliquo ducem genere*]. I am surprised those learned men did not see that it should be restored as: *“lest he should not seem to act as a leader in any way”* <note>original: "ne non aliqua Ducem agere videretur." Tollius is correcting a grammatical gender/case error to make the Latin more idiomatic</note>.

> *And if you had not harmed him in some way <note>original: "aliqua"</note>, you would have died.*

A little later we read: *“Absent, therefore, and defeated, he fled to the seas and the island of Samothrace <note>An island in the northern Aegean Sea, famous in antiquity for its Mystery Cult and the sanctuary of the Great Gods</note>, relying on its famous sanctity: as if temples and altars could defend him, whom neither his own mountains nor his weapons could.”* One should maintain that Samothrace was most famous and sacrosanct; but that very fame seems to stand in the way of adding this specific adjective as if it were a mere indicator of its celebrity. The words of Velleius <note>Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian who wrote a compendium of Roman history</note> regarding the same Perseus confirm my opinion: <margin>Book 1</margin> *“Leaving which, he fled to the island of Samothrace; and as a suppliant, he entrusted himself to the sanctity of the temple.”* And those of Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a historian who epitomized the works of Trogus</note>: <margin>Book 39, ch. 1</margin> *“When he had sought Tyre, intending to defend himself by the sanctity of the temple.”* 

But even the antithesis that follows demands the same. Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil</note> abundantly teaches what a shrine <term>delubrum</term> <note>A sacred space, often specifically a place for ceremonial cleansing or the sanctuary surrounding a temple</note> is in his commentary on Virgil, where <margin>Aeneid II, lines 225 & 296, and Aeneid IV, line 56</margin> he discusses this very Samothracian temple. For the sanctity of this temple, one should consult Livy <note>Titus Livius, the preeminent historian of Rome</note>, from whom these details were expressed by Florus. 

It follows in <margin>Book 45</margin> the same chapter: *“When the enemy <note>original: "hostis"</note> had come into sight, he received him into the temple, and invited him to banquets, and warned his children, etc.”* What place is there here for the word "enemy"? I read it, therefore, as: *“when he had come into sight, he both received him hospitably <note>original: "hospitaliter," which Tollius suggests in place of "hostis"</note> and invited him to a banquet.”* Before this emendation had occurred to me, I had conjectured: *“and he received him into his assembly <note>original: "consessum"</note>”*; for "temple" [*templum*] or "tent" [*tentum*], as others have been pleased to read, are too far-fetched here. 

The words of Valerius Maximus <note>A Roman writer of a famous collection of historical anecdotes</note> favored my conjecture: <margin>Book 5, ch. 1</margin> *“Who, when he had heard that Perseus—who in a tiny moment had turned from a king into a captive—was being led to him, ran to meet him, decorated with the ornaments of Roman command: and he raised up with his right hand the man who attempted to fall at his knees, and in the Greek language exhorted him to have hope.”* Having introduced...

...and they increase strength: but the waters of an old woman are bitter, like wormwood, and they weaken strength: like a cistern which had waters that the wind, by drawing them out, consumed. This is a clever comparison indeed, in which an excellent account of the nature of each <note>referring to the young versus the old</note> is maintained. 

Moreover, that use of "waters" for sexual matters occurs in another proverb in the same place: *“Let the scribe who teaches others marry a virgin; and let him not marry her who has had a husband. For the waters of a virgin shall be yours alone; but the waters of her who has had a husband, someone else besides you has drawn before.”* 

You may also read in the Proverbs of Solomon: <margin>chapter 5</margin> *“Drink water from your own cisterns, and flowing waters from your own well; let your springs be dispersed abroad, and streams of water in the streets, which you alone should have, and not strangers with you. Let your fountain be blessed: and enjoy the wife of your youth, a lovely hind and a graceful doe; may her breasts satisfy <note>original: "irrigent," literally "water" or "moisten"</note> you at all times; may you always be possessed by her love.”* 

And in the same book of Proverbs: <margin>chapter 9</margin> *“Stolen waters are sweet, and stolen bread is pleasant,”* where one and the same thing is expressed by a double metaphor. To this corresponds that line of Pindar: *“Something sweet is a stolen labor of Venus”* <note>original Greek: γλυκύ τι κλεπτόμενον μέλημα Κύπριδος</note>. <margin>In the Epistles</margin> And this from Philostratus: *“Everything stolen is more delightful”* <note>original Greek: πᾶν δὲ τερπνότερον τὸ κεκλεμμένον</note>. Here too, in the Poet <note>referring to Homer</note>, are the tricks and "sweet thefts" of Vulcan and Mars <note>referring to the mythological affair between Ares and Aphrodite</note>. <margin>Greek page 395</margin> And there are more of that kind in Clement of Alexandria <margin>Book 3 of The Instructor, ch. 2</margin> and in Athenaeus from Ariphron. <margin>Book 16 of The Banquet of the Learned</margin> 

But in Artemidorus: <margin>Book 2, ch. 27 of The Interpretation of Dreams</margin> *“A river flowing out of a house for a poor man slanders his wife, suggesting that someone in the house is being unfaithful, or even being wasteful with money”* <note>original Greek: ἐξ οἰκίας ποταμὸς ἐκρέων πένητι ἀνδρὶ διαβάλλει τὴν γυναῖκα, ἥτινα τῶν ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ μοιχευόμενον, ἢ καὶ ἀχρημονεῦτα</note>. This passage is excellently illustrated by those words of Pausanias, where he says that a statue of Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> was dedicated in shackles at Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, so that women would be faithful to their husbands and not flow out to other men like a river. 

In the same place in Artemidorus: *“To see a well in a house or in a field, where none was before, is good; for to an unmarried man it signifies a wife. For there are nymphs in the well”* <note>original Greek: Φρέαρ ἰδεῖν ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ ἢ ἐν ἀγρῷ, ἐκ ὂν πρότερον, ἀγαθόν. ὅτι ἀγάμῳ γυναῖκα σημαίνει. νύμφαι γὰρ εἰσιν ἐν τῷ φρέατι</note>. Likewise: *“A well-proportioned lake, and a very small one, signifies a woman”* <note>original Greek: λίμνη σύμμετρος, καὶ μικρὰ λίαν, γυναῖκα σημαίνει</note>.

<margin>in Laconia.</margin> ...signifies abundance; they rejoice in the pleasures of Venus <note>original Greek: ἀφροδισίοις, referring to Aphrodite</note>. To this metaphor derived from waters also belongs that which Alcman deduced from the act itself, saying:

Where the word *to flow down* <note>original Greek: τὸ κατείβειν</note>, or to irrigate, is a term related to water. Truly notable is the ancient custom of the Segobrigii <note>a Celtic tribe in ancient Gaul</note> mentioned in Justin’s writings, where he discusses the founding of Marseilles: the royal maidens were accustomed to offer water to their future grooms. But it is now time to provide the reason why sexual pleasure is signified primarily by this word *water*; then, we shall see shortly why the waters of old women weaken one’s strength, while those of virgins flourishing in age increase it. Many things exist regarding this sentiment, carefully gathered by Plutarch; but it seemed particularly remarkable to me that for the worshippers of Osiris, it was a crime to destroy a garden tree or to block a spring of water. Furthermore, the Egyptians depicted the southern region of the world—that is, the meridian and moist southern quarter of the Earth—with a fig leaf; by this, both the moistening and the generation of all things were signified, and even the genital member itself, whose shape it seemed to express. # FORTUITOUS REMARKS
<sig>F 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

<margin>On the Scholiast of Idyll 13. Table Talk, Book 5, Question 9.</margin>
...the Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator</note> on [Theo]critus. Plutarch, however, believes that he derived that term from "roughness." But leaving aside the dispute over the etymology of the name, which matters little to us, let us examine the matter itself. For it seems to me that the leaf of the fig tree is attributed to reproduction because the fig alone lacks a flower and immediately produces fruit. Furthermore, while it sends all its sweetness and richness into the fruit, the leaf itself remains devoid of sweetness. This concept of "fruit without a flower" is a clear matter in man, appearing both in reality and in the philosophical image of truth. Moreover, I could easily prove that nothing is sweeter than that fruit, and nothing weakens the tree itself more—whether we consider the act of generating or the offspring generated. For Venus <note>the Roman goddess of love</note> was called and held by the ancients to be *Most Beautiful* because the pleasure found in sexual intercourse is most fittingly joined to humans, as it surpasses all others <note>original Greek: διὰ τὸ μάλιστα ἀρηρέκεναι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τὴν κατὰ συμπλοκὴν ἡδονὴν, ὡς πάντων τῶν ἄλλων διαφέρουσαν</note>. Indeed, this passage in Cornutus <note>a Stoic philosopher of the 1st century</note> should be corrected in this way; in the common editions, it is read as *anērokenai* <note>meaning unknown/corrupt</note>, but in the manuscript, it is read as *ararēkenai* <note>meaning "to be joined" or "fitted"</note>. Augustine <note>the influential Christian theologian</note> taught the same regarding that pleasure, as did Philo <note>a Jewish philosopher from Alexandria</note> before him in his work *On Generation*. Regarding the physical toll or detriment of the act, Clement of Alexandria <note>a Greek Christian theologian</note> will provide some information, as will Plutarch, both in his *Table Talk* <note>original Latin: Problemata Convivalia</note> and in his treatise *On Preserving Health*. Geverhart Elmenhorst also collected several points in his notes on Apuleius regarding the fruit itself. As for the fruit, nothing is sweeter to us than our children; hence they are called the *lights of the eyes* <note>original Latin: Oculi lumina; original Greek: φῶτα</note>, named after the most precious part of our body because of the similarity of the pleasure they bring. For the eyes resemble children, because they are beloved <note>original Greek: Ἐοίκασι γὰρ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ παισὶν, ὅτι ποθεινοί εἰσι</note>, as Artemidorus <note>an ancient professional diviner and author</note> says somewhere—or as Tzetzes <note>a 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian</note> puts it:

<margin>Plutarch, in the same place. On the Nature of the Gods. Book 10: see City of God, ch. 16. The Pedagogue, Book 2, ch. 10. Book 11, page 161. Book 1, ch. 28. Chiliads VII. 149. ch. 74.</margin>

> Children seem better than light to those who plant them.

But these children also drain from us all our juice and sweetness, as we are weighed down by an immense mass of cares and anxieties that we undertake for their sake. Hence, an unknown author cited in Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of Greek extracts</note> says:

> Children are cares; and it is a misfortune if they should suffer anything. 
> Even while they are alive, they are no small cares.
> <note>original Greek: Φροντίδες οἱ παῖδές εἰσι· κἀκὸν, εἴ τι πάθοιεν. Εἰσὶ δὲ κᾀ ζῶντες φροντίδες οὐκ ὀλίγαι.</note>

That is, as we translate these and the following lines:

> *Children are a care and a grief to a father, if anything happens to them:*
> *Even living, children are a care and a grief to a father.*

Nor is that Greek proverb different from these,

<margin>Artemidorus, Book 16.</margin>
> *A son is a care to his father for all time.*
> <note>original: Ὡς υἱὸς ἦ λύπη πᾶς πατρὶ πάντα χρόνον.</note>

For this is how the text should be restored in Artemidorus <note>a 2nd-century professional diviner and author</note>. In place of which, he says Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon, a renowned Renaissance scholar</note> reads "he saw how great a grief." Rigaltius <note>Nicolas Rigault, a 17th-century classical scholar</note> testifies that this is expressed by Plutarch, quoting Evenus, as follows:

> See how great a grief a son is to his father for all time.
> <note>original Greek: Ἴδε ὅδη λύπη παῖς πατρὶ πάντα χρόνον</note>
> *A son is either a joy to a father, or he is a wolf.*
> <note>original Latin: Aut jovis est patri filius, aut lupus est.</note>

However, Heraldus <note>Desiderius Heraldus, a French jurist and philologist</note> thinks it should be corrected to:

<margin>page 8, on Arnobius.</margin>
> Or to those for whom a son is also a wolf to his father for all time.
> <note>original Greek: Ἢ οἷς ἠδὲ λύκος παῖς πατρὶ πάντα χρόνον.</note>

Therefore, for these reasons, the *thrion* <note>original: Ἵριον, likely a typographical error for θρίον (thrion), meaning a fig leaf</note> is to me a symbol of generation <note>reproduction</note>; and perhaps for the same reason (unless someone prefers to attribute it to the moisture of the leaf itself, or the warm humidity of the fruit) "for the plant of all is milky <note>original Greek: ὀπωδές, referring to the sap</note>, so that the fig itself, the wood, and the leaf (I read *phyllo* <note>leaf</note>, or *thrion* <note>fig leaf</note>) are filled with it." It was sacred to Bacchus, its discoverer, who was therefore called by the Greeks *Sykites* <note>the Fig-god</note>, as well as *Phloios* <note>Bark-like</note>, *Phleon* <note>Abounding</note>, *Phlous*, and *Phlyeus*, as seen in:

<margin>Plutarch, Book 6, Table Talk, Question 10.</margin>

### FORTUITOUS REMARKS.

<sig>F 5</sig>

Moist vapor creates all things: it is the male, while water is the female. The nature of both, but especially the latter, must be considered more deeply, so that we may understand that third point: why the followers of Osiris <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and fertility; his followers viewed water as his essence.</note> were forbidden from blocking wells. At the same time, let us explain what we promised shortly before: why the fig and its sticky quality were a symbol of the **sexual act** <note>original Latin: "rei Venereæ", literally "the matter of Venus".</note>. Just as heat diffuses, so **dryness solidifies** <note>original Greek: "τὸ ξηρὸν πήγνυσι"</note>. Indeed, all water **contains something sticky and slippery, holding it together by its moisture and solidifying it** <note>original Greek: "ἔχει τι κολλητικὸν, καὶ γλισχρὸν, τῇ ὑγρότητι συνέχον, καὶ πηγνῦον"</note>; for this reason, it was called **Friendship** <note>original Greek: "φιλότης"</note> by Empedocles, while he called fire **destructive Strife** <note>original Greek: "νεῖκος ὀλόμενον"</note>, seeing as it is **separating and dividing** <note>original Greek: "διαστατικὸν καὶ διαιρετικόν"</note>.

Rightly, then, is Water held to be a symbol of the sexual act, both because <term>Materia Prima: the formless, primal substance from which all things are made</term> **of the universe** <note>original Greek: "τοῦ παντὸς"</note> is the mother. This matter, by its own coldness and fatty tenacity, binds and contains the generative power of the descending warm spirit. While fire struggles with water, the finest part of the fire and the thinnest part of the water are tempered together, producing a subject of the most perfect, stable nature, most fit for further generation. This, when we speak of our [alchemical] work, we call the **Philosopher's Stone**. For it comes forth from opposites reconciled: Peace, union, generation, life.

Moreover, all life is of the nature of air, warm and moist; and hence Love is **of a dual nature** <note>original Greek: "διφυὴς", often meaning hermaphroditic or possessing two forms</note>, neither male nor female, but **ALL THINGS**—just as Barnaudus elegantly and truly explained that enigma of *Aelia Laelia Crispa* <note>A famous, cryptic Latin inscription from Bologna that fascinated Renaissance alchemists.</note>, interpreting it as the Philosopher's Stone, while Gevartius, more learnedly, interpreted it as Love. And mention of this brings back to my memory those things regarding the "marine Venus" <note>Venus Anadyomene, or Venus rising from the sea foam.</note> which we either neglected to say or deferred a little earlier. At the same time, we shall lightly correct Cornutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher known for allegorical interpretations of myths.</note> from a manuscript. He, then, speaking of Venus, says:

"And it is probable," he says, "that **Aphrodite** <note>The Greek goddess of love, known as Venus to the Romans; she was famously born from the foam of the sea.</note> was handed down as having been born in the sea for no other reason than that for all things to come into being, there is a need for **motion and moisture** <note>original Greek: "κινήσεως καὶ ὑγρασίας"</note>. Both of which are abundant in the sea." I add that by conjecture it seems to me that instead of "since" <note>original Greek: "ἐπειδὴ"</note> one should read "because indeed" <note>original Greek: "ὅτι δὴ"</note>, or simply "because" <note>original Greek: "ὅτι"</note>. One might also bring up that pleasures—of which Venus holds the **summit** <note>original Greek: "τὴν ἄκραν", meaning the highest point or perfection.</note>—are defined by Empedocles as **those arising from moisture according to the movements of the fibers and nerves** <note>original Greek: "τὰς ἐξ ὑγρᾶ κατὰ τὰς τῶν ἰνῶν καὶ νεύρων κινήσεις"</note>. These things should be read this way in Plutarch, though the versions commonly circulating are highly corrupt.

Now, **moisture** <note>original Greek: "ὑγρότης"</note>, as we have seen, is characteristic of water. And water is often contained in wells. These wells, therefore, are not to be blocked. If you take this literally, it is so that the support of life is not removed (which is the origin of the phrase for those stripped of the community of life: **forbidden water and fire** <note>original Latin: "aqua & igni interdictum"; a Roman legal formula for exile, depriving a person of the basic necessities of life.</note>). If you take it symbolically, it is so that generation is not hindered—whether that happens through potions for women that destroy fertility (a crime now counted among the more secret arts, or the arts of the court, among [the corrupt]) or through **castrations** <note>original Greek: "ἐκτομαῖς"</note> in males.

XXIII.
