We must now move to the second part of the Hebrew proverb, and the reason must be given why the "waters of old women" are so wicked and harmful, while on the contrary, those of "young women" are pleasant and healthy. Whoever has read Plato regarding the **human being divided into male and female** <note>A reference to the myth in Plato's *Symposium*, where original humans were split in half and thereafter spent their lives searching for their "other half."</note>—or rather, whoever has more precisely contemplated nature itself and the wisdom of God the Architect—will immediately recognize how exceedingly admirable is the appetite by which both sexes are drawn and swept toward mutual union, so that through it the propagation of the human race may be continued. ### CHAPTER XII.
->*The colors of the Moon and the Sun.*<-

Justus Lipsius and Nicolas Rigaltius <note>Two famous 16th and 17th-century scholars known for correcting and editing ancient manuscripts.</note> have excellently purged the errors from the thirty-third chapter of Book II of Artemidorus <note>Artemidorus was a 2nd-century Greek author who wrote a famous manual on the interpretation of dreams called the "Oneirocritica."</note>. Tollius is proposing a textual correction to the Greek manuscript of Artemidorus.</note>. The following passages confirm this: **"for she yields, and is covered, and the armor itself is more beautiful than the former. But if he fights as a <term>secutor</term>** <note>A "follower," a specific type of heavy-armored gladiator usually paired against a net-fighter.</note>**, he will take a wife who is beautiful and rich, but very haughty."** That the color silver is a symbol of beauty is proven by even a single epithet of the Moon, whom the poets call **"silvery"**; in the same way, Thetis is called **"silver-footed"** <note>original Greek: "ἀργυρόπεζα."</note> and the Peneus river **"silver-swirling"** <note>original Greek: "ἀργυροδίνης Πηνειὸς."</note> by Homer.

<margin>Olympiad IX.</margin>

I will explain this as briefly as I can. We have shown elsewhere, following Aristotle and Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD known for interpreting Greek mythology as allegory for natural phenomena.</note>, that *light is the color of fire*, and for that reason both *Phoebus* and the *Sun* are called "golden-haired." Therefore, when the Earth is not fully exposed to the sun's rays because the Moon stands in the way, or when thicker clouds intervene and intercept the light of the solar rays, it is necessary that the golden color of the sun diminishes and fades into a bright whiteness. Thus, the Moon appears to be of a *silvery* color; yet she is conversely *golden* when the sky is clear, or when she enjoys the "whole sun"—that is, the full light. The same reasoning explains why a *silver* *bow* is assigned to Apollo (or the Sun): namely, because his brilliance appears more blunt or dimmed when the air is pestilential, or thicker than usual, so that the solar rays can neither disperse nor penetrate it. Indeed, one finds that Physical discipline is exercised in Homer, and <term>Chemical discipline</term> <note>In this context, "Chemical" refers to Alchemy, which Tollius viewed as the hidden meaning behind ancient myths.</note> in Pindar. For that Pindaric fable is entirely <term>mysterious</term> <note>original Greek: "μυστηριώδης" (mystēriōdēs), implying it contains hidden, initiatory knowledge.</note>, and contains more in its inner corner than it promises at first glance. For the *Bow* of Phoebus is the <term>acid faculty</term>, and the *Arrows* sent forth from it are <term>volatile spirits</term>. Against these, Hercules opposes his own <term>fixed acid</term> and carries away the victory. In the same way, he resists Neptune—that is, the <term>volatile Alkali</term>—and Pluto—that is, the <term>fixed Alkali</term>—who otherwise leads mortal bodies down to the hollow street of the dying with his staff. I will set down Pindar's words so that the matter itself may be better perceived.

Therefore, when Neptune, armed with his <term>trident</term>, resisted Hercules at Pylos—that is, at the very "gate of birth" <note>A pun on the Greek word "pylē," meaning gate.</note>—Hercules was the victor. For once the matter has been agitated and stirred up, and is now ready for birth, Hercules soon emerges as the <term>Averter of Evil</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀλεξίκακος" (alexikakos), a traditional title for Hercules.</note> and the <term>Subduer of Evils</term>, destined to be the victor over the three Gods: those of the heavens, the sea, and the underworld—representing the animal, vegetable, and mineral realms. As for Pindar saying this happens "according to the divinity," he received this idea from others, just as Virgil did when he wrote of the <term>Golden Bough</term>:

<margin>Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VI</margin>
> *It will follow willingly and easily,*
> *if the fates call you.*

That <term>Golden Bough</term> is the same as the <term>staff</term> <note>original Greek: "ῥάβδος" (rhabdos).</note> of Pluto. The trident, however, is attributed to Neptune, just as the <term>triad</term> <note>original Greek: "τριάς" (trias).</note> was attributed to justice by the Pythagoreans. Hence, the trident here stands for Neptune himself. For Mercury is—as was noted above in Chapter IV—a <term>mediator</term> <note>original Greek: "μεσίτης" (mesites).</note> between both the nature of Acid and the Sun <note>original: "Acidi Sol." The text likely continues to describe the union of acidic and solar/sulfuric principles.</note>...

...and of fixed <term>Alkali</term> <note>original: "Alkali fixi." In early chemistry, this refers to stable salts (like potassium carbonate) that do not vaporize when heated.</note> is the common bond; the scourge related to both is the efficacy of the <term>spirit of Neptune</term> <note>original: "Neptuni spiritus." Tollius uses Neptune to represent the volatile, watery principle—Mercury—which acts as the "promoter" or catalyst of the alchemical work.</note>, the promoter of the work. Regarding the "Equestrian Neptune," I shall say more later.

I will add to these points a sort of corollary and a solution to that question which likewise pertains to the nature of light: why the color of the sky, and also that of the sea, becomes blue—though the sea’s color is darker, which is why it is called <term>purple</term> <note>original Greek: "πορφύρεος" (porphyreos). In ancient Greek literature, especially Homer, this term described dark, churning, or iridescent surfaces, famously the "wine-dark" sea.</note> by Homer. 

The blue color is born from the purest light—that is, the fiery particles of the Sun's rays—combined with water and air. Where the color is darker, earthy particles have been mixed in. Therefore, when the Sun directs and pours its rays onto the Moon, the rays reflected from the Moon imbue the air of the opposite sky with that color which we see during the day when the Moon is below our horizon; yet while she shines for us at night, she is above the horizon for those at the <term>antipodes</term> <note>The people living on the exact opposite side of the earth.</note>. These same rays falling into the sea <note>The Latin OCR "more" is a likely error for "mare" (sea).</note>, partly reflected from the sky, show the sea to us as green under a clear sky, because the earthy particles of the sea receive more light and, through the heat of the Sun, become purer and more refined. 

However, when the Sun is covered by clouds and does not shine so brightly, the color of the sea is blue. When it is completely cloudy and the Sun is driven away, the sky turns blackish or "purple," as the poets call it. They describe death in the same way: as the extinguishing of the <term>vital fire</term> <note>original: "vitali igne." The animating heat or "innate heat" believed by early physicians to sustain life.</note> in a man, whose rays previously illuminated his entire body.

### CHAPTER XIII.

## A COMPARISON OF VIRGIL WITH HOMER.

<margin>chapter 3. discussions 11, 12, 13.</margin>

I do not fear envy, reader, where the mind is conscious of what is right and good, and the reason for the deed is clear. I promised earlier that I would compare **Virgil** with **Homer**, and the Tragedian **Seneca** with **Sophocles**. What I had once conceived and begun for the sake of illustrating my edition of <term>Longinus</term> <note>Dionysius Longinus, the supposed author of the ancient Greek treatise *On the Sublime*, which Tollius edited in 1694.</note>, I shall now complete for the sake of exercising, strengthening, and even delighting the mind. 

But you, if I bring forth anything ill-advised, or alien to reason and truth, or supported by a less-than-firm judgment, correct me with that same kindness with which I serve your benefit or leisure. *Let envy be absent; let ill-will be gone!* <note>original Greek: "Ἀπέστω φθόνος: ἀπίτω βασκανία" (Apestō phthonos: apitō baskania).</note> Let that preconceived opinion also be absent, which is so often imposed upon most people. I have undertaken to defend the Greeks and to assert for them the primary glory—which now, through the laziness of the age, is most unjustly granted to the Latins—with arguments that seem to me, at least, not invalid. 

I do not blame or criticize the Latins for this; rather, I award them the second <term>palm</term> <note>The "palm" was a traditional symbol of victory in ancient contests.</note>, not the first. And in a most fair judgment, I have those very authors favoring me, even though I pronounce against them. In addition to this, if I love any of the ancient Latins, I love Virgil and hold him in the highest esteem; I give infinite thanks to him, as to all other excellent writers, because he devoted his time to the pleasure and utility of posterity, and thus to mine as well. Far be it from me that I, like another <term>Zoilus</term> <note>An ancient Greek grammarian known as "Homeromastix" (the whip of Homer) for his notoriously harsh and pedantic criticisms of Homer; his name became a byword for a spiteful critic.</note>, should [exalt] myself <meta>catchword: memet (myself)</meta> through the censure of him or anyone else who has deserved well of posterity.

<vocab>Virgilius, Homerus, Sophocles, Seneca Tragicus, Longinus, Zoilus, Comparatio, Græci, Latini</vocab>

<summary>Jacob Tollius introduces a literary comparison between Greek and Latin masters, arguing that while Virgil and Seneca are excellent, the primary "palm of victory" belongs to Homer and Sophocles. He defends his critical approach against charges of envy, positioning himself as a scholar aiming to restore the rightful status of Greek literature.</summary>

I do not strive to prove myself or build a reputation for my own talent by insulting others. To do so is the mark of an unhappy and wicked character, the suspicion of which must be avoided far more than any small glory for intellectual sharpness should be sought. However, if I still do not satisfy someone by saying this, I will whisper in that more troublesome person's ear what I remember learning from <term>Fabius</term> <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, the famous Roman rhetorician known as Quintilian.</note>:

<margin>Book 12, ch. 19.</margin>

*Whatever is dedicated to books and published as a model ought to be polished, refined, and composed according to law and rule; for it comes into the hands of the learned, and it has as its judges the masters of the craft.* <note>original: "Quicquid Libris dedicatur, & in exemplum editur, tersum, ac limatum, & ad legem ac regulam compositum esse oportet; quia venit in manus doctorum, & judices artis habet artifices."</note>

**Virgil** gave his **Aeneas** two adversaries in whom he might exercise the virtue of his soul: **Dido** and **Turnus**. Indeed, he presented Dido to us as a woman who became unchaste from a state of the greatest purity; in this, he did the opposite of what **Homer** did, who fashioned from the "unchaste" **Penelope** a model of chastity for all ages. <note>Tollius refers to the tradition that Virgil altered the historical Dido—who was said to have died to remain faithful to her husband—to make her Aeneas's lover, whereas Homer took Penelope (whom some ancient traditions suggested was less than faithful) and made her the icon of the loyal wife.</note> Here was a topic for talent, and a very broad subject matter supplied for judgment, sufficient for a long dispute. But leaving this aside and neglecting many other points, let us look at the final moments of Turnus compared with the final moments of Homer’s **Hector**, after whose image Turnus was fashioned by Virgil. Rhetoricians are accustomed to teaching in their schools that the fame of a brave man is all the more illustrious according to the greatness of those he has conquered. Glory quickly fades when won from lowly enemies, and it is no great mark of goodness to merely be "better than the worst."

<margin>Martial.</margin>

> ->Do you wish to win in the race and boast of your feet?<-
> ->Surpass the tiger and the swift horse <term>Passerinus</term>.<- <note>Passerinus was a famous racehorse in ancient Rome.</note>
> ->There is no glory in overtaking little donkeys.<-

<margin>book 1.</margin>

**Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note> remarks on those lines of Virgil: *I have twice seven [nymphs]...* <note>original: "sunt mihi bisseptem..." from Aeneid 1.71.</note> He says that the poet does well to praise even these minor nymphs, so that the glory of **Deiopeia’s** beauty might be greater. *For it is more praiseworthy to overcome those who are themselves praised*, just as Virgil himself praises Turnus to enhance the greater glory of Aeneas. They hold these views, as they do all others...

...all things from our **Homer**, whom we are about to bring forth: who, in order to amplify the glory of **Achilles**, fashioned **Hector** to be many times the strongest—not only among the Trojans, but also among all the Greeks, if you set aside **Ajax** <note>In the *Iliad*, Ajax the Greater is often described as the strongest Greek warrior after Achilles.</note> alone—powerful not just in physical strength, but also in the immense greatness of his soul. Therefore, in Homer, the doomed Hector—deceived by the goddess **Minerva** <note>Tollius refers to the Roman name for Athena. In Book 22 of the *Iliad*, she takes the form of Hector’s brother, Deiphobus, to trick Hector into standing his ground against Achilles.</note> and frustrated by the false image of his brother, and about to fight an adversary equal neither in divinity nor in strength—what does he say?

> No longer, son of Peleus, will I flee you, as before
> I fled three times around the great city of Priam. Nor did I ever dare
> To await your onset. But now my heart has driven me
> To stand against you: I might take you, or be taken myself.
> But come here, let us call the gods to witness, for they will be the best
> Witnesses and overseers of our pacts.
> For I will not treat you with cruel outrage, if **Jupiter** <note>Zeus in the original Greek text.</note>
> Grants me the strength to endure, and I take your life;
> But after I have stripped your glorious armor, **Achilles**,
> I will give your body back to the Achaeans; and you should do the same. 
> <note>original: "Οὐ σ' ἔτι Πηλέος υἱὲ φοβήσομαι... ὣς δὲ σὺ ῥέζειν." — *Iliad* 22.250–259.</note>

Admirable here is the Poet’s skill in expressing Hector’s silent premonition of death; for since he is struggling with almost no hope of winning, he offers milder conditions to the vanquished, so that he might perhaps obtain the same from the victor, whom he recognized was stronger than himself. Hence, he assigns the praise of victory—should it perhaps befall him—not to himself, but to **Jupiter** himself, who has often struck down a victor by means of one already cast down. In contrast, that fierce, pitiless, and inexorable soul of **Achilles**, conscious of his own vigor and unconquerable strength, and provoked by the grief for his lost **Patroclus**, shines forth in what follows, so that I seem to see him...

...[so that Achilles] might seem to breathe a slaughter more bitter than any harshness, claiming victory for himself not with doubtful hope, but with certain confidence, and intending insult upon the corpse once his enemy was slain. But after the trickery of **Minerva** <note>Tollius refers to the Roman name for the goddess Athena, who disguised herself as Hector's brother to trick him into fighting Achilles.</note> was discovered and **Hector** felt his fate pressing upon him, did he seek safety or flight with a dejected spirit or a degenerate voice? Not at all. What then?

> Let me not die, at least, without a struggle or without glory, 
> but after performing some great deed for men yet to come to hear of. 
> <note>original: "Μὴ μὰν ἀσπουδίγε καὶ ἀκλειῶς ἀπολοίμην. Ἀλλὰ μέγα ῥέξας τι καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι." — *Iliad* 22.304–305.</note>

Well done, Hector, with such a spirit! What then? Stricken with a lethal wound, he prays for this one thing: that his lifeless body not become prey for birds or dogs, but be returned to his parents for burial. These were his final prayers, and thereafter came death with a great and unconquered soul.

In **Virgil**, everything is more refined, and adorned with every cultivation and care: grand indeed, and magnificent, splendid, illustrious, and although surpassing praise; yet they do not approach that truth of Homeric emotions and <term>forcefulness</term> <note>original: δεινότητα (deinotēta) — a Greek rhetorical term referring to a powerful, even terrifying, intensity or skill in expression.</note>. For anyone to feel this perfectly, they must be of a great mind, raised far above fawning humility and dejection, looking down from their height upon the broken and depressed spirits of a servile nature. As for us, we attempt what we cannot fully do. Let us try, then.

That which we said **Homer** did above, **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his influential commentary on Virgil.</note> has already taught that **Virgil** imitated. What **Achilles** is to Homer, **Aeneas** is to Virgil; what Hector is to the former, **Turnus** <note>The primary antagonist of Aeneas in the *Aeneid*.</note> is to the latter. Come then, let them be compared. Thus, indeed, Achilles speaks in Homer:

Huge here is the bitterness of a mind exasperated by pain; and first, what could be more bitter than that insult with which he addresses him as a "dog," deigning to call him not only by a name other than his own, but one not even human? Take away the phrase *fired by furies and anger*, which are the poet’s own words—what demonstration of fury or anger, I ask you, is found in that actual speech? *Are you to be snatched from me?* Are these the words of a man in a fury? I admit indeed that the doubling of the name **Pallas** holds much bitterness, so that **Turnus** might die with even greater sorrow; furthermore, the word *sacrifices* <note>original: *immolat* — a term used for ritual slaughter.</note> indicates that he is being slaughtered as a sacrificial victim to the spirit of Pallas, which is itself not ineffective in increasing Turnus’s pain. Nevertheless, these things fall far below that anger which is neighbor to madness. As for the insult regarding his "criminal blood"...

...penalty Aeneas inflicts upon Turnus—I am not sure whether he does so deservedly. For in killing Pallas, Turnus had acted only as an enemy; nor was the cause of the war unjust for Turnus. Furthermore, Turnus was not a barbarian to Aeneas, but rather Aeneas might have seemed a barbarian to Turnus; hence that passage:

<margin>

Aeneid line 97.

->*of this half-man Phrygian, and foul in the dust his hair*<-
->*curled with a hot iron, and dripping with myrrh.*<-
<note>original: "Da sternere corpus / Semiviri Phrygis..." — *Aeneid* 12.97-100. Turnus is here insulting Aeneas’s Trojan (Phrygian) heritage, mocking his "effeminate" groomed hair.</note>

In contrast, things were different for Hector. For to the Greeks, all foreigners were "barbarians." Furthermore, the cause of the Trojans, who defended the abduction of Helen by Paris, was wicked and most unjust. Then, indeed, the Homeric Achilles is described as far more monstrous than the "pious" Aeneas. Thus the term <term>wretched one</term> <note>original: "ἄλαστε" (alaste)—literally "unforgettable" or "accursed," used as a bitter insult by Achilles to Hector in *Iliad* 22.345.</note>, with which insult Achilles addresses Hector, becomes tolerable in Achilles, especially since he himself had been much more severely wounded by the slaughter of Patroclus—his beloved and comrade—than Aeneas was by the death of Pallas, a recently joined ally in war. 

But if Aeneas’s gentler character protects that mercy in his words, or the sentiment expressed before, it seems that the same insult [used by Achilles] ought rightly to have been very far removed from him. Yet Aeneas’s words do not approach the bitterness of the term <term>wretched one</term>, because his address of "criminal" is directed not at Turnus himself, but at his blood, as if to a third and nearly separate person. <note>Tollius refers to Virgil's line: "Pallas takes the penalty from your criminal blood."</note> But these things could have been overlooked. Yet will that dejection of spirit in Turnus also be possible—by which he humbly begs for his life from his enemy, and so calmly yields to him his betrothed Lavinia, for whose sake that long and dreadful war had been waged by both nations, the victors and the vanquished alike?

# FORTUITA

He, humble and a suppliant, stretching forth his eyes and his pleading right hand, said: "I have indeed deserved it, nor do I ask for mercy; **use your good fortune. If any care for a wretched parent can touch you, I pray—you too had such a father in Anchises. Have pity on the old age of Daunus.** And return me to my people, or, if you prefer, my body despoiled of light <note>Meaning "deprived of life."</note>. You have conquered, and the Ausonians <note>An ancient name for the people of Italy.</note> have seen me, the conquered, stretch forth my palms. Lavinia is your wife. **Do not press further in your hatred.**"
<note>original: "Ille humilis, supplexque..." — Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.930-938. This is the final plea of Turnus to Aeneas before he is killed.</note>

Let us compare the prayers of Hector:
Then, his strength failing, Hector of the shimmering helmet addressed him: "I entreat you by your life, by your knees, and by your parents: **do not let the dogs of the Achaeans devour me by the ships, but rather accept the bronze and the gold, gifts that my father and lady mother will give you.** Give my body back to my home, so that the Trojans and the wives of the Trojans may grant me, in death, my portion of fire <note>The "portion of fire" refers to the ritual cremation required for a proper burial.</note>."
<note>original: "Τὸν δ' ὀλιγοδρανέων..." — Homer, *Iliad* 22.338-343. Hector's final plea to Achilles.</note>

I have always loved that old saying, *Nor did he suffer prayers to perish in vain*. And never does any matter cause me more regret or annoyance than when, at the urging of my own [feelings], I sink into this **smallness of soul**. *For this reason, in the case of heroes—to whom I am not even to be compared—I find nothing less [tolerable] than a dejected spirit, and especially the fear of death, which even women who are not overly timid have very often overcome.* Yet how does this Turnus differ from Phineus, of whom 

Ovid writes: — Suppliant,
stretching out his yielding hands and slanted arms, he said: "You conquer, Perseus! Remove these grim monsters, and take away the stone-making face of Medusa, whoever she may be. **Take it away, I pray. It was not hatred, nor the desire for a kingdom, that drove us to war: we took up arms for a bride.**"

Yet Perseus <note>Perseus of Macedon, the last king of the Antigonid dynasty, who was defeated by the Romans.</note> rightly calls this man most fearful, because such a defect of the soul was absent from Turnus—and indeed, it ought to have been as far from him as possible. **For even the bold flee, whenever they see death already near their life;** <note>original: "Φεύγουσι γάρ τοι..." — Sophocles, *Antigone* 580-581.</note> as Creon speaks in the works of Sophocles. But to beg for one's life is plainly feminine, and is detested and held in contempt even by those from whom it is sought or by whom it is granted. Thus, in the case of Perseus, Paulus Macedonicus <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, the Roman general who defeated King Perseus at Pydna in 168 BCE.</note> mocked this insane love of life; conversely, in the case of Porus <note>An Indian king who fought Alexander the Great.</note>, Alexander admired and grew to love the greatness of soul he showed in his contempt for death. Having finished this sample of the comparison between Virgil and Homer—though many and perhaps not absurd things could be said regarding the entire work of both and Virgil's art of imitation—let us move to the second part of our promise: that is, to the comparison of Seneca with Sophocles.

# MISCELLANY

...my dear friends, I have decided to insert here my little work in the very words with which that brief commentary—originally conceived to illustrate my edition of Longinus <note>Refers to Cassius Longinus, the presumed author of the influential ancient Greek work of literary criticism, *On the Sublime*.</note>—began. The matter stands thus: To illustrate these two chapters, Seneca alone will suffice. In his *Hercules Oetaeus* <note>A Roman tragedy attributed to Seneca the Younger, depicting the death of Hercules on Mount Oeta.</note>, he took the examples of the most excellent poets before him as his models, yet he imitated them with so little judgment that I fear—if I speak with total honesty and reveal my true feelings—I might appear to be an overly harsh judge of other men's writings.

Nevertheless, a certain part of this tragedy must be examined to show how cautiously and closely the footsteps of the ancients ought to be followed. In Sophocles' *Trachiniae* <note>The Women of Trachis, a Greek tragedy where Hercules' wife Deianira accidentally kills him while trying to win back his love.</note>, whom Seneca follows most closely, there is that famous passage concerning Deianira. It is a portrayal worthy of a lady of holy and noble upbringing, occurring at the moment she learns that her husband, Hercules, has been captivated by a love for the captive Iole, who had been sent ahead to her. Let us hear her lamenting at the first news of such a great misfortune:

> "Alas," she says, "wretched me, where on earth do I stand? What hidden ruin have I received under my roof?" <note>original: "Οἴμοι, τάλαινα, πῆ ποτ’ εἰμὶ πράγματος; Τίν’ εἰσδέδεγμαι πημονὴν ὑπόστεγον Λαθραῖον;" — Sophocles, *Trachiniae* 375-377.</note>

And shortly after:

> "What must I do, women? For I find myself struck senseless by the words I have just heard." <note>original: "Τί χρὴ ποιεῖν γυναῖκες, ὡς ἐγὼ λόγοις Τοῖς νῦν παροῦσιν ἐκπεπληγμένη κυρῶ." — Sophocles, *Trachiniae* 385-386.</note>

And although she felt great sorrow of soul—not a mad sorrow, however, but one ruled by reason—she desired to learn the whole truth exactly from Lichas <note>The herald who brought the news and the captive Iole to Deianira.</note>. With what moderate and wise speech she addresses him while he hesitates!

> "I beseech you, by Zeus who sends lightning over the high glens of Oeta, do not hide the truth. You will not be speaking to a wicked woman." <note>original: "Μὴ πρός σύ τ’ κατ’ ἄκρον οἰταῖον νάπος Διὸς καταστράπτοντος ἐκκλέψῃς λόγον. Θνητῇ γυναικὶ τοὺς λόγους ἐρεῖς κακῇ." — Sophocles, *Trachiniae* 436-438. Deianira appeals to the sanctity of the location to demand honesty.</note>

> "Does she not know among mortals that it is not her nature to always rejoice in the same things? Whoever stands up against Love like a boxer at close quarters is not wise. For Love rules even the gods as he wishes, and me as well—so why not another woman like me? Thus, if I blame my husband for being seized by this sickness <note>original: νόσῳ (nosō) — Deianira refers to Hercules' lust as a disease or madness rather than a moral failing.</note>, I am surely mad. Or if I blame this woman, who is the cause of nothing shameful or evil to me."

And a little later:

> "Not to learn the truth—that is what would pain me. But to know it, what is so terrible? Has not one man, Hercules, married many others before? And yet none of them ever received a harsh word or reproach from me; nor shall she, even if she is completely consumed by her love. For I pitied her most of all when I looked at her, because her beauty has destroyed her life, and she, hapless girl, unknowingly ruined and enslaved her own fatherland. But let these things drift away with the breeze." <note>Sophocles, *Trachiniae*, lines 438–448 and 457–467. The "breeze" refers to letting her sorrows and the past be carried away.</note>

From these lines, her spirit shines forth—one that endures her husband's insults, yet is struck by profound grief. She surrenders her indignation to her love for him. Nor does she lash out bitterly at the mistress, even though the girl has been brought right before her eyes; instead, she pities the unfortunate woman’s fate. Just as the character was established from the beginning, so she is maintained until the very end. <note>Tollius is referencing a rule from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*: "servetur ad imum," meaning a character should remain consistent throughout a play.</note> She loved Hercules; she knew his heart was prone to such pleasures <note>original: "ad voluptates illas procliviorem"</note>, while she herself was most virtuous and of a very peaceful mind. She was well aware of the custom of her age, by which female captives were taken into the company <margin>of the household</margin>

...concubines of the marriage bed were admitted, without shame or disgrace to either party. Nevertheless, jealousy <note>original: *zelotypia*</note> burned; which some wit once quite aptly called the "illegitimate daughter of love." Hence arose that anxiety in her mind to retain her husband, lest he incline entirely toward his love for the beautiful girl <note>Deianira refers to Iole, whom Hercules has brought home as a captive.</note>. Hence the sending of the robe <note>The Shirt of Nessus, which Deianira believed was treated with a love-charm.</note>, and after the unhappy outcome of the attempted love-potion <note>original: *philtri*</note>, violence was done to her own life, and her spirit was earnestly driven out.

All these matters are handled with such propriety <note>original: *decore* — referring to the classical concept of "decorum," where a character's actions perfectly suit their nature and status.</note> by Sophocles that they could not be improved. Among other things, it is truly notable that once the treachery of Nessus and the final agony of Hercules were understood, she does not break into wailing or tears, but is led away speechless: for indeed no speech could be devised that would suit a woman so afflicted or such immense grief. For the magnitude of a vast and especially unexpected sorrow does not admit words or complaints; furthermore, nothing better suits that sad plan of taking one’s own life. Nature itself teaches this. We see this also in the *Antigone*, where likewise the mother of Haemon <note>Eurydice, who kills herself after learning of her son’s death.</note>, having understood the unworthy death of her son, departs without uttering a single word. The chorus then foretells some more serious misfortune looming:

> What can you make of this? The woman has gone back
> without a word, before saying anything good or bad?
> <note>original Greek: Τί τ’ ἂν εἰκάσειας, ἡ γυνὴ πάλιν / φρούδη, πρὶν εἰπεῖν ἐσθλὸν ἢ κακὸν λόγον;</note>
> and shortly after: To me, at least, an excessive silence seems
> to portend something heavy, just as much as loud crying in vain.
> <note>original Greek: Ἐμοὶ δ’ οὖν ἥτ’ ἄγαν σιγὴ βαρὺ / Δοκεῖ προσεῖναι, χἠ μάτην πολλὴ βοή.</note>

Furthermore, however diligently this entire work is examined, nothing in it will be found that is childish, nothing frivolous, nothing inept, nothing "swollen" <note>original: *tumidum* — referring to bombastic or over-the-top rhetorical style.</note>, and nothing that is not drawn from truth itself. In short, everything is sober, chaste, excellent, and observant of propriety. But how different are those writings of Seneca? <note>Tollius here transitions to a critique of the Roman playwright Seneca the Younger, implying his style lacks the dignified restraint of Sophocles.</note>

Who would not call these lines grand? Who would not call them truly tragic? However, let us see what it is in these lines that so displeases us. First, it seems to me no small sin that he has given Deianira an <term>inappropriate disposition</term> <note>original Greek: τὴν πρέπουσαν διάθεσιν — referring to the character's internal state or "mood" being ill-suited to her traditional role.</note>, and has introduced her as a raving woman. Nothing moved Seneca to do this (as far as I can gather by conjecture) except that this emotion has more noise, allows for grand sententious maxims, and is much more suitable and abundant for showing off his talent than that other [Sophoclean] style. Even if we grant that Seneca achieved what he intended, should for that reason <term>decorum</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ πρέπον — the classical principle of "appropriateness" or "what is fitting" in art.</note> be despised? And yet that is the primary thing in every matter. Moreover, the poet must avoid this as the greatest vice—the one who sins even when he attributes a worthy speech to an unworthy person, or the speech of a wise man to a fool: much more so when he acts against art itself, and against...

and, if there is any truth in fictional fables—indeed, even against the nature of a holy woman, endowed with the most upright morals and most loving of her husband even when he sins—he attributes to her not just madness, but such wicked plans as would not be forgiven even in <term>Medea</term> <note>A mythological sorceress famous for murdering her own children to spite her husband, Jason; she represents the absolute extreme of female vengeance in tragedy.</note> herself. ->*Either follow tradition, or invent things consistent with themselves, O writer.*<- 
<note>original Latin: *Aut famam sequere, aut sibi convenientia finge Scriptor.* from Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note>

And what is less consistent with tradition—that is, the descriptions of the ancient poets—and what is less consistent with itself, than that he should bring onto the stage a Deianira who is first raving, and so mad that she contemplates the slaughter of her husband, and then suddenly, with the help of a verse or two, transitions to the arts of love and magic potions? What does Horace say to this?

->*I shall bid the learned imitator to look upon the model of life and character, and from there draw forth true voices.*<- 
<note>original Latin: *Respicere exemplar vitæ, morumque jubebo Doctum imitatorem, & veras hinc ducere voces.*</note>

For those <term>verses poor in substance and melodious trifles</term> <note>original Latin: *versus inopes rerum, nugæque canoræ* — a phrase used to describe poetry that sounds beautiful but lacks intellectual or emotional depth.</note> could not greatly delight him.

The other sin, no less grave, is that although a double example of silent, wordless grief existed in Sophocles that he could have followed, Seneca nevertheless attributes to Deianira such a long and inept speech: in which she openly declares that she will do violence to herself, and only then hurries inside and kills herself; as if her son, to whom she speaks and who is already trying to comfort his mother and call her back from this monstrous purpose, would have been unable to prevent it. But he also introduces her as raving once more, now from repentance, just as before she raved from <term>jealousy</term> <note>original Latin: *Zelotypia*.</note>. Indeed, there occur...

# CHANCE REMARKS

<page-num>115</page-num>

<header>CHANCE REMARKS</header>

There are so many things that should not escape notice that I am overwhelmed by their very number. Therefore, I shall not say a word about the childish laments of Hercules, nor about his most absurd apparition; instead, I shall return to that first speech of the raving Deianira, and I will examine it—and several other things of the same stamp—somewhat more accurately. How much <term>swelling</term> <note>original Latin: *tumor*. In classical rhetoric, "tumor" refers to a "swollen" or "puffy" style—bombastic language that lacks substance or genuine emotion.</note> is there immediately?

> *Whatever part of the heavenly seat you occupy,*
> *Wife of the Thunderer* <note>original Latin: *Conjux Tonantis*. A reference to Juno, the queen of the gods and wife of Jupiter (the "Thunderer"), who was the eternal enemy of Hercules.</note>

And how inept is what follows?

> ------- *send against Hercules a beast*
> *Which might be enough for me.* <note>original Latin: *mitte in Alcidem feram / Quae mihi satis sit.* "Alcides" is a common epithet for Hercules, referring to his grandfather Alceus.</note>

How rotten are the remaining parts?

> ------- *if any Serpent, vaster than the whole marsh,*
> *moves its fertile head,*
> *ignorant of being conquered:* <note>original Latin: *si qua foecundum caput / Palude tota vastior Serpens movet / Ignara vinci*. This refers to the Hydra of Lerna, which grew two heads for every one cut off.</note>

Even this empty swelling of epithets was not enough. Therefore:

> ------- *if anything has surpassed the wild beasts.*
> *Monstrous, dreadful, horrible—at the sight of which Hercules*
> *would turn away his eyes—let it emerge from this immense fold.*

From what "immense fold," I ask? From the raving Deianira's? <note>Tollius is mocking the ambiguity of the Latin word *sinus*, which can mean a "fold" in a garment, a "bosom," or a "womb." He suggests the playwright's phrasing implies the monster is literally coming out of Deianira's clothes or body.</note> Were such great monsters to be expected from there?

> *Or if beasts are denied, I pray, convert*
> *this soul into something: I could become any evil whatsoever*
> *with this mind.*

This is what <term>Longinus</term> <note>An ancient Greek literary critic, author of *On the Sublime*.</note> warned of elsewhere: *playing on mouth-pipes, indeed, but without a mouth-band.* <note>original Greek: <gloss>στοματικοῖς μὲν αὐλίσκοισι, φορβειᾶς δ’ ἄτερ</gloss>. This is a metaphor for a musician (or writer) who "blows" too hard without the leather strap (*phorbeia*) used by flute players to control their breath, resulting in uncontrolled, harsh noise rather than music.</note> But the tone is not consistent everywhere. And so it immediately fails, and...

...from that, *if anything exceeded the beasts, etc., it falls into something else, and any evil*, which soon follows:

> —— Provide me an image
> Equal to my grief; my breast cannot contain [merely] threats,

nay, nor even true sublimity.

> Why do you shake the depths of the farthest earth
> And turn the world upside down? Why do you ask Dis <note>The god of the underworld, also known as Pluto.</note> for evils?
> You will find within this breast all the beasts
> That he feared.

I seem to hear Longinus <note>A Greek philosopher and literary critic, famous for his treatise *On the Sublime*.</note> whispering: *these things are not sublime, but merely bombastic* <note>original Greek: οὐχ ὑψηλὰ ταῦτα, ἀλλὰ μετέωρα. Longinus used the word "meteōra" (aloft) to describe writing that tries too hard to be grand but ends up being puffy and hollow.</note>. But what other place is there for talent, what place for that little maxim?

> —— Why do you ask Dis for evils?

Should not that most celebrated Virgilian sentence have been imitated? *If I cannot bend the gods above, I will move the underworld.* <note>original Latin: *Flectere si nequeo superos, acheronta movebo*. One of the most famous lines from Virgil's *Aeneid* (VII.312), spoken by Juno.</note> He proceeds:

> —— Take up this weapon for your hatred.

But this weapon here is weak. Yet with how many threats shall it be compensated!

> I am a stepmother: you can destroy Hercules! <note>original Latin: Alcidem. Hercules was often called Alcides after his grandfather, Alceus.</note>
> Stretch forth your hands anywhere. Why do you hesitate, Goddess?
> Use me in my madness. What crime do you command to be done?
> Find it. Why do you pause? Even you may now cease;
> This rage is enough.

What says Longinus again? Many, he says, *who think themselves to be in a divine frenzy in many ways, are not truly inspired, but are merely playing.* <note>original Greek: πολλαχῇ ἐνθουσιᾷν ἑαυτοῖς δοκοῦντες, οὐ βακχεύουσιν, ἀλλὰ παίζουσιν. Tollius is accusing the playwright of "faking" a poetic trance or "Bacchic" frenzy.</note> Moreover, this very thing will appear much more in the other madness of the dying Deianira, where that *vision* <note>original Greek: φαντασίαν (*phantasia*). In classical rhetoric, this refers to a mental image so vivid that the speaker seems to see it before their eyes.</note> of the Furies must be compared with that of Euripides, of which Longinus speaks in chapter 15. Lest anyone should think there is nothing of good in these lines; those [words] might not even be unworthy of a Sophoclean Deianira:

<header>RANDOM THOUGHTS</header>

<sig>H 3</sig>

> "Shall a captive girl give brothers from the Sun <note>original Latin: *Sole*. This refers to the lineage of Iole, the daughter of Eurytus, who was said to be descended from the Sun god.</note>
> To my children? And shall she, once a slave, become Jove's daughter-in-law?"

Here you have an indignation expressed that is quite suitable for even the most noble matron. Even Sara might prove this point from the Sacred Scriptures; when her son Isaac was born, she spurned Ishmael, who was born of a slave-woman, for she could not endure that he should be the heir to his father’s fortunes. But again, what follows is not so good:

> "Shall flame and torrent run their courses together?
> And shall the dry Bear <note>The "dry Bear" refers to the constellation Ursa Major, which, in the northern hemisphere, appears to never "bathe" or set below the horizon into the sea.</note> drink of the blue sea?"

To say nothing of the first line—what? Were the women of that time so skilled in astronomy? Even when they were in a mad rage? Why did she not also refresh Juno's memory of Calypso, so that Juno might conspire more excitedly with her for the destruction of Hercules? But let these points suffice, although there are many more things here that deserve a censor's mark. Truly, <term>nothing in excess</term> <note>original Greek: μηδὲν ἄγαν (*mēden agan*). One of the famous maxims inscribed at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, advising moderation.</note>. This must be repeated now and many times elsewhere: these critiques do not proceed from any malice or a desire to attack the faults of others, but from a love of helping the "Republic of Letters" <note>A term for the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note>. Truly, the many other parts adapted from the Greek writer <note>Tollius refers to Sophocles, whose play *The Women of Trachis* served as the source for this story.</note>—such as Deianira’s narration about the gift and death of Nessus, the sad premonition of treachery after the robe was sent, the speech of Hyllus, and other things of that kind—certainly deserve the same care of comparison, but that is a task any reader can now easily perform for themselves.

> *“To the lands, the sea, the stars, the Ocean, the underworld.*
> *Flee beyond the labors of Alcides <note>original Latin: *Alcidae*. A patronymic name for Hercules, referring to his grandfather Alceus.</note>, mother.”*
> and immediately after: *“Rule, triumph, seek the temples of Juno.”*

> *“That glory of the world, etc.”*

“O *mother*,” he said, “he is gone.” He ought not to have called her “mother,” especially with that particle *“O,”* which indicates a certain filial affection. Such a feeling should not be present—or certainly should not be expressed—in the midst of such anger and indignation. How much better is Sophocles, who shows pure rage in the same exclamation?

> <note>original Greek: ὦ μῆτερ, ὡς ἂν ἐκ τριῶν σ’ ἓν εἱλόμην... from Sophocles' *The Women of Trachis*.</note>
> *“O mother, how I wish I could choose one of three things for you:*
> *either that you were no longer living, or that if you stayed alive*
> *you were called the mother of another, or that you could somehow*
> *exchange your current mind for a better one.”*

How does this happen? I will tell you. In Sophocles, this is Hyllus’s first address to her, and as the situation required, it is full of a son’s indignation and loathing toward a mother he believes to be so wicked. Thus, after she leaves, he adds:

> <note>original Greek: Οὔκουν γ’ ἄλλως ὀνόμαθ’ τί δεῖ τρέφειν...</note>
> *“Why then should I cherish the name of ‘Mother,’*
> *for one who acts in no way like the mother who bore me?”*

In the Latin play, however, that word is placed there after the anger has supposedly been poured out, yet such rage should not be extinguished so quickly, as if the stinger were lost after the first strike. But there are more "sores" in that same passage which I do not wish to touch, as this is not the place for it.

### Examples of Childish Sayings.

Hercules, in Seneca's play:

> *“Among all others, he seeks and pursues Lichas alone.*
> *Clutching the altars with a trembling hand,*
> *he consumed his death through fear, and left little of himself*
> *for punishment. And while he [Hercules] held*
> *the trembling corpse in his hand, he said: ‘By this hand, by this one—*
> *O Fates!—shall I be called defeated? Lichas slays Hercules.*
> *Behold another disaster: Hercules slays Lichas.’”*
> <note>original Latin: from *Hercules Oetaeus*, lines 814–822. The scene describes Hercules, driven mad by the poisoned robe, murdering the innocent messenger Lichas.</note>

Who could refrain from tears when saying such things—though they be tears shaken out by excessive laughter? O Hercules, the Gauls once fashioned you as an Orator <note>A reference to "Hercules Ogmius," a Gallic version of the hero described by the author Lucian as an old man who draws crowds not by strength, but by the chains of eloquence attached to his tongue.</note>; here you become even a sophist <note>A teacher of rhetoric, often used pejoratively to mean one who uses clever but fallacious reasoning.</note>. O, what cleverness, worthy not only of Seneca but also of a "Philosopher Hercules"! 

If the nature of things and the logic of time had allowed Seneca to recite these lines to a living Hercules, what reward do you think he would have received for such a "beautiful" sentiment? Hercules would not have sent him—him whose *“torso falls into the deep like a trunk, while his neck does not hit the rocks; a funeral lies for both”* (which is itself a line of the same low quality)—he would not have sent the poet to other cities or an unknown world as Deianira wished, but into the middle of the Caspian snows, where they say the cold is most intense. Truly, since that brave Stoic *“consumed his death through fear with a trembling hand,”* let that *“trembling corpse”* be dismissed from our hands.

And let us move on to shaking our heads at the *Natural Questions* <note>Another work by Seneca the Younger, a scientific treatise on the natural world.</note>, where he asks: *“when the fatal...”*

...the fatal day of the flood has come, just as a great part of the earth is overwhelmed by the waves. This is Chapter 27 of Book 3 <note>Tollius is quoting Seneca the Younger's *Naturales Quaestiones* (Natural Questions), Book 3, Chapter 27, which describes the end of the world by water.</note>. Pay attention, Pamphilus! <note>A common address to a listener, likely borrowed from the character names in Roman comedies by Terence.</note> First, immoderate rains fall, and without any sun the sky is sad with clouds; and a continuous fog, and a thick darkness from the moisture, with winds never drying things out. > *“Why do you strip me from myself?” he says.*
> *“Ah, I regret it! Ah!” he shouted, “the flute is not worth this much!”*
> <note>original Latin: *Quid me mihi detrahis, inquit, / Ah piget! ah! non est, clamabat, tibia tanti.* In Greek mythology, the satyr Marsyas lost a musical contest to the god Apollo; his punishment was to be flayed alive. Tollius finds Ovid’s description of Marsyas making puns and complaining about the "price" of his flute while being skinned to be in very poor taste.</note>

It is a wonder that he did not also depict Marsyas playing the flute at that moment—so playful are the words of this man: *“why do you strip me from myself?”* The other verse is of such foolish simplicity it would be a joke if the matter were not serious. But in a serious matter, in such great pain, must we think that wretched Satyr was in the same frame of mind as that man who, while being roasted over a fire, told the judge he should be turned over, lest he be forced to eat half-burnt meat? <note>This is a reference to St. Lawrence, a 3rd-century Christian martyr who, according to legend, joked with his executioners while being grilled alive, saying, "I'm well done on this side. Turn me over!"</note>

Let Ovid’s account of the flood in *Metamorphoses* Book 1 be compared, and let the individual details be examined.

The same author [Ovid], at the end of the same Book, where he speaks of Boreas <note>The North Wind, personified as a god.</note>:

> *“While he flies,” he says, “the fires, being stirred, burned more strongly.”*
> <note>original Latin: *Dum volat, inquit, arserunt agitati fortius ignes.* Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, line 264.</note>

I am truly ashamed of such a rotten artifice. For that which belongs to the wind, insofar as it is wind, to attribute that same thing to Boreas—who is then depicted as a God, and affected by human emotions—is not the mark of a silly man, but of a madman. <note>Tollius is criticizing Ovid for mixing metaphors: treating Boreas as a literal wind that fans a fire while simultaneously treating him as a personified deity with a soul.</note>

He had read, if I am not mistaken, in Lucretius, Book 6:
> *It also happens that sometimes the force of the wind, sent without fire,*
> *nevertheless catches fire in space and by its long journey,*
> *while it comes, losing certain large bodies in its course*
> *which cannot penetrate the air in the same way:*
> *and gathering other very small ones from the air itself it carries them,*
> *which, mixed together, create fire by flying.*
> <note>original Latin: *Fit quoque, ut interdum venti vis missa sine igni / Ignescat tamen in spatio...* Tollius is quoting Lucretius’s *De Rerum Natura*, which attempts to explain natural phenomena like lightning and heat through the movement of atoms.</note>

But there was no place for these fires now; nor for that reason, while it flies, should Boreas <note>The North Wind</note> burn with greater flames, just as in Virgil, Book 5 of the *Aeneid*:

> *The flying arrow caught fire among the liquid clouds.*
> <note>original Latin: *Volans liquidis in nubibus arsit arundo.* This refers to a famous omen in the *Aeneid* where an arrow shot by Acestes catches fire in mid-air.</note>

Since the fires of love are very far removed from those other fires, lovers do not—through their movement—either lose certain large bodies or, in turn, scrape up other tiny ones from the air so that they may become more inflamed, and perish with a greater love for their pretty little girlfriends. <note>Tollius is mocking an unnamed author for using a scientific explanation of friction and atomic heat to describe the "heat" of romantic passion, which he finds ridiculous.</note>

### Regarding Chapter 29 of Longinus: On the Choice of Words.
<note>Longinus is the traditional name given to the author of *On the Sublime*, a Greek work of literary criticism that discusses how to achieve greatness in writing.</note>

"And it captivates the listeners." <note>original Greek: Καὶ κατακλεῖ τοὺς ἀκούοντας.</note> No one does this better, or more effectively, than Pindar. We shall examine one or two particles selected here and there from him, so that from these examples, students <term>tirones<gloss>literally "recruits" or "beginners" in Latin</gloss></term> may learn what they should follow in the art of composition. Let the first one taken in hand be the first strophe of the *Nemean Odes*:

> Hallowed breathing-place of Alpheus,
> Ortygia, offshoot of famous Syracuse,
> Couch of Artemis,
> Sister of Delos! From you the sweet-sounding
> hymn sets out to give...
> <note>original Greek: Ἄμπνευμα σεμνὸν Ἀλφεοῦ / Κλεινᾶν Συρακοσᾶν θάλος Ὀρτυγία... Pindar is addressing the island of Ortygia in Sicily, linking its mythology to the river-god Alpheus and the goddess Artemis.</note>

<page-num>122</page-num>

<header>OF JACOBUS TOLLIUS</header>
<meta>catchword: more fittingly</meta>

->Great praise of storm-footed horses,<-
->a gift for Aetnaean Zeus.<-
<note>original Greek: "Αἶνον ἀελλοπόδων μέγαν ἵππων, Ζηνὸς Αἰτναίου χάριν." These are lines from Pindar's *First Nemean Ode*, celebrating a chariot race victory.</note>

We shall examine almost every single word, so that from this example it may be understood with what judgment they must be selected by those composing such works. He says *ampneuma* <note>original: *ἄμπνευμα*, meaning a breathing-place or respite</note>. This is a melodious word because of the two most excellent vowels it contains at the beginning and the end. Furthermore, the very conjunction of three consonants that are difficult to pronounce creates a grander sound through the delay of time it requires; this is something Longinus also observed regarding a verse by Euripides in his chapter *On the Composition of Words* (chapter 38). To this we add that *ampneuma* is a magnificent term for the river Alpheus, as it attributes "breathing" to it as if it were a living thing—an elegant metaphor indeed for a river that finally bursts forth after a long course beneath the sea, as if exhausted. It is just like horses who, after a long run, finally catch their breath once they are allowed to rest. Moreover, Chromius—for whom Pindar sings this *victory ode* <note>term: *ἐπινίκιον* (epinikion), a song celebrating a victory in the Greek games</note>—had won with a four-horse chariot. Thus, no more fitting metaphor could have been devised. As for the word *semnon* <note>original: *σεμνὸν*, meaning august, holy, or stately</note>, nothing can be given that is weightier than its own gravity. Here, too, are noble vowels, especially the final one, which is full of dignity.

The name *Alpheus* <note>original: *Ἀλφεοῦ*</note> returns in this magnificent composition with the resonance of its first vowel. But here we should observe the elegance and grandeur of the *circumlocution* <note>term: *τῆς περιφράσεως* (periphrasis), the use of indirect or descriptive speech</note>, as well as the splendor of the epithets for the island of *Ortygia*. First, the "breathing-place" (*ampneuma*) is not merely simple, but *august* (*semnon*), specifically because of the virginity of Arethusa <note>A reference to the myth where the nymph Arethusa was transformed into a fountain in Ortygia to escape the river god Alpheus; Tollius suggests the site is "holy" because of her chastity</note>. Nor is it the breathing-place of just any common river, but of the *Alpheus*, famous for the Olympic games. There is a second point.

Replace the word *kleinān* <note>original: *Κλεινᾶν*, meaning famous or renowned</note> with *klytān* <note>original: *κλυτᾶν*, a synonym</note>, which conveys the same meaning, and consult your own ears. Therefore, I shall not add another word regarding the sound. But it is also more fittingly...

<summary>Tollius performs a technical analysis of Pindar’s poetry, focusing on how specific Greek words like "ampneuma" and "semnon" use phonetics and mythology to create a sense of grandeur. He highlights the metaphor of the river Alpheus "breathing" as a masterful link to the athlete Chromius’s chariot victory.</summary>

<header>CHANCE REMARKS.</header>

No more fitting epithet could be given to Syracuse. Regarding this, Cicero says: *“You have often heard that the city of Syracuse is the largest of the Greek cities, and the most beautiful of them all.”* <note>original Latin: "Urbem syracusas maximam esse Graecarum urbium, pulcherrimamque omnium saepe audistis." This is from Cicero's speeches against the corrupt governor Verres.</note>

*Bloom* <note>original Greek: Θάλος (Thalos), meaning a young branch, scion, or offshoot</note>, used in a most pleasant sense. Demetrius Phalereus observes somewhere that Sappho was a wonderful artist at selecting charming, elegant, and pleasant subject matter, and even more so at handling it with much more brilliant vocabulary. *“There are,”* he says, *“graces found in the subject matter, such as gardens of the nymphs, wedding songs, and loves—indeed, the whole of Sappho’s poetry. For such things, even if spoken of by Hipponax* <note>Hipponax was a poet known for his harsh, ugly satire; the point is that some subjects are so beautiful they shine even in the hands of a crude poet</note>, *are graceful, and the matter is cheerful in and of itself,”* etc. *“Thus, while there is a certain grace in the subject matter, there are also things that the wording itself makes more charming. For example: 'As when the daughter of Pandareus, the greenwood nightingale, sings beautifully when spring has newly begun.' Here, the nightingale is already a graceful little bird, and spring is naturally graceful, but it is much more adorned by the interpretation. Certain elements are even more charming, such as the word 'greenwood'* <note>original Greek: χλωρηὶς (chlorēis), suggesting the fresh green of spring</note> *and calling the bird the 'daughter of Pandareus,' which are the poet's own inventions.”* Pindar therefore calls Ortygia a *bloom*; by this word, the pleasantness of springtime is recalled to our memory and almost placed before our eyes. It is likewise a distinguished metaphor.

*Ortygia*, about which Virgil wrote:
> An island lies stretched out before the Sicanian bay,
> facing wave-beaten Plemmyrium; the ancients called its name
> Ortygia. Fame tells that Alpheus, the river of Elis,
> forced secret paths here beneath the sea; and now,
> O Arethusa, it mingles with the Sicilian waves at your mouth.
<note>This passage from the *Aeneid* (Book 3) describes the legend of the river Alpheus, which was said to flow from Greece under the Ionian Sea to emerge in the fountain of Arethusa on the island of Ortygia in Syracuse.</note>

At this point, it occurs to me as especially worth observing that the divine poet [Pindar], when he was about to praise Chromius of Aetna as a victor—though in the Nemean games—did not begin his song with the fires of Mount Aetna...

...to have begun <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page, likely referring to Pindar beginning his poem.</note> both because the status of this victor was lower in majesty than the other, and because this contest <note>The Nemean Games</note> was not as noble as the Olympic or Pythian, since those two *belong to the gods, while this is a festival of men*, as my favorite author Ausonius says. Therefore, in the case of Hiero—who was both a king and a winner at the Olympics and the Pythian games—Pindar used a loftier subject and style. In the case of this man <note>Chromius, the victor celebrated in the First Nemean Ode</note>, who was a private citizen (noble, yes, but less renowned than those others), Pindar sought a certain charm, though still mixed with much gravity and brilliance. Compare, if you like, the first odes of both the Olympian and Pythian series, or perhaps more pleasingly, the second Pythian, which begins like this:

> O great-citied Syracuse <note>original Greek: Μεγαλοπόλιες (Megalopolies)</note>,
> sacred precinct of Ares deep-in-war,
> divine nurse of men
> and of horses who rejoice in iron!
> To you I come, bringing from shimmering Thebes
> this song, news of a chariot-race that shakes the earth.
> In which Hiero, victorious with his fine chariot,
> has crowned Ortygia with far-shining wreaths,
> Ortygia, the seat of Artemis of the River, etc.

You see how he uses *great-citied*, where in this current ode he uses *renowned* <note>original Greek: κλεινᾶν (kleinan)</note>; and to pass over other such examples, he calls the place a "seat" <note>original Greek: ἕδος (edos)</note> there, which is somewhat more solemn, whereas here he has said "resting-place" <note>original Greek: δέμνιον (demnion)</note>. In my judgment, he does this out of a desire to be *more charming* <note>original Greek: χαριεστέρᾳ (chariestera)</note>, though both terms are honorable and splendid.

*Sister of Delos* <note>original Greek: Δάλου κασιγνήτα (Dalou kasigneta). Ortygia was often called the sister of the island of Delos because both were associated with the goddess Artemis.</note>: again, a most sweet and beautiful metaphor, drawn from the tenderest bond of human kinship—*Sister of Delos*—and

<summary>Jacobus Tollius analyzes Pindar's shift in poetic register, noting that the poet uses more "charming" and intimate language for private citizens while reserving "solemn" and majestic terms for kings like Hiero of Syracuse.</summary>

# FORTUITA

...because both are sacred to Artemis, and because Delos was also once called Ortygia.

**Sweet-speaking** <note>original Greek: Ἁδυεπὴς (haduepēs)</note>, do you see how all these words bloom with charm and grace? What more elegant epithet could have been fashioned for this passage? He says, "a **sweet-speaking** hymn." Indeed, in that 11th Pythian Ode which we mentioned, he wrote: *he finished a sweet-sounding song for kings* <note>original Greek: εὐαχέα βασιλεῦσιν ὕτελευσεν (euachea basileusin uteleusen)</note>. What of it? Do you think he chose these words without care? Without judgment? Consider also the 1st Olympian Ode: *a hymn of many voices is cast around the thoughts of wise men, to shout aloud the son of Kronos* <note>original Greek: πολύφατος ὕμνος ἀμφιβάλλεται σοφῶν μητίεσι, κελαδεῖν Κρονόπαιδα</note>. And in the 11th Olympian <note>Tollius likely means the 2nd Olympian Ode</note>, **hymns, lords of the lyre** <note>original Greek: ἀναξιφόρμιγγες ὕμνοι (anaxiphorminges hymnoi)</note> are invoked to sing the praises of gods, heroes, and men. I do not believe for a moment that the poet used these contrasts at random. Do I believe it? "Let the Jew Apella believe it," not I <note>original: "credat Judæus Apellas"; a reference to Horace’s Satires, used to express skepticism or that only the gullible would believe something</note>.

**Of the starts** <note>original Greek: Ὁρμάτων (hormaton)</note>: this word is also full of efficacy, and very fitting for the rush of horses charging forward. Their **impulse** <note>original Greek: ὁρμὴ (hormē)</note>, or rather their "aroused fire," is elegantly expressed by Virgil:

> Not so headlong in the two-horse contest do the chariots
> Seize the plain and rush forth, poured out from the starting-gate.
> <note>Quoting Virgil, Aeneid V.144–145</note>

**On the foundation** <note>original Greek: Θεμέλῳ (themelo)</note>: used to suggest something stable and grand.

**Praise** <note>original Greek: αἶνον (ainon)</note>: this is also most appropriate, derived from the word **to delight** <note>original Greek: ἰαίνω (iaino)</note>, because it delights the mind and affects it with pleasure; for it is the **sweetest sound to a man** <note>original Greek: ἥδιστον ἀκούσμα (hediston akousma)</note>, as Xenophon says, and as we have shown at greater length in our commentary on Cicero’s *Pro Archia*.

**Storm-footed** <note>original Greek: Ἀελλοπόδων (aellopodon)</note>: A magnificent epithet, drawing a comparison from rapid storms, and also in its composition, which possesses a certain **stateliness** <note>original Greek: ὄγκον (onkon)</note>.

**Great** <note>original Greek: Μέγαν (megan)</note>: this word, placed after such high-sounding vocabulary, wonderfully elevates and raises the sentiment.

**For the sake of Aetnaean Zeus** <note>original Greek: Ζηνὸς Αἰτναίου χάριν (Zenos Aitnaiou charin)</note>: a phrase at once sublime and alluring...

Having previously discussed the specific epithets Pindar uses for hymns and the movement of horses, Tollius now transitions into the power of poetic language itself, using the literary critic Longinus to support his argument that Pindar's word choices provide a "majesty" and "strength" that physical objects alone cannot possess. # JACOBUS TOLLIUS

<margin>hymn</margin> For Chromius was of Etna, and **victory lies on the knees of the gods** <note>original Greek: Διὸς ἐν γούνασι κεῖται (Dios en gounasi keitai); a Homeric idiom meaning the outcome is yet to be decided by divine will</note>.

You see therefore, reader, the truth of what Longinus affirmed: that **nothing remains of physical bodies—whether selection, grandeur, beauty, clarity, weight, strength, power, or any other quality—that words do not provide** <note>original Greek: μηδὲν λοιπὸν τῶν σωμάτων ἐκλογὴν μέγεθος, κάλλος, σαφήνειαν, βάρος, ἰσχὺν, κράτος, ἄλλα δὲ εἴ τιν, τοῖς λόγοις παρασκευάζειν. Tollius is citing Longinus’s famous treatise "On the Sublime," which argues that great writing reflects a great soul and elevates the listener</note>. If you do not believe it, pay attention to this noble sentiment from the 6th Isthmian Ode:

> For if any man, rejoicing in expense
> And in labor, achieves god-built virtues,
> And the divinity plants for him
> Lovely glory, already at the furthest reaches
> Of bliss he casts his anchor,
> Being honored by God.

Are not all these words select, beautiful, magnificent, and sonorous? Does it not, as Longinus says, **bring forth noble living things and charm the listeners** <note>original Greek: γενναῖα προσάγει ζῶτα, καὶ κατακηλεῖ τοὺς ἀκούοντας</note>? One observes in these lines such distinguished marks as **rejoicing** <note>original: χαρεὶς (chareis)</note>, **god-built** <note>original: θεοδμάτους (theodmatous)</note>, **plants** <note>original: φυτεύει (phyteuei)</note>, **lovely** <note>original: ἐπήρατον (eperaton)</note>, **casts anchor** <note>original: βάλλετ’ ἄγκυραν (ballet’ agkyran)</note>, and **honored by God** <note>original: θεότιμος (theotimos)</note>. Even the word **being** <note>original: ὢν (ōn)</note>, which might seem contemptible at first glance, possesses a notable charm here. In this instance, the accent concurring with the length of the final syllable creates a most excellent poetic rhythm. You will only truly understand this if you try to read the phrase with a single syllable removed, as "honored by God [is]" <note>original: θεότιμος ὢν</note>, an example that very opportunely illustrates chapter 37 of our Longinus’s work *On Composition*. But what I shall now serve you will be pure nectar, or if you prefer, **the milk of Zeus** <note>original Greek: Διὸς γάλα (Dios gala); a metaphorical term for something divinely sweet or nourishing</note>.

**Kindly** <note>original: Φιλόφρον (Philophron)</note>, he says in the 8th Pythian Ode, **Peace, daughter of Justice, you who make cities great,**

> Daughter, who of counsels and of wars
> Holds the supreme
> Keys, [receive] the Pythian victory
> Honor for Aristomenes.

### C A P. XV.

#### *On the Chemical Matters concerning the Horses of Neptune.*

<margin>
Book 1.
Interpretation of Dreams
Ch. 58.
</margin>
If ever by chance a rose appears among sharp thorns, its sight is all the more pleasing because it is rare and unexpected. This very thing happened to me, with great pleasure, as I found a little flower—both beautiful to look upon and sweet to smell—among the thorny dreams of Artemidorus <note>Artemidorus Daldianus was a 2nd-century professional diviner who wrote the *Oneirocritica*, a manual on dream interpretation</note>. **To ride a racehorse**—he says—**that is well-obedient to the rein, and also carries its rider, is equally good for all.** For a horse **has the same relationship to a woman and a beloved** because it takes great pride in beauty and carries its rider; **in the same way, it also relates to a ship.** Indeed, even the Poet <note>Homer</note> called ships **horses**, and we call Neptune **Lord of Horses** <note>original Greek: ἵππον... κέλητα ἐλαύνειν καλῶς πειθόμενον τῷ ῥυτῆρι... (hippon... keleta elaunein kalos peithomenon to rheuteri...). Artemidorus, *Oneirocritica* 1.58.</note>. I could have offered much from both sacred and profane writers regarding the comparison of women with horses, and from those, I could have discussed the very name of the horse, which shares certain similarities with that part of the female body that makes them women; however, because my purpose is now different, I shall bring forward only one passage of Aeschylus, because it requires a medical hand <note>In philology, a "medical hand" refers to the correction or "healing" of a corrupted text</note>.

Correct this to: *I knew these things*, etc. <note>Tollius is correcting the Greek text from "Having" (Ἔχων) to "I knew" (Ἔγνων)</note> I will also add the deed of Hippomenes, a prince of the Athenians, memorable for its cruelty; he shut up his daughter, who had allowed herself to be corrupted, in a house together with a horse, and having denied food to both, delivered her to be torn apart by it. And so I return to where I left off, namely to the explanation of the epithet which Artemidorus <note>The 2nd-century dream-interpreter mentioned on the previous page</note> teaches us was attributed to Neptune, in such a way that he even supplies an investigation of the cause. For in this matter the Ancients did not look to lust, but to nature. We have said elsewhere that Ocean was considered the father of things. Hence Neptune is given not only the title **Equestrian** <note>original Latin: *Equestris*; Greek: ἱππίῳ (hippiō)</note>, but also **Phytalmios** <note>original Greek: φυταλμίῳ (phytalmiō), meaning 'nurturing' or 'generative'</note>, that is, the **generative power of living offspring** <note>original Greek: ζωογόνῳ γεννήματι (zōogonō gennēmati)</note>; this same title was also given to Jupiter by Aeschylus. The horses of Neptune, **greatly prideful and exulting in their beauty** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ κάλλει μεγαφρονεῦντες καὶ γαυριῶντες</note>, are **volatile alkali spirits**; nothing is more beautiful than these. Of each of them you might say what is read in the third book of Virgil’s *Georgics*:

> — *If by chance the sound of arms is heard from afar,*
> *He cannot stand still; his ears quiver, his limbs tremble,*
> *And pressing back the collected fire, he rolls it beneath his nostrils.*
> *Such also was Saturn himself, when at the arrival of his wife*
> *He poured out a horse's mane from his neck, swift as ever,*
> *And fleeing, filled high Pelion with a sharp neighing.*

Here, if anyone pays attention to the etymology of **Pelion**, or of the fleeing Saturn himself, and of the **Oceanid Philyra** <note>A nymph, daughter of Oceanus, whom Saturn loved while in the form of a horse</note>, and understands that "sharp neighing," he will easily unlock the inner sanctums of **Chemistry** <note>original Latin: *Chemiæ*; Tollius uses this term to mean alchemy or the secret science of matter</note>, and see what this horse desired to beget for himself. Nor should anyone wonder at Saturn appearing in place of Neptune...

I have substituted Saturn for Neptune based on Virgil: the same story and the same deed are attributed to Neptune and Ceres. For Neptune, captured by love for her when she had turned herself into a mare to hide from him, likewise took the form of a horse. From her, he sired a daughter, Hera, and the horse **Arion** <note>original: *Ariona*</note>, as if from the word **more excellent** <note>original Greek: ἀρείωνα (*areiona*)</note>, signifying a son more excellent than himself. It is said that Ceres, most angry and as if in a frenzy, initially took this union very badly; but later, having been appeased, she washed herself in the river Ladon. From this, she received the surnames **The Fury** <note>original Greek: Ἐριννύς (*Erinnyes*)</note> and **The Deliverer** <note>original Greek: Λυσιάς (*Lysias*), which can also mean "the washer" or "one who loosens"</note>. To Neptune was given the title **Equestrian** <note>original Greek: ἱππίῳ (*hippiō*)</note>, as recorded by Pausanias in the *Arcadics* <note>Pausanias was a 2nd-century travel writer; "Arcadics" refers to his book on the region of Arcadia</note>. Those lines by the Prince of Poets <note>Homer</note> concerning Neptune are distinguished:

> He drove over the waves, and the sea-beasts gambolled beneath him
> From all their hidden depths; nor were they ignorant of their lord.
> In joy the sea parted, and they flew forward.

These are the lines I once translated thus:

> — He through the waves
> Proceeds, driving his chariot. The whales of the deep leave
> Their inner chambers, and leap around their master in a gathered line.
> The sea, swollen with joy, parts its waters:
> And with the rush of winged horses, the axle flies swiftly.

It is necessary for one to believe that this is no vain poetic fiction, but a most hidden <term>secret of nature<note>original: *arcanum*, a term used by alchemists to describe the fundamental, hidden laws or substances of the natural world</note></term>, so that one may understand the **Keys of Basil Valentine** <note>Basil Valentine was a legendary alchemist, likely a pseudonym, whose "Twelve Keys" are a series of influential alchemical allegories</note>. A certain image appears in every distillation, but it appears much more clearly in the preparation of the **Starred Regulus** <term>Regulus stellatus<note>When the metal antimony is purified in a specific way, it cools into a crystalline structure resembling a star; alchemists saw this as a sign of planetary or celestial influence</note></term>, about which we shall speak more broadly later. 

But now, for the sake of the mind’s pleasure, we shall propose a few small questions from ancient fables, the solution of which is not too difficult:

II. Why was Neptune’s horse first seen on the highest mountain, and why are Centaurs <note>Mythological creatures with the upper body of a human and the lower body of a horse</note> said to inhabit the mountains?

VI. From where did Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> get the surnames **tamer of horses** <term>ἱπποδαμεία (hippodameia)</term> and **Equestrian**?

VIII. Why was Chiron, the son of Saturn and Philyra, a centaur and a physician? <note>Chiron was the wise tutor of many Greek heroes.</note>

IX. Why is Pegasus, the son of Neptune, winged, and why did Bellerophon defeat the Chimera with his help? And what is the origin of Hippocrene, the **fountain of the Muses**? <note>Hippocrene literally means "horse's fountain"; it was said to have been created by the strike of Pegasus's hoof.</note>

**These things** <note>original Greek: Ταῦτα (tauta)</note> we shall pray for Apollo, the **Leader of the Muses** <term>Μουσαγέτην (Musagetēn)</term>, with his golden four-horse chariot, to assist us—provided the Muses, being winged, desire a **melodious** <term>μεθώδῃ (methōdē)</term> path—while in the meantime the impulse of my mind carries me elsewhere.

### CHAPTER VI.

### *On the Salutation Formula "Peace be with you."*

While I was living among the Turks, I frequently heard from them the greeting *Salemnalik* <note>original: "Salemnalik," a phonetic rendering of the Arabic *Salam alayka*</note> when individuals met one another; or *Salemnalikom* <note>original: "Salemnalikom," the plural *Salam alaykum*</note> if there were several people. Since I was not indifferent to such matters, I began to ask my interpreter what those words meant. When I understood they meant, "Peace be with you" <note>Latin: *Pax tecum* or *vobiscum*</note>, I was greatly amazed that such an ancient custom had not been abolished by any migrations among the barbarians or by any changes of time. Even now, that salutation formula, which was used in the East since the most ancient times, has been transmitted intact and secure <note>Tollius uses the Latin legal idiom "sartam tutam," meaning well-patched and safe</note> to the Arabs first, and then from them to the Africans. 

<margin>
Genesis 43.
Judges 6 & 19.
<note>Tollius cites these Biblical chapters as they contain early examples of the "Peace be with you" greeting in a Semitic context.</note>
</margin>

Nor would that little observation have seemed worthy to me to hold a place in these *Chance Thoughts*, had I not come across a poem in the *Greek Anthology* in which almost the same salutation formula occurs, except that the latter pertains to the dead, while the former pertains to the living. I will set down the whole poem as it is read in Book III, in the section "To anonymous poets" <note>Tollius is referring to a famous epigram by Meleager of Gadara, though he attributes it here to an anonymous source.</note>:

> Step softly, O stranger, for among the pious the old man
> Sleeps, having fallen into the sleep that is owed to all.
> This is Meleager, son of Eucrates, who joined sweet-teared love
> And the Muses with cheerful Graces.
> Whom Tyre, daughter of the gods, and the sacred land of Gadara made a man,
> And lovely Cos, land of the Meropes, nurtured in his old age.
> But if you are a Syrian, say *Salam* <note>original: "Σαλάμ" (Salam), the Semitic word for Peace</note>; or if you are a Phoenician...

There is also another custom among the same Turks retained from antiquity, by which the *Morabaudi* <note>A Latinization of "Marabout," referring to Muslim religious leaders or holy men</note>, or leaders, pray for peace for the people during the sacred rites, which they call *Sala* <note>Likely referring to the *Salat* (prayer) or the *Salawat* (blessings)</note>. The poem goes as follows:

<margin>Book II. *To the witty.*</margin>
> "Peace to all," the Bishop said, entering.
> How can he give to all that which he alone has at home?
<note>This is a joke based on the Greek name *Eirene* (Irene), which means "Peace." The Bishop wishes "peace" to his congregation, but the poet jokes he is keeping his "Peace" (his mistress) to himself.</note>

->we translate this playfully:<-

> *Lately, "Peace to all," the Bishop said, entering,*
> *How can it be for all, which he alone has for himself?*

This formula of greeting is frequent in the sacred books, such as 2 Kings 18:28; Matthew 10:12, 13; Luke 10:5 and 24:36, and elsewhere. It was subsequently used by Christians with the "holy kiss," as is evident from Justin Martyr, Tertullian, Origen, and others. For it follows by antithesis: *but the name of the wicked shall perish*: that is, his memory shall be blotted out.
