### CHAPTER XVII.

### *Several Emendations to Cicero's Paradoxes.*

Recently, while comparing the *Paradoxes* of Cicero <note>The *Paradoxa Stoicorum*, a work where Marcus Tullius Cicero explains six Stoic ethical principles that seem counter-intuitive (paradoxical) to the general public</note> with a manuscript from our public library, I encountered several points—not so much remarkable as they are unworthy of being passed over in silence. I decided to include them in this single chapter, as they are not very numerous. In the preface to Brutus, the common reading is: *Indeed, I have playfully cast into commonplaces those very things which the Stoics themselves barely prove in the gymnasiums and at leisure.* <note>original Latin: "Ego vero illa ipsa, quæ vix in gymnasiis & in otio Stoici probant ludens conjeci in communeis locos."</note> In our book, it was: *I [send] you those very things...* <note>original Latin: "Ego tibi illa ipsa"</note> which is not inelegant; it certainly follows the custom of the ancients, who often insert "to you," "to me," or "to himself" into speech for emphasis, as many have already noted. There follows immediately: *Because these things are admirable and contrary to everyone's opinion, they are even called "paradoxes" by the Stoics themselves; I wanted to try whether they could be brought into the light.* <note>original Latin: "Quæ quia sunt admirabilia, contraque opinionem omnium, ab ipsis etiam παράδοξα appellantur; tentare volui, possentne proferri in lucem."</note> Insert a conjunction <note>copula</note> as the manuscript suggests, and read: *and they are even called "paradoxes" by them.* <note>original: "and ab ipsis etiam παράδοξα [paradoxa] appellantur"</note> In this way, the sentence will be tightened and connected, whereas otherwise it is loose and disjointed. The Greek title of the first Paradox, with the words transposed, is rendered this way in our book:

->That only what is morally noble is good<- <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι μόνον τὸ καλὸν ἀγαθόν"</note>

In the first Paradox, the common reading is: *What force held Cocles alone on the bridge against all the enemy forces? What force devoted the father Decius, and what force devoted the son and sent them against the armed forces of the enemy?* <note>original: "Quæ vis Coclitem contra omnis hostium copias tenuit in ponte solum? quæ patrem Decium, quæ filium devotavit, atque immisit in armatas hostium copias?" Horatius Cocles and the Decii were legendary Roman heroes famous for their self-sacrifice in battle.</note> In our manuscript, it is: *what force called down the son.* <note>original: "quæ filium devocavit"</note> That is: it demanded and summoned them to sacrifice themselves and hurl themselves at the enemy.

In the second Paradox: *Fear of judgments and laws paralyses you; wherever you look, your injustices encounter you like Furies; they do not allow you to breathe in*

He highlights specific linguistic nuances, such as the use of the ethical dative and the correction of "devoted" to "called down" in the context of Roman heroism.</summary>

in our manuscript, the word is not poorly read as *to sigh for* <note>original Latin: *suspirare*</note>, which is an elegant word in this sense, and less common, and thus more liable to corruption by later scribes.

In the third Paradox: *For sins are not to be measured by the outcome of things, but by the vices of men.* <note>Cicero’s third paradox argues that all "sins" or moral failings are equal because they all represent a deviation from the single line of "Right."</note> Our manuscript had *by the outcomes of things* <note>original: *rerum eventis*, plural</note>. This is more in the style of Cicero, though the common reading can be defended by this verse from Ovid:

> *The result justifies the deeds: I pray that he may lack success,*
> *Whoever thinks that actions should be judged by their outcome.* <note>From Ovid’s *Heroides*, II.85–86</note>

In the same place: *Since to sin is, as it were, to leap over the lines.* Read with our manuscript, *as it were to cross over* <note>original: *tamquam transire*</note>, as the same verb is repeated twice immediately after. Although that other reading <note>to "leap over" or *transilire*</note> is not bad either. Thus in Plato: <margin>In the *Cratylus*.</margin> *to question with too wide a circuit, and to leap beyond the boundaries.* <note>original Greek: μακροτέρᾳ τῇ περιθήκῃ ἐρωτᾷν, καὶ ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα ἅλλεσθαι. The "boundaries" or *eskanmena* were the dug-out lines in a gymnasium marking the limits for jumpers.</note> Again, by the same author in the same book: *But why do you watch me as if I were being carried outside the track?* <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ὁ γὰ ἐπισκοπεῖς με ὥσπερ ἐκτὸς δρόμου φερόμενον.</note> This is what Justin Martyr <note>An early Christian apologist (c. 100–165 AD)</note> calls *to run outside the rule* <note>original Greek: ἔξω τοῦ κανόνος τρέχειν</note>. Faber <note>Tanaquil Faber, a 17th-century French scholar</note> discusses more on this in Book II of his *Agonisticon*, chapter VII; and we shall say some things—if God permits <note>original Greek: ἐάνπερ ἐπιτρέπῃ, ὁ θεός</note>—in our second thoughts on Lucian's *On Slander*.

In the same Paradox, a somewhat more corrupt passage occurs: *Therefore this cause, not nature, distinguishes: which, since it has approached either [of the two], that becomes more inclined; if it be joined to both, it is necessary that they become equal.* Here the book failed me; therefore, the remedy had to be entrusted to conjecture. A light change of a letter or two suggested this: *which, since it has approached either one of the two* <note>original Latin: *quae quum alterutro accessit*</note>, *it becomes more inclined: if it be joined to both, it is necessary that they become equal.*

The Greek inscription for the fourth Paradox is much more elegant in our manuscript: *That every fool is a madman.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι πᾶς ἄφρων μαίνεται. This refers to the Stoic idea that any person not living according to "Reason" or "Wisdom" is technically insane.</note>

In the same Paradox, these words are stained: *All the wicked and impious, of whom you profess yourself to be the leader, whom the laws wish to be punished with exile, even if they have not changed their soil...* <note>This likely refers to Cicero's attacks on his political enemy Clodius, arguing that a person is an "exile" by their character and crimes, even if they haven't physically left the country.</note>

Thus says the Manuscript, in which those words, *you will not be an exile*, were not present—they were added by a translator—just as those words, *is he not called an enemy!* were also added. Gruterus <note>Janus Gruter (1560–1627), a famous Flemish-Dutch philologist and librarian.</note> did not correctly retain these, and changed them into *should he be called an enemy?* which makes no sense. But if that sentiment should strike anyone as too pleasing—*when all the laws command you to be an exile, will you not be an exile?*—then one should further read: *Do those laws not command him to be an exile who was found with a weapon?* instead of, *is he not called an enemy who was found with a weapon!* as is clear enough from what follows.

### C H A P T E R XVIII.

->*Why Diana was born before the Sun. Alchemical matters.*<-

Many things often occur both in the works of the poets and in the writings of those who explain them which usually pass us by unnoticed. Truly, when you apply your mind to them, they are typically very delightful and even instructive. Of such a kind is this which is read in Servius <note>Servius (late 4th century CE) was a famous grammarian and commentator on the works of Virgil.</note>: <margin>On the Aeneid, Book III, 73.</margin> *Latona,* he says, *expelled from all lands, was finally received by her sister (add here what was omitted: Asteria) who was reaching the shores; and there she gave birth first to Diana, and afterwards to Apollo.* He then adds: *Moreover, the fact that we said Diana was born first is a matter of reason. For it is established that the first state was Night, whose instrument is the Moon—that is, Diana—and afterwards Day, which the Sun creates—who is Apollo.* 

As soon as I read these things, I was seized with wonder as to where the ancients received this knowledge, seeing as they lacked the light of Divine history <note>By "Divine history," Tollius refers to the Book of Genesis, where the creation of light follows a state of darkness.</note>. So too says Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet, often cited alongside Homer.</note>:

<margin>In the Theogony.</margin>
> Truly first of all Chaos came into being; but then
> Broad-bosomed Earth, the secure seat of all things forever <note>original: "Ἤτοι μὲν πρώτιστα χάος γένετ᾽. αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα / Γαῖ᾽ εὐρύστερνος, πάντων ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς αἰεί"</note>

<summary>Tollius concludes his technical corrections of Cicero's "Paradoxes" before beginning a new inquiry into why ancient mythology places the birth of the Moon (Diana) before the Sun (Apollo). He links this mythological sequence to the philosophical and "chemical" idea that darkness or chaos preceded the organized light of the world.</summary>

Immediately, the Poet <note>Referring to Hesiod.</note> recognizes the true and one God, the creator of this universe, when at the beginning of the genealogy of the Gods (as they were commonly called), he says *was born* <note>original: *ἐγένετο* (egeneto). Tollius argues that by saying the gods "came to be," Hesiod implies they are created beings, not eternal.</note>. By this word, he silently rejects the opinion of those who imagine some kind of eternal matter for themselves and place it beneath God. (For that which has been made and created cannot be called eternal. Furthermore, that word *first* <note>original: *πρῶτον* (proton)</note> is a word of order, which implies succession; but in eternity there is nothing first, nor second.) And this term presupposes a certain author, since nothing can happen without an efficient cause. These are almost the very same words with which Moses begins the history of creation: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* In the beginning, that is, *first of all* <note>original: *πρώτιστον* (protiston)</note>. Heaven and earth were then still a chaos, *a rough and unordered mass, nothing but sluggish weight.* <note>Tollius quotes Ovid’s *Metamorphoses* (Book I, 7) to bridge the Roman, Greek, and Biblical descriptions of the primordial state.</note> The ancients called this by the single name <margin>Second Epistle [of Peter], Chapter III, 5.</margin> *Water*: and this is that noble principle of Thales <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624–546 BCE) was a pre-Socratic philosopher who claimed that water was the fundamental substance of the universe.</note>. Now, the Physicists say that *all things grow by means of the day*. Over this <margin>Servius on Aeneid, Book I, 310.</margin> water was borne the *spirit of the Lord*, that is, heat...

From this, a resulting effervescence came forth as *Eros* <note>original: ἔρως</note>, which is to say **Love**, or **Air**. For Air is born from water that has been thinned by fire; and thus it is the "dross" or byproduct of Saturn and Rhea. <margin>Plutarch, *On the Primary Cold*.</margin> *Either because these things happen in ordered measures of time, or because they have been completed through combination. Or, what is more probable, because Air then existed at the moment when nature was moved by fire to mix and perfect all things.* <note>Tollius is translating and commenting on a passage from Plutarch’s philosophical essay *De primo frigido*.</note> This is how the text of Cornutus <note>Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, a 1st-century Stoic philosopher who wrote on Greek mythology.</note> stands, as corrected by me.

Now, this son of **Acid** and **Alkali** is called **First-born** <note>original: Πρωτόγονος (Protogonos)</note> by Orpheus—or rather by Onomacritus <note>A 6th-century BCE poet often credited with compiling the "Orphic" hymns.</note>—because <margin>From the *Hymns to the Nature of the Gods*.</margin> he was the first of the entire count of creatures to be born from Fire as the father and Water as the mother. For this reason, he was also called **double-natured** <note>original: διφυὴς (diphyes)</note> by him, meaning he shares in the nature of both parents. 

But what stops us from explaining almost that entire hymn, which contains the mystery of creation? Nothing, I think; let us try then. He is called **great** <note>original: μέγα (mega)</note> because he occupies all things. He is called **aether-wandering** <note>original: αἰθερόπλαγκτος (aitheroplanktos)</note> because he is closest to fire. He is **egg-born** <note>original: ὠογενὴς (oogenes)</note> because Chaos is like an egg, in which the **Water** provides the white, the **Earth** the yolk, and the **Fire** (or Acid) the seed. He is described as **rejoicing in golden wings** <note>original: χρυσείαισιν ἀγαλλόμενος πτερύγεσσιν</note> because the color of fire is golden, and he partakes in it; furthermore, nothing is more mobile than air once it has been set in motion by heat. Additionally, this color is supplied to the air by the nearby sun, which gilds it with golden rays. Finally, he is called **bull-roaring** <note>original: ταυροβόας</note> and **whistling** <note>original: ῥοιζήτωρ</note> from the sound he makes; for sound, like the voice, comes from the striking of the air. He is the **origin of the blessed gods and mortal men** because...

---

<margin>Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 1.</margin>
> *When moisture and heat have found their balance,*
> *They conceive; and from these two, all things arise.*

And so he found the much-remembered Paean <note>Paean is an epithet of Apollo, the god of healing and light, whom Tollius here associates with the "First-born" element.</note> of many rites <note>original: "Ὥστε πολύμνησον, πολυόργιον εὗρε παιὰν"</note>, because from him came the beginning of health, life, and generation, which was the theme of all the mysteries. And for this reason he is called **ineffable** <note>original: "ἄρρητον"</note> and **hidden** <note>original: "κρύφιον"</note>, no differently than how Onamacritus <note>A 6th-century BCE poet and seer who compiled the Orphic hymns.</note> called him **one who rushes with a whirring sound** <note>original: "ῥοιζήτορ"</note>, because those sacred rites were performed far from the profane common folk, at night with a noise in imitation of the celestial motion: **an all-shining offspring**,

> Who dispelled the dark mist from all things, <note>original: "Ὅσων ὃς σκοτόεσσαν ἀπημαύρωσεν ὁμίχλην"</note>

because as the **Alkali** matter was thinned by the active heat of the **Acid**, the heat of the **Acid**—or **Fire**, <margin>Aristotle, *On Colors*, Book 1.</margin> that is **Light** (for thus Aristotle speaks of light)—mixed itself into the **Air** at the very moment of its birth. Hence in the sacred books, **Darkness** is said to have preceded **Day**, just as we have seen that Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet whose *Theogony* describes the origins of the gods.</note> imagined that **Aether** and **Day** were born from **Erebus** and **Night**. The Germans seem to have learned this from the Hebrews, about whom Tacitus <note>A Roman historian; Tollius suggests here that Germanic and Hebrew traditions share a common ancestral logic regarding time.</note> wrote: *They do not count the number of days, as we do, but of nights. Thus they establish their dates, thus they make their agreements. Night seems to lead the day.* And indeed, it could not have happened otherwise. For whatever is born or arises, it arises from that which did not exist before. Hence I wonder that there are, and have been, philosophers who said and still say, ***Nothing comes from nothing*** <note>original: "Ex nihilo nil fieri." This was a standard maxim of ancient philosophy which Tollius, as a Christian, seeks to refute.</note>. For in order for the world to be made, it had to be created and made from that which was not the world—that is, "**nothing**"—because in the world are **All things**. Yet **All** and **Nothing** are opposites to one another. And from this comes "**Strife**" <note>original: "Inimicitia," referring to the force that separates elements in the system of Empedocles.</note> among the principles of the world in the philosophy of Empedocles. Indeed, that all things were created out of nothing should seem a wonder to no one who knows God as God—that is, as omnipotent. And what, I ask, is so incredible about that power in God to create both matter and form out of nothing, when we men daily [produce] forms out of nothing...

...we might bring forth: unless someone perhaps objects to us with Platonic ideas <note>Plato’s Theory of Forms suggests that physical objects are merely shadows of perfect, abstract "Ideas." > *Immediately follows the shining, bright air,*
<margin>Book VI <note>This citation actually refers to Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book IV, lines 312–315.</note></margin>

> *Of that former air: for this bright air is by many degrees*
> *More mobile, and many parts smaller, and more powerful.*

Indeed, those things seem to me to shine which, being composed of smooth and solid particles, receive every most volatile particle emitted from fire by continuous and swift motion into their center, and send them back into the eyes of viewers: just as the heat of the sun, reflected from a wall or other solid body, reaches our sense of touch; or as the image of a voice <note>An echo.</note> struck against rocks reaches the ears. These are the physical principles which seem to provide the truest explanation for what the ancients wrote regarding the origin of the Moon—or rather of night and darkness—before the sun and the day. For the fact that **Diana** <note>The goddess of the Moon.</note> is imagined by some to have been born before **Apollo** <note>The god of the Sun.</note>, so that she might assist her mother **Latona** <note>In myth, Latona (Leto) gave birth to the twins Artemis (Diana) and Apollo. Now, Latona is the **Philosophical Earth** <term>Philosophical Earth: In alchemy, this is the "prime matter" or the purified base material required to begin the Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>, in which the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>In alchemical symbolic shorthand, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold or the active masculine principle, and the Moon (Luna) represents Silver or the passive feminine principle.</note> lie hidden; they cannot come forth into the light unless the mother has grasped the olive and the palm. We have dealt with the **Olive** elsewhere; perhaps a place will be given for the **Palm** as well. But as offspring <note>original: "ἐκγόνους"</note>...

The alchemists’ **raven** is linked to **Apollo** <note>Apollo represents the Sun or the sulfurous principle.</note> by the ancients; the **white swan**, or **Diana** <note>Diana represents the Moon or the mercurial principle.</note>, follows it, and after her comes the **golden eagle**, or the **winged Sun**, destined to be changed into a **Phoenix** so that a better offspring may rise from its ashes. <note>These animals represent the color changes in the alchemical "Great Work": the black raven for *nigredo* (decay), the white swan for *albedo* (purification), and the phoenix for the final *rubedo* (perfection/reddening).</note> Reeds are the receivers of air, as is clear from the story of **Pan** and **Syrinx**. <note>In myth, the nymph Syrinx turned into reeds to escape the god Pan; Tollius likely views this as an allegory for the capture of "vital air" or spirit in a vessel.</note> I have dealt elsewhere with ***mountains*** and mountain gods, which are **volatile spirits**. Likewise, I have explained the name of the **world** <gloss>Latin: *orbis*</gloss> and what it signifies. It is known what **Delos** is; the matter itself will teach you why that island had to be "light" <note>Tollius plays on the Latin *levis*, meaning both weightless (floating) and bright (light-filled).</note> at first. Likewise, why **Juno** becomes the enemy of **Latona**; but it is especially notable that Latona is said to have fled into ***Lycia***, that is, the **Region of Wolves**, about which I have written more extensively elsewhere. So too, the reason why the triple-formed monster, the ***Chimera***, is in Lycia—which is not added here in vain—is easy for the seeker to track down.

Furthermore, consider what that **thirst** of hers signifies when the heavy Sun scorched the fields. What are these fields? Who is this Sun? For **Apollo** himself was carried by her ***in her bosom***, along with **Diana**. Why are her breasts said to be exhausted of **milk**? What is this milk? Why are her children called **acid**? From whence comes that ***lake in the depths of the valleys***, and indeed of "better water"? What is "water," and what specific water is this? Why was it called "better"? <note>Tollius refers to the scene where Latona, exhausted and thirsty, tries to drink from a pond. Local peasants stir up the mud to stop her; she curses them to become frogs. Alchemically, this represents the struggle to extract pure "water" or solvent from crude matter.</note> I explain the greatest part of these things elsewhere, and therefore I do not repeat them. Look back, reader, and you will marvel; you have read these things often, yet never understood them. Like many other things of this kind, once they have borrowed light from these explanations, they will thereafter strike your eyes more brightly, and they will no longer allow themselves to be passed over as they were before.

### CHAPTER XIX.

->*Florus Corrected.*<-

We often attempt several small tasks; and although sometimes we beat the air and our effort falls in vain, we do not for that reason despair or lose heart. For that saying of **Theocritus** always comes to mind: *By trial, indeed, all things are accomplished.* <note>Original Greek: Πείρῃ θὴν πάντα τελεῖται. Tollius uses this quote to justify his persistent attempts to fix difficult passages in ancient literature.</note>
<margin>Chapter 7.</margin>
We shall therefore try once more—something attempted once before in vain—to see if we can apply a remedy to a "diseased" passage in **Florus**. <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus was a Roman historian who summarized Roman history.</note> In his fourth book, speaking of the danger facing **Brutus** and **Cassius** after the murder of **Caesar** <note>This refers to the immediate chaos in 44 BCE after Caesar was killed in the Senate.</note>, which was imminent from Caesar's veteran soldiers, he says: *Therefore, when it appeared what slaughter was threatening the Republic, the revenge was displeasing, and it was decreed along with the abolition of the consul.* <note>Original Latin: "displicuit ultio cum consulis abolitione decreta." This sentence is grammatically and historically confusing in the original Latin manuscripts.</note> Even before I knew the opinion of **Anne Dacier** <note>Tollius refers to her as "Anna Fabri f." (daughter of Tanneguy Le Fèvre); she was one of the most famous female scholars of the 17th century.</note>, who substituted "by a decree of the senate" <gloss>Latin: *senatusconsulto*</gloss> for the phrase "with the consul," I had conjectured that Florus wrote: *By a decree of the senate, an amnesty was decided.* <note>Original: "Senatus consulto oblivione decreta."</note> However, the conjecture of **Freinshemius** <note>Johann Freinsheim, a German classical scholar known for his work on Roman historians.</note>, who suspects it was written "by the counsel of **Cicero**," is not unpleasing. But whatever the case may be, the word "amnesty" <gloss>Latin: *oblivionis*, literally "forgetfulness"</gloss> certainly seems to me to be the correct replacement for that word "abolition." For thus says **Cicero**: 
<margin>Philippics, Book 1, Chapter 1.</margin>
> *In this temple of Tellus, as much as lay within me, I laid the foundations of Peace: and I renewed the ancient example of the Athenians; I even used the Greek word <note>The word Cicero refers to is "amnestia," meaning a "forgetting" of past grievances to ensure peace.</note> which that state had used at the time in settling discords, and I moved that every memory of the discords should be erased by everlasting forgetfulness:*

I am not unaware, however, that in **Suetonius**, in the *Life of Tiberius* chapter 4, we read: *Yet, Caesar having been slain, when all were decreeing an "abolition" of the deed for fear of riots, etc.* But here, the word "deed" is added. Yet this seemed like a gloss <note>A "gloss" is an explanatory note added by a later scribe that accidentally gets copied into the main text.</note> to **Torrentius**. For which reason, "Amnesty" <gloss>Latin: *Oblivione*</gloss> should be restored here as well. **Velleius** says: *that most famous decree of the Athenians...*

<meta>The catchword "rimi" at the bottom of the page is the end of the Latin word "celeberrimi," meaning "most famous."</meta>

He supports his argument by citing similar phrasing in Cicero, Suetonius, and Velleius Paterculus regarding the legal pardons issued after Caesar's assassination.</summary>

<page-num>145</page-num>
<header>II MISCELLANY</header>

The most famous example, reported by **Cicero**, of an *Amnesty for past things*, was approved by a decree of the Senate. <note>original: "Oblivionis præteritarum rerum"; Tollius refers to the "Act of Oblivion" or "Amnesty" of 44 BCE, where the Senate attempted to stabilize Rome by pardoning Caesar's assassins while upholding his acts.</note> But the words that follow in the text of **Florus** are not "healthy" enough <note>In philology, a "healthy" (sana) text is one that is considered original and uncorrupted by copying errors.</note>: *However, lest they should bear the eyes of public grief, they withdrew into the provinces given by that very Caesar whom they had killed, Syria and Macedonia.* <note>original: "Ne tamen publici doloris oculos ferrent..."</note> By inserting just a single little letter, I read it as: *lest they should **strike** the eyes of public grief.* <note>Tollius is suggesting changing the Latin word "ferrent" (they might bear/carry) to "ferirent" (they might strike). This is a common type of textual correction called an emendation.</note> This "public grief" <margin>Book II.</margin> is treated here as a living thing, representing the people themselves. It is just as good an expression to speak of "the eyes of public grief" as it is to say "the eyes of the afflicted state." Furthermore, *to strike the eyes* is a phrase very familiar to the poet **Lucretius**. <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BCE), a Roman poet and philosopher.</note> For he writes:

<margin>Book IV. line 217; line 257; line 328.</margin>
> Bodies which **strike the eyes**, and provoke the sight. <note>original: "Corpora quæ feriant oculos, visumque lacessant."</note>
And: Why those images, which **strike the eyes**, seem to be seen, etc. <note>original: "Cur ea, quæ feriant oculos, simulacra videri, &c."</note>
Likewise: And they **strike the eyes**, disturbing their structures. <note>original: "Et feriunt oculos, turbantia composituras."</note>

If by chance my correction does not satisfy someone, let him recall these words of **Cicero**:
<margin>1st Oration against Catiline, Chapter VII.</margin>
> *And if I saw myself so heavily suspected by my fellow citizens and an object of offense, I would prefer to be deprived of the sight of my citizens than to be looked upon by the hostile eyes of all. You, since by the consciousness of your crimes you recognize the just hatred of all, which has long been your due—do you hesitate to avoid the sight and presence of those whose minds and senses you wound?*

"To wound the senses" and "to strike the eyes" <margin>Letters to Friends, Book II, Epistle XVI.</margin> are equivalent terms. <note>original Greek: ἰσοδυναμοῦντα (isodynamounta).</note> The same author says elsewhere: *But this laurel of ours runs into not only the eyes, but now also the petty voices of the malevolent.* "Running into the eyes" is the same as striking or wounding the eyes. In the same letter, Cicero uses another quite elegant metaphor; "You know," he says, "not only the disgust of my stomach, but also of my eyes at the unworthiness of insolent men." After the pagan Cicero, let the Christian **Lactantius** follow. <margin>Book V, Chapter IX.</margin> For he says: *Rather, let those be removed in whose presence one is ashamed to live poorly; those who **strike** and beat the brow of sin, if not with words—because they remain silent—then by their very different way of life.* As for the matter itself, he could...

### C H A P T E R XX.

->*A Physical Explanation of Vision.*<-

I have judged that it would be a useful deed if I were to add some remarks on **Vision** to illustrate the preceding chapter. For you see the rest. For if we saw by the **falling-in of images** <note>original Greek: κατ’ εἰδώλων ἐμπτώσεις. For it is not the "images" of things, as he called them, but light reflected from things that reaches our eyes, and in their **crystalline humor** <note>The lens of the eye, which early scientists believed was the primary organ of sight.</note> represents the image of those things. What light actually is, we have discussed elsewhere—namely, that it consists of the most subtle and most volatile fire particles. 

It is described excellently by Bartholomaeus Anglicus <note>A 13th-century Franciscan monk known for his encyclopedia *On the Properties of Things*.</note>: *Light,* he says, *is a substance most simple, most manifold in its power, most mobile, of absolute penetration, the principle and origin of all natural motion: most perfectible, most delightful, and most communicable. Light multiplies itself by begetting. For light begets light, and the light thus begotten simultaneously begets the light that succeeds it.* 

Therefore, this light, falling upon the **crystalline membrane** <note>term: crystalloides — the lens of the eye or its surrounding membrane.</note> after being reflected from objects, forms an image there. The sense of sight—residing in the junction of the **optic nerves** above the **sphenoid bone** <note>A butterfly-shaped bone at the base of the skull.</note>—perceives this through the continuation of the parts ending in the crystalline or "spider-web" membrane <note>term: aranea — a term used by early anatomists to describe the delicate vascular membrane or the lens capsule.</note>, with the help of the **optic spirits** <note>historical term: spirituum opticorum — invisible "vapors" or fluids once believed to travel through nerves to carry sensory information to the brain.</note>. It then transmits this to the mind for recognition via the **medulla oblongata** <note>The base of the brainstem.</note>, wherever the mind may ultimately have its seat.

...[natura]l light, when light is emitted from bodies into the related air—which, being easy to diffuse and turn, is penetrated by the fiery force of sight. However, these opinions of the two greatest men <note>Likely referring to Plato and Epicurus, whose theories of vision were debated on the previous page.</note> can easily be refuted. For it can be immediately proven from the rest of the senses that **emissions** <note>original: "emissiones"</note> do not occur from the Senses, but rather **receptions** <note>original: "receptiones"</note>. 

Thus, the ears do not emit particles to attract sounds; nor do the nostrils for odors, nor the tongue for flavors: nor does the body scatter anything from itself to feel other bodies through touch. In these and those greatest men—and even now in many other most acute thinkers—an error has occurred that is entirely contrary to the error of sailors. To sailors, some lands seem to approach and others to recede while they themselves seem to stand still; these thinkers, however, believe they are emitting something and acting, when in fact they are receiving and being acted upon. 

Moreover, as for those who attribute a certain native light to the eyes, they seem to do so correctly, provided one interprets it properly. For much heat is implanted in the **optic spirits** <term>spiritus optici: In early modern science, these were believed to be subtle, refined fluids or gases that traveled through the nerves to convey sensory information to the brain.</term>, which accounts for that ineffable speed with which they revolve through the **optic nerves** and carry things seen back to the sense and the mind. 

But this interior light illuminates the internal parts when aided by external light, while it more easily processes and distributes that external light. Furthermore, the greater the heat of these spirits, the sharper the sight: so that in moments of anger, sparks often seem to leap from the eyes—which is an abundance of heat squeezed out by the excessive agitation of the spirits. This is similarly evident from a heavy blow to the eyes, where those same fiery particles, condensed and forced together by the strike, present to us the appearance of sparks falling from the eyes; this is due to a reflection directed from all sides toward the **crystalline tunic** <term>tunica crystalloides: A historical term for the lens of the eye or the membrane surrounding it.</term>. Therefore, here too there are fiery particles, <term>cutting particles, carried upwards by their lightness toward the senses of the head</term> <note>original Greek: μόρια τέμνοντα, φερόμενά τε ὑπὸ κουφότητος ἄνω πρὸς τὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς αἰσθήσεις</note>, as Plato says in that same *Timaeus*. Moreover, what smoke and other sharp things are to the eyes, so those people are to the mind whose appearance is unpleasant to us. They strike our eyes, therefore, and wound them, just as Florus says of Caesar's assassins, and Cicero says of Catiline <note>Catiline was a Roman senator who led a famous conspiracy to overthrow the Republic, famously denounced by Cicero.</note>: to the illustration of whom this chapter was dedicated and intended.

->*This man shall be Marcellus.*<-
<note>original Latin: *Hic Marcellus erit.* This refers to Marcus Claudius Marcellus, a nephew of Augustus who died young; in the poem, his soul is seen in the underworld before being born.</note>

For Anchises says that regarding one not yet born. But if the same should be read in Florus, then I would think *let it grow* <note>original: *crescat*</note> should be put in place of *it grows* <note>original: *crescit*</note>.

In the same chapter, it seems to me that a more correct reading can be found in John of Salisbury <note>A 12th-century English author and diplomat, famous for his work *Policraticus*.</note>, with a little help: *"If (as they say that Panus, or rather Adherbal the son of Bomilcar, said) if Hannibal had known how to use victory just as he knew how to win."* Commonly it is read as *"just as he might know how to win, so he might have known how to use victory."* A little later in the same chapter we read: *"From this he received a new surname, and one beneficial to the Republic: the Delayer."* <note>The Latin *Cunctator* refers to Quintus Fabius Maximus, the Roman general whose strategy of avoiding direct battle and wearing down Hannibal's forces saved Rome, though he was initially mocked for his "slowness."</note> Those who substitute *true* for *new* do not seem to me to have grasped the author's meaning. Write instead: *a shameful surname, but beneficial to the Republic.* For this was initially given to him as an insult; but because it was found to be beneficial to the state, it later turned into a mark of glory. And indeed, the name "Delayer" is quite shameful for a leader if the matter exceeds proper measure. Notable is the speed of Alexander, who "put nothing off" <note>original Greek: μηδὲν ἀναβαλλομένῳ</note>. Notable is the saying of Sallust: *"Before you begin, there is need for deliberation; when you have deliberated, there is need for timely action."* That golden saying of Augustus, *hasten slowly* <note>original Greek: σπεῦδε βραδέως</note>, although it seems to approve of hesitation, is nonetheless far removed from the vice of the Delayer.

It is a minor matter that a fault lies hidden in the same chapter from an omission: *Tarentum,* he says, *had returned to us by law.* Read: *Now Tarentum had returned to us.* Then later: *so that you may know there were even omens for the fates;* replace with *of fate*. Thus a little later—

...a little: *"This was that man's first confession, not without a certain omen of his imminent fate."* <note>original: *Hæc fuit illius viri non sine præsagio quodam fati imminentis prima confessio.* Tollius is concluding a previous thought regarding a historical figure’s admission before their downfall.</note>

In Book II, chapter 11, a passage occurs that has been troubled by many, which we shall also attempt to address: *“The ruin of the Syrian war also,”* he says, *“engulfed Gallogrecia <term>Gallogrecia: Also known as Galatia, a region in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey) settled by Celtic Gauls in the 3rd century BC.</term>.”* *“Whether they had been among the auxiliary forces of King Antiochus <term>Antiochus III (the Great): The Seleucid king who fought against Rome in the early 2nd century BC.</term>, or whether Manlius <term>Gnaeus Manlius Vulso: The Roman consul who led a campaign against the Galatians in 189 BC, though some questioned if he did so merely to win military glory (a triumph).</term>, being eager for a triumph, pretended they were seen there, is doubtful. A twin passage to this occurs in Book III, chapter 3: *"The enemy held the valley and the river in the middle; for our men, there was no abundance of water. Whether the general did this by design, or turned an error into a plan, is doubtful; certainly, courage increased by necessity was the cause of victory."* In a manuscript from our Library, it reads: *"Whether they had been among, or whether they would have been, or whether eager for a triumph, etc."* But the reading *"Whether they were among the auxiliaries of King Antiochus, or whether he was eager, etc."* is also not inconvenient. However, I prefer the former.

A little later, I find the judgment of some lacking, who rejected the conjecture of Salmasius <note>Claude Salmasius (Saumaise), a famous 17th-century French classical scholar.</note>, which is also confirmed by our own manuscript, reading: *"Furthermore, the race of the Gallogrecians, just as the name itself is evidence, is mixed and adulterated; the remnants of the Gauls, who under the leadership of Brennus <term>Brennus: The leader of the Gauls who famously invaded Greece and attacked the sanctuary at Delphi in 279 BC.</term> had devastated Greece, and soon followed toward the East, settled in the middle part of Asia,"* where I would prefer to read, *"they settled together <note>original: *confederunt*</note> in middle Asia."* As in Virgil: *"And he settled in an Italian city."* <note>original: *Atque itala confederat urbe.* A reference to the Aeneid, emphasizing the use of the verb for settling/founding.</note> Book II, chapter 18. *"Numantia, as much as Carthage, as much as Capua..."* <note>Numantia, Carthage, and Capua were the three major cities whose defiance or rivalry most threatened Roman power.</note>

"Inferior to Corinth in wealth; yet in the name and honor of valor equal to all; and, if you judge by the quality of its men, the supreme glory of Spain." <note>original: "Corinti opibus inferior; ita virtutis nomine & honore par omnibus; summumque, si viros æstimes, Hispaniæ decus." Tollius is quoting Florus’s description of the city of Numantia, which resisted Rome for years.</note> This reading seemed acceptable to everyone else, but to me it appears corrupted. I would replace the word "yet" <note>original: *ità*</note> with "to such an extent" <note>original: *in tantum*</note>, were it not for the fact that I know that in that era the word "how much" <note>original: *quantum*</note> was often used in place of "in the manner that" <note>original: *quemadmodum*</note>. <margin>In *Vespasian*, chapter 6.</margin> For example, Suetonius writes: "This prophecy regarding a Roman emperor, as it later became clear by the outcome, the Jews applied to themselves and rebelled." <note>original: "id de imperatore Romano quantum eventu postea patuit, prædictum, Judæi ad se trahentes, rebellarunt." Suetonius was a Roman biographer; Tollius uses him here to prove a grammatical point about how Latin was used in the Imperial period.</note>

### CHAPTER XXII.

#### FLORUS freed from several glosses.
<note>A "gloss" is a marginal note or explanation made by a scribe that accidentally gets copied into the main text of a book over centuries of rewriting.</note>

The text of Florus is quite condensed; hence, many things have been added to it by foreign hands. Thus, in Book III, chapter 13, you may read in the common editions: "Now, so that we may touch upon the more showy vices, was not the ambition for honors incited by those same riches?" <note>original: "Jam ut speciosiora vitia tangamus, nonne ambitus honorum ab iisdem divitiis incitatus?"</note> Delete the word *vices*, which adds no value here. The same applies a little later: "Finally, that very desire for supremacy and lordship, whence does it come if not from excessive wealth?" <note>original: "Denique illa ipsa principatus & dominandi cupido, unde nisi nimiis opibus venit?"</note> Consult and compare the preceding parts; you will say immediately that the word "comes" <note>original: *venit*</note> is from a "bad hand" <note>meaning a clumsy scribe’s addition</note>. Conversely, in this same chapter, two words seem to me to have fallen out, which must be restored. In the common editions, it is: "From where did the gladiator armies against their own masters come, if not the lavish bribery to win the favor of the common people, when it indulges in spectacles, it makes a skill out of what was once the punishment of enemies." <note>original: "Unde gladiatorii adversus dominos suos exercitus, nisi ad conciliandum plebis favorem effusa largitio, quum spectaculis indulget, supplicia quondam hostium artem facit."</note> This is a disconnected sentence, which can be repaired by adding a single word: "if not *that* [bribery]..." <note>original: *nisi quod...*</note>. Furthermore, instead of "when it indulges in spectacles," I would prefer "while it indulges in spectacles" <note>original: *dum* instead of *quum*</note>. If this insertion of a single little word does not please someone, they might—not against my will—change "makes" <note>original: *facit*</note> into <unclear>faceret</unclear>. A little further down, before "These things of Catiline..."

...*the power of the most holy right.* A little earlier we read: *Nor was the whole nobility lacking with a ready hand.* I would prefer that the phrase *with a ready hand* <note>original: "obvia manu"</note> be deleted, because the word *hand* <term>manu</term> follows shortly after, and then again, *with a ready hand of the nobles*, which is foreign to the usual elegance of Florus.

In **Chapter XVII**, I would gladly eject two more spurious <note>Meaning "fake" or "incorrectly added."</note> words. He says, "*in this state of affairs, equal in resources, spirit, and dignity (whence also a rivalry with Livius Drusus had arisen), Servilius Caepio asserted the cause of the knights, and Livius Drusus the senate.*" **Grævius** <note>Johann Georg Graevius (1632–1703) was a leading German classical scholar and critic.</note> is correct in his reading: *whence also a rivalry with Livius Drusus had arisen.* For Florus is usually so concise. But I would prefer, both here and in what follows, to strike out the name *Livius*. It could also be read: *and from there a rivalry had incited Drusus.* Not much later, we find: *To resist these movements, Drusus [raised up] the common people to himself by the Gracchian laws, and the allies to the common people by the hope of citizenship.* Read it as: *he drew <term>traxit</term> the common people to himself by the Gracchian laws, and the allies to the common people by the hope of citizenship.* The rest of the phrasing comes from unskilled copyists who wished to "clarify" Florus’s style. In **Freculphus** <note>A 9th-century bishop and chronicler who frequently quoted from classical Roman histories.</note> we read, *enticed by the hope of liberty.* This favors the conjecture of **Lipsius** <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), one of the most famous humanist scholars of the Renaissance.</note>, who prefers the word *enticed* <note>original: "allexit"</note>. However, I prefer *drew* <note>original: "traxit"</note>, and the word *to raise up* <note>original: "erigere"</note> has no place here. It is better used in the following chapter, where we find: *to which hope Drusus had carried them forth by the desire for power.* For I hardly think *to raise someone to oneself by hope of power* is proper Latin.

In the following **Chapter XVIII**, immediately at the beginning, the word *war* <note>original: "bellum"</note> should be deleted and we should read: *Although it may be called the Social War, so that we might diminish the hatred of the event, if we want the truth, however, it was a civil war.* For that extra word comes from a commentator. Indeed, the sentence refers back to the title of the chapter, which had been noted by Florus himself: **THE SOCIAL WAR.** <note>The Social War (91–87 BC) was a rebellion of Rome's Italian allies (the *socii*) who fought for the right to Roman citizenship.</note>

**Chapter XVII.** I would gladly cast out two more spurious words: *in this*, he says, *state of affairs, equal in wealth, spirit, and dignity (whence also a rivalry born against Livius Drusus had approached) Servilius Caepio asserted the knights, and Livius Drusus the senate.* <note>Tollius is discussing the political tensions leading to the Social War (91–87 BCE).</note> Graevius <note>Johann Georg Graevius (1632–1703), a leading German classical scholar and contemporary of Tollius.</note> correctly notes: *whence also a rivalry born against Livius Drusus.* For Florus is usually so concise: But I would prefer, both here and in what follows, to strike out the name *Livius*. It could also be read: *and from there a rivalry born had incited Drusus.* <note>original: "and inde nata Drusum æmulatio accenderat."</note> Not much later: *In order that Drusus might resist these movements, [he raised up] the common people to himself by the Gracchan laws. The same man raised up the allies to the common people by the hope of citizenship.* Read it as: *he drew the common people to himself by the Gracchan laws, and drew the allies to the common people by the hope of citizenship.* <note>original: "plebem ad se Gracchanis legibus, socios ad plebem spe civitatis traxit."</note> The rest of the phrasing is from inept scribes <note>original: "ineptis librariis."</note> who wished to "illustrate" or clarify Florus's text. In Freculphus <note>Freculphus of Lisieux, a 9th-century bishop and chronicler who often quoted earlier Roman historians.</note> it is read, *enticed by the hope of liberty.* This favors the conjecture of Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), one of the most famous Renaissance philologists.</note>, who prefers the word *allured* <term>allexit</term>. I prefer, however, *drew* <term>traxit</term>; the word *to raise up* <term>erigere</term> has no place here. It is used better in the following chapter; where it says: *to which hope Drusus had carried them out of a desire for dominance.* For I think the phrase *to raise someone to oneself by hope of dominance* <note>original: "erigere aliquem ad se spe dom."</note> is scarcely proper Latin.

In the following **Chapter XVIII**, the word *war* <term>bellum</term> must be deleted right at the start, and it should be read: *It may be called the Social [War], so that we may diminish the odium; if we wish the truth, however, it was a civil war.* <note>The "Social War" was fought between Rome and its Italian allies (socii), but Tollius argues it was effectively a civil war.</note> For that word *war* is also from an interpreter <note>meaning a later commentator whose notes were accidentally merged into the main text.</note>. The speech here is looking back to the title of the chapter, which had been noted by Florus himself: *THE SOCIAL WAR.*

In the same chapter is a passage that is all but given up for lost <note>original: "tantum non conclamatus." Literally "cried out," an idiom referring to a funeral rite or a hopeless case.</note>: *Since all the strength of the bravest.* Most faithful—

### CHAPTER XVII.

I would gladly cast out two more spurious words: "in this state of affairs," he says, "equal in resources, spirit, and dignity (from which also a rivalry had arisen for Livius Drusus) Servilius Caepio asserted the rights of the knights, and Livius Drusus the rights of the senate." <note>original: "in hoc statu rerum, pares opibus, animis, dignitate (unde & nata Livio Druso æmulatio accesserat) equitem Servilius Cæpio, senatum Livius Drusus asserere." Joannes Georgius Graevius was a contemporary scholar of Tollius.</note> For Florus is usually so concise. But I would prefer, both here and in what follows, to strike out the name *Livius*. It is better in the following chapter, where: *to which hope Drusus had carried them out of a desire for power.* <note>original: "ad quam spem eos cupidine dominationis Drusus evexerat."</note> For *to raise someone to oneself with the hope of power* <note>original: "erigere aliquem ad se spe dom."</note> I think is scarcely proper Latin.

Immediately at the beginning, the word *war* <note>original: "bellum"</note> should be deleted and it should read: *Though it may be called Social, so that we may lessen the odium, yet if we want the truth, it was a civil war.* <note>original: "Sociale vocetur licet, ut extenuemus incidiam si verum tamen volumus, civile bellum fuit." But he tries in vain. that is, when these substances are liquefied in the crucible or philosophical vessel, the fiery spirit—which cannot be reduced to a fixed state—leaves behind all Lycaonian impurity to be consumed by the flames, while it escapes intact and returns to heaven. Regarding Jupiter as the Sun and Jupiter as Mars, one should consult Macrobius; all of which can hardly be explained unless one recurs to Chemistry. Indeed, the *wolf* <note>original: "lupus"</note> is added to the Sun and Mars. We also read of *Lycus*, or the *wolf*, as the son of Mars in Hyginus; and the *wolf* was worshipped as a god by the Lycopolitans in Egypt. Likewise, there were two sons of Osiris, Anubis and Macedon: the former bore a *dog* as his military emblem, and the latter a *wolf*. Now, this pertains most especially to the night in which Lycaon plotted against Jupiter, because the Sun is called "born of light" <note>original Greek: λυκηγενὴς (lyke-genes), which Tollius punningly associates with "wolf-born"</note> by Homer, and years are called "wolf-paths" <note>original Greek: λυκάβαντες (lykabantes), an ancient word for years</note>; and even the Sun himself is elsewhere called "wolf-slayer" <note>original Greek: λυκηκτόνος</note> and "wolf-destroyer" <note>original Greek: λυκοφθόρος</note> for a twofold reason, similar to this...

...the cruelty of the Lycaonian Lyncus, King of the Scythians, who lay in wait by night for Triptolemus—as is found in Ovid at the end of the fifth book of the *Metamorphoses*, of which more shortly:

> "My homeland is famous Athens," he said:
> "My name is Triptolemus: the open air lay pathless before me.

Both the location of Athens—which is under the protection of Minerva <note>Goddess of wisdom, often associated with the "Salt of Wisdom" in alchemy</note>—and the name of Triptolemus <note>A mythical hero who spread the knowledge of agriculture</note>, in which the <term>triple mystical number</term> is found, must be noted above all others. Regarding Triptolemus, so that the harmony of these myths may be more clearly revealed, it will not be troublesome to add what is read in the same Poet [Ovid], in the fourth book of the *Fasti*, where he writes thus of Ceres:

> It was the middle of the night, and the silence of peaceful sleep:
> She lifted Triptolemus into her lap:
> Three times she stroked him with her hand; she spoke three charms,
> Charms not to be repeated by a mortal voice.
> And so, in the hearth's live embers, she buried
> The boy’s body, that fire might purge the burden of mortality.
> <note>original: "Noctis erat medium, placidique silentia somni: Triptolemum gremio sustulit illa suo: Terque manu permulsit eum; tria carmina dixit, Carmina mortali non referenda sono. Itaque foro pueri corpus vivente favilla Obruit, humanum purget ut ignis onus." Ceres's act of placing the boy in fire is an alchemical metaphor for "calcination," using heat to strip away impurities from a substance.</note>

We have already seen the nature of the Lycaonian fire. Regarding the "attainment of immortality," more will be said in what follows. Furthermore, the homeland of Lycaon is Mount Lycaeus, or certainly its borders—a mountain sacred to Pan; whence Virgil says:

> Leaving his native grove and the glades of Lycaeus,
> Pan, the guardian of the sheep.
> <note>original: "Ipse nemus linquens patrium, saltusque Lycæi, Pan ovium custos."</note>

But even Jupiter himself is called Lycaeus; indeed, so is Apollo Lycaeus. We have seen regarding Pan above. Sleep, however, is a matter of rest and of winter. Hence, that god of the Phrygians is himself one who sleeps in winter, but wakes in summer; or, as the Paphlagonians <note>An ancient people of northern Anatolia</note> would have it, he is one who is restrained by chains in winter, but is set in motion in the spring.

...could be, that is, the sons of heat. Nor does it escape me that Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a renowned French Protestant biblical scholar and geographer</note>, a most learned man, derives the etymology of the word *Chemistry* <margin>Book IV, Chapter I of *Phaleg* <note>Bochart's famous work on sacred geography</note></margin> from the Arabic *Chema*, which signifies "to hide" or "to conceal," because that art wraps its secrets in all sorts of evasions, and its writers hand everything down obliquely <note>original Greek: "λοξῶς"</note>, veiling them with a greater obscurity than even the Sphinx was accustomed to use. But while I do not condemn that view, I also do not see why the other, derived from heat, might not be equally true. 

Furthermore, I cannot at all approve of that same man's clearly absurd opinion by which he condemns this art as a novelty. Since he himself admits that Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Latin writer and astrologer</note> mentioned it—who was a contemporary <note>original Greek: "σύγχρονος"</note> of Constantine the Great—he could have seen from that very testimony that the Chemical art is much older than he thinks; for Firmicus mentions it not as something recent, or found "yesterday or the day before" <note>original Greek: "χθὲς καὶ πρώην"</note>, but simply as if it were known through long and ancient usage. 

I, however, believe that it became better known around those times and was shared with more people, having previously lain hidden among a few. For love, or brotherly charity so highly commended in the Gospel, persuaded some—who were passing from the Pythagorean sect or even the order of Egyptian priests to the Christian faith—to reveal that great secret to some of their brothers, especially in the age of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor (reigned 284–305 AD) known for the "Great Persecution" of Christians</note>, when the Christian cause was afflicted in a marvelous way. They did this so that by this aid, those pressed by poverty could be more abundantly helped <note>Tollius suggests that converted alchemists used their knowledge to create gold to support Christians suffering under Roman persecution</note>. For I am as thoroughly convinced as one can be that it is much older even than the times of Moses and Joseph; and from that remarkable [evidence] of all things, which...

To this place, they say Deucalion <note>The survivor of the Greek version of the Great Flood</note> was saved on Mount Athos when the waters rose; some even add the specific time, namely, *on the ninth day*.

The name Deucalion comes from *Deukes* <note>original: Δευκὴς</note>, which to the Greeks means "bright" or "splendid"; and from *deukein* <note>original: δεύκειν</note>, meaning "to care for" or "to consider." An etymology for Deucalion can be sought from either word, but I would prefer the former. For splendor is attributed to fire, and for us, this Deucalion of ours is the son of fire. Hence, according to Hesychius <note>An ancient Greek lexicographer</note>, the Satyrs are called "Deucalidae" <note>Descendants of Deucalion</note>, of whom we spoke above. ...offspring <note>original: *suboles*; the text continues from the previous page's discussion of Deucalion's children</note> without birth <note>original: *ἄτερ γονᾶς*</note>.) In the ninth year afterward, he was to be sent to Lycomedes—the ruler of wolves <note>original: *τῶν λύκων μήδοντα*</note>—the king of Scyros, an island of clay (just as Deucalion reached Parnassus on the ninth day), so that hiding there in female attire, he might bear the name *Pyrrha*. Moreover, he was called Pyrrha because he had yellow hair, and in *Greek*, one who is "fire-red" is called *Pyrrhon*. Go now, you who understand Greek, and deny that our art <note>Tollius refers here to Alchemy, the "Hermetic Art"</note> is ancient.

<margin>Hyginus, Fable 96.</margin>

*By a small boat, in the belly of the wind, by the Mercurial spirit.* Hermes says in the *Emerald Tablet*: *The wind carried me in its belly.* <note>This is a foundational line from the *Tabula Smaragdina*, the most famous text of Western alchemy, symbolizing how the "spirit" or vaporous matter contains the potential of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> This is that ship <margin>Diodorus Siculus</margin> of Jupiter Hammon, and of Horus the Sun; likewise of Isis. *It adhered, by a sympathetic glue, or the suitability of nature, by Philosophical magnetism.*

*The Corycian Nymphs. Hesychius says: "korykos" means a sack or small bag; but others say a ship.* <note>Hesychius was a 5th-century lexicographer. Tollius is using etymology to link "caves" (the sack) to "ships," suggesting both are vessels for the alchemical spirit.</note> We have seen this regarding the small boat: likewise regarding the placement of the Egyptian Gods upon a ship. Indeed, Nymphs, or Naiads, are the powers presiding over waters, and souls undergoing generation. Furthermore, since caves are sacred to Nymphs, none is surely more suitable for them than the Corycian cave on twin-peaked Parnassus. There was also another very famous cave of the same name in Cilicia, in which there was a shrine of Mercury, the god most friendly to the Nymphs; whence he calls those the *secret shrines of Hermes* <note>original: *ἑρμαῖα ἄδυτα*</note>.

And thus, having finally been purified, she becomes the mother of the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical symbolism, the Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver, the "children" of purified matter.</note>. 

Themis is the sister of Theia, the offspring of the same mother; or rather she is the same, but from another perspective. She sits beside Jupiter and grants to each their own, so that in the bed of love the husband may not prevail over the wife, nor the wife over the husband. When that conjunction <note>A technical term in alchemy for the chemical or spiritual union of opposites, often symbolized as a marriage.</note> is completed, she herself hands over the seat of the oracle to Phoebus <note>Apollo.</note>, as to one more worthy. 

Furthermore, there is another consideration of Themis. For the number five <term>quinarius<gloss>the number five</gloss></term> is sacred to her, which we have discussed extensively above. # THE WORKS OF JACOB TOLLIUS
<page-num>178</page-num>
<header>JACOB TOLLIUS</header>
<sig>M</sig>
<meta>catchword: Prin- (The beginning of the next page likely refers to "Principles")</meta>

...is introduced by Basilius Valentinus in his eleventh key <note>Basilius Valentinus was a legendary 15th-century alchemist. His "Twelve Keys" describe the sequence of the alchemical Great Work; the Eleventh Key specifically deals with the multiplication of the Stone through "marriage" or union.</note>. Let him who understands, understand. A great secret has been revealed here.

<margin>page 374.</margin>
O sister, O spouse—of these things we must say what Plutarch says of Isis and Osiris: <note>Tollius is drawing a parallel between the chemical union of substances and the divine marriage of the Egyptian gods.</note> "And so one must think of her [Isis] as always partaking of the male [Osiris], and being joined with him through a love for the good and beautiful things associated with him, just as it is lawful and just for a man to love in justice." <note>original: "Οὕτω δὲ διανοεῖσθαι χρῆ καὶ ταύτην τοῦ ἀνδρὸς μεταλαγχάνουσαν ἀεὶ, καὶ συνέσαν ἔρωτι τῶν περὶ ἐκεῖνον ἀγαθῶν καὶ καλῶν, ὥσπερ ἄνδρα νόμιμόν ἐσι, καὶ δίκαιον ἐρᾶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ."</note> From this "fraternal marriage," which was not correctly understood, that perverse custom of marriage between brothers and sisters was born among the Egyptians; it seems possible that this, along with several other Egyptian sacred rites, passed over to the Athenians.

They are of a "cousinly origin," most truly. For **Acid** and **Alkali** are born from the same parents. <note>In 17th-century chemistry, the reaction between acids and alkalis was seen as a foundational "marriage" or combat between opposing principles that resulted in a neutral salt.</note>

Now the very dangers join them; they are themselves the reduction into a **regulus** <note>The *regulus* is the pure metallic heart or "button" found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting, often considered a "lesser king" in the alchemical process.</note>.

*There is no trust in a certain life*, because they can do nothing, being not yet sufficiently cooked out and fixed, nor yet capable of generating.

Clouds still terrify the mind; even now there is some external combustible sulfur present in the regulus, which must be expelled again through fire. <note>original: Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book 5, lines 92–96. Tollius uses this famous Epicurean poem to introduce the idea of the world's eventual physical dissolution.</note>

<margin>verse 42, book 4, *On the Gods*, in Servius's commentary on the 4th Eclogue.</margin>
Servius, in his commentary on Virgil’s *Sixth Eclogue*, says: *It should certainly be known that both through the flood and through conflagration, a change of the ages is signified.* <note>Servius was a 4th-century grammarian whose commentaries on Virgil often preserved older Roman religious and philosophical lore.</note> The things reported by Nigidius are remarkable: *Certain people,* he says, *distinguished the Gods and their kinds by times and ages:* (this passage is to be supplemented thus) among whom was Orpheus. First was the kingdom of Saturn, then of Jupiter; then of Neptune, and after that of Pluto: *some also say, as the Magi (that is, the Chemists) tell us, that the kingdom of Apollo is to come.* <note>Nigidius Figulus was a Roman scholar and Pythagorean. And the Stoics say rightly (provided we understand them as we should) that in the <term>apokatastasis</term> <gloss>the restoration or renewal of the universe</gloss> of the world after this conflagration, seeds fall from heaven, by which the human race is restored. For our HUMANITY is born from a heavenly seed, and what Virgil flatteringly attributed to the son of Pollio truly applies to it:

> Now a new generation is sent down from high HEAVEN:
<note>original: Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, line 7. This poem was famously interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of Christ, but Tollius reads it as a description of the alchemical "new man" or perfected substance.</note>

<margin>Eclogue 4.</margin>
Indeed, man is the most perfect image of the universe. Basilius Valentinus says: *Now concerning this seed, which works upon the metals, understand it thus: a certain celestial influence is sent down from on high by divine will, and being mixed with the properties of the Stars, from this marriage a third thing is born, which is of an earthly essence. And this is the beginning of our seed, and its first origin. From those three come forth the elements, which then, with the Aetnean fire <note>original: "igne Aetnæo." This refers to the subterranean fire of Mount Etna, used here as a metaphor for the intense, steady heat of the alchemist's furnace.</note> driving them, give birth to a perfect body.* This seed is the Mercurial, Neptunian spirit, which, when mixed with the sulfurous Jovial spirit, falls into the Plutonian womb of the earth (or of the salt), and there it is nourished and grows.

...until he is formed into a **Chemical Man**, and comes forth into the light by birth. You will find more things pertaining to this in the same author's <note>Referring to the author mentioned on the previous page, likely Gerhard Dorn or a similar Paracelsian writer.</note> Chapter 6, *On Natural and Supernatural Things*, and in Sendivogius, <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a famous Polish alchemist known for his theory of "the food of life" in the air.</note> Treatise 6 of the *New Chemical Light*. To this pertain the Orgies and <term>initiation rites <note>Greek: *teletai*</note></term> of the ancients, and the purifications by water and fire. "Now every purification is threefold," says Servius; <margin>On *Aeneid* VI.</margin> *For either souls are purified in the **Earth**, those which have been too greatly weighed down by filth, devoted namely to bodily charms—that is, they pass into earthly (that is, **Saline**) bodies; and these are said to be purified by **Fire** (the infernal fire of Etna, the punisher of Typhon), for fire is from the earth, by which all things are burned away. Or in **Water**; that is, they pass into marine bodies (into **Mercurial** bodies, like Glaucus and Palaemon), if they lived a little better. This we also read in Statius where he treats of auguries. Hence also in all sacred rites there are those three purifications. For they are purified either with torches and sulfur, or they are washed with water, or they are fanned by air; which was the case in the rites of Liber [Bacchus].* For this is what he says in the second book of the *Georgics*:

->And for you<-
->They hang soft **MASKS** <note>original: *oscilla*. These were small ritual masks or figures of Bacchus hung from trees to swing in the wind, believed to purify the air and grant fertility to whatever direction they faced.</note> from the tall **PINE** tree.<-

For it was a kind of purification: and in the purifications themselves he followed the order of good merits, so that he spoke of the purification of air first, then of water, and finally of fire.

Let the fair reader now judge, who knows the preparation of the **Starry Regulus**, <note>The "Starry Regulus" of antimony is a crystalline metallic substance that forms a star-like pattern on its surface as it cools. In alchemy, it was considered a crucial "signature" of the celestial influence on matter.</note> whether anything more true could have been said. But every cause for doubting will be removed if those things which Ovid sang concerning the **Palilia** <note>The Palilia was an ancient Roman agricultural festival held on April 21, aimed at cleansing sheep and shepherds.</note> are compared. <margin>Book 4 of the *Fasti*.</margin> This poem is no less full of mysteries than is this fable of the flood; where among other things:

>Turning yourself toward the **EAST** [the Rising].
>Say it **THREE TIMES**, and wash your hands in **LIVING DEW**.
>Then, with a wooden bowl placed there like a **MIXING BOWL** [KRATER]...

You drink snow-white milk, and PURPLE **boiled wine**. <note>Original Latin: *sapam*. Sapa was a thick syrup made by boiling down grape juice, used as a sweetener or preservative.</note>

Devouring fire purges ALL things, and it cooks the vice out of METALS.
For that reason, it purges SHEEP with their LEADER. <note>In the original Ovidian context, the "leader" is the shepherd; in Tollius's alchemical reading, this likely refers to a "leading" or "primary" metal or agent in the crucible.</note>

*Are two discordant gods, FIRE and WATER;*
*The fathers joined the Elements: and thought it fit*
*To touch the body with fires and scattered water?*
*Or because the cause of LIFE is in these; the EXILE has lost these:* <note>Ancient Roman law punished exiles by "forbidding them fire and water," effectively cutting them off from the community.</note>
*By these a NEW WIFE is made; they think these two things GREAT?* <note>Traditional Roman wedding rites involved the bride touching fire and water as symbols of the domestic hearth and life.</note>
*I scarcely believe it: there are those who believe PHAETHON is referred to,* <note>Phaethon was the son of the Sun-god who scorched the earth when he lost control of the solar chariot; he represents the destructive power of fire.</note>
*And the excessive WATERS of DEUCALION, etc.* <note>Deucalion was the survivor of the great flood in Greek mythology, representing the destructive power of water.</note>

I am often accustomed to wonder, when I read these and other things of this kind, that the Ancients so ignored the treasure which they possessed. So much so that I might deservedly assign to them the same complaint that Phaedrus assigns to the rooster; which I will correct in this very work:

> *What a great thing, he says, you lie in an unworthy place!*
> *Oh, if someone eager for your value had seen you,*
> *Long ago you would have returned to the greatest splendor.*
> *But because I found you, I for whom food is much more preferable,*
> *Neither can anything benefit you, nor can you benefit me.*
<note>Tollius is referencing Phaedrus's famous fable of the Rooster and the Pearl. A rooster finds a precious pearl in a dungheap but wishes it were a grain of corn instead. Tollius argues that the ancient poets (the "rooster") held the "pearl" of alchemical secrets in their verses without understanding their true worth.</note>

<margin>Plato, in the *Timaeus*.</margin>
Rightly therefore did that Egyptian priest say that the Greeks were always children: <note>In Plato's *Timaeus*, a priest of Sais tells the Greek statesman Solon, "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old Greek," referring to their lack of ancient tradition and scientific memory compared to the Egyptians.</note> and that very thing could deservedly be proclaimed about the Latins, who received almost all their knowledge from the Greeks.

# THE WORKS OF JACOBUS TOLLIUS

<page-num>182</page-num>
<header>JACOBUS TOLLIUS</header>

"What is for you if without me, since one without the other can achieve nothing." <note>This likely refers to the "Chemical Wedding" or the necessary union of opposites in alchemy.</note> Therefore, just as that masculine, sulfurous, and hot spirit is extinguished, it is necessary that the feminine, mercurial, and moist spirit undergoes the same fate, and returns into the deep, or the "sea of the philosophers," from whence it had come forth. <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active/male principle and Mercury the passive/female principle; their "death" and return to a primal state is a stage in the transmutation process.</note>

"Oh, if only I could!"—this is that solemn vow of the fathers, namely that desire for propagating by whose power man becomes immortal while he is reborn in his children.

By paternal arts, Deucalion is fashioned to have been the son of Prometheus, who first fashioned men from mud. Prometheus, however, is *the Word ordering all things, and the overseeing Providence.* <note>Original Greek: ὁ λόγος ἐστὶ πάντα κοσμῶν, καὶ πρόνοια ἐπιτροπεύουσα.</note> Cornutus interprets him as *the mistress of the soul of the universe,* <note>Original Greek: τοῦ δὲ τῇ τῶν ὅλων ψυχῇ κυρίαν. Cornutus was a Stoic philosopher known for allegorizing myths.</note> *which the younger philosophers called Providence.* <note>Original Greek: ἣν οἱ νεώτεροι πρόνοιαν ἐκάλεσαν.</note> Furthermore, this same Prometheus is the same as Jupiter. Concerning the "Mud," more will be said later regarding the fable of Peleus and Thetis.

*And he fashions souls from the shaped earth below,* <note>Tollius is quoting or paraphrasing various commentaries on the creation of man.</note> Servius in his commentary on Virgil’s *Eclogue IV* writes: *Prometheus, the son of Iapetus and Clymene, is said to have ascended to heaven with the help of MINERVA after humans were made by him; and having applied a torch to the wheel of the SUN, he stole fire, which he showed to humans.* I shall spare my efforts here and be briefer, for there are otherwise many things which could be profitably said concerning the help of Minerva, the ascent into heaven, the torch, the wheel of the sun, and the showing of fire to men. But a word to the wise is enough. <note>Original Latin: *sapienti verbum sat est*. This is a common phrase in alchemical texts, suggesting that the "true" meaning is hidden and only intended for the initiated.</note>

*So it seemed to those above,* to heaven, or to the celestial spirit, from which help comes.

*And we remain as examples of men,* because while they were living, they were dead—*living corpses.* <note>Original Greek: ἔμψυχοι νεκροὶ. This refers to the state of "philosophical death" or the *nigredo* stage in alchemy where the matter is dark and inert.</note> For they were at rest.
<margin>In Camilla page 139.</margin>
For rest (which is the opinion of Heraclitus found in Plutarch) is proper to the dead. *But generation is either a kind of motion, or at least occurs with motion,* as found in the same author. <note>Original Greek: Κίνησις δέ τις, ἢ σὺν κινήσει πάντως ἡ γένεσις.</note>

<summary>Tollius interprets the myth of Prometheus and Deucalion as an alchemical allegory for the creation of "life" in the crucible, identifying Prometheus with the Divine Word and the necessary infusion of celestial "fire" (sulfur) into the "mud" (mercury).</summary>

<margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 357.</margin>
The same is read elsewhere in Plutarch. Let these things be compared with the eleventh key of Basil Valentine. <note>Basil Valentine was a legendary 15th-century alchemist; his "Twelve Keys" are a series of allegorical descriptions of the steps to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

"**He had spoken, and they were weeping**," <note>Original: *Dixerat, & flebant*. A quote from Ovid describing Deucalion and Pyrrha’s despair after the flood.</note> there will doubtless be many who will judge this to be a mere poetic flourish. I once thought so myself; now I feel differently, and I believe this "weeping" is not much different from the weeping of Isis at the fountain. <note>In alchemy, weeping or "tears" often symbolize the process of liquefaction or the "mercurial water" released during the breakdown of matter.</note>

"**It pleased them to pray to the heavens**," <note>Original: *Placuit cæleste precari*.</note> this is most excellent, for new life comes to the Chemical man from heaven: from there comes that angelic happiness which Basil discusses in his keys. However, Apollodorus does not record that Deucalion betook himself to the oracle of Themis, but rather that he sacrificed to Jupiter Phyxius <note>Jupiter as the "God of Escape" or "Protector of Fugitives."</note>, who sent Mercury to him. One may compare this to Basil’s "winged sun," which is discussed in the eleventh key. <note>The winged sun often represents the volatile principle or "philosophical mercury" that has been purified.</note>

"**Through the sacred lots**," <note>Original: *Per sacras sortes*.</note> the Chemical art is obscure if ever there was one, and it cannot be understood without divine revelation.

"**There is no delay**," <note>Original: *Nulla mora est*.</note> one must press on in the work. This reflects that precept of the adepts <note>An "adept" is someone who has mastered the secrets of alchemy.</note>: that one must not cease the work once it has been started.

<margin>Vitruvius, Book 8, Ch. 3. Diodorus, Book 1, Ch. 4.</margin>
"**The Cephisian waves**," <note>Original: *Cephisidas undas*. Referring to the river Cephisus.</note> *kephos* <note>Original Greek: κῆφος</note> signifies "silver" to the Greeks. <note>Tollius is using a creative etymology here to link the river to the purification of metals.</note> And the river Cephisus makes sheep white, just as the Melas, rising from the same lake, makes them black. It is said, moreover, to carry a great deal of "fat earth" or mud, so that it may be compared in this regard to the Achelous and the Nile. I shall ignore the Hebrew etymology here, although it is not foreign to truth and nature itself. In our work, however, the Cephisus is the Alkaline spirit: moist, cold, and carrying much "fatness" <note>In alchemy, "fatness" or "unctuosity" refers to the sulfurous or oily principle that allows substances to bond and become fertile.</note> by which our earth is rendered more fertile.

"**Then when they were tasted**," <note>Original: *Inde ubi libatos*. Referring to the ritual sprinkling of water.</note> that is, when the material has been imbued with that spirit...

# CHANCE OBSERVATIONS
<page-num>185</page-num>
<header>FORTUITOUS OBSERVATIONS</header>
<sig>M 5</sig>

...I shall first trace this story of Deucalion back to its Syrian nurse, and from her to its Egyptian parents; having first added this: that the **veiling of the head** <note>original: *velationem illam capitis*</note> which is commanded by the goddess Themis, the **loosening of garments** <note>original: *vestium recinctum*</note>, and the **bones of the mother** <note>original: *ossaque matris*</note>—along with the act of throwing them behind one's back—contain the entire mystery of **multiplication** <note>The alchemical stage where the power or quantity of the Philosopher's Stone is increased.</note>, which can be uncovered and revealed by comparing it to the eleventh key of **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary alchemist; his 11th key involves the "multiplication" of the Stone through symbolic "marriage" and "regeneration."</note>. Furthermore, that rite of adoring the gods with a veiled head could seem to me to have drawn its origin from here, the cause of which is sought in vain from elsewhere. For I am not troubled by the authority of **Virgil** <note>The Roman poet Publius Virgilius Maro.</note>, where Aeneas is commanded:

<margin>Aeneid, Book III.</margin>
> To veil your hair, covered with a **PURPLE** cloak.
> *Lest any hostile face appear among the holy FIRES in honor of the Gods,*
> *And disturb the omen.*

Thus, however, it should be read there *as an omen* <note>original: *pro omina*</note>. Although, when I look at the matter correctly, this reasoning also seems **Chemical** <note>alchemical</note>.
