# JACOBUS TOLLIUS

*Teaching that the great Earth hangs in the space of the air;*
*and that earth cannot stand upon earth.*
<note>original: *Aeris in spatio magnam pendere docentes / Tellurem; neque posse in terra sistere terram.* These lines argue against the idea of a flat earth resting on a physical foundation, suggesting instead a planet suspended in a void.</note>

And these things are indeed believed, but it is not the true reasoning.
<margin>On Virgil's Aeneid, Book 1</margin> Regarding the chariot of Juno, **Servius** <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century Grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil.</note> says: *It is certain that Juno possesses chariots. Furthermore, it is established that this is the case from the sacred rites of the people of Tibur <note>Modern-day Tivoli.</note>; where they pray thus: Juno Curitis <note>A title for Juno as a protectress of the "curiae" or divisions of the people, often depicted with a spear and shield.</note>, protect the home-born servants of this assembly with your chariot and shield.* For I would prefer to read this passage in this way, rather than as it is commonly read: *The home-born servants of the assembly are for the entrance, managing the care of the temples.* For a *Curia* is a temple, because it exists only in a place inaugurated by augury, as we learn from the same author elsewhere.

<margin>On Aeneid, Book VII, line 174.</margin> <note>Tollius here translates or quotes a passage describing a statue of the Syrian Goddess, often identified as Juno/Hera, from Lucian's *De Dea Syria*.</note> And indeed, the image of Jupiter looks in every way like Jupiter: the head, the eyes, and the throne. But Juno displays a multifaceted form. While the whole work is accurately called Juno, she possesses something of Athena, Aphrodite, Selene, Rhea, Artemis, Nemesis, and the Fates. In one hand she holds a scepter, and in the other a spindle; on her head she wears rays, a tower, and a girdle <note>original: *keston* (the cestus), a magical belt usually associated with Aphrodite that made the wearer irresistible.</note>, with which they adorn only the Celestial Goddess. On the outside, she is covered in gold and very precious stones. Some of these are white, some the color of water, and many are the color of fire. 

The fact that he says the head, face, and seat of Jupiter are recognized immediately refers to the property of the **ethereal spirit**, which is recognized instantly because it never changes. **Homer** also joined the head and the eyes; where he says of Agamemnon: *His eyes and head like Zeus who delights in thunder.* <note>original: *Ὄμματά καὶ κεφαλὴν ἴκελος Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ* (Iliad 2.478).</note> Hence there is also a temple to him at Lacedaemon [Sparta], dedicated to *Agamemnon Zeus*, as **Tzetzes** <note>original: *Tretres*; likely a typo for Joannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine philologist.</note> teaches in his commentary on Lycophron. # THE WORKS OF JACOBUS TOLLIUS

Aëtius Cornutus <note>A Stoic philosopher of the 1st century AD who wrote on Greek mythology.</note> states: **"He is the ruler over the first and archetypal essence of the world."** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ ἀρχηγός ἐσι τῆς πρώτης καὶ ἀρχετύπε ἐσίας τοῦ κόσμου</note> The *Cestus* <term>Cestus: The magic girdle or belt of Venus/Aphrodite, which had the power to excite love.</term> was sought from the belongings of Venus. For this reason, Juno, intending to thoroughly warm her Jupiter, in the works of Homer:

->**"Sought the warm Cestus from the bosom of Venus."**<-

However, this **Cestus** is not what the most learned Rigaltius <note>Nicolas Rigault (1577–1654), a French classical scholar.</note> considers it to be in his notes on the military strategies of Onosander—namely, some kind of tunic. Rather, it is that attractive or magnetic force by which she:

->**"Poured around him as he lay back with her holy body"**<- <note>A reference to Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, describing Venus embracing Mars.</note>

soothes and caresses her Mars. If we were to call this force the **Iynx** <note>original: *Iÿnga*. In Greek mythology, a magic spinning wheel or a bird used in love charms.</note> of Theocritus, or even the **"inclining fore-gate"** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλινόν πρόφυλον (*ekklinon prophylon*). A term from Michael Psellus, a Byzantine polymath, referring to a point of transition or attraction in Neoplatonic thought.</note> mentioned by Psellus, or the **Hippomanes** <term>Hippomanes: A substance associated with horses, used in ancient times as a powerful ingredient in love potions, mentioned by Virgil.</term> of Virgil, we would not be mistaken.

Our philosophers call Love a **magnet**, which not only sends out rays from the center to the circumference in every direction to give life to all things, but also, by a magical virtue and a kinship of natures, draws them back. It recalls them from the circumference to the center and joins these irradiated bodies in a mutual embrace. In this circuit, penetrating all things, it turns them up and down in a continuous motion and drives them in a circle.

Hence, Love itself was compared by the ancients to a **circle**; and hence also the **girdle**, or **Cestus** of Venus, of which it is said: **"wherein there is love, and desire, and seductive speech."** <note>original Greek: ἔν’ θ’ ἔνι μὲν φιλότης, ἐνδ’ ἵμερος, ἐν δ’ ὀαριστύς — Homer, *Iliad* 14.216.</note> This girdle is fashioned as **variegated** <note>original Greek: ποικίλος (*poikilos*)</note> or diverse, most suitably matching nature, according to the varying account of magnetism.

Because of this perpetual <margin>II Kings 17</margin> motion, that God of the Hivites <note>Referring to the Avvites, a people mentioned in the Bible.</note> mentioned in the Sacred Books was called **Thartak**. He is the Sun, who surveys the circle of the world in his constant circuit; the name comes from *rathaq* <note>original Hebrew: רתק</note>, meaning **"to survey by going around in a circle,"** and *rathaq*, **"to bind,"** from which comes *rattuq* <note>original Hebrew: רתוק</note>, meaning a **"chain"** or **"girdle."** The Jews, mocking this and alluding to the origin of the name... <note>The page ends here; the catchword "ludentes" suggests the next page continues with "mocking/playing."</note>

<summary>Tollius interprets Venus's magic girdle (the Cestus) as a symbol for a universal magnetic force that binds and vivifies the cosmos. He links this "magnetic love" to classical magic charms and the biblical sun-god Thartak through creative etymology.</summary>

We have just now attributed this sign to Deucalion: but as far as the name bestowed by the Syrians is concerned, anyone will easily recognize that it has been corrupted from the Phoenician word *Samajim* <note>original: *Samajim*, the Hebrew/Phoenician word for "Heavens" (*Shamayim*).</note>. This was rightly explained by them regarding the beard: that by it, the perfect and virile power of Apollo is indicated. <meta>This page continues Tollius’s exploration of the alchemical meanings hidden within ancient mythology and seasonal cycles. ->JACOBUS TOLLIUS<-

"For spring," as Plutarch says, "is blooming, fertile, and pleasant" <note>original Greek: Τὸ γὰρ ἔαρ... θαλερὸν καὶ γόνιμον, καὶ προσηνές</note>. For this reason, a festival was celebrated by the Egyptians at the new moon in the month of Phamenoth (which corresponds to our March); they called this the "entry of Osiris into the Moon." Virgil also writes:

<margin>Book II of the *Georgics*</margin>
> *In spring the earth swells, and demands the seeds of life:*
> *Then the almighty father, the Sky, descends with fertile showers*
> *Into the lap of his joyful spouse.*

In this passage, "to swell" <note>Latin: *tumere*</note> means "to be in heat" <note>original Greek: ὀργᾶν</note>, which Hesychius interprets as "to desire intensely" <note>original Greek: ἐπιτεταμένως ἐπιθυμεῖν</note>. But the Chemists <note>Alchemists</note> also seek the beginning of their work from this point. Indeed, even learned men have considered that the creation of the "greater world" <note>the macrocosm or universe</note> began in its own "spring," but was finally completed in "autumn"; hence the beginning of the Jewish civil year is in autumn. 

Certainly, the Chemical World is perfected in autumn—that celebrated Stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>, whose birth we do not limit to the ninth or tenth month (following the example of the "lesser world" <note>the human fetus</note>). Instead, we regulate it by the lyre of Orpheus. In that lyre, although there are only **seven** strings, the harmony of the **nine** circles is completed by the Muses, with Phoebus, the Leader of the Muses, presiding—as we already stated in Chapter IV. 

Nor is it of no significance that that Egyptian festival was called the "pyre" <note>original Greek: πυρὰ</note> or "torch" <note>original Greek: λαμπὰς</note>, since the beginning of the work comes from fire. Nor is it in vain that in our author Lucian—as in Ovid’s account of Latona—*there is a stone altar in the middle of a lake, crowned with garlands, and warm with burning incense.* For that altar is a symbol of the "fixed fire" lurking in the midst of the still-confused world <note>the *massa confusa* or initial chaotic state of alchemical matter</note>. We discussed this earlier in this very chapter, and also in another where we treated Latona. You may also find these "garlands" <note>Latin: *ferta*</note> mentioned in the story of Pandora, whom Pallas <note>Athena</note> crowned with a wreath of various flowers. 

But as for Juno entering the lake—

### CHANCE REMARKS.

What is permitted to the gods is not permitted to Jupiter <note>a play on the proverb *Quod licet Jovi, non licet bovi*—what is allowed to a leader is not allowed to a commoner</note>, lest he look upon the **Fishes** <note>The zodiac sign Pisces</note> first; and this is drawn from the innermost secrets of the Art: lest the spirits be burned up, or the volatiles be driven out, if they are exposed too suddenly to the heat of the fire without the aid of a protecting moist **Alkali** <term>Alkali: a basic substance used in alchemy to "fix" or hold volatile substances</term>, into which they might retreat. Regarding the former: **Venus**, when she was fleeing from **Typhon**, was transformed into a fish. On **Atergatis** the Half-fish, one should consult **Selden** <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a polymath who wrote on Syrian deities</note>; on **Nemesis**, see **Athenaeus**, Book 8, page 334. <margin>On Isis and Osiris.</margin>
For onions are airy and corrosive spirits; and for this reason they were so hated by the Egyptian priests that they always abstained from them. The reason added by Plutarch is also valid: that this plant alone flourishes and grows while the **Moon** is waning. We can also affirm this regarding the sharp **Sulfurous** spirits in our own work. For it is the Moon that restrains them, as we hinted at above when discussing the river Cephisus. # JACOBUS TOLLIUS

<margin>Book II.</margin>...unfolded the fable [of Isis and Osiris], he says that he cut out some of the harsher parts, such as those found in **Diodorus Siculus** <note>Diodorus Siculus was a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note>, regarding **Osiris** being torn limb from limb and **Isis** being decapitated. He adds: *“Therefore, that we must spit out and (as Aeschylus says) cleanse the mouth, if they believe and say these things about the blessed and incorruptible nature—the very essence of the divine—as if they truly happened and occurred, I need say no more to you.”* <note>original Greek: Ὅτι μὲν οὖν, εἰ ταῦτα περὶ τῆς μακαρίας καὶ ἀφθάρτου φύσεως, καθ’ ἣν μάλιστα νοεῖται τὸ θεῖον, ὡς ἀληθῶς πραχθέντα καὶ συμπισόντα δοξάζουσι καὶ λέγουσιν, ἀποπτύσαι δεῖ, καὶ καθηήρασθαι τὸ στόμα κατ’ Αἰσχύλον, οὐδὲν δεῖ λέγειν πρός σε.</note> 

From this, it seems abundantly clear to me that this fable was not invented by the wisest men merely to involve the history of the creation of the universe and the knowledge of the Supreme Being in such intricate and obscure riddles to keep them from the eyes of the common people (even though participation in such things is of the greatest interest for the glory of the Divine and the practice of piety). Rather, it was done so that they might preserve the true knowledge of the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Philosophicus Lapis: the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting immortality</term> safe, hidden, and uncorrupted for themselves and the fellow-initiates <note>original: *symmystae*</note> of their order. 

Thus, of all the philosophers who are said to have come to them from Greece in ancient times, none besides **Homer** and **Pythagoras** seem to have been made partakers of so great a secret. In the case of Pythagoras, his "golden thigh," his symbols, and his five-year vow of silence prove this; in the case of Homer, it is proven by the divine work woven into his fables—indeed, even the entire plot of the **Trojan War**. 

But to return to the purpose: this fable of **Plutarch** concerning Isis and Osiris is too long for the whole of it to be conveniently described here. I will, therefore, extract the principal points in which a miraculous harmony with the fables of the Greeks is observed, even if they seem very different. From the secret union of **Rhea** with **Saturn**, five gods are imagined to have been born on five consecutive days: **Osiris** was the first; on the second...

**Aroveris** <note>Also known as the Elder Horus</note>, is called by some **Apollo**, or the elder **Orus**; then **Typhon**; fourth is **Isis**; fifth is **Nephthys**, who is also called **Venus**, and **the End**, and **Victory**. **Rhea’s** husband is imagined to be the **Sun**, and **Mercury** likewise lay with her: so that **Osiris** and **Aroveris** are said to be sons of the Sun, **Isis** the daughter of Mercury, and **Typhon** and **Nephthys** the children of **Saturn**. These matters are explained physically <note>Meaning through natural philosophy or the laws of nature</note> <margin>p. 375.</margin> by **Plutarch** himself: but their alchemical <note>original: *Chemica*</note> explanation will be immediately obvious to anyone who considers the nature of each parent. 

For just as the **Sun** is the god of heat and dryness, so **Saturn** is the God of cold <margin>Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* Book 1, lines 12 & 335.</margin> and of rains; and he makes these most heavy when in the sign of Capricorn. **Mercury**, being androgynous <note>original Greek: ἀνδρόγυνος; possessing both male and female qualities</note>, is the intermediate air, participating in both heat and cold, dryness and moisture; he is the glue and bond of both—the Egyptian **Anubis**, the "defining circle" <note>original Greek: ὁ ὁρίζων κύκλος; referring to the horizon where different states meet</note>. Where **Osiris** was born, a voice was heard at the same time: *“The Lord of all things comes forth into the light.”* 

This **Osiris** of ours is **Deucalion** <note>The hero of the Greek flood myth</note>; **Isis** (or *Iseha*) is the Heroine, **Pyrrha** <note>The wife of Deucalion</note>. **Deucalion** is the son of **Prometheus**, while **Osiris** is the son of the Sun, "who possesses an all-seeing eternal eye" <note>original Greek: τοῦ πανδερκὲς ἔχοντος αἰώνιον ὄμμα</note>; *He who sees all, and through whom the earth sees all things, the eye of the WORLD.* <margin>Onomacritus in the Hymns.</margin> <margin>Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book IV.</margin> He is also renowned by other titles; **Isis** was born of **Mercury**... she is volatile <note>original: *volatilis*; in alchemy, a substance that easily vaporizes</note>, just like him, to whose feet the ancients added winged sandals. The **Sun** received the surname of **Prometheus**, "since the constitution of the world was suitably disposed toward this at the beginning" <note>original Greek: ἐπιτηδείως πρὸς τοῦτο ἐχούσης κατ’ ἀρχὰς τῆς τοῦ κόσμου συστάσεως</note>: as stated in the works of **Cornutus**.

...of the **bearing of palm branches** <note>original: *βαϊοφορίας* (baiophorias)</note>, and so on, regarding the rites. We have treated above the subject of **Bacchus *of the trees*** <note>original: *δενδρίτῃ* (dendritē)</note>, as well as **Pan *of the forest***, a title by which **Hercules** is also known. However, **Linen** <note>original: *Linum*</note> actually signifies **Alkali**; for "flax grows from the immortal earth and yields an edible fruit (that is, a **volatile alkaline spirit** <term>A "spirit" in alchemy refers to a highly reactive or vaporous substance; "alkaline" suggests it acts as a base in chemical reactions</term>), and it provides a simple and clean garment, not heavy upon the wearer, and well-suited for every hour and season. It is, as they say, the least likely to breed lice." This last phrase, once added, is enough to open the eyes of even the blind. For who is ignorant of what "to destroy" <note>original: *φθείρειν* (phtheirein)</note> means to the Greeks, what "lice" <note>original: *φθεῖρες* (phtheires)</note> are, and from where they are generated? It is not necessary to explain at length that new linen clothes are sought after by them; therefore, these **"lice"** mentioned here are **corroding spirits**, smoky vapors, which must be absent from our work, as they would surely corrupt it. I believe it is now clear why the followers of **Isis** are called "linen-wearers." In those rituals, there were also **libations** <note>original: *χοαὶ* (choai)</note>, which are **nourishing rains** sent down from heaven to water the earth. Hence that line from the Poet:

> We pour in foaming bowls of warm milk.

For that entire rite of the underworld comes from the Egyptians, as does every libation used in sacred ceremonies. **Apuleius** says that **Milk** was poured to **Isis** from a golden vessel rounded in the shape of a breast. <margin>Book 11, *The Golden Ass*</margin> **Diodorus** records that three hundred and sixty-five urns used to be filled daily with **Milk** by the priests in honor of **Osiris**. <margin>Book 1, ch. 2</margin> To the **Muses**, it was customary to offer **Milk** and water, according to **Varro** in the writings of **Servius**; to the **Nymphs**, **Milk** and oil; and a shepherd in **Theocritus** promises he will offer **Milk** and honey to **Pan**. <margin>On Virgil's *Eclogue* 7</margin> **Triptolemus** was nourished with divine **Milk** by **Ceres**, as found in **Hyginus**. <margin>fable 147</margin> **Ovid** writes in the sixth book of the *Fasti*:

> Bountiful Ceres abstains; and she gives you, boy,
> causes of sleep <note>Poppy seeds or juice</note> to be drunk with warm **Milk**.

<summary>This page interprets the use of linen and milk in ancient religious rites as alchemical metaphors, specifically equating linen with alkali and "lice" with corrosive impurities. The author argues that classical offerings (milk, honey, oil) represent specific stages or substances in the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

# JACOB TOLLIUS

<margin>Anthology on the God.</margin>Antipater commands that milk and honey be poured in libation to **Mercury**:
> "Be favorable, Hermes, to the shepherds. One who rejoices in milk and the pouring of honey from the oak." <note>original: *Εὔχολο- ἑρμείας, ἴο ποιμλύες. ἐν δὲ γάλακτι / Χαίρων, καὶ δρυΐνῳ σπενδόμενο- μέλιτι.*</note>

<margin>Ovid, *Fasti* Book IV.</margin>The offerings to **Pales** <note>The Roman goddess of shepherds and livestock</note> and **Cybele** were made with milk. Now, all milk is full of spirit, and is a **Symbol of the fatness of the earth** <note>original: *Symbolum pinguedinis terræ*</note>, which is born in the udders of the earth, or is preserved from decay by the **Salt of nature** <term>A fundamental alchemical principle thought to preserve and give form to substances</term>. So says **Sendivogius** <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist</note>. Our **Basil** <note>Basil Valentine, a legendary alchemical author</note> also has some things to say about milk in various places, where he compares it to our work, and from it he extracts cream, cheese, and **whey** <note>original: *Serum*</note>.
<margin>Tract 10.</margin>

Furthermore, **Plutarch** mentions the serpent **Cneph** <note>An Egyptian deity often depicted as a winged serpent or creator god</note>, about which you may see **Porphyry** in the writings of **Eusebius**. This serpent is a symbol of **the All** <note>original: *τοῦ παντὸς* (tou pantos)</note>. Indeed, what he says regarding the colors—**Osiris's black**, **Horus's white**, and **Typhon's red**—is easily understood by anyone, provided they are not a complete stranger to chemical books. For the chemists say that every **moisture** in their work is **black**, and must be drawn out by the power of fire: but where **dryness** dominates because all moisture has been consumed, **whiteness** <term>Known in alchemy as the *albedo* stage, representing purification and the "White Stone"</term> is born. This is **Apollo**, born on the second day. Now, beneath all whiteness, **redness** lies hidden. "**Whatever is white on the outside is red on the inside**," says **John Isaac Holland** <note>A 15th-century Dutch alchemist</note>; and "whatever is white on the outside, **Typhon** <note>In alchemy, Typhon often represents the violent, 'combustive' aspect of the process</note> is truly the fiery effervescence of the red color": because through him the work is brought to maturity. These are the riddles of our art. Therefore, **Osiris** will soon become **Pluto**, equipped with the three-headed **Cerberus**; he is also **Serapis** and **Bacchus**, "**when he changed his nature**" <note>original: *ὅτε τὴν φύσιν μετέβαλε* (hote tēn physin metebale)</note>. However, **Plutarch** errs gravely when he refuses to believe the Phrygian writings which revealed **Charopon**—that is, Ovid's **Pyrrha**, the daughter of **Hercules**—and **Typhon** as the son of the Isiac Hercules. For **Hercules** is the same as **Pluto**, the **Sun**, **Jupiter**, and so on.

Regarding this, Servius also offers some commentary on Virgil. In the same way, he wrongly accuses Phylarchus of error—erring himself—who had recorded that Bacchus brought two bulls from India (that is, from **fiery salt** <term>In alchemy, "India" often symbolizes the source of a specific mineral salt, and "fiery salt" refers to a reactive chemical agent</term>), which were two "fiery spirits," namely Apis and Serapis. For later, he compares Bacchus—or Dionysus—to Osiris, describing him as **animal-shaped** <note>original: *ζωόμορφον* (zōomorphon)</note>, appearing with a **bull's foot** <note>original: *ποδὶ βοείῳ* (podi boeiō)</note>, and **bull-born** <note>original: *βουγενῆ* (bougenē)</note>, asserting they are one and the same. Here now we have the bull upon which Jupiter sat in the temple of the Syrian Goddess. Here are the related bulls of Neptune, from which he is called "the Bellower" <note>original: *μυκητὴς* (mykētēs)</note>; from this it is clear why black bulls were sacrificed to him. Related also is the calf of Mercury and the cow of Minerva. Whence Ovid says:

<margin>Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book IV.</margin>
> *For three gods he builds as many altars of turf:*

> *A calf to the wing-footed one; a bull for you, highest of the Gods.*
<note>Minerva is the "warlike Maiden" and Mercury is the "wing-footed one."</note>

And who is he who builds these altars? Perseus, begotten from a golden shower, whom we shall later show to be a symbol of the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>The legendary substance capable of perfecting matter and transmuting base metals into gold</term>. Who would not stand struck with wonder at this consensus of myths fabricated by the Greeks, Syrians, or Phoenicians, and Egyptians? But let us add a few more things. A female bovine, or cow, was led seven times around the temple of the Sun near the winter solstice among the Egyptians, as our same Plutarch testifies. Note also the fable of the cattle of the Sun from Homer and Apollodorus. Furthermore, Apollo is called *Thurius*, from "bulls," which the Chaldeans call *thor*. You may read of Bacchus as **the bull** <note>original: *ταῦρον* (tauron)</note> in Athenaeus and as **the bull-eater** <note>original: *ταυροφάγον* (taurophagon)</note> in Hesychius. Neptune...

...just as he was called **"the Bellower"** <note>original Greek: *μυκητὰς* (mykētās)</note>, of whom I spoke a little before, so also he is called **"the Bull"** <note>original Greek: *ταῦρος* (tauros)</note> and **"Bull-like"** <note>original Greek: *Ταύρειος* (Taureios)</note>, and his festival is the **"Bull-feast"** <note>original Greek: *ταύρεια* (taureia)</note>. But Diodorus also relates that the bull was assigned to Pluto, Isis, and Osiris. The chariot of Rhea, though usually drawn by lions, was also sometimes drawn by *bulls*, as is clear from Onomacritus. Regarding Diana, it is too well known to need recounting here. Minerva also appears as the **"Bull-tender"** <note>original Greek: *ταυροπόλος* (tauropolos)</note> in the writings of Hesychius. Indeed, the cow of Cadmus, of which Ovid speaks in the *Metamorphoses*, belongs entirely to our work <note>Tollius refers to alchemy as "our work," suggesting Cadmus's cow is a symbol for a specific chemical substance or process</note>. Furthermore, among the delusions of the Gnostics <margin>Book III, Origen *Against Celsus*, page 295.</margin> we find *Uriel*, that is the God of fire, with a *Bull-like* face. Therefore, he who has learned that bulls are Gods, or are attributed to the Gods, will no longer wonder at the horned gods: the Sun, Bacchus, Ocean, Neptune, Pan, Serapis, the Moon, Isis, Ceres, Astarte, and so on.

That view of Plutarch seems more correct—though it is not entirely so—which derives the etymology of Serapis from the *joy* <note>original: *lætitia*</note> of the god, because cheerfulness is a property of purity. He goes even further, but is himself unaware of what he says: when he speaks of the *Amenthe* of the Egyptians—which is, as he explains, **"giving and receiving"** <note>Amenthe usually refers to the Egyptian underworld; Tollius interprets it as a chemical exchange of properties</note>, where the souls of the dead depart—he approaches the mystery of the bones of the mother thrown behind the back by our Deucalion <note>In myth, Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulated the earth by throwing stones ("the bones of the mother") behind them; in alchemy, this often refers to the "stone" or "salt" of the earth</note>. He does this so that Serapis may emerge from there, who is at once Osiris and Isis, Deucalion and Pyrrha, but now raised to the number of the heavenly ones, joined and unified into a single form, after Typhon <note>Typhon usually represents "chaos" or "impurity" in alchemical texts</note> was slain by the victorious Venus. To this Goddess, by her own right, a **"four-angled"** <note>original Greek: *τετράγωνος* (tetragōnos)</note> or square figure is attributed by the Pythagoreans, as it is also to Rhea, Ceres, Vesta, and Juno, and likewise to Mercury; while the *triangular* figure is assigned to Pluto, Bacchus, and Mars. To these latter also belong the *three-forked* lightning of Jupiter, and Neptune's trident, and *three-formed* Hecate, and the triple Pallas, and the **"three-headed"** <note>original Greek: *τρικέφαλον* (trikephalon)</note> Mercury—though in another respect—and...

<gloss>having a triple phallus <note>original Greek: τριπλάσιον αἰδοῖον ἔχοντα</note></gloss> it would have been permitted to add to Osiris: whether that threefold number <gloss>denotes the moist nature <note>original Greek: τὴν ὑγρὰν φύσιν</note>, which is the beginning and the birth of all things from the start, and having made the first three bodies: earth, air, and fire <note>original Greek: ἀρχὴν καὶ γένεσιν οὖσαν πάντων ἐξ ἀρχῆς, καὶ τὰ πρῶτα τρία σώματα, γῆν, ἀέρα, καὶ πῦρ ποιήσασαν</note></gloss>, as Plutarch maintains; or whether it signifies the three principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsian alchemy, believed to be the base components of all matter</note>; or whether it expresses the nature of fire rising into a triangular shape. For this reason, the Pyramids are sacred to the Sun god, and the idol of the Amathusian Venus was a *pyramidal stone*; she who was the mistress of Cnidus and Paphos was both male and female <note>Tollius refers to the hermaphroditic nature of the alchemical "Rebis" or the union of opposites</note>. The same was the figure of the Sun-god Elagabalus and of <gloss>Aguyieus <note>original Greek: Ἀγυιέως; a title for Apollo as protector of streets, often represented by a conical pillar</note></gloss>. <margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book III, chapter 2.</margin> Indeed, more can be read concerning these shapes in the works of Eusebius.

What can be said about the *seven-day* flight of Typhon <note>Typhon represents the chaotic, destructive force in Egyptian myth, often equated by alchemists with crude or volatile matter</note>, anyone can now easily suggest for themselves. However, we shall pass on to other simpler and more obvious reasons in Plutarch, and then to the more hidden and <gloss>more mystical <note>original Greek: μυστικωτέρας</note></gloss> accounts of the Egyptian priests. Thus, the Nile *running into the sea*, and Osiris *thrown into the sea by Typhon*, and Deucalion *suffering the flood when all was sea*, are one and the same preparation of our <term>regulus</term> <note>The "regulus" is the metallic heart or purified core of a substance, often associated with antimony in Tollius's era</note>, when the entire Matter is dissolved by a "flood of fire." Typhon is *foam*, that is, an effervescing heat. For he is born from the spirituous motion of the waves; Hippocrates teaches that this occurs not only in this "philosophical" man <note>The alchemist's metaphorical creation</note>, but also in the natural man. <margin>Hippocrates, *On Generation*, books 5 and 6.</margin> Hence Priapus was considered to be Typhon, as is found in Diodorus, and Venus was called <gloss>Aphrodite, the Foam-born <note>original Greek: Ἀφροδίτη, Ἀφρογένεια</note></gloss>. To her the *myrtle* is sacred, which delights in the shores. You may find the former meaning in Aristophanes as well. And *Myrtile* is a woman’s name, which was once the name of Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great. Furthermore, he is described <margin>Servius on Virgil’s *Aeneid*, 8. 801. Scholiast on Sophocles' *Oedipus at Colonus*.</margin>

This is even more evident in the descriptions of Isis, where Plutarch explains her philosophically in this way:

<gloss>For Isis is the female principle of Nature, receptive of every kind of generation; in this role she is called "nurse" and "all-receiver" by Plato, and is known by the masses as "she of ten thousand names." This is because, being transformed by Reason [Logos], she receives all forms and ideas. She possesses an innate love for the first and most sovereign of all things, which is identical to the Good; she longs for and pursues it. She shuns and repels any portion derived from Evil. Although she serves as the place and the matter for both, she always inclines of her own accord toward the better, offering herself to be impregnated by it and to be sown with emanations and likenesses. In these she rejoices and is glad as she conceives and is filled with new births. <note>original Greek: Ἡ γὰρ Ἶσίς ἐστι μὲν τὸ τῆς Φύσεως θῆλυ, καὶ δεκτικὸν ἁπάσης γενέσεως... καὶ ὑποπιμπλαμένη τῶν γενέσεων.</note></gloss>

But to return to Deucalion: Anticlides, says Plutarch, makes Isis the daughter of Prometheus and the wife of Dionysus. In this way, she would be both the sister and wife of Deucalion, and Deucalion would be Dionysus, whose son is Horus. Isis bore Horus as <gloss>a perceptible image of the intelligible world <note>original Greek: εἰκόνα τοῦ νοητοῦ κόσμου αἰσθητὴν</note></gloss>, and so on.

...the bodily. But the element of Hermes <note>original Greek: τοῦ Ἑρμοῦ</note>—that is, of Reason—prevails and conquers, bearing witness and showing that nature, being transformed toward the intelligible, restores the world. This Horus <note>The OCR reads "σῖρος" (siros), likely a printer's error for "Ὧρος" (Horus).</note> himself is defined and perfect; he has not utterly destroyed Typhon, but has taken away his activity and strength. 

In this context, Horus must be understood as the Starred Regulus <term>The "Regulus" (Little King) is the purified metallic heart of a substance; "Starred" refers to a specific crystalline pattern alchemists sought as a sign of success.</term> of the Philosophers. He is born from the marriage of Deucalion and Pyrrha, yet he is at once both Deucalion and Pyrrha joined together and made more perfect; however, he is not yet the completed Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the final goal of the alchemical work.</note>.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

->*Hesychius corrected and supplemented.*<-

In the preceding chapter, we discussed the Goddess Venus as being both male and female. I would add nothing further to such a well-known matter, were it not for a notable error occurring in the works of Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note> where he treats this same Goddess. 

He says: <gloss>Aphroditus: Theophrastus calls him Hermaphroditus. But the one who wrote about Amathus says the god was fashioned in Cyprus as a *paianison* man. <note>original Greek: Ἀφρόδιτος, Θεόφραστος μὲν Ἑρμαφρόδιτόν φησιν. ὁ δὲ τὰ περὶ Ἀμαθοῦντα γεγραφὼς παιάνισον ἄνδρα τὸν θεὸν ἐσχηματίσθαι ἐν Κύπρῳ λέγει.</note></gloss> <margin>p. 286</margin>

The illustrious Isaac Vossius, having noticed this flaw, corrected it in his observations on Catullus to *equal to Paean* <note>original Greek: Παιᾶνι ἴσον</note>, meaning equal to Apollo or Aesculapius. For this god, too, was sometimes depicted as beardless, according to the testimony of Pausanias. 

But here, judgment and memory failed even this great man. <margin>On Virgil's *Aeneid* 11. 632.</margin> For it is likely he had read in Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note>: *There is also in Cyprus an image of a Bearded Venus, with a female body and dress, but with a Scepter and male nature, which he calls Aphroditus; to whom men sacrifice in women's clothing, and women in men's clothing.* 

Therefore, read [the Greek text] as *bearded* <note>original Greek: ὡς πωγωνίαν</note>, or *as a bearded man* <note>original Greek: πωγωνίαν ὡς ἄνδρα</note>. Do not doubt that you would find even Vos- <meta>catchword: Vof- (Vossius)</meta>

<summary>Tollius interprets the Egyptian god Horus as the alchemical "Starred Regulus" and argues that the mythical "Bearded Venus" of Cyprus represents a union of male and female principles, correcting a textual error in the lexicographer Hesychius.</summary>

### CHAPTER XXV.

->*A Play of Wit.*<-

The mind must be refreshed for a little while; it must be released from its long concentration and restored. We shall wander out, therefore, a little way into the pleasant greenery of the Muses; and there, if not among the laurels, we shall certainly rest beneath the shade:

> — *Where the earth pours out various flowers*
> *Around the rivers; where the white poplar leans*
> *Over the cave, and the flexible vines weave a canopy of shade.*
> <note>These lines are adapted from Virgil's ninth Eclogue, depicting a pastoral ideal of peace and poetic inspiration.</note>

But as I wish to do with your permission, kind Reader, I will not address you now, but another most distinguished foster-son of the Muses. With that extraordinary “finest flower” <note>original Greek: ἀώτῳ (aōtō)</note> of a noble mind, I shall sweetly pass this time of quiet and harmless pleasure—a pleasure both honorable and humane. Do you long to know who he is? It is GISBERT CUPER <note>Gisbert Cuper (1644–1716) was a prominent Dutch humanist scholar and statesman.</note>, a man of consular rank, a great glory of his own Deventer <note>A city in the Netherlands where Cuper served as mayor.</note>, and no less a glory of these letters which we cultivate. To his honor—because amidst the public affairs and infinite business encountered in the council of the States-General <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>, he still holds and grants no small honor to the Muses—we shall give, dedicate, and consecrate this chapter. There is no reason for me to describe the subject at greater length. <gloss>“The work itself will soon show.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: Τοὔργον τάχ’ αὐτὸ δείξει (Tourgon tach' auto deixei)</note>

### CHAPTER XXVI.

->*Florus attempted several times.*<-
<note>This chapter begins a series of philological "attempts" or trials to correct errors in the text of the Roman historian Florus.</note>

<margin>Book I, Chapter 10</margin>
"Second thoughts are wiser," <note>original Greek: "Δευτέραι φροντίδες σοφώτεραι"</note> is an old saying, but it is not always true. For sometimes the first concerns are the better ones. Freinshemius <note>Johann Freinsheim (1608–1660), a noted classical scholar and editor of Roman historians.</note> will serve as an example for us in correcting a most corrupt passage of Florus: he rejected an excellent and most true <term>conjecture</term><note>A scholar's proposed correction of a corrupted word in an ancient manuscript.</note> simply to please his father-in-law. 

These are the words of Florus concerning Scævola: <note>Gaius Mucius Scaevola, a legendary Roman hero who, after failing to assassinate the king Porsena, thrust his right hand into a fire to prove Roman bravery.</note> *“So that you may know,” he said, “what kind of man you have escaped, three hundred of us have sworn to do the same.”* 

“What does this,” says Freinshemius, “have to do with the estimation of the man—whether he has three hundred comrades, or more, or less! I had thought it should be read: *how little*...” 

But

<summary>This page presents five poetic variations of a Greek epigram about the philosopher Epictetus before transitioning into a philological critique of Johann Freinsheim's editorial choices regarding the historian Florus.</summary>
<keywords>Epictetus, Stoicism, Irus, poverty, Jacob Tollius, Johann Freinsheim, Florus, Scaevola, philology, textual criticism</keywords>

--- Page 271 ---
<meta>This page continues Chapter 26 of Jacob Tollius’s philological commentary. On the previous page, Tollius began a critique of the Roman historian Florus, discussing various textual emendations. Here, he focuses on specific word choices regarding the Roman struggle against King Pyrrhus and the famous use of war elephants.</meta>

<page-num>221</page-num>
<header>CHANCE REMARKS.</header>

But since the manuscripts have *whom scarcely* <note>original Latin: "quemvix"</note>, Bernegger <note>Matthias Bernegger (1582–1640), a noted philologist and professor at Strasbourg</note> better emends it to *which you will have scarcely escaped* <note>original Latin: "quam vix effugeris"</note>, that is, which you will be scarcely able to escape; so that this word *effugeris* [you will have escaped] denotes the future tense. Before Freinsheim’s <note>Johann Freinsheim (1608–1660), a scholar famous for his "supplements" to lost books of Livy</note> edition was at hand for me, I myself had already conjectured that it should be restored as: *How little you will have escaped* <note>original Latin: "Quam parum effugeris"</note>. Nor could I condemn a conjecture that was so effective at inspiring terror. Later, I saw the same confirmed by Freculph <note>Freculph of Lisieux, a 9th-century bishop and chronicler who often quoted ancient texts</note>, who transcribed this passage from old manuscripts in no other way, except that in the preceding verse he has *brought in* <note>original Latin: "intulit"</note> instead of *casts in* <note>original Latin: "injicit"</note>. Livy also seems to favor him, who expresses these things thus:
> *Nor was I the only one to bear this spirit against you: behind me is a long line of those seeking the same glory. Therefore, prepare yourself for this struggle, if it pleases you, so that you may fight for your life every single hour, etc.* <note>This quote is from Livy’s History of Rome (Book 2, Chapter 12), depicting the defiance of Mucius Scaevola before the Etruscan King Porsena.</note>

In the same Florus, I can scarcely stomach <margin>Book 1, chapter 18</margin> *elephants running forward into the spectacle of war.* For he [Florus] says it like this: *It would have been all over, had not the elephants, having been turned around, run forward into the spectacle of war.* <note>Tollius is critiquing Florus's account of the Battle of Heraclea (280 BC), where King Pyrrhus's elephants terrified the Romans.</note> He had already mentioned the elephants just before, so there was no need for a repetition of that word. I read it, therefore, as: *It would have been all over, had not the Beasts, having been turned toward the front line, run forward: with whose size, etc.* <note>Tollius suggests replacing "elephants" with the more poetic "beasts" (belluæ) to avoid repetition and improve the Latin style.</note> I know that those who have a <term>critical nose</term> <note>A scholarly metaphor for someone with a keen sense for detecting errors or stylistic flaws in ancient texts.</note> will not wrinkle their nostrils at this conjecture, especially when they read a little later: *For when the elephants were again led out into the front line, a heavy blow from a spear driven into the head of one of their young turned them away.* If he says "again," then they must have been there once before. It follows: *who, while running back through the slaughter of his own kind and seeking with a trumpeting cry, his mother recognized him, and as if to avenge him, she leapt forward; then she threw everything around the enemy into a state of grave fear.* I think it should be read: *when he, running back through the slaughter of his own kind, sought his mother with a trumpeting cry, she recognized him and leapt out to avenge him; then everything around... etc.* Phaedrus. <note>Phaedrus was a Roman fabulist; Tollius likely cites him here for his descriptions of animals or as a stylistic parallel to the dramatic scene described in Florus.</note>

<margin>Book III, folio XVI.</margin>
> Among the goats, a dog says to a bleating lamb:
> Foolishly, he says, you wander; your mother is not here:
> And he pointed to the sheep separated in the distance.

<margin>Book II.</margin>
*I do not seek her who conceives when she pleases.* <note>original Latin: "Non illam quæro, quæ cum libitum est, concipit."</note> This should be read there instead of *this is not your mother* <note>original Latin: "non est hæc mater tua"</note>. The ancient way of writing "here" as *heic* <note>A common archaic spelling in Latin manuscripts</note> provided the occasion for the error. Compare Lucretius:

> Furthermore, the tender kids with their trembling voices
> know their horn-bearing mothers, and the butting lambs 
> [know] the bleating flocks.

Basil the Great: "Therefore God, who created them, compensated for their lack of speech through the abundance of their senses. Furthermore, I argue that the phrase *is and as if he were claiming* <note>original Latin: "est & quasi vindicaret"</note> should be retained, meaning he acted willingly, or thinking that he was claiming [vengeance]. In the same chapter, there follows: *For no triumph entered the city more beautifully or more splendidly by chance.* Our manuscript, and some others, as well as Freculph <note>Freculph of Lisieux, a 9th-century chronicler</note>, with the approval of Salmasius <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a titan of 17th-century classical scholarship</note>, have *another* <note>original Latin: "alius"</note>. If I know the talent of Florus correctly, he wrote: *Not by chance at another time* <note>original Latin: "Nec temere alias"</note>. So also a little before: *nor by any other more than the Tarentine victory, etc.* <note>original Latin: "nec alia magis, quam Tarentina victoria &c."</note> Where likewise...

...should be restored from an old book, and not more so than in other places. Thus, in Book III, chapter VI: *Not at any other time have we enjoyed such a bloodless victory.* <note>original Latin: "Non alias tam in cruenta victoria usi sumus." Tollius is likely arguing for the reading "incruenta" (bloodless) rather than "in cruenta" (in a bloody one).</note>

In Book II, chapter 15, he speaks thus concerning the Carthaginian wars: *And if anyone should consider the turning points of the three periods, the war was begun in the first, pushed forward in the second, but truly finished in the third. But the cause of this war was that, against the law of the treaty, they had once prepared a fleet and army against the Numidians; moreover, they frequently harassed the borders of Masinissa.* <note>Masinissa was the first King of Numidia and a key Roman ally against Carthage.</note> I would think it better to read it as: *Therefore, if anyone should consider the turning points of the three periods, he will say that the war was begun in the first, pushed forward in the second, but finished in the third. The cause of the war was that, against the law of the treaty, they had indeed once prepared a fleet and army against the Numidians, but they were frequently encroaching upon the borders of Masinissa.* So also in Book IV, chapter 5: *He had indeed offered as the cause of that war, before the legate Cassius, that his borders were being encroached upon by Nicomedes of Bithynia.* And among the legal experts <note>original Latin: "Jctos," an abbreviation for "Jurisconsultos"</note>, theft is defined as: *The handling of another's property against the owner's will.* <note>original Latin: "Contractatio alieni invito domino." This is a standard Roman legal definition of "furtum" (theft).</note> 

A little later, Freinsheim <note>Johann Freinsheim (1608–1660), a German classical scholar known for his "supplements" to lost books of Roman history</note> correctly removes the word *city* <note>original Latin: "urbis"</note> once, which learned men approve of, but in the wrong place: for it should be removed after the word *rival* <note>original Latin: "aemulae"</note>. The same should have been done in the very next sentence, where, instead of *so that it might only be moved from its place*, you would more correctly read, *rather than that the city only be moved from its place*. Velleius <note>Velleius Paterculus, a Roman historian writing in the 1st century AD</note> supports the former judgment: *This end,* he says, *did Carthage, the rival of the Roman empire, reach.* The latter is supported by the elegance of the language, which rejects such inept additions. Furthermore, a *city* <note>original Latin: "urbs," referring to the physical buildings and walls</note> could not be moved from its place; I might grant that for a *state* <note>original Latin: "civitate," referring to the body of citizens</note>, which is contained not by walls, but by its citizens. 

Soon after, that phrase, *they were commanded to migrate from their borders*, somehow pleases me less. I would prefer simply: *they were commanded to migrate*; or, if something must be added, *they were commanded to migrate from their dwellings*. For that former phrasing is contrary to historical truth. There follows a little later a remarkable passage which many...

...exercised the talents of the generals in vain: *Then, with Mancinus as consul, the siege raged by land and sea. The work having been bared of its port* <margin>At the end of chapter 26.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Ad finem cap. XXVI."</note> *the first, then the second, and now even the third wall [was taken], yet nevertheless Byrsa, which was the name for the citadel, resisted like a second city.* If I have any insight in this kind of study, I think it should be read as: *Then Mancinus [pressed] them. The siege raged by land and sea. The first, then the second, and now the third wall were stripped piece by piece.* Instead of *stripped* <note>original Latin: "nudatus." Tollius refers to the walls being "bared" or breached of their defenses.</note> (which is nonetheless an excellent and elegant word to use elsewhere regarding a siege), the word *captured* <note>original Latin: "expugnatus."</note> could also be read. For our author will soon say concerning the port that it was blocked by Scipio.

In the same book, chapter 17: *That Metellus, who had his surname from Macedonia, deserved to become "Celtiberius" as well, since he had captured Contrebia with a memorable example, and spared the Nertobriges with greater glory.* So says the Illustrious Man who recently published this edition. <note>Tollius is likely referring to a contemporary editor of Florus, such as Graevius or a similar scholar.</note> But it seems to me that Florus used a far different elegance of speech, which no one here has noticed. Read it, therefore, as: *Cato (the Censor) broke the Celtiberians, that is the strength of Spain, in several battles. Gracchus (the father of the Gracchi) punished the same with the destruction of one hundred and fifty cities. Metellus (he with the surname from Macedonia: for the title "Celtibericus" was of less value) having captured Contrebia with a memorable example, spared Segobriga with greater glory.* In the old writings it was: *Celtiberius's son*; *to become Celtibericus*, etc. At the beginning I had conjectured: *for he scorned the title Celtibericus,* which even now does not displease me. <note>Roman generals often took "agnomina" or honorary surnames from the regions they conquered, such as "Macedonicus" or "Celtibericus." Tollius is debating the prestige of these titles.</note>

At the end of the same chapter: *He slaughtered the army of Claudius Unimanus almost to total destruction: and he fixed the trophies in his mountains, including the insignias with our robes and bundles of rods which he had captured. At last, even Fabius Maximus the consul had crushed him.* <note>The "trabeis and fascibus" (robes and bundles of rods) were symbols of Roman magisterial authority.</note> Read: *He slaughtered the army of Claudus Unimanus almost to total destruction: and he fixed the trophies in his mountains, including the insignias with our robes and bundles of rods, which he had captured.* <note>Tollius suggests correcting the name from "Claudius" to "Claudus" (meaning 'The Lame'). Claudius Unimanus was a Roman praetor defeated by the Lusitanian leader Viriathus.</note>

### CHAPTER XXVII.

->*A Petitionary Booklet for an English Captive.*<-

It is generally the ease of nature among men who are not ill-tempered to look kindly upon the foolish love of parents toward their children—those children who stand out for some gift of beauty or good character—and to forgive this human weakness. I now presume, kind reader, with almost certain hope, that you will show me that same humanity. I trust you will not take it ill that I have inserted among these miscellaneous pieces a petitionary booklet, once written for an English captive. This work is all the more pleasing to me because of the sincere and envy-free judgments it earned at that time. 

There were some men—such as I still experience even now—who were malevolent and envied my labors and (if I may say so without bragging) <note>original Latin: "præfiſcini." This is an old Latin expression used to ward off the "evil eye" when one is about to praise themselves.</note> my diligence. They sought any opportunity to pluck at and slander my studies because of my infrequent use of the Latin tongue, and they denied that I possessed any skill in it. But it happened to me through which... <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword for the next page is "quam."</note>

I therefore wrote this letter, and I managed to have it delivered to the consuls in the Englishman's own name by that excellent and most distinguished man, **Mr. AEMILIUS COOLIUS** <note>Adriaan Cools (1624–1689) was a prominent Dutch magistrate and supporter of the arts.</note>, whose virtue placed him among the illustrious glories and ornaments of our age, even when he withdrew during those riots of the raging mob in the year <term>1672</term> <note>original: "CIƆ IƆ CLXXII." Then, too, the spirit of my dear **CANTIUS** <note>Likely a reference to a deceased friend or relative of Tollius.</note> will feel the glory won by his virtues flourish anew, and will rejoice to be remembered among the *nobles of more distinguished character*. 

But, to return to the point from which *I digressed*: *Envy was then caught in the act.* However, it would be unbecoming for me to set forth exactly what was decreed or what actions were taken. I will say only this: that I then reaped the most abundant fruit of my labors, and most bitterly punished Envy with its own poison, which it was forced to swallow back after it had been spewed out. You will therefore forgive that common human failing: namely, that I was led by affection to share this letter—which once brought me much pleasure and which I happened upon while searching through some of my papers—

### ON BEHALF OF AN ENGLISH CAPTIVE

If it is permitted to complain at all about you, Fortune, my first grievance will be this: that being needy, destitute, and a prisoner, I am forced to beg for the help of others. It is a heavy thing for a noble spirit to be a burden to anyone before you have been of use to them. But far heavier is the weight of this most sorrowful misfortune itself, which in a brief moment has rendered me—who was not unhappy until now—the most miserable of men. 

Bitter Fortune, enemy to good men, where have you thrust me? Into what abyss of evils have you thrown me? What addition of glory comes to you from the calamity of a dejected man like me? What title of honor could be hoped for from such an ignoble victory? 

You will grant this to a most justified grief, most Distinguished Men and Lords <note>The "Viri, ac Domini Ampliffimi" refers to the *Burgemeesters* or high magistrates of the city.</note>; you will grant it to the <term>vicissitude</term> <note>The natural "turning" or unpredictable change of human affairs from good to bad.</note> of human affairs, that I demand an account for a few things from that unfair Fortune, and with a few sobs play a prelude to a greater complaint. And oh, that I might pour out from my innermost heart groans mixed with tears, by which your minds—which never deny anything to the prayers of suppliants—might be moved to bring help even to me, a wretched man! 

Yet it is not primarily out of concern for myself that I throw myself at your knees. A greater care twists me, and a deeper pain chokes my spirit, as often as I remember that dearest person, my mother. The sight of her torn garments and her face stained by grief drive sleep from my eyes; and even if sleep, that conqueror of evils, occasionally offers a brief rest to my sick mind, the mournful image of my elderly, afflicted mother continuously appears before me, weeping for her fate and mine. Let others, whom the same fortune as me...

The disaster of our nation has engulfed me—just reasons for grieving. Let those parents whose children have had their liberty snatched away along with me have a reason to speak harshly of Fortune. But without controversy, those lamentations are the most justified, and that grief the most sincere, which are forced out against what is right from those who never deserved such a thing and who were not expecting it. 

A greed for abominable slaughter may have sent others to this war; others the <note>original: "auri sacra fames." A famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid referring to the "accursed hunger for gold."</note> accursed hunger for gold; others the desire for empty glory; or, which is the most noble cause for fighting, love of country. But as for me, shaped for peace by my father's precepts—for what herald of peace would have taught his son anything but charity, of which peace is the nursling?—imbued with peace by my father's warnings, Royal authority, or rather Royal ministers governing everything by their own whim, cast me onto a ship. 

Known is that dire custom of our nation <note>A reference to "press-ganging," the practice of forcibly recruiting men into the Royal Navy.</note>: willing or unwilling, we are driven away like cattle by those to whom the blood of others is too cheap. A pharmacist or medical professional in training.</note>, into this war, so that I might stain hands destined for the healing of the human race with what is almost civil blood.

Far from me now are my parents' prayers, far the times given to my studies, far a mind conscious of what is right and pure of stain: captured in war, alas! captured, I am held in prison, in shackles, among the guilty. The evils of my life would bring a weariness upon me and extinguish me with sickness of mind and mourning, were it not that hope—which is always present for the afflicted—now solaced me, weary as I am with pain. Promising all these things, hope sustains my unhappy and faltering spirit; she commands me to approach You with a suppliant prayer, and to beseech you that, mindful of the human lot, you might deign to grant an unfortunate youth to the grief of his exhausted mother. 

I, if returned to my own people, shall not have harmed this commonwealth; nor shall I have been of any use if I am retained. The common safety does not depend upon this head <note>original: "capite." Literally "head," but used here to mean his life or individual person.</note>, for which I would otherwise devote it with a willing mind. When you spare me, you will be looking out for my mother; and when you consider her age, look also upon my youth. 

My slender means promise a wretched old age, unless, imitating the industry of the ant, I sow seeds now in this, the springtime of my life, so that I may harvest in summer what must be brought out in winter. <note>The narrator uses the metaphor of the ant—a common classical trope for foresight—to argue that he must spend his youth learning his trade to avoid poverty later.</note> But also for uncertain accidents, and for the support of my mother, certain things must be set aside; and from where shall they come? For what protection, what hope is there from a craft only recently begun and not yet properly mastered? 

While I linger here in the filth of prison, those things which I thought I already held will slip away, and that age will fly past which is most suitable for acquiring and learning the arts. Thus all my hope, life, and safety, Most Distinguished Men and Lords, are placed in your kindness. You are able to restore me to my former liberty; you can return me to my parent, and return me to health. That you might wish to do so, I pray and entreat you by your knees, by your own safety and that of your children, and by the fortune and <term>genius</term> <note>original: "genium." In Roman tradition, the "genius" was the protective spirit or guiding essence of a person, place, or institution.</note> of this commonwealth. Nod your assent, I beg, with a benevolent countenance: and you shall have within you the conscience of a [benevolent deed] <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "bene-" which likely continues as "beneficii" (benefit/deed).</note> rightly bestowed.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.
->*Sacred Frauds.*<-

<margin>Observations on Human Affairs, book 5, chapter 20.</margin>
It is my intention here to bring forward a remarkable example of fraud, devised by that class of men who, under the appearance of piety, most shamefully mock human credulity. The Jesuit scholar Andreas Schottus, learned in the Greek language, brought this to our attention from an old manuscript belonging to Antonio Agustín <note>A Spanish jurist and historian (1517–1586) known for his collection of ancient manuscripts.</note>, which contained the *Physical Eclogues* of Stobaeus. He says it is a "small fragment" <note>original: "Ἀποσπασμάτιον"</note> from the commentaries of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note> titled *On the Styx*. Because the knowledge of this fragment seemed to me extremely useful for recognizing several other frauds of this kind, I thought I would be doing something worthwhile if I translated this fragment into English <note>Tollius translated it into Latin; the current translation renders it in English for the reader.</note>, even though it is defiled by many errors. 

"Hear," he says, "what certain travelers coming to Syria from Mesopotamia once told Bardesanes <note>A Syriac Gnostic and philosopher (154–222 AD).</note> during the reign of Antoninus of Emesa (this is Elagabalus <note>The Roman Emperor Elagabalus, who reigned 218–222 AD and was known for bringing Syrian religious rites to Rome.</note>), just as these things were recorded and handed down in writing by Bardesanes himself."

# FORTUITA.

They reported that there is even now a certain lake which among the Indians is called "The Proving Ground" <note>original: "Exploratorio"</note>; into this lake, any of the Indians who, being accused of some crime, denies the deed, is led.

The trial is conducted by the Brahmins <note>The priestly and scholarly caste of India, often described by ancient Western writers as philosophers.</note> in this manner: they first ask the man whose name has been brought forward whether he is willing to have the truth about him sought through that water. If he refuses, he is sent away to the tribunal as a self-confessed criminal, there to pay the well-deserved penalties for the crime committed. But if he accepts the inquiry, they lead him, along with his accusers, into that lake we mentioned. For the accusers are also forced to descend into the water, so that their own minds may be tested to see whether they have accused the defendant truly or through false slander. Therefore, when both the accusers and the accused have entered the lake, they make their way toward the opposite bank. Now, the depth of the lake in most places barely reaches the knees; nor does it rise any higher if the defendant is innocent, so that he may cross the lake safely. But if he should be guilty of the crime, as he progresses a short distance, the waters gradually increase and overwhelm him, until he is submerged up to his head. Then, those they call the Brahmins pull him out from there and hand him over to the accusers, asking that he be reformed through a punishment short of death. However, it rarely happens that anyone dares to deny a crime, as everyone everywhere fears being refuted and exposed by this water. This, therefore, is the method of discovery <note>original: "indicinam"</note> the Indians have for crimes committed by choice.

But regarding those things committed unintentionally or against one's will—indeed, for any actions, even voluntary ones, and thus for the conduct of an entire life—they have another method and way of testing. Concerning this, Bardesanes <note>Bardaisan (154–222 AD), a Syrian philosopher and Gnostic teacher whose writings often blended Eastern and Western thought.</note> records these things, which I have decided to transcribe word for word. He said they also reported that there is a natural, immense cave there, situated roughly in the middle of a very high mountain, in which a statue is seen. It was about ten or twelve cubits tall, as they estimated, standing with its body upright and its hands spread out almost in the shape of a cross. The right side of its face represents a man, the left a woman; and it is not just the face, but the arm, the foot, and indeed the whole side is distinctly feminine. Thus, at the very first glance, this diversity of both sexes, joined in one body and compared with one another, miraculously strikes the spectators—

In that place, Sandates <note>Sandates (or Sandales) was an Indian ambassador to the Roman court in the 3rd century AD; his accounts are a primary source for Western views on Indian "gymnosophists."</note> used to say that he encountered annual assemblies of the Brahmins <note>The priestly and scholarly caste of ancient India, often romanticized by European writers as ancient philosophers.</note> on a set day. But I believe that Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker of the 1st century AD who allegedly traveled to India.</note> also remembered this water which is in the cave. For in writing to the Brahmins, he composes a certain oath: **"Not by the Tantalic water by which you initiated me."** <note>original: "Non per aquam Tantaliam qua me initiastis."</note> For I think he calls it "Tantalic" for this reason: because it tortures and punishes with perpetual expectation those who strive with great zeal to approach it and desire to seek a drink from it.

It is easy to reveal the tricks <note>The author uses the term "technas," implying deceptive craft or artifice.</note> of this deception: for inside there were subterranean passages equipped and adorned with lead pipes, from which water was secretly released by priests who were in on the trick. For these priests, both from a person's face and speech, and many other signs, could easily make a guess about anyone's innocence and integrity. Hence, once a signal was given and the valves secretly opened, the water released into the pool would suddenly rise to the height that was needed. Nor was any other machine used in moving the door in the cave. If anyone doubts this matter, I would wish him to look to Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a satirist famous for exposing the fraudulent methods of "prophets" and "oracle-mongers" of his time.</note>, who recounts more than one example of frauds of this kind.

### JACOBUS TOLLIUS

How easily, truly, miracles of this kind are faked! Sweat can be simulated by placing grains of salt on the statue in the evening, which liquefy during the night; a statue can be turned, twisted, and moved from its place by strings—just as **puppets** <note>original: νευρόσπαστα (neurospasta), literally "string-pulled" figures or marionettes.</note> usually are—and by little wheels, twisted and arranged with mechanical skill. Finally, shouts and voices can be faked, even without any magical art, through tubes inserted into the walls and ending in the mouths of the statues. Our own age is well-acquainted with such things, often circumventing the foolish credulity of the stupid commoners with tricks of this sort. 

Furthermore, Lucian relates in that same little book (if indeed he is the author of that commentary) <note>Tollius expresses scholarly doubt about the authorship of "On the Syrian Goddess," a debate that continues among modern classicists.</note> that the image of Apollo in that temple used to move of its own accord and gave oracles by itself without the intervention of priests. "He himself moves," he says, "and carries the prophecy to its end by his own will." <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ... αὐτός τε κινέεται, καὶ τὴν μαντηΐην ἐς τέλος αὐτογνωμέει.</note> 

I shall also add what follows, so that the fraud may be recognized more clearly from it: 

"The manner of it is this: whenever he wishes to deliver an oracle, he first moves in his seat. The priests immediately lift him up. If they do not lift him, he sweats and moves into the middle. But when they go under and carry him, he leads them, spinning all around and leaping from one to another. Finally, the high priest meeting him, asks him about all matters. If he does not wish to do it, he moves backward. But if he is persuaded, he leads the porters forward, just like a charioteer." <note>original Greek: Τρόπος δὲ αὐτῆς τοῖόσδε. εὖτ’ ἂν ἐθέλῃσι χρησμηγορέειν, ἐν τῇ ἕδρῃ πρῶτα κινέεται. οἱ δέ μιν ἱρέες αὐτίκα ἀείρουσι. ἢν δὲ μὴ ἀείρωσι, ὁ δὲ ἱδρώει, καὶ ἐς μέσον κινέεται. εὖτ’ ἂν δὲ ὑποδύντες φέρωσι, ἄγει σφέας, πάντη περιδινέων, καὶ ἐς ἄλλον ἐξ ἑτέρου μεταπηδέων. τέλος ὁ ἀρχιερεὺς ἀντιάσας, ἐπερέεται μιν περὶ ἁπάντων πρηγμάτων. ὁ δὲ, ἢν μὴ θέλῃ ποιέεσθαι, ὀπίσω ἀναχωρέει. ἢν δὲ πειθομένη, ἄγει ἐς τὸ πρόσω τοὺς προφέροντας, ὅκωσπερ ἡνιοχέων.</note>

On my French journey, I remember seeing many **mechanical devices** <note>original: μηχανήματα (mechanemata).</note> of that kind in Lyon <note>original: Lugdunum.</note>, in the museum of Servierius <note>Nicolas Grollier de Servière (1596–1689), a soldier and inventor famous for his "cabinet of curiosities" featuring elaborate mechanical clocks and automatons.</note>, a nobleman; and I pleasantly marveled at the wonderful [device] of the Bishop...

...[the Bishop’s] intellect, I laughed at his slowness. Even a man of Episcopal dignity, if those mechanical devices <note>original: "mechanemata," referring to the hidden pulleys and tubes described on the previous page.</note> had been employed in temples and upon sacred images, would undoubtedly have been persuaded that they were directed and moved not by a devilish power, but by a divine one. Through the works of such "revelers"—or rather, "calves" <note>Tollius uses a pun here: "vitulantium" (those celebrating or frisking like calves) and "vitulorum" (calves, often used as a metaphor for fools or simpletons).</note>—that **False Prophet** <note>Alexander of Abonoteichos, a 2nd-century charlatan exposed by Lucian.</note> of Lucian had reached such a reputation for holiness, and his god **Glycon** <note>A snake-god established by Alexander, which was actually a puppet with a human-like mask.</note> had seemed so present, that Lucian had cause to congratulate himself for escaping the most immediate danger to his life from the man. And certainly, if it were handled with more frequent use, we would perhaps have fewer coarse and "fat-headed" men putting their faith in any sort of fables and frauds of that kind.

### CHAPTER XXIX.

-> *Some corrections in the works of Florus.* <-

<margin>Chapter 19, Book II.</margin> I believe I perceive a flaw in Florus <note>Lucius Annaeus Florus was a Roman historian who wrote a brief sketch of Roman history from the founding of the city to the time of Augustus.</note> that no one has noticed until now. Whether I have been more sharp-eyed than others, or whether my eyes have seen too little, let the judgment be yours, Reader. Thus, indeed, says Florus: *The following hundred years were truly made of iron and blood, and if anything is more monstrous: since they mixed the Gracchian and Drusian slaughters with the Jugurthine, Cimbrian, Mithridatic, Parthian, Gallic, and German wars—by which glory itself ascended to the heavens—added to these the slave wars, and so that no shame might be missing, the gladiatorial ones.* When I compare the preceding and following passages with these, and observe the confused and obscure shifting of subjects in the common edition—tangled and without any distinction—I conjecture that Florus actually wrote: *since by these* <note>original: "quippe quis," suggesting a change from the relative pronoun "who" to a form meaning "by which things."</note> *the Jugurthine wars, etc., it mixed*... referring to those hundred "iron" years. This matches the previous phrase: *by which it [the Roman people] subdued Africa, Macedonia, Sicily, and Spain.* In this way, all these deeds are ascribed in a single flow to the persona of the Roman people; otherwise, if the *years* were said to have done something in the meantime, the name would have to be repeated before the word *ascended*; though even then, the following parts would not fit together well. In the same chapter of a recent edition, another tiny flaw remained, which I had already pointed out some years ago in my notes on Ausonius: *Finally, it [Rome] turned against itself. By the hands of Marius and Sulla, and most recently of Pompey and Caesar, as if through madness and fury...*

<meta>This page continues Jacobus Tollius’s philological commentary on the Roman historian Florus. ## JACOBUS TOLLIUS
<meta>catchword: phus,</meta>

Mithridates’ plan was to cross from Colchis <note>An ancient kingdom on the Black Sea coast, in modern-day Georgia.</note> into the Tauric Chersonese <note>The Crimean Peninsula.</note>, and from there to cross into Thrace. Once he had traveled through Thrace, Macedonia, and Greece, he intended to board his fleet again—which would have been waiting for him by a direct course through the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara.</note> and the Hellespont <note>The Dardanelles.</note> near Apollonia, Dyrrachium, or the neighboring shores—to skirt the coasts of Sicily, and, having instilled terror in that almost suburban province, to land his army in Campania itself. In this way, he planned to march on Rome and overwhelm it with an unexpected assault. In the same chapter, a much more difficult passage occurs, which I hardly know if I dare to attempt. But what is the harm in trying? For this is not a life-or-death matter, but one of honest and laudable study, provided that recklessness is absent. *The Jews,* he [Florus] says, *attempted to defend Jerusalem: but he [Pompey] also entered this city, and saw that great secret of an impious race lying open, under a golden sky.* <note>original: "sub aureo uti cælo." This refers to Pompey the Great’s entry into the Holy of Holies in 63 BCE, an act considered a great sacrilege by the Jews.</note> 

Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a renowned Flemish philologist.</note> very ingeniously conjectured the reading: *a vine under a golden sky* <note>original: "sub aureo vitem cælo"</note>. For you may read in Tacitus: *A golden vine was found in the temple.* Vossius and others defend the common reading. Others substitute the word for "veil" <note>original: "velo"</note>; others "a platform" <note>original: "cillo"</note>. However, I seem to see this: that the words *and lying open* <note>original: "& patens"</note> should be referred to the following clause and separated from the preceding one. Then, that word *uti* (or *utis*, as it was in Salmasius’s <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a French classical scholar.</note> manuscript) is part of a corrupted word for *openings* <note>original: "uris," likely from "aperturis"</note>. Therefore, it could be read: *and he saw that great secret of an impious race, the sky lying open from the openings*; or *the sky with wide openings*; or, if anyone prefers it this way, *the sky visible through the openings*. That the sanctuaries <note>original: "adyta"</note> of the ancients were open, or rather <term>subdivalia</term> <note>Open-air areas or shrines exposed to the sky.</note>, is too well known to need proof. Concerning *Openings* <note>original: "Aperturis"</note> in sacred buildings, one should consult Vitruvius, Book IV. As for the matter itself, Freculphus <note>Freculphus (died 853), a Carolingian bishop and historian.</note> writes of it as follows:

# CHANCE OBSERVATIONS.

In Chapter VI of the same Book III, a <term>glossema</term><note>A "gloss" or marginal note written by a later reader that accidentally became part of the main text during copying.</note> from the margin seems to have crept into the flow of the text. It says: *Never before did we enjoy so bloodless a victory; but nor was any race found more faithful in the future. And this was provided for by the singular strategy of the general, who removed this seafaring people far from the sight of the sea and bound them, as it were, to inland fields.* One should read it as: *Nor was any race found more faithful in the future: By the singular strategy of the general, etc.* 

Similar but likewise corrupted passages occur in Book IV, Chapter XII: *Soon there was certain loyalty and eternal peace, both because of their own character being more inclined toward peace, and because of Caesar’s strategy; fearing their confidence in the mountains into which they were retreating, he ordered them to inhabit and dwell in his camps, but those which were on the plain.* That too was a sign of great strategy: *The nature of the region all around is gold-bearing, and fertile in cinnabar, chrysocolla* <note>A green mineral, often copper silicate, used in antiquity as a pigment or for soldering gold.</note>, *and other pigments. He ordered them to work the soil.* The remaining words are not by Florus, but by commentators; they have committed fraud not only in these passages, but in many others. 

Thus at the beginning of the following chapter: *The Cretan War, if we wish to know* <note>original: "noscere"</note> *the truth, we started ourselves.* The word "know" is from an unreliable hand. They were trying to match the phrasing found in Chapter XVIII of this book: *Though it may be called a Social War, so that we may diminish the ill-will: yet if we want the truth, it was a civil war.*
