<meta>catchword: tia.</meta>

Freinshemius <note>Johann Freinsheim (1608–1660), a German classical scholar known for his "supplements" to lost works of Roman history.</note> noticed something similar in Chapter VIII; where [Florus writes], *At the same time the Balearic islands had corrupted the seas with the madness of piracy*: here, the word *islands* is rightly suspect to him. To me, however, that other word *corruperant* <note>original: "corruperant" (had spoiled/corrupted)</note> seems like it should be changed to *corrupuerant* <note>likely a variant or error for "corripuerant," meaning "had seized."</note>. Likewise in Book III, Chapter VI: *The Cilicians had invaded the seas*, that is, *they had seized them*. For these words are <term>equivalent in meaning</term> <note>original Greek: "ἰσοδυναμοῦσαι"</note>.

Indeed, at the end of Book I, Chapter IX: *And having seized the closest [regions], he brought all of Italy under his control.* For that is how it should be read there. And in Book IV, Chapter II: *The madness of Caesar and Pompey gripped the city, Italy, races, nations, and finally the whole empire as far as it stretched, like some kind of flood or fire.* <note>original: "corripuit" (seized or gripped)</note>.

I shall also free the next chapter from a no less inept <term>glossema</term> <note>A "gloss": a marginal note that a later scribe accidentally included in the main text.</note>. *The following*, he says, *and by far more bloody, was the battle of the Belgians; since they were fighting for liberty.* These are the final words, [drawn] from Caesar’s *Gallic War*, Book I. In the preceding parts, the word *battle* <note>original: "pugna"</note> should be deleted; the preceding word *movement* <note>original: "motus"</note> should be understood in its place. The author had said, *The first movement of Gaul began from the Helvetii.* Therefore, here it should be: *the following, far more bloody [movement] of the Belgians.*

In Chapter XI, the common reading is inept and quite foul: *Gazing greedily at the royal treasures, he [gave] no answer, not even by a sham right. But he replied that he would answer at Seleucia.* Read it as: *with no right, not even a sham one, he replied that he would answer at Seleucia.* I know that some will think a certain sharpness exists in the common reading; but how can it be said *he replied nothing* when he *replied that he would reply at Seleucia*? Dio <note>Dio Cassius, a Roman historian who wrote in Greek.</note> says: <quote>But Crassus said to that man that he would state the causes of the war in Seleucia.</quote> <note>original Greek: "Ὁ δὲ Κράσσος ἐκείνῳ τε ἐν Σελευκίᾳ τὰς αἰτίας τοῦ πολέμου ἐρεῖν ἔφη."</note> Plutarch says the same: <quote>When Crassus boasted that he would give his responses in Seleucia, the elder [ambassador] laughed, etc.</quote> <note>original Greek: "Κράσσος κομπάσαντος, ὡς ἐν Σελευκίᾳ δώσει τὰς ὑποκρίσεις, γελάσας ὁ πρεσβ. &c."</note> Otherwise, it would have to be read as *nothing of even a sham right*.

In the same chapter, Florus wrote twice that the head of Crassus was a mockery to the enemy, which is due to his elegance of style.

### CHAPTER XXX.

->*Miscellaneous Emendations.*<-

I have decided to gather into this chapter certain miscellaneous emendations, or rather conjectures, just as they have come into my hands. In the third *Catilinarian Oration* of Cicero, Chapter 1, the common reading is: *For we have extinguished the fires that were already applied and set around the temples, shrines, roofs, and walls of the whole city.* <note>original: "Nam totius urbis templis, delubris, tectis, ac mœnibus subjectos prope jam ignes, circumdatosque restinximus."</note> It is written more elegantly in an old book <note>A "vetus liber" refers to an ancient manuscript source.</note>: *For [we have extinguished the fires applied] to the whole city, to the temples, shrines, roofs, and all the walls, etc.* <note>The difference is a subtle grammatical shift from "temples of the city" to "the city [itself] and its temples."</note> I would not have turned my mind to this—since the city's temples, shrines, etc., are contained within the word "city"—unless Favorinus <note>A philosopher and polymath (c. 80 – c. 160 CE) who appears as a character in the works of Aulus Gellius.</note> had "plucked my ear" <note>An idiom meaning to give a reminder or warning.</note> in the writings of Aulus Gellius, and warned me that this method of writing was used by Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> with deliberate care. For in Book XIII, Chapter XXIV, Gellius has this to say: *Just as in the book of the same Marcus Tullius, "On the Appointing of an Accuser"* <note>original: "de constituendo accusa-", referring to Cicero's "Divinatio in Caecilium."</note>

...in the role of an accuser, one and the same matter is expressed with many words, forcefully and fiercely: *If all of Sicily were to speak with one voice, she would say this: whatever gold, whatever silver, whatever ornaments were in my cities, homes, and shrines.* <note>original: "Sicilia tota, si una voce loqueretur..." from Cicero's "Against Verres."</note> For when he [Cicero] had once mentioned the cities as a whole, he added homes and shrines, which are themselves also within cities.

In Dion Cassius <note>A Roman historian of Greek origin who wrote a massive history of Rome in Greek.</note> there is a shameful error in Book 39, where he discusses Gabinius <note>Aulus Gabinius, a Roman politician and general who returned to Rome in 54 BCE to face charges of corruption.</note>, who was in low spirits due to the consciousness of his crimes: *so that he arrived in Italy at length, and was brought into the city by night, and for many days did not dare to appear outside of Italy.* <note>original Greek: "ὥστε καὶ χρόνῳ ἐς τὴν Ἰταλίαν ἀφικέσθαι... ἔξω τε τῆς Ἰταλίας συχναῖς πάνυ ἡμέραις μὴ τολμῆσαι φανῆναι."</note> Read instead: *outside of his house.* <note>Tollius suggests changing the Greek word "Italias" (Italy) to "oikias" (house).</note> For he was already in Rome at his own home; nor did he dare to come out into public because of the consciousness of the shames he had committed, and out of both shame and fear.

In the same author [Plutarch], in the *Life of Marius*, a single corrupt letter has brought a great stain upon the speech. Thus he writes of Marius, now returning from exile: <margin>page 430.</margin> *“But wearing mean clothing and with his hair long since the day he fled, being over seventy years old, he approached slowly, wishing to appear pitiable, but to this pity was mingled his habitual look, which was more <note>Tollius notes that the Greek word "πλέον" (pleon), meaning "more," is a corruption.</note> terrifying.”* The correction is easy, yet it seems it was not noticed by the translator. Read instead: *“breathing <note>Tollius suggests the word "πνέον" (pneon), meaning "breathing" or "emanating." The difference in Greek is a single letter: a Nu instead of a Lambda.</note> terror.”* That is, *Breathing out terror.* Calavius Offilius says something not much different in Livy regarding the Romans sent under the yoke <note>A ritual of humiliation for a defeated army.</note> at the Caudine Forks: <margin>Book IX.</margin> *“That obstinate silence and eyes fixed on the ground, and ears deaf to all comforts, and the shame of looking upon the light, were signs of a great mass of wrath being stirred up from the depths of the soul.”*

Suetonius, in his *Life of Julius Caesar*, chapter 24, discussing the imprudence of Lucius Domitius; *“But when Lucius Domitius,”* he says, *“a candidate for the consulship, threatened that as consul he would effect what he had been unable to do as praetor, and would take his armies away from him [Caesar], Caesar compelled <note>Latin: "compulit"</note> Crassus and Pompey, who had been drawn out to the city of Luca in his province, to seek a second consulship for the sake of ousting Domitius; and he achieved both: and that his command should be extended for five years.”* I think the text should be restored as: *“Crassus and Pompey, having been drawn out to the city of Luca in his province so that they might seek a second consulship for the sake of ousting Domitius, he achieved both: and that his command should be extended for five years.”* The word *compelled* <note>Latin: "compulit"</note> instead of *persuaded* <note>Latin: "perpulit"</note> crept into the text from the margin. Yet perhaps it might be better to read: *“so that they might seek a second consulship for the sake of ousting Domitius, and that his command should be extended for five years: and he achieved both.”* But the first reading is closer to historical truth. For it was Caesar's plan that these two should seek a second consulship: but they were so generously inclined toward him that, for the sake of protecting his dignity, they sought both; on which matter Dio writes at greater length...

…and in the *Life of Caesar* by Plutarch. The diligence of Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a renowned Flemish philologist and humanist famous for his definitive editions of Tacitus.</note> in cleansing <note>The process of "emending" or correcting errors introduced by medieval scribes into ancient manuscripts.</note> the works of Tacitus was remarkable. In the same author [Tacitus], Book XV, dealing with the Pisonian conspiracy and giving the reason that drove Lucan <note>The poet Lucan, author of the Pharsalia, who was forced to commit suicide by Nero.</note> to join the criminal plot: *“Lucan,”* he says, *“was incited by his own reasons, because Nero suppressed the fame of his poems and had forbidden him from showing them off, being vain in his pretense.”* <note>original: "Lucanum propriae caussae accendebant, quod famam carminum ejus Nero premebat, prohibueratque ostentare, vanus assimulatione."</note> Lipsius suggests, *“vain in his rivalry.”* <note>Changing "assimulatione" (pretense) to "aemulatione" (rivalry).</note> More correctly: *“in the most vain rivalry.”* And so much for these matters.

#### ->Description of the Starred Regulus, and a chemical explanation of several myths.<-

<margin>Book 12 of the *Thebaid*</margin>I am about to describe here the Starred Regulus <term>Regulus stellatus: A term in alchemy referring to a purified metallic substance (usually antimony) that, when cooled properly, forms a star-like crystalline pattern on its surface.</term>, as I promised in earlier pages—that common one which is the image of the true and Philosophical one, and in which, as if in a mirror, you may recognize all the things that have been said before. It will provide the key to almost all the most ancient myths; and, lest I seem to have said this rashly, I will add some of the best examples, which may serve as a model for them all.

> ℞. <note>The symbol for "Recipe," meaning "Take."</note> Two parts of the best, shining **antimony** <note>Specifically stibnite, the sulfide ore of antimony, which forms long, needle-like crystals.</note> with long striations—Hungarian, if it is at hand; 
> One part of **steel** filings, or the purest steel nails; 
> One and a half parts each of **saltpeter** <term>Saltpeter (potassium nitrate)</term> and the best **white tartar** <term>White tartar (potassium bitartrate), a sediment from winemaking used as a flux.</term>.

The steel—whether nails or thin plates—should be heated in a crucible until it is white-hot using a very intense fire. The crucible should be large enough that the material occupies only a fourth part of it. Into this, the **antimony** should be poured with an iron spoon; once the lid is placed and the fire is stirred up, let it melt. When it flows like water, cast in the **tartar** mixed with **saltpeter** using a spoon, bit by bit, immediately covering the crucible after each addition. When the mixture has finished "detonating" <note>Referring to the violent deflagration or rapid burning that occurs when saltpeter and tartar react.</note>, cast in another portion, and repeat until all the saltpeter and tartar have been added and fused. 

The fire must be intensified so that everything is thoroughly melted and mixed. Then, pour it into a concave bronze cone, commonly called an **antimonial horn** <note>A conical casting mold used by alchemists to separate metal from slag.</note>, though it should first be smeared with tallow or a bit of a candle and moderately warmed by the fire. By carefully but gently striking the sides of the mold with an iron rod, ensure that the **regulus** <term>Regulus (literally "little king"): the purified metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible or mold.</term> settles to the bottom and the **scoriae** <note>The dross or slag that separates from the metal.</note> rise to the top. 

Once everything has cooled, the slag is separated by light tapping, and the **regulus** often appears—on the very first attempt—marked with a magnificent **star** <note>The "Starred Regulus of Antimony" displays a beautiful, star-like crystalline pattern on its surface when cooled slowly; alchemists saw this as a sign of the "signature" of the heavens on the metal.</note>, provided the temperatures were correctly observed. Indeed, I have often seen the "star" consumed by an overly intense fire, which exhausts the "water" or **Mercurial humidity** <note>original: "humiditate Mercuriali." Alchemical theory held that metals contained a fundamental "mercury" or moisture that gave them their luster and fluidity; if overheated, this essence was thought to be lost.</note>. But if the star does not appear, the regulus should be reduced to a powder and melted a second or third time in a fresh crucible with an equal weight of saltpeter and tartar, until the slag turns reddish. One must, however, be careful...

In this passage, almost every individual word suggests **something more musical** <note>original Greek: *μουσικώτερόν τι*</note>. As Euclid says in his *Division of the Monochord*: <term>If there were stillness and immobility, there would be silence. Where there is silence and nothing moves, nothing can be heard. Therefore, if anything is to be heard, a blow and movement must first occur.</term> <note>original Greek: *Εἰ ἡσυχία εἴη...* Euclid was a Greek mathematician; here Tollius uses his theories on sound to explain that the "noise" of the chemical reaction proves the "movement" of the elements.</note> From the reaction of the sulfurous nature and the saline nature, a "third thing" arises: the **Gas** of Helmont <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644) was a chemist who coined the word "gas" from the Greek "chaos."</note>, or the **wild spirit**, which is the first effect of fermentation. Because of this, according to Plutarch, the Pans and Satyrs—who are forest gods, or spirits—were said to be the first to sense Osiris when he was cast into the sea by his brother Typhon. They lived around Chennin; and "Chen" signified a **plant** to the Egyptians. <margin>Treatise 7 of the New Light of Alchemy. Chem.</margin> <term>The first matter,</term> says Sendivogius, <term>is a herb or a tree, which you do not know how to create; the second matter is the seed; in this the herb or tree is multiplied.</term> <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a famous Polish alchemist. This quote emphasizes that the alchemist works with natural life-forces rather than creating matter from nothing.</note> 

After these "wild spirits" come the more refined parts of the fermented substance itself; and thirdly, the very substance of the fermented matter, which is like the **blood of the plant**. Therefore, when the plant is separated from all its earth—taken from its trunk and transplanted from its own root into another earth—it is **Water**. This "Earth" is the substance of nature, which is called **Oil** and **Fire**, together with the **spirit of the Quintessence**; the water carried this away with it from the stinking earth from which it exited and flowed out by distillation. This **Water** possesses the nature of those things from which it is drawn and separated. The trunk which is separated, or the root from which it came, are the dregs of the **Earth** which are cast aside; for indeed, these three—**Water**, **Air**, and **Fire**—have emerged as one. The other Earth, into which the plant (or Water) is implanted, **is**...

However, so that each detail may be better understood, and the nature of the **starred regulus** <term>regulus stellatus: a piece of purified metallic antimony that exhibits a star-like crystalline pattern on its surface upon cooling</term> itself better perceived, we shall excerpt some relevant points from Becher, Tachenius, and several others. 

All minerals, of whatever kind they may be, which contain hidden metallic bodies, have attached acids—namely various sulfurs—which prevent the metal from being freed from the impurity of the mines. In this difficulty, one must necessarily flee to alkalis, which offer swift aid. Hence **steel** <note>original: *chalybs*. Represented by the planet Mars in alchemy.</note> is added to antimony along with **tartar** <note>original: *tartaro*. Potassium bitartrate, often used as a flux.</note> and **saltpeter**: which, when ignited by the sulfur, partly burns away, while another part, together with the tartar, is turned into an alkali. By this alkali every acid is absorbed, which would otherwise cause all the **Mercury of antimony**—which is its metal—to flee away. But in this way, with the filing of **iron** <note>original: *martis limatura*. "Mars" refers to iron.</note> greatly assisting, the Mercury of Antimony, released and freed from its acidic sulfur, falls down and seeks the bottom. 

Or, as others maintain, the arsenical sulfur of Iron and of the salts themselves seizes the related sulfur of antimony; and this is what **Basil Valentine** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, credited with influential works on antimony.</note> says: *Poison which is driven out by poison.* Some have thought that the **Star** <margin>Key 1.</margin> arises from the abundance of the added salts. For salt joined with sulfur exhibits a striated form. I, although I do not reject this, nevertheless think it is born chiefly from the abundance of the **mercurial water** <note>original: *aquae Mercurialis*. A theoretical alchemical solvent or the "spirit" of mercury.</note>, or the internal volatile alkali salt, joined with a bright and pure earth, through freezing: just as from there—

...they are called **elements** <note>original Greek: στοιχεῖα (*stoicheia*)</note>; by their constant change, as Cicero says, *the nature of the WORLD is sustained*. For from earth comes water; from water, air is born; and from air, the ether. Then, in a reverse cycle, from ether comes air; from air, water; and from water, the lowest earth. Thus, by these natures—from which *ALL THINGS* are composed—moving up and down, back and forth, the connection of the parts of the **World** is maintained.

<margin>Plutarch, *On the Principle of Cold*.</margin>
"Air," says another Philosopher, "changes into water when it is condensed, and into fire when it is divided. Just as, conversely, that which is divided is destroyed into air, while by union it is destroyed into earth." <note>This refers to the ancient theory that the four elements are simply different densities of a single underlying substance.</note>

<margin>On the Soul of the World.</margin>
Timaeus of Locri <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and character in Plato's dialogues.</note> attributed earth to the Moon, water to Mercury, air to Venus, and fire to the Sun: then, in reverse order, he assigned fire to Mars, air to Jupiter, water to Saturn, and earth to the eighth Sphere: in which last one lies hidden that which is hidden to many. The ancients even persuaded themselves that these elements were living beings.

<margin>Servius, commentary on *Aeneid* Book IV, line 524.</margin>
From these elements, the Egyptians created four Gods who preside over **MAN** at his birth: the **Daemon** (or the Sun), **Fortune** <note>original: *Τύχην* (*Tychen*)</note> (or the Moon), **Love**, and **Necessity**. Of these, it should be noted that Love was represented by a kiss, and Necessity by a knot.

<margin>Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 1, Chapter 19.</margin>
Seneca speaks slightly differently: *The Egyptians,* he says, *made four elements and then divided each into two, male and female. They judge the Air to be male where it is wind, and female where it is misty and still. They would call the sea the masculine Water, and every other kind of water feminine. They call Fire masculine where the flame burns, and feminine where it shines harmless to the touch. The stronger Earth they call male, such as rocks and cliffs; they assign the name of female to this earth which is workable for cultivation.*

<margin>Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book III, Chapter 14.</margin>
To these is added the **Fifth Essence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth element" or ether, believed to be the pure substance of the celestial bodies</term>, which Aristotle called **Entelechy** <note>original: Ἐντελέχειαν; here used to mean the fundamental "formative principle" of matter</note>. It is unlike those first four elements; from it are made the *STARS* and *individual Minds*. It is the Matter that lies beneath all things, without any outward appearance and lacking any quality, from which *ALL THINGS* are shaped and brought into being.

Yet, I would prefer it to be derived *from the mud*. <note>original: *ἀπὸ τοῦ πηλοῦ* (apo tou pelou).</note> In this sense, the poet called Ocean, the father of all things, the *eternal mud*; <note>original: *ἀΐδιον πηλὸν* (aidion pelon).</note> and in Plato, the *rivers of liquid mud* <note>original: *ὑγροῦ πηλοῦ ποταμοὶ* (hygrou pelou potamoi).</note> are the rivers of liquefied millstones, or rather of sulfurous stones; concerning which Severus writes in *Aetna*:

<margin>Phædo v. 394.</margin>

> *A part lies manifest to the eyes: it grows red, and is itself hard,*
> *As stone: fires boil within the thick juice.*
> *Nay, even certain stones under various pressures*
> *Melt throughout the whole mountain: to them a true*
> *And tenacious guardianship of flame is given: but indeed the greatest*
> *Millstone-rock of that burning stone claims Etna for itself,*

Regarding this passage, Scaliger very opportunely brought forward these words of Strabo: <margin>in Theogonia.</margin> *“When the rock has melted in the craters and then been cast up, that which overflows from the summit is a liquid black mud, flowing down the mountain-side; then, having taken on a solid form, it becomes millstone.”* <note>original Greek: Τακείσης ἐν τοῖς κρατῆρσι τῆς πέτρας... λίθος μυλίας.</note> Our Peleus is of the nature of this *black* <note>original: *μέλανος* (melanos).</note> and bituminous *mud*, to whom Thetis is joined; for *Thetis*, says Hesychius, *is the mother of Achilles, and the sea; but the earth is called Tethys:* <note>original Greek: Θέτις δὲ... ἡ δὲ γῆ λέγεται Τηθύς.</note> whom Hesiod not without reason calls *lovely* <note>original: *ἐρατεινὴν* (erateinēn).</note> and gives to Ocean in marriage. Thus we also read in Homer;

<header>JACOBI TOLLII</header>
<page-num>256</page-num>

->Ocean, the origin of the gods, and Tethys the mother. <note>original Greek: Ωκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν, καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν. A quote from Homer's *Iliad*.</note><-

But to return to Peleus: in the mud, or *pēlos* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ πηλῷ (en tō pēlō). Tollius is using a wordplay between the hero's name, Peleus, and the Greek word for mud or clay.</note>, there is much of the "Acid": because there is also much of Mars <note>In alchemy, "Mars" is the standard term for iron or iron oxides, often associated with a red color and reactive properties.</note>, as has been recognized through many experiments. Some things were said above concerning the mud of the rivers Cephisus, Achelous, and the Nile, and regarding the Hebrew etymology of the city of Thebes, which signifies "mud." It was fated that from this mud—that is, Peleus—and Thetis, a son would be born who would be greater than his father. Therefore, all the Gods assembled to celebrate these nuptials <margin>Book 3, Mythology</margin>: just as they also attended in great numbers at the marriage rites of Cadmus (or Jasius) and Harmonia. Thus, in the "marriage" of our Work <note>The *Opus Magnum* or Great Work of alchemy, which involves the symbolic marriage of opposing elements.</note>, all the planets are wedding guests: about whom Basil <note>Basil Valentine, a legendary (possibly pseudonymous) alchemist.</note> and Philalethes <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a famous 17th-century alchemist whose name means "peaceful lover of truth."</note> have written extensively.

It is worthwhile here to transcribe some things from Fulgentius <note>Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, a Late Antique mythographer who provided allegorical interpretations of Greek myths.</note>, so that it may be seen from them how closely the Greeks perceived the truth. "They wanted *Thetis*," he says, "to be called water, from which she is also called a Nymph. Jupiter, acting as God, joins her to Peleus. For *Pēlos* <note>original Greek: Πηλὸς</note> is said in Greek, which in Latin is called *lutum* [mud]. Therefore, they maintain that HUMANS were born from earth mixed with water. Hence, they also say that Jupiter wanted to lie with Thetis, but was forbidden, lest—if he should father one greater [than himself] (as it should be read here)—that son might expel him from his kingdom. For fire, which is Jupiter, if it should unite with water, is extinguished by the power of the water. Therefore, in the joining of water and earth—that is, Thetis and Peleus—only Discord is not sought (that is, she is not invited to the wedding): for the evident reason that through the CONCORD of both elements, a HUMAN is brought forth. At these nuptials, moreover, three Goddesses contend over beauty, the <margin>in Practice.</margin> prize of which is a golden apple. This is given by Paris to Venus—that is, to that spirit which, in our Work, is clothed in a more abundant color; whose body is pure tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent substance capable of transmitting its color and properties to other metals.</note>, not unlike the color seen in the finest metal, and which, because of the abundance of color, [turns] into redness..."*

<summary>Tollius uses the myth of Peleus and Thetis as an alchemical allegory, where "mud" represents the material base and their marriage signifies the union of Earth and Water. He quotes the mythographer Fulgentius to argue that this union produces the perfected alchemical "redness" rather than discord.</summary>

# FORTUITOUS REMARKS.

...stretches out, as it is found in the works of Basil <note>Basil Valentine, the legendary alchemist</note>: for whom *MUSIC* holds forward a mirror of red color as a banner, in which is depicted a most beautiful *CHARITY* in green garments: for whom *SATURN* acts as the chamberlain <note>original Latin: "curopalates," a high-ranking Byzantine court official, here serving as an attendant to the planetary allegory.</note>. 

<margin>Apollodorus, Book III.</margin>
Thetis, therefore, the woman, is the Alkali <term>Alkali: In 17th-century chemistry, the passive or "receptive" salt that reacts with an acid</term>, or the matter capable of receiving all forms, no less changeable than Proteus himself; she was captured by the same trick as he was and bound by the bond of marriage. At this point, there was need for the penetrating force of the Acid. Therefore, Chiron presents Peleus with an *ashen spear*, Neptune gives him the horses Balius and Xanthus, and Vulcan gives him a sword: the other Gods give other gifts. 

<margin>Fulgentius, Book III.</margin>
From these parents, *ACHILLES* is brought into the light—our Chemical hero, the fated victor and destruction of *TROY*: whom, like a *PERFECTED MAN*, his *mother dips into the Stygian waters*. Others relate that Thetis, wishing to grant immortality to her son, secretly hid him in the fire on the hearth. Plutarch narrates the same of Isis, and Hyginus, Ovid, and others tell it of Ceres. But since they were all disturbed by the accidental intervention of the fathers, they were unable to entirely burn away the defect of mortality. For there is present in our *MAN* <note>The alchemical substance or "rebus"</note>, and inherent in him—though not deeply—an impure sulfur <term>Impure Sulfur: The combustible "dross" or earthly impurity that alchemists sought to purge through fire</term>: and for this reason he must die, so that he may rise again clarified from that state and be made equal to the *CELESTIAL* spirits.

<margin>The Book of Alze, p. 334.</margin>
Nor is it without mystery that the commentator on Homer relates that *the seventh* child was snatched from the fire by Peleus, while the others were extinguished. Let us now hear the Chemists. *If the body*, they say, *becomes fluid and is burned, it turns itself back toward its progenitor, and a subtle aerial MAGNESIA is made, and it is turned toward the earth, which makes it spiritual and gives it life.* The Seventh Key of Basil Valentine will provide more information, of which this story is a kind of interpretation.

<summary>Tollius interprets the birth and "dipping" of Achilles as an alchemical process where the union of acid (Peleus) and alkali (Thetis) creates a perfected substance that must still be purified by fire to remove "impure sulfur."</summary>

He is killed by Achilles and dragged three times around the walls of Troy: once he is removed, the conquest of Troy is easy thereafter, though in such a way that the Arrows of Hercules are needed <note>The "Arrows of Hercules" likely refer to sharp, penetrating chemical reagents required to finalize the process</note>.

Having finished the story of Peleus, I shall approach the story of Perseus. His mother was Danaë,

> Whom, when she was shut up, Jupiter filled with fertile gold. <note>A quote from Horace, Odes 3.16.1</note>

How much nonsense have the Greek and Latin interpreters given us about her? in which he is said to have been enclosed with his sister Hemithea by his father Cycnus, and carried to the island—not Leuce, but Leucophrys: and all these more-than-Gordian knots [he] solved with a single Tenedian axe—

**R 2**

...would have lived through the blow. But even the boat of Brizomantis <note>A name likely related to Britomartis, a Cretan goddess of nets and fishing; Tollius treats her boat as an alchemical vessel</note>, <margin>Athenaeus, Book 11.</margin> of which Athenaeus speaks, would have been recognized; when the inhabitants of Delos performed sacred rites to her, **they offered her vessels full of all good things, except for fish.** <margin>Homer, Book VIII.</margin> This Ark, or boat, or ship, is the **Belly of the Wind** <note>original: "Venter venti est." This is a direct reference to the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus: "The wind carried it in its belly." In alchemy, this represents the volatile spirit or gas contained within the apparatus</note>. Concerning the fish, I have spoken above. You may also add to these the cup of Hercules (for his cradle does not belong in <margin>Servius on Aeneid VII.</margin> this place), in which he set out, as if in a ship, to lead away the three-bodied cattle of Geryon. Add also the cup of the Sun, in which he is accustomed to be carried from the east to the west. For that will lead us to the famous place in Illyricum named *Cylikes* <note>original: "Κύλικες," meaning "cups" or "drinking bowls"</note>: near which is the monument of Cadmus and Harmonia. There it will be granted to drink leisurely from the cup of Heroes, and to feast with the **Abundant Ceres** <note>Ceres is the goddess of grain; Tollius links her to the "abundance" of the completed alchemical material</note>. <margin>Athenaeus, Book XI.</margin> Nor should anyone expect the threats of a Cyclops here, saying: **"I shall eat No-man last"** <note>original: "Οὔτιν ἐγὼ πυμάτον ἔδομαι." A reference to Homer's *Odyssey*, where the Cyclops Polyphemus promises to eat Odysseus (disguised as "No-man") last</note>. For that creature has already been deprived of his only eye by Ulysses, after he drank three times <margin>Scholiast on Homer, Iliad 319.</margin> from the cup of red wine.

The foster-father and educator of Perseus (for we must return to him) is said to have been **Polydeuces**, a name meaning "much sweetness." He was also the **Temperer of Acid**: perhaps because of a kinship with Deucalion <note>Tollius is playing on the Greek *deukos* (sweet wine/must) and Deucalion's name to suggest the neutralization of corrosive chemical acids</note>. But when Perseus grew up, he attacked the three Gorgons, who were accustomed to share a single eye and a single tooth among themselves. He slew Medusa by holding out a crystalline or polished, shining bronze shield: her hair was full of serpents. From the blood of Medusa was born Pegasus, the winged horse: by whose help, and with the curved sword given by Minerva, he killed the sea-monster and won Andromeda, the daughter of Cepheus, King of the Ethiopians, and granddaughter of Phoenix. We shall refer Cepheus to the river Cephisus, and Phoenix to the tutor of Achilles. From Andromeda, a wife of "manly care," a son was born to Perseus named **Erythras**, and another named **Pyrrhus** <note>Both names, *Erythras* and *Pyrrhus*, derive from words for "Red" in Greek. In the alchemical "Great Work," the appearance of the color red (*rubedo*) marks the final perfection of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. These are the things, Kind Reader...

### JACOBUS TOLLIUS

Kind Reader, these are the things which Chance <note>original: "Fors"; the personification of Luck or Fortune</note> suggested to me while I was turning over nothing less in my mind, and while the lack of certain editions delays the work I had intended for Lucretius <note>The Roman poet Lucretius, author of *On the Nature of Things*. Tollius was a renowned classical scholar who published an edition of Lucretius in 1695</note>; for an ardor impatient of any longer delay commands me to seize upon whatever lies in my path. **Farewell, and use and enjoy these things, of whatever sort they may be.**

->THE END.<-

# JACOB TOLLIUS
# ->CUPID<-
# ->SLEEPING,<-
### SLEEP THE GENEROUS GIVER.

Among the monuments of Antiquity that have been left to us—either by the injury of long time or the savage madness of barbarian nations—there are statues and images that usually bring me the greatest pleasure. For they do not only delight the eyes, but often instruct the mind with healthy precepts, or at least increase the knowledge required to understand the words, deeds, and writings of the ancients. Therefore, I welcomed the opportunity that once presented several marbles of this kind to me. Among these was a statue of Cupid sleeping upon a lion; his right hand was folded back over his left shoulder, while his left hand grasped two poppies, toward which a lizard crawls. Near the right side of the statue, these letters were found, and no traces of any others are visible: O. V. A. R. N. M. This is a task for an Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the only one capable of solving the Sphinx's riddle; here it means a master riddle-solver.</note>. But although I am neither Davus <note>Davus is a clever servant character from the plays of Terence, often contrasted with Oedipus in the proverb "I am Davus, not Oedipus," meaning "I am a simple man, not a riddle-solver."</note> nor Oedipus, I will nonetheless offer an interpretation: if it is good, it will not be without benefit; if it is bad, let others do better. I explain it, therefore, in this way: *Every Force of Love Grows Mild through Nightly Rest* <note>original Latin: "Omnis Vis Amoris Requie Nocturna Mitefcit." Tollius suggests the letters O.V.A.R.N.M. are an acronym for this sentence.</note>. For Sleep is the "releaser from care" <note>original Greek: λυσιμέριμνος (lysimerimnos)</note>, "possessing a sweet rest from labors, and stealing over us as a sacred consolation for every grief," <note>original Greek: κόπων ἡδεῖαν ἔχων ἀνάπαυσιν, καὶ πάσης λύπης ἱερὸν παραμύθιον ἕρπων</note> as Orpheus says, <margin>In his hymns.</margin> or rather...

> — And you, O Sleep,
> tamer of evils, rest of the soul.

<margin>Book 3, Argonautica.</margin>
A shining example of this matter occurs in Apollonius, where, having described the cares of Medea who was seized by love for Jason, he adds this:

> A deep sleep, having relieved her from her sorrows, soothed her. <note>original Greek: Κέρση δ’ ἐξ ἀχέων ἀδινὸς κατελώφεεν ὕπνος.</note>

<margin>Book 3, elegy 4.</margin>
Indeed, there is hardly anything more frequent among the writers of love. Hence for Tibullus:

> — *A God useful to the sick mind.*

<margin>Book 4, page 433; in Protrepticus, page 125; Book 1, chapter 84.</margin>
And in Achilles Tatius, he is called *the medicine for all diseases* <note>original Greek: πάντων νοσημάτων φάρμακον</note>. By Critias, in the works of Athenaeus, he is called *the harbor from labors* <note>original Greek: καμάτων λιμὴν</note>, and by Iamblichus, *the rest from evils* <note>original Greek: ἀνάπαυμα κακῶν</note>. The reason is obvious; *for he delivers from every anxiety* <note>original Greek: πάσης γὰρ ἀπαλλάττει φροντίδος</note>, as is found in Artemidorus's work *On the Interpretation of Dreams* <note>original Greek title: Onirocritica</note>. And from this comes those words of Propertius’s Cynthia:

> *Sometimes, abandoned, I complained heavily to myself*
> *of the long delays often found in a foreign love.*
> *Until pleasant slumber struck me as I fell upon its wings.*
> *That was the final cure for my tears.*

<margin>In Orestes, and from him Plutarch in the book On Superstition.</margin>
Moreover, what I said about the sickness of love growing mild through sleep is wonderfully confirmed by these lines of Euripides; although they refer to the raving Orestes:

> O dear enchantment of sleep, helper against disease,
> how sweet you came to me in my hour of need. <note>original Greek: Ὧ φίλον ὕπνου θέλγητρον, ἐπίκουρον νόσου, Ὡς ἡδύ μοι προσῆλθες ἐν δέοντί γε.</note>

<meta>catchword: Ὧ πό- (the start of the next line of Euripides: Ὦ πότνια λήθη, "O lady oblivion")</meta>

<summary>Tollius provides a wide-ranging survey of classical authorities—including Cicero, Catullus, Seneca, and Euripides—to demonstrate the ancient consensus that Sleep serves as a divine remedy for mental anguish and the pains of love. This serves as scholarly support for his interpretation of the sleeping Cupid statue.</summary>

# MISCELLANY

> "O mistress Oblivion of evils, how wise you are, and a goddess to be prayed for by those in misfortune." <note>original Greek: Ὦ πότνια λήθη τῶν κακῶν, ὡς εἶ σοφὴ, / Καὶ τοῖσι δυςυχοῦσιν εὐκταία θεὸς. From Euripides’ tragedy *Orestes*.</note>

Where he likewise joins Oblivion to sleep, just as here the symbol of Oblivion is added to it, about which we will say more shortly. For we shall not dwell long on this conjecture of ours. However, we shall illuminate those symbols that are more easily understood, as much as we can, so that the sculptor's intention becomes crystal clear. It was a most praiseworthy custom of the ancients to cloak in symbols those ideas which, if presented plainly and openly, would have offered less delight and beauty. They did this both to stir the minds of diligent and curious people to investigate and penetrate their meaning, and to bar the uneducated masses from these sacred mysteries of the Muses and refined scholarship. For instance, among the ancient statues still standing in Rome, another **Cupid** is seen, deep in thought. The artist wisely expressed this hesitation of judgment by depicting him sitting and pressing his right foot upon a **tortoise** <term>testudo: used here as a symbol of slowness or domesticity</term> as it crawls along.

<margin>In the later books of the Description of Elis.</margin>
**Pausanias** <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler whose writings provide a detailed account of ancient Greek art and monuments.</note> mentions another example, reporting that a statue of **Venus Urania** <note>The "Heavenly Venus," often associated with spiritual love and domestic virtue, as opposed to "Venus Pandemos" or common love.</note>, a work of the master sculptor **Phidias**, stood in Elis, and she too pressed a tortoise with her foot.

<margin>In Advice on Marriage and On Isis and Osiris.</margin>
**Plutarch** <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer who often sought moral lessons in myths and customs.</note> believes this was done because the tortoise carries its own house; thus, a woman might learn to stay at home and not wander through the houses of neighbors or strangers while neglecting her own family affairs. For, as the Greek maxims teach:

> "It is the duty of a good woman to preserve the home." <note>original Greek: Γυναικὸς ἐσθλῆς ἐστι σώζειν οἰκίαν.</note>

Or, as Eteocles says in the works of **Aeschylus**:

<margin>In Seven Against Thebes.</margin>
> "Let no woman take counsel on matters outside; and while staying within, let her do no harm." <note>original Greek: Μὴ γυνὴ βουλευέτω / Τἄξωθεν. ἔνδον δ' οὖsa μὴ βλάβην τίθει.</note>

That posture of the body, and the casting of the right hand over the opposite shoulder with limbs relaxed in languor—as Ovid speaks of the god Sleep himself—suggests a weariness that is settled by rest; just as the right hand folded over the head denotes one resting from long labor, according to Lucian. Of this sort, among <margin>Part VI, page 5.</margin> other ancient statues in Boissard <note>Jean-Jacques Boissard (1528–1602), an antiquarian famous for his drawings of Roman statues.</note>, is one of a certain Nymph sleeping in this physical posture. Nor is it without reason that he sleeps on his left ear. For that is a sign of repeated sleep, and thus of a mind relieved of care. For at first, if the physicians are to be heard, it is healthier to sleep on the right side, as that sleep is the first and the deepest. But to fall back asleep once awakened is not so easy, except for those free from all care. Well known are the <margin>Erasmus, in his *Adages*.</margin> adages *to sleep on either ear*, and *to sleep on the right ear*—and what also seems to have some place here, *with feet stretched out*. In this posture of the feet, Boissard presents to us the very image of Sleep.

<margin>Virgil, *Georgics* Book 1, line 78 and Book 4, line 212.</margin>

->*While she gathers, she is said to have tasted with a forgotten palate,*<-
->*and unwittingly satisfied a long hunger.*<-

<margin>Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3. *On the Nature of the Gods*. Galen, *On the Properties of Simples*, Book 7. Virgil, *Georgics* Book 4, line 131; Book 1, line 212. *Aeneid* Book 4, line 486. Pliny, *Natural History* Book 19, chapter 8.</margin>

And he rightly used the word *forgotten* <note>Latin: *oblita*</note>. For the poppy, as Hesychius says, is **a certain herb that induces forgetfulness** <note>original Greek: μήκων... πόα τις λήθην ἐμποιεῦσα</note>.

Although other reasons are also brought forward by the ancients: namely, that it stands as a symbol of fertility, as Eusebius has recorded; and this is clear from a coin of the people of Hierapolis, and from the "Apotheosis of Augustus" found on that famous noble gemstone, the explanation of which Tristan and Rubens <note>Jean Tristan de Saint-Amant and Albert Rubens were prominent 17th-century antiquarians and scholars of ancient coins and gems.</note> have given us. Or perhaps because its roundness and cone-like shape signify that the earth is round in the manner of a sphere, as Phurnutus <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher who wrote on Greek mythology.</note> would have it. Or, what is more credible, because the ancients once used the poppy as food: which is why Virgil called it **edible** <note>Latin: *vescum*</note> and **Ceres’ poppy**; though elsewhere he calls it **sleep-bringing**. For in both ways it is suitable for consumption. The farmers of old were not ignorant of this. Indeed, because both forms of bodily restoration were necessary for those exhausted by rural labor and toil, they were accustomed to **sprinkle the seeds of the white poppy onto the crusts of their bread**. There is an excellent passage on this matter in Philostratus: **And if you have need of seasoning, here you have it. For they share in fennel, and in celery, and also in the poppy, which is the seasoning of sleep.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ εἰ μ’ ὄψῳ π’ χρήζεις, αἱ δ’ ἔχεις. Ἔτε γδ, μαραίθρῳ μετέχουσι, κὶ ὅ σελίνῳ, κὶ ἔti μήκωνι, ἥπέρ ἐστιν ἥδυσμα ὅ ὕπν8.</note> Athenaeus mentions somewhere **ox-dung bread** <note>A type of bread likely named for its shape or color rather than its ingredients.</note>, which, before it was baked, was smeared in the kneading-trough with oil, and poppy seeds were sprinkled underneath. But more notable in the same book, and more relevant here, is another passage from the same author. He says that **Alcman mentions poppy-breads in his fifteenth book, thus:**

<margin>Book 2, *Images*</margin>

> **Seven couches, and as many tables of poppy-breads,**
> **crowned with celery and sesame in bowls.**
<note>original Greek: Κλίναι μὲν ἑπτὰ, τόσσαι τράπεζαι μακωνίδων ἄρτων, Ἐπιστεφεῖς σελίνῳ τε σακάμῳ κἤν πελίχναις πίδαισι.</note>

Regarding this subject, Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar who produced extensive commentaries on ancient texts.</note> cites a passage from Hesychius’s twenty-seventh chapter: "figures made in the inner chamber from poppy and sesame" <note>original Greek: ἐνθαλάμια πλάσματα ἐκ μήκωνος καὶ σησάμης</note>. He also brings forward words from Petronius, "sesame and poppies scattered," <note>original Latin: sesamo & papavera sparsa</note> used to describe things that are honeyed and sweet. He could also have added those lines from Plautus’s play *The Little Carthaginian* <note>Latin: *Poenulus*</note>, where a girl seems to her lover to speak of nothing but "little cakes, sesame, and poppy, and wheat, and roasted nuts," because, just like all of those, the flavor of the poppy is sweet and most pleasing. For this reason, toasted poppy with honey was once served at the second course <note>essentially as a dessert in the Roman meal structure</note>. Furthermore, there is a garden variety of poppy that physicians call <term>thylakitis</term> <note>Greek: θυλακῖτιν, meaning "pouch-like," referring to the shape of the seed pod</note>, which is highly suitable for baking and very healthy.

<margin>Plautus, *Poenulus*, Act 1, Scene 2.</margin>

<margin>Dioscorides, Book 4, Chapter 6.</margin>
Regarding this kind of poppy, Dioscorides writes: "The *rhoias* <note>the common corn poppy</note> is a cultivated, garden poppy, the seed of which is made into bread for healthy use; they also use it with honey instead of sesame, and it is called *thylakitis*." <note>original Greek: Μήκων ἡ ῥοιάς ἐστιν ἥμερος, κηπευτὴ, ἧς τὸ σπέρμα ἀρτοποιεῖται εἰς τὴν ὑγείαν χρῆσιν, καὶ σὺν μέλιτι δὲ ἀντὶ σησάμης αὐτῇ χρῶνται, καλεῖται δὲ θυλακῖτις</note>

Because there was an abundance of the fruits of Ceres <note>grain</note> in times of peace, I believe it came to pass that on an ancient gemstone, when Concordia—the mother of peace—was depicted with right hands joined, those hands held a poppy positioned between two ears of grain. Similarly, Victoria <note>the goddess Victory</note>, who brings about such peace, had a poppy, an ear of grain, and a ship’s rudder assigned to her as symbols.

<margin>Gorlæus, Gemstone 94.</margin>
<margin>Gemstone 7.</margin>

<margin>Porphyry as quoted in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 3, Chapter 11. Aelian.</margin>
Furthermore, the poppy is sacred to the Moon, the Goddess of the Night, both because of its sleep-inducing power and because its outer edges resemble crenellated walls <note>referring to the "crown" atop the poppy pod, which resembles a mural crown</note>; its seeds are also like a great crowd of people, and indeed, it suggests the fertility that the Moon bestows upon worldly things. Ausonius, however, in his poem *Cupid Crucified*, notes that the poppy is also dedi- <note>The Latin text *dicatum* is cut off by the catchword; it refers to the poppy being dedicated to Proserpina, queen of the Underworld.</note>

# JACOBI TOLLII

<page-num>278</page-num>

<header>JACOBUS TOLLIUS</header>

<meta>catchword: Nam- (For-)</meta>

> *And afterward comes silent Sleep, surrounded by tawny wings,*
> *and dark dreams with a wavering foot.*
<note>original Latin: "Postque venit tacitus fulvis circumdatus alis Somnus, & incerto somnia nigra pede." These lines are from the Roman poet Tibullus (Elegies 2.1.89-90).</note>

<margin>Sanchuniathon according to Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book I, chapter x.</margin>
So too is Night described by Euripides as the *mother of black-winged dreams*. <note>original Greek: μελανοπτέρυγων μῆτηρ ὀνείρων.</note>

For Sleep is no less winged than Time itself, the image of which—as everyone knows—is winged. Because, therefore, humans are given times for both sleep and waking, the Egyptian Thoth <note>The Egyptian god of wisdom and time, often identified by the Greeks with Hermes or Mercury.</note> fashioned an image of Saturn <note>Tollius likely refers here to the Orphic or syncretic Chronos/Saturn, associated with the passage of time.</note> which, in addition to its four eyes:

<margin>Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book I; *Silvae* Book V, iv.</margin>
> *Whence in their turns two took their rest,*
> *And two kept watch, and remained on guard,*
<note>original Latin: "Unde suis vicibus capiebant bina quietem, Binaque servabant, atque in statione manebant." These lines from Ovid originally describe the hundred eyes of the giant Argus, which never all slept at once; Tollius applies this symbolism to the alternating nature of rest and alertness.</note>

It also had as many wings, of which two were unfolded and two were folded and lowered, to signify both the "rest of the wakeful" and the "wakeful cares of the resting."

<margin>In Stobaeus, sermon vi, end. Themistius, Oration II. Lucretius, book iv. Orpheus in the hymns, l. xxxi. Dionysius, Odyssey, book v, 373. In [Sophocles'] Ajax, book viii. Agathon.</margin>
Sleep is also depicted with a youthful face, which is why Papinius Statius <note>A 1st-century AD Roman poet.</note> calls him the *most peaceful of the young gods*. Euclides <note>Possibly a reference to a commentator or a different Euclides than the mathematician.</note> makes two [Sleeps], one *younger and giving shape to dreams*, the other *gray and old*. <note>original Greek: νεώτερον & μορφωιώδη (younger and form-shaping), πολίον & γέροντα (gray and old).</note> Whoever considers human nature will easily see the reason for this. Moreover, as for the *sleeping* lion, <note>original Greek: καθεύδοντα.</note> that itself denotes that Sleep is *limb-loosening* and *all-subduing*. <note>original Greek: λυσιμελῆ (limb-loosening) and πανδαμάτορα (all-subduing). These are traditional Homeric epithets for sleep.</note> Thus says Nonnus: *Sleep, why are you called all-subduing?* And before him, Homer:

-> *And he lulled him [Zeus] in sleep for Hera, the all-subduer,* <-
<note>original Greek: Κὰδδέ μιν ὕπνῳ Ἥιρῃ πανδαμάτωρ. From the *Iliad*, Book 14.</note>

Sophocles, however, calls him *master of all*. <note>original Greek: πασικρατῆ.</note> And Valerius Flaccus, interpreting Sophocles as far as can be guessed, calls him *omnipotent*.

---

> *—And she summoned you, he says of Medea,*
> *Father Sleep, omnipotent one of sleep; I, the Colchian, call you from the whole*
> *world.*
<note>original Latin: "Teque ciebat... Somne pater, somni omnipotent; te Colchis ab omni Orbe voco." From Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* 8.62-73, describing Medea calling upon Sleep to charm the dragon guarding the Golden Fleece.</note>

# FORTUITA

<page-num>279</page-num>

<header>FORTUITA.</header>

<sig>S 4</sig>

For by Sleep *the body becomes weak; all the limbs grow faint;* <note>original Latin: "Namque Somno debile fit corpus; languescunt omnia membra;" likely a poetic paraphrase or quotation regarding the physiological effects of rest.</note> And indeed he is *the king of all living things, as many as the wide earth nourishes.* <note>original Greek: ἄνακτα πάντων ζώων, ὁπόσα τρέφει εὐρεῖα χθών.</note>

<margin>Pindar, *Pythian Odes* ix; quoted in Aristotle, *On Sleep and Waking*; see also Cicero, *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, book v, chapter xix.</margin>
*For it takes away the senses,* as Cicero says, *and removes all action.* <note>original Latin: "Aufert enim sensus, ut ait Cicero, actionemque tollit omnem."</note>

From that union of the lion and sleep, it will be immediately clear to anyone how aptly he was called by Pindar a *sweet companion of the revel to sleep*; <note>original Greek: ὕπνῳ σύγκωμος γλυκύς. Tollius is likely interpreting an artistic depiction of a lion alongside a personification of Sleep.</note> and there is a noble passage from Themistius <note>A 4th-century Byzantine philosopher and rhetorician.</note> giving the reason why he is <gloss>thus</gloss> called *sweet*: *"Because,"* he says, *"of the experiences that affect us, sleep is the sweetest; for first, it extinguishes the sensation of pain in everyone through a pleasure mixed with much of its own nature. Then, it masters other desires, even if they are most intense."* <note>original Greek: Ὅτι τῶν περὶ ἡμᾶς παθῶν ὁ ὕπνος ἡδιστός ἐστι πρῶτα μὲν γὰρ αἴσθησιν ἀλγηδόνος πᾶσι σβέννυσι διὰ τὴν ἡδονὴν πολλῷ τῷ οἰκείῳ κεραννυμένην. ἔπειτα τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιθυμιῶν κρατεῖ, κἄν ὦσι σφοδρόταται.</note> But nothing is *more intense* <note>original Greek: σφοδρότερον (sphodroteron).</note> than a lion, which is a symbol of impetuous passions; especially since the lion is very sparing of sleep, and has eyes that are not entirely closed while sleeping, but shining—though here they clearly blink. For which reason the lion's head was also a hieroglyphic symbol of watchful guardianship for the Egyptians. Indeed, there were even those who believed lions were sleepless, among whom was Manetho the Egyptian; <note>An Egyptian priest and historian (3rd century BCE) who wrote on Egyptian history and religion.</note> and for that reason they were dedicated to the sun, from whose all-seeing eyes nothing escapes. Whence comes that line of Ovid:

<margin>Pierius, *Hieroglyphica*, book i; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book iv.</margin>
> ——— *This God sees all things first.* <note>original Latin: "Videt hic Deus omnia primus." Referring to the Sun (Sol/Helios).</note>

And this line from Homer,

> *He who sees all and hears all.* <note>original Greek: Ὃς πάντ’ ἐφορᾷ καὶ πάντ’ ἐπακούει. A standard Homeric description of the Sun.</note>

<margin>Pindar, *Pythian Odes* 1.</margin>
As for the closed eyes, in a matter so natural and common, I would not want to begrudge Sleep that most sweet epithet of Pindar, who calls it *a dark-eyed cloud* and *a sweet shutter of the eyelids.* <note>original Greek: κελαινῶπιν νεφέλαν (dark-eyed cloud) and βλεφάρων ἁδὺ κλαΐστρον (sweet shutter of the eyelids).</note>

The remaining things agree so beautifully, that to [waste] effort... <note>Tollius is concluding that the literary evidence perfectly matches the visual evidence he is studying.</note>

Recently, a print of a quite curious *Ancient Artifact* fell into my hands. It depicts a Lion and a Boy sleeping together. The Lion is leaning on one of its claws, and the Boy on the Lion, holding some kind of fruit in his left hand. Below, there is a Lizard that seems to want to pounce on this fruit; and on the right hand there are these letters *OVARNM*, which are claimed to be mysterious. As I had just finished reading the *Anthology* <note>The *Greek Anthology*, a collection of poems and epigrams from the classical and Byzantine periods.</note> when I was shown this print, I first believed it was the Cupid of *Argentarius*, <note>Marcus Argentarius, a poet included in the Greek Anthology known for his witty epigrams.</note> who, after having run a long race on horseback upon a Lion, was resting peacefully with his mount. In truth, one does not notice either a quiver, nor arrows, nor torches in the Figure. But the Sculptor might well have forgotten all these little things. Usually, people of his trade are not very exact. And then, one does not need so much gear to recognize Love. Beauty is an indelible character in this Boy. One has only to see him; the heart soon says that it is he.

# DE RONDEL
### Professor at Maastricht <note>Trajectum ad Mosam is the Latin name for Maastricht.</note>
# EXPOSITION
### OF THE ANCIENT TOLLIAN ARTIFACT

Not many days have passed, distinguished Sir, since an engraving <note>original: "ectypon"; a cast or molded image of an original work.</note> of an ancient marble fell into my hands—one which is, if I understand anything of these matters, truly elegant. A lion is seen there, and a youth: both overcome by sleep. The former rests on his front paws; the latter on the lion. He holds in his left hand some sort of fruit, which a lizard a little lower down gapes at and lies in wait for. On the right side, these letters occur: O. V. A. R. N. M., which some consider enigmatic. 

As I had recently been reading the *Greek Anthology* when this engraving was shown to me, I immediately suspected that this was the Cupid of Argentarius <gloss>1</gloss>, <note>Marcus Argentarius, a poet in the *Greek Anthology*. His epigram (9.221) describes Cupid taming a lion as a symbol of love’s power over even the fiercest nature.</note> exhausted from driving the lion and resting with his steed. Although neither the quiver, nor his arrows, nor torches appeared on the marble—equipment of which I attributed the omission to the carelessness of the sculptor, as if it were a matter of little importance; for one expects accurate diligence in such works from that class of men in vain. 

Furthermore, there was no need for such elaborate equipment for Love to be recognized; the very charm of his form <gloss>2</gloss> provides the most certain evidence, so that at the first glimpse of him, the mind itself suggests to us that this is the son of Venus. But after considering the matter more deeply shortly thereafter, while [evaluating] the nature of the lion...

</margin>

...to have between a **Lion**, a **Boy**, a **Lizard**, and some fruits, I believed—and still believe—that it must be something else entirely than **Cupid**. I have been confirmed in my opinion by the explanation that a certain learned man named **Tollius** <note>Cornelius Tollius (c. 1628–1654) was a Dutch philologist who published works on ancient artifacts.</note> gave for these letters. He believes that **O V A R N M** signifies, or can signify, *All the power of Love softens with nightly rest* <note>original Latin: "Omnis Vis Amoris Requie Nocturna Mitescit."</note>. But he has not considered, it seems to me, that the night is the true time for **Lovers**. It is the "inn of Love," says **Propertius** <note>Sextus Propertius, a Roman elegiac poet.</note>:

> Love has prepared a guest-chamber for the whole night. <note>original: "Hospitium tota nocte paravit Amor."</note>

It is the **Bacchanals of Venus**, the *Rites of Venus* <note>original: "Veneris Orgia."</note>, according to what the good man **Hephaestion** <note>Likely referring to the Greek grammarian Hephaestion of Alexandria.</note> says; and it is the "Banner of Pleasures," as an old poet of Greece sings: *a sacred image of pleasure* <note>original Greek: "ἱερὸν ἡδονῆς ἄγαλμα."</note>, etc. You know the impatience of **Lovers**. They hurl a thousand insults at the Sun; they grow restless for the darkness; a single day seems like a year to them. Thus, **Sir**, even if this were **Cupid**, far from concluding, as **Tollius** does, that these letters **O V A R N M** can mean *All the power of Love softens with nightly rest*, I would conclude the opposite: *Every power of lovers, when resting, is of no consequence* <note>original Latin: "Omnis Vis Amantium Requiescens Nullius Momenti."</note>. Why is that? It is, **Sir**, because...

1. But from this passage, which appears at the end of Book III, you can hardly derive that specific epithet for Night.

...of **Milo**, of the youth, of the lizard, and the harmony among the fruits, or what their relationship to one another might be, I began to think differently (nor do I regret that opinion even now), and I came to believe that the matter is something far different from **Cupid**. My view was greatly confirmed by the explanation of a certain **Tollius** <note>Cornelius Tollius (c. 1628–1654), a Dutch philologist.</note>, a man of no small learning, who thinks those letters signify, or can conveniently signify: *All the Power of Love Softens with Nightly Rest* <note>original Latin: "Omnis Vis Amoris Requie Nocturna Mitescit."</note>. But in truth, it seems to me that he has not noticed that the night-time is by far the most suitable of all for **lovers**. For this reason, **Propertius** <note>A Roman elegiac poet of the 1st century BCE.</note> calls the Night the "inn of Love": <margin>1</margin> *Love,* he says, *has prepared a guest-chamber for the whole night.* <note>original: "Hospitium tota nocte paravit Amor."</note> And **Hephaestion** <note>Likely referring to the Greek grammarian Hephaestion of Alexandria.</note> calls them the "Bacchanals of Venus" <note>original: "Veneris orgia," referring to secret rites or celebrations.</note>; while a Greek poet calls it *a sacred image of pleasure* <note>original Greek: "ἱερὸν ἡδονῆς ἄγαλμα."</note>. Nor does the desire of lovers, impatient of delay, escape you; nor the six hundred insults they constantly hurl at the Sun while it lingers, fleeing into the lap of **Thetis** <note>In mythology, the sun (Helios) was said to descend into the ocean (Thetis) at dusk. So much so that, even if I were to concede that this was a statue of **Cupid**, my opinion differs so much from that of **Tollius** that, on the contrary, I judge those letters to signify: <margin>2</margin> *All Power of Lovers, when Resting, is of No Consequence* <note>original Latin: "Omnis Vis Amantium Requiescens Nullius Momenti."</note>. *Every lover serves as a soldier, and Cupid has his own camp.*
<note>original Latin: "Militat omnis amans, & habet sua castra Cupido." This is the famous opening line of Ovid's *Amores*, 1.9.1.</note>
However, as for saying more about the "bed-wrestling" <note>term: <term>Clinopale</term>; a Greek-derived word used by the Emperor Domitian to describe his sexual activities as a form of "bed-wrestling."</note> instituted by **Domitian** for that purpose, neither your modesty nor mine allows it. Nevertheless, let us assume this is a sign of **Love**: where then, in the individual elements that this marble shows us, are the characters and indicators of this passion? For this God never fails to leave certain traces of himself everywhere and at every turn. *Injuries, suspicions, enmities, war,* <note>original Latin: "Injuriæ, suspiciones, inimicitiæ, bellum." A reference to the volatile nature of love described in Terence's play *The Eunuch*.</note> and other things of that kind, perpetually accompany him. Who could find or detect those things here? He himself rests, seized by peaceful sleep; nor is the **Lion's** appearance any different; only the **Lizard** remains awake!

"What of it?" someone might say. "Is this not a sufficiently grand argument for doubt? Indeed, she does not watch in vain." Believe me, the nature of this little beast is not so happy; and little animals of that kind do not rise to such intellectual distinction. > And Nature in her sluggishness established a secure home.

<note>original: "Securumque larem segnis Natura locavit..." from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book XI, describing the House of Sleep.</note>

*But what is most convincing is that Sleep, in the work of the Poet I just cited, never appears without his Horn.* <note>original: "Mais ce qu'il y a de plus convainquant..." The "Poet" is Ovid. In ancient art, Sleep often carries a horn from which he pours out slumbering liquids or vapors.</note>

<margin>Metamorphoses, Book 11.</margin>
> The older one passes these by; and from all the brothers, Sleep

<margin>Topography, part III, p. 69; part IV, p. 72; part III, p. 48.</margin>
Do you prefer one of middle age—not yet advanced, but rather in his prime? An ancient marble in the work of **Boissard** <note>Jean-Jacques Boissard (1528–1602), a famous antiquarian who published engravings of Roman monuments.</note> shows him to us thus. Is a youth sought? With such a face, sleeping peacefully with his chin resting on his left hand and holding a downward-turned torch <note>A common symbol for the end of life or deep sleep.</note>, he is shown on another marble in the same Boissard with this inscription: *And secure rest, and a life that knows no deception.* Also on another, with these words inscribed above: *To the sleep of daughter Orestilla.* Does someone desire a boy? Many ancient stones occur in the same author where winged boys, like **Cupids** or **Spirits** <note>original: "Geniorum"</note>, also with downward torches, represent the perpetual sleep of those who have passed from life. Especially notable is the one where two figures stand on either side of a building with closed doors, pointing with outstretched hands to the shut gate, indicating no hope of return to life. By this, those words of **Horace** are wonderfully illustrated:

> Soon night will press upon you, and the ghosts of myth,
> and the meager house of Pluto; once you have traveled there,
> you will neither cast lots for the lordship of the wine,
> nor admire tender Lycidas.

Another stone supplies us with the image of just such a house or temple, through whose half-open doors **Mercury** returns, he who had led the dead to the lower regions. He is the **Guide** <note>original: "πομπαῖος" (pompaios), an epithet of Mercury/Hermes as the conductor of souls to the underworld.</note>, of whom the same Poet says:

> You place the pious souls in joyful
> dwellings, and with your golden staff you shepherd the
> airy throng, pleasing to the gods
> above and those below.

> *temple; this other, having forgotten the horn, has let it drop.*

Which horn, however, you would seek in vain in this marble. Furthermore, if this is the figure of Sleep which Pausanias mentions, and which Tollius <note>Jacobus Tollius (1633–1696), a Dutch scholar of antiquities.</note> accepted from him, it would be necessary for it to have <gloss>2</gloss> twisted feet; yet in this youth—whoever he may be—the feet are most beautiful and positioned in a manner familiar to those sleeping, as far as can be seen from the one that is still intact. At this point, if the subject and time permitted, some things could be explained more extensively concerning the "twisted feet" of Sleep according to the opinion of the ancients, who wished to denote by this symbol the ambiguous nature of dreams, which are deceitful and twisted with obscure evasions. 

But omitting these for the present, I will rather address this: I will say that these fruits could just as well be <gloss>3</gloss> mandrakes (and perhaps they are) as poppies. There is no reason for me to prove here to you—who are most skilled in all these fine arts—with many arguments that the Mandrake is a symbol of oblivion <note>Forgetfulness or the loss of memory.</note>, nor likewise to teach you the proverb that once arose among the Greeks from this. Just as the poppy induces sleep, it <gloss>1</gloss> does not take away memory; but he who drinks mandrake—if any faith is to be placed in the ancients—forgets all those things which he did or said. 

Indeed, Lucian <note>A 2nd-century Syrian-Greek satirist.</note> says that memory is lost if rest is taken under a mandrake. But as for it being some taller plant, such that one could sleep under its shade, the naturalists <note>original: "naturæ interpretes," referring to early botanists like Pliny or Theophrastus.</note> do not even attribute a stalk to it, except perhaps to a certain third kind of the plant, and even then quite ambiguously. Moreover, it is known that the Greek preposition <term>hypo</term> <note>original: "ὑπὸ"; usually meaning "under."</note> can signify "by" or "from" as much as "under"; thus in Plato, we find the phrase <term>altered by food and drink</term> <note>original: "ὑπὸ σιτίων καὶ ποτῶν ἀλλοίωτον."</note>. Furthermore, it is not Lucian’s opinion that Jupiter actually lost his memory, but rather that, being lulled by Mandrake, he heard nothing and understood nothing of the crimes being committed on earth. He refers, therefore, to the power of the Mandrake to induce a deep stupor rather than to its ability to remove memory. On this power, Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and the father of pharmacognosy.</note> and the Greek proverbs speak quite enough; but regarding the sleep...

I recall that he had some fine and sturdy ones on the day of the Titans, when fear melted all his divine form, and he became the prettiest Raven in the world <note>A reference to the myth where the Olympian gods fled from the monster Typhon by transforming into animals; Apollo took the form of a raven.</note>. *Arachne*, out of malice or otherwise, once depicted him disguised as a Hawk for some young lady whose name we no longer know <note>Referring to Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, where Arachne weaves a tapestry showing the gods' various deceptions and disguises.</note>. I would tell you something more serious here if we still possessed the *Praises of Apollo* contained in twenty-five Sermons, which we have lost along with several other *Indigitamenta* <term>Indigitamenta: ancient Roman lists or books of names for gods used in official invocations to ensure the correct deity was addressed for a specific need</term> of Antiquity. The Hymn sung to him at one of his Festivals contains, among ninety-six attributes, that of "myriomorphos" <note>original: "μυριόμορφος", meaning "of ten thousand shapes" or "multiform."</note>. And as one cannot doubt this under penalty of the *Poetic Inquisition*, Apollo could well have wings, claws, fins, etc., when it was a matter of displaying all that, and not otherwise. I will tell you yet another thing: in the East, the Sun was worshipped among several peoples under the figure of a winged Globe with a Serpent around it <note>A reference to the "Winged Sun" motif common in Egyptian, Persian, and Mesopotamian iconography.</note>. Thus, the Sculptor of our antiquity—either by hearsay or by following the design of a man slightly more skillful than himself—may have inferred something that belonged to Apollo, so that there might be enough in his marble to satisfy all the various devotees.

<meta>This page continues the defense of depicting Apollo (the Sun) with wings, moving from poetic examples of his transformations into birds to theological and archaeological evidence from Eastern and Biblical sources.</meta>

<page-num>(301)</page-num>

...which you would find to be fiction. Indeed, since the horses of the Sun are said to be winged, and wings are attributed to the very wheels of his chariots, what reason is there why they should be denied to Apollo himself? I remember that to certain Poets he once appeared not unfeathered, when the fear cast upon him during the Battle of the Giants <term>Gigantomachy: the mythical war between the Olympian gods and the Giants</term> shook off his former shape and displayed Apollo to us as a quite beautiful raven. But also *Arachne*—whether she did it out of the wickedness of her mind or for some other reason—depicted him on her tapestry as having changed at one time into a hawk, seized by love for a maiden whose name is unknown. You see, therefore, Apollo winged when the situation seems to require it; nor is anything easier or more natural for a God of such bird-like swiftness. Some arguments of greater weight and importance could be brought forward here, had not the injury of time begrudged us those twenty-five discourses and several other ancient *Indigitamenta* <term>Indigitamenta: ancient Roman priestly lists of the names and functions of various deities used for official invocations</term> in which the praises of Apollo were contained.

But I do not think we have been left without a defense for that reason. If indeed that hymn, which was sung on a certain festival day of his, among those ninety-six surnames attributed to him, designates Apollo as *myriomorphon* <note>original: "μυριόμορϕον" (myriomorphos), meaning multiform or having ten thousand shapes</note>; if he was thousand-formed, why should we hesitate to believe that he sometimes possessed wings, claws, and feathers? Especially since many peoples of the East worshipped him in the likeness of a winged globe, surrounded by a serpent—or something similar? This is not foreign to the genius of sculptors, and so we may not unjustly suspect of our own sculptor that he received—either by hearsay or by seeing it in a design provided by those more skilled—certain things pertaining to Apollo which he thought should be added to his marble.

...devotees of this Divinity. Because they adopted all the Religions of the world, they represented a Divinity under several forms, or took the most significant portion of each effigy under which it appeared in various countries, to incorporate it into a single image. Thus, *Venus* in Cyprus was both man and woman; in Assyria, a semi-circle of rays; at Paphos, a pyramid; at Rome, whatever one wished. Thus, our Mithras or Apollo is a Discus in Paeonia, a Dog and a Wolf in Egypt, all the animals of the Zodiac in Chaldea, and in Greece, he is all things. Witness this prayer of the Theologians of Paganism: *O almighty Sun, spirit of the world, power of the world, light of the world* <note>original Greek: "ἥλιε παντοκράτωρ, κόσμου πνεῦμα, κόσμου δύναμις, κόσμου φῶς"</note>. This is all very strange. I admit it, Monsieur. However, these Pagans had some reason. The Gods hardly ever appeared in the same form to different Peoples. It was the needs of the people, the misery of the Nations, and the occasions for rewarding or punishing that determined these Gods to appear under various figures. It was also the Valleys, the Mountains, the Caves, and every other dwelling of either solitude or pleasure that engaged them to leave the Celestial Court and come to sport among us. "O Sun, all-ruling, spirit of the world, power of the world, light of the world." <note>original Greek: Ἥλιε παντοκράτωρ, κόσμου πνεῦμα, κόσμου δύναμις, κόσμου φῶς.</note> Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and writer known for his commentary on Cicero’s Dream of Scipio.</note> also confirms this with these words of Orpheus:

You will marvel, I know, and not without cause; but the ancient nations did not lack their own reasoning. For the Gods did not appear in the same form to every people. Indeed, necessity sometimes demanded this—the sorrowful fates of nations, and the very opportunities that presented themselves for repaying the turns of fortune, whether well-deserved or ill-earned. But secluded valleys, shaded mountains, caves dripping with springs, and other places of that kind—which either lead one into solitude or entice with their beauty—often invited the Gods so that, having left the temples of heaven, they might enjoy human delights and pleasures. 

Indeed, a certain famous Platonic philosopher <note>Referring to Maximus of Tyre, a 2nd-century philosopher who often used this hypothetical argument.</note> once used to say: *"If another Prometheus were to arise and fashion a new world for me; or if another soul were given to me from this mind of ours, to be formed by my own laws and institutions, I would forbid men from fashioning any other image of the divine than that which nature shows us beforehand. I would forbid them from representing it in gold, or silver, or ivory; and I would suffer even less for the divine to be expressed in the form of a fir tree, a river, or a bird. But I would perhaps grant this: that with their eyes fixed upon the rising sun, they might look up at and admire that stupendous variety of a thousand colors with which the first rays of the rising orb illuminate the air. Furthermore, I would command them to gaze upon the moon, whose purest and sweetest brightness seems to me to dispel the horrible and foul shadows of the night for no other reason than to offer us some comfort, however thin, for the loss of the light of day. Finally, I would command that they contemplate with their whole mind that entire mass of the heavens, whose vastness is as great as its rich decoration and polish, and which is perfectly composed by the admirable arrangement of all its parts."* 

But in truth, since this age of ours is inferior <note>The author refers to the "Iron Age" or a later, diminished era of humanity where abstract thought is more difficult.</note>, and we must live as it has happened to be given to us, let us obey the established laws whose utility we experience every day. Let us not change what is forbidden to change, nor let us [take away] anything from this opinion regarding the Gods...
