### Inscription on the ancient Sixian marble.

You arrived, unsummoned, at three-times-ten years,
> Theodotus, to the path that is owed by all who live;
And for you, who rejoiced in festive libations among the citizens,
> Your mother, the presiding official, wails in mourning.
This stone shall cry out to strangers how, like a shadow,
> Fortune has granted nothing secure to mankind.
May you be joyful with your father, so that likewise,
> Sostratus may hold infinite praise among the departed.
<note>original: Ἤλυθες ἐκ ἀβόατος... This is a Greek funerary epigram. The "three-times-ten years" refers to the deceased being thirty years old.</note>

### Interpretation:

<margin>Barely completing his sixth five-year period <term>lustrum</term>.</margin>
*Within the sixth five-year period of life, but not without lamentation,*
*Theodotus, you tread the path fated for all.*
*And while you presided over the festive offerings among the citizens,*
*In the middle of the joy, your mother groans that you have passed away.*
*Stranger, you may learn from this stone that all things are turned*
*By the blind whim of unstable Fortune.*
*But may you dwell happily with your father, so that in this way*
*Sostratus may also receive great praise among the spirits of the dead <term>manes</term>.*
<note>This Latin verse section is a poetic translation of the Greek epigram provided above. A "lustrum" was a Roman period of five years.</note>

### Subject matter of the inscription.

This Theodotus had been a *Prytanis*, which is to say a curator of the republic; it was the duty of these curators to take their meals at public expense in the town hall <term>prytaneum</term> <note>The Prytaneum was the civic heart of a Greek city-state, where officials and distinguished citizens were fed at the state's expense.</note>. Therefore, at this banquet, on a certain feast day, when libations had been made to the Gods (perhaps also after a treaty was struck with a neighboring city), he had celebrated quite cheerfully. But that same night, his life having been exchanged for death, he gave a notable lesson to mortals through his mother's great grief: that human affairs are uncertain, and that Fortune intervenes even in our joys, making them mournful by some sudden, opposing accident. This unexpected...

...the author of this funerary poem laments the so sudden and untimely death of Theodotus.

### Notes.

**You came** <note>original: "Ἦλθες" (Elthes)</note>] Everything is seen to be written, or rather carved, in square letters <note>This refers to the "majuscule" or all-capital style used in ancient inscriptions</note>, joined together in such a way that they are not separated by any spaces. In almost all Greek monuments, this same sequence of continuous letters appears without any accents or breathing marks.

**Without a cry** <note>original: "ἀβοά" (aboa)</note>] Written in the Doric dialect <note>A regional variety of ancient Greek often used in choral and funerary poetry</note>, as are all the other words; this term indicates the mourning and the loud cries of the mother, the relatives, or the citizens complaining about the misfortune, as is customary in bitter funerals. Thus, it could be said of him what was said of another Theodotus in the *Greek Anthology*: *You left wailing and grief to your sweetest mother* <note>original: "Κάλλιπες ἡδίστῃ μητρὶ γόος ἠδ’ ἄχη"</note>. Similarly, in the same *Anthology*, Book III:
> When Agathon, son of Ainesias, died before them in Abdera,
> The whole city wailed at his funeral pyre.
> <note>original: "Ἀβδήρων προθανόντα τὸν αἰνεσίην Ἀγάθωνα / Πᾶσ’ ἐπὶ πυρκαϊῆς ἤδ’ ἐβόησε πόλις."</note>

**Theodotus** <note>original: "Θεόδοτε" (Theodote)</note>] Among the Arundel Marbles <note>A famous collection of ancient Greek inscriptions brought to England in the 17th century</note>, there is a seventh entry by a recent editor which also mentions a Theodotus who lost two sons in their early youth. However, neither the age of the children nor the dialect of that inscription allows us to suspect that this is the same man. The spelling *Theodotos* for *Theodotus* <note>original: "Theodotus pro Theodotus"</note> is very common, just as *Theodosius* is used for *Theodosius* in Claudian’s poem *Against Rufinus*.

**The path owed** <note>original: "Οἶμον ὀφ." (Oimon oph.)</note>] This is that famous *path of death that must be trodden once* mentioned by Horace. In the *Anthology*, we find phrases like *at the final path*, and *the dark shadow of Hades*. It is also used in a much gentler sense as *the sleep that is owed*.

The Latins say *To go to the common place*. Indeed, the Greeks say it no differently. Thus, we find *the common place that receives the dead* in Artemidorus, Book I, chapter 80. By contrast, in Clement’s *Letter to the Corinthians*, Peter and Paul are said *to have journeyed to the holy place* and *to the profitable place of glory*. Ignatius used a similar expression in his *Letter to the Magnesians*, and in the *Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 1:25, Judas is said *to have turned aside to go to his own place*.

**In the libations** <note>original: "Ἐν σπονδαῖσι" (En spondaisi)</note>] Meaning in the ritual offerings of wine. These were performed on festival days in honor of the gods; furthermore, they were used extensively in the sealing of treaties, which is why the word is sometimes used to mean the sanctioning of a treaty itself, or the treaties themselves. It was then the duty of the Prytanes <note>term: Prytanes — the leading executive magistrates in many ancient Greek city-states</note> to invite the ambassadors of the people with whom treaties were being made to a sacred feast in the Prytaneum <note>term: Prytaneum — a public hall that housed the city's eternal flame and where official guests were entertained</note>. This is described by the Greeks as *to call someone to the Prytaneum for hospitality*. In Homer you may read:

namely, onto the slaughtered lambs, by which sacrifice that treaty was sanctioned: just as in **Virgil**, Book VI of the *Aeneid*: *The priest pours wine upon the forehead.* **Claudian**, Book I, *On the Praises of Stilicho*:

[**Giver of Honors**] <note>original: "Γεραδόχα" (Geradocha)</note> From this word, I have elicited what I believe to be the true meaning of this epitaph, which is also confirmed by the sixth verse.

[**Prytane**] <note>original: "Πρυτάνιν" (Prytanin)</note> Regarding who the Prytanes were in Athens, **Casaubon**, **Selden**, and others teach with sufficient accuracy; namely, the leaders and Governors of the city, in whose hands lay the care of laws, treaties, and sacred rites. Indeed, the stewards <note>original: "ταμίαι"</note> and choral leaders <note>original: "χορηγοὶ"</note> were also often called Prytanes, being the providers and moderators of libations. **Hesychius**: *Prytane: king, ruler, choral leader, steward, administrator.* For it should be read thus in that source, as is clear from **Suidas**, and not "of the lake" <note>original: "λίμνης"</note> as is commonly read. So that it can be said of these what **Cicero** said of another in Chapter X of *On the Responses of the Haruspices*: *To your priesthood belong the sacred wagons, the chariot, the opening chant, the games, the libations, and the banquets of the public games.* Furthermore, on these festival days and assemblies, he records that the Prytanes of the Naucontitae were clothed in white tunics. **Athenaeus**, Book IV, page 149.

[**Invisibly**] <note>original: "Αϊδήλως" (Aidēlos)</note> I would take this not so much as the cruelty of fortune, but as its unknown and obscure outcome. Thus, I remember reading in some place of an "invisible fire" <note>original: "ἀΐδηλον πῦρ"</note>; a fire whose origin was unknown. This interpretation fits exceptionally well with the word "certain" <note>original: "ἀσφαλὲς"</note>, which signifies something fixed and stable, and which one may trust. For what is more unforeseen than sudden death in the midst of the joy of a festival day? What is more uncertain...

<summary>This page provides a scholarly analysis of the religious and civic terms in Theodotus's epitaph, comparing the use of wine libations and the role of "Prytanes" (city leaders) to examples in classical literature by Homer, Virgil, and Cicero.</summary>
<keywords>libation, Prytanes, Homer, Virgil, Hesychius, funerary rites, Athenian government, sacrifice, religious festivals</keywords>

(310)

Arela

is certain, than the hope of a long-lasting life, even if one's strength is intact and their health unshaken? *Can it be certain to anyone*, says **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator</note>, *how the body will behave, I do not say for a year, but even until evening?* And the same author says elsewhere: *Who is so foolish, however young he may be, as to be certain he will live until evening?*

[*It was fated*] <note>original: "Εἵμαρτ’" (Heimart')</note> This word seems to fit here perfectly, especially when considering **Nemesis** <note>The Greek goddess of divine retribution and justice</note>, whom the learned are persuaded is the same as Fortune, distributing good and bad things to men at her pleasure, and bitterly punishing excessive prosperity or pleasure: we have written more on this in our notes on Adonius.

[*With*] <note>original: "Σὺμ" (Sym)</note> written instead of *syn* <note>original: "σὺν"</note>, because a labial letter <note>A sound made with the lips, like 'p' or 'b'</note> follows it. Thus, in the **Arundel Marbles** <note>A famous collection of ancient Greek inscriptions brought to England in the 17th century</note> and other Greek stones, you may often see the 'n' changed into an 'm' when followed by the labials 'm', 'p', 'b', or 'ph'. Conversely, it changes to a 'g' <note>gamma</note> before 'k' and 'ch'.

[*Rejoicing*] <note>original: "Κεχαρμέν@" (Kecharmenos)</note> According to ancient custom. Hence, in sepulchral inscriptions, we find: *Farewell, Eupere. Farewell, good and painless one. Farewell, good Nicephorus.* &c. *Be of good cheer*, and similar phrases. The **Latins** said either *Greetings*, *Hail*, or *Farewell*. Regarding this, you may consult **Servius** <note>An ancient commentator on the works of Virgil</note> in his notes on **Virgil's** *Aeneid*, Book 5, verse 80, and the inscriptions collected by **Gruter** and **Reinesius** <note>Famous 17th-century scholars of ancient inscriptions (epigraphy)</note>.

[*I was buried*] <note>original: "Εσάφω" (Esapho)</note> To one looking closely at the marble, it easily appears that *sealed and buried* <note>original: "σφραγισάφω" (sphragisapho)</note> was written on it. In place of this, some otherwise very learned and sharp-eyed men read *Oeranus your...* <note>original: "οἵρανε τῶ" (oirane to)</note>, and translated it as *to your Oeranus* in both prose and verse. But hardly anyone could persuade me that the same man was called both **Theodotus** and **Oeranus**. For the Greeks did not do such things. In the other parts, there is no difficulty.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

It often happens that while we are searching for one thing, we find another. This very thing happened to me recently. For while I was looking through the book *On Airs, Waters, and Places* by our own <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>A famous Greek physician of the 5th century BCE, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, I happened upon chapter 43: where he discusses the <term>Scythians</term> <note>Ancient nomadic people who lived in the regions north of the Black Sea.</note> and their impotence in the matters of <term>Venus</term> <note>The Roman goddess of love; here used as a polite term for sexual function.</note>. "Furthermore," he says, "among the Scythians, many become eunuchs; they perform women's work and speak in the same manner as women. Such people are called <term>Enarees</term> <note>A class of Scythian shamans who took on feminine roles.</note>. The local people attribute the cause to a god, and they revere these men and bow before them, etc." <note>original Greek: "Ἔτι τε πρὸς τούτοισιν, εὐνουχίαι γίγνονται οἱ πλεῖστοι ἐν Σκύθησιν, καὶ γυναικεῖα ἐργάζονται, καὶ ὡς αἱ γυναῖκες διαλέγονταί τε ὁμοίως. καλέονται δὲ οἱ τοιοῦτοι ἐναρέες. Οἱ μὲν ἐπιχώριοι τὴν αἰτίην προστιθέασι θεῷ, καὶ σέβονται τούτους τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, καὶ προσκυνέουσι, &c."</note>

And he goes on to provide a natural explanation for this fact, namely the cutting of the veins behind the ears—a remedy that many were accustomed to using when they were seized by <term>sciatica</term> <note>Pain affecting the back, hip, and outer side of the leg, caused by compression of the sciatic nerve.</note> due to constant horseback riding. 

At that same time—specifically around the beginning of the <term>Peloponnesian War</term> <note>The great war between Athens and Sparta (431–404 BCE).</note>, which began in the first year of the 87th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks for dating; this specific date corresponds to 431 BCE.</note>—lived <term>Herodotus</term> of Halicarnassus <note>The Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note>. He records almost the same details regarding this disease among the Scythians, but he assigns the cause to a committed act of sacrilege. "Concerning those," he says of the Scythians returning from their Egyptian expedition, "when they were on their way back and had reached the city of <term>Ascalon</term> in Syria, and after the majority of the Scythians had passed through without doing harm, a few of them stayed behind and plundered the temple of the <term>Heavenly Aphrodite</term>. Upon these men, and upon their descendants forever, the goddess inflicted a 'female disease'." <note>original Greek: "Οἱ δὲ... ἐπεί τε ἀναχωρέοντες ὀπίσω ἐγένοντο τῆς Συρίης ἐν Ἀσκάλωνι πόλι, τῶν πλεόνων Σκυθέων παρεξελθόντων ἀσινέων; ὀλίγοι τινὲς αὐτέων ὑπολειφθέντες ἐσύλησαν τῆς οὐρανίης Ἀφροδίτης τὸ ἱρόν. τοῖσι δὲ, καὶ τοῖσι τούτων αἰεί ἐκγόνοισι ἐνέσκηψε ἡ θεὸς θήλειαν νοῦσον."</note> 

It seems, however, that Hippocrates had either heard Herodotus giving a recitation of his work, or had read the history already published, since he believes this disease should not be attributed to a God or Goddess and, as I have said, he offers a natural reason for it. The most noble critic <term>Longinus</term> <note>A Greek teacher of rhetoric, likely from the 1st century CE, famous for his work on literary style.</note> cites this passage of Herodotus in his treatise *On the Sublime* <note>Greek title: περὶ ὕψους.</note>, and remarks that this <term>periphrasis</term> <note>A roundabout way of speaking; here, the "female disease" as a polite way to describe impotence.</note> is "inimitable" <note>Greek: ἀμίμητον.</note>. Whence

(320)

I have always felt that I understood the nature of that disease; however, all those who have written commentaries on it seem to have fallen into a similar error. Therefore, I believed it would be appropriate to include here the notes I previously made regarding this passage in <term>Longinus</term> <note>Referring to the ancient Greek work *On the Sublime*, traditionally attributed to Longinus, which discusses the use of indirect language to describe the Scythian condition.</note>, specifically section XXVIII (or section XXV, as others divide it).

<term>Tanaquillus Faber</term> <note>A 17th-century French classical scholar (Tanneguy Le Fèvre).</note> interpreted the term as "monthly purgings" <note>original Greek: *καταμήνια* (menstruation).</note>. Being a man who, during his life, was exceedingly witty and marvelously refined in both Greek and Latin scholarship, he jokingly tells the reader to hold their nose. <term>Boileau</term> <note>Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux, a French poet and critic who translated Longinus into French with remarkable elegance and learning.</note>, who translated this treatise into French with remarkable elegance and learning, interprets it as a flux of <term>hemorrhoids</term> <note>Swollen veins in the rectum; Boileau suggested this as a more plausible explanation for bleeding occurring in men.</note>. This was because it seemed as incredible to him as it did to me that men could be afflicted by a woman's condition. However, observing the same condition in a rather famous individual taught me a better lesson.

Boileau’s view was supported by a similar story in the Holy Scriptures (though he did not notice it) which occurred among the same people. In the <term>First Book of Samuel</term>, chapter 5, the <term>Philistines</term> were struck with hemorrhoids because they had captured the <term>Ark of the Covenant</term>. It is recorded that they even dedicated golden images of their "posteriors" <note>original Latin: *culi* (anuses or buttocks).</note> [as offerings]. Similarly, in chapter 28 of <term>Deuteronomy</term>, this same disease is listed among the punishments that <term>Moses</term> pronounced to the Israelites in God's name, should they abandon the law and the worship of the true God.

But this disease seemed to me to be no more feminine than it was masculine. For this reason, I initially attributed it to <term>dysentery</term> <note>A severe intestinal infection; the author suggests the symptoms might be confused with menstruation.</note>, as its infection and foul odor correspond quite closely to those of "monthly purgings" <note>original Greek: *τοῖς καταμηνίοις*.</note>. Yet this, too, is common to both sexes. Finally, <term>Philo Judaeus</term> <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher from Alexandria.</note> dispelled the darkness from my eyes and enabled me to see the truth. In his treatise titled *Every Good Man is Free* <note>original Greek: *ὅτι πᾶς σπουδαῖος ἐλεύθερος*.</note>, he relates the following story about <term>Diogenes</term> <note>Diogenes of Sinope, the famous Cynic philosopher.</note>: "It is said, at any rate,"

<insert>Having observed one of the buyers, who was afflicted by the feminine disease and appeared non-male in his aspect, he approached and said: "Buy me, for you seem to me to have need of a man."</insert> <note>original Greek: "θεασάμενός τινα τῶν ὠνεομένων... σύ με πρίω. σὺ γὰρ ἀνδρὸς χρείαν ἔχειν μοι δοκεῖς." Now, <term>Ascalon</term> <note>An ancient coastal city in Palestine, modern-day Ashkelon.</note> was a city of Palestine in which <term>Caystrus</term>, the son of Penthesilea, married <term>Derceto</term> and from her fathered <term>Semiramis</term> <note>A legendary queen of Assyria.</note>. From this arose the cult of Venus in that place, whom we learn from <term>Diodorus</term> <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC Greek historian.</note> and others was actually Derceto herself. But even among the Israelites, under the reigns of the kings, there was a sacred grove of <term>Astarte</term> <note>A Phoenician goddess of fertility and war, often identified with Venus/Aphrodite.</note> (Venus), whose priests were effeminate and castrated. As <term>Selden</term> <note>John Selden (1584–1654), a renowned English polymath and scholar of ancient Near Eastern religions.</note> explains in *On the Syrian Gods* (Part II, Chapter 2), citing <term>Jerome</term> and <term>Aquila</term> the translator. By these examples, I believe it is clear how much <term>Longinus</term> <note>The author of "On the Sublime," who praised the term "feminine disease" as a sophisticated literary device.</note> was in error when he decorated this <term>periphrasis</term> <note>A roundabout or indirect way of speaking.</note> with the praise of being "inimitable"; for nothing is more common among the Greeks and Romans than this way of describing <term>Cinaedi</term>.

*   First, I will speak on the **abundance of natural talent**; <term>ingenii copia: The innate mental capacity and creativity a person is born with.</term>

*   And finally, on the **aids of long and diligent practice**, <term>exercitatio: The constant application and rehearsal of one’s skills.</term>

...of all those who have followed their opinion <note>original: "pedibus ivere"—literally "to go with their feet," a Roman idiom for voting in agreement with a motion</note>, it may be said that they were greatly mistaken. They believed that Sallust <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–35 BCE), a Roman historian known for his concise and sometimes archaic style.</note> looked to a restricted interpretation by learned men rather than to the etymology of the word and the familiar, common way of speaking. This is especially true since Fabius <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 CE), the most famous Roman teacher of rhetoric.</note> called eloquence "lustful," and the author of the short commentary *On the Causes of Corrupted Eloquence* <note>This likely refers to the "Dialogus de oratoribus," a work often attributed to Tacitus.</note> called it "lucrative" and "bloody"—to omit many other arguments which are not appropriate to mention here. 

Nor did Julius Candidus and the younger Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus (61–113 CE). In his letters, he discusses the distinction between mere talkers and true orators.</note> fail to brilliantly separate **eloquence** from **talkativeness**. They snatched eloquence away from wicked men—those who, like Catiline <note>Lucius Sergius Catilina, the Roman conspirator famous for being articulate but dangerous.</note>, have too little wisdom despite being articulate and fluent—and declared it the sole property of wise and upright men. 

However, we must rather blame the poverty of the Latin language here and, in contrast, the wealth of the Greek language, which is to be highly praised and proclaimed. For since true **Eloquence** is the faculty (as we said shortly before) of expressing a well-thought-out opinion of the mind elegantly and appropriately, and since no one thinks correctly unless their heart is imbued and equipped with **wisdom**; the ancient Greeks first called this method of thinking and explaining thoughts, and this power of speaking, *sophia* <note>original: "σοφίαν"—wisdom.</note>. Then, even more precisely, they called it *logiotēta* <note>original: "λογιότητα"—the quality of being "logios," meaning learned, eloquent, or rational.</note>, and called the eloquent man *logion* <note>original: "λόγιον"—an eloquent person or a scholar.</note>. Within these words, both **reason** and **speech** are contained <note>The Greek word "Logos" famously means both "word/speech" and "reason/proportion."</note>; through both, humans are reminded of their divine origin and distinguished from brute animals. 

I could, if the time permitted, wander further and, shaking out the cabinets of deeper learning, bring forward some points about Mercury <note>The Roman god Mercury (Greek: Hermes) was the patron of both commerce and communication.</note>, the inventor of the art of speech and, among the pagans, the presiding official of eloquence and its tutelary God. We learn that this very surname *Logios* <note>original: "Λογίς," likely a scribal variant or error for "Λόγιος"—the eloquent/rational one.</note> was attributed to him by the ancients. I could also go into praises of my native language by comparing it with the principal languages flourishing in Europe, which [shares] the abundance of Greek...

...and its proper nature, which it <note>Eloquence</note> most closely emulates; and from this, I could show what true Eloquence really is. Descriptions of Fame exist in Virgil <note>Virgil describes Rumor (Fama) in Book 4 of the Aeneid.</note> and of Philosophy in Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD); he describes the personification of Philosophy in his "Consolation of Philosophy."</note>; both of these figures, by the license of poetic imagination, are spoken of as if they were numbered among the Goddesses:

> She walks upon the ground, and hides her head among the clouds. <note>original: "Ingrediturque solo, & caput inter nubila condit" — Virgil, Aeneid 4.177. This describes a figure so vast it spans from earth to heaven.</note>

> — — — as many feathers as are on her body,
> So many eyes she has, and just as many tongues: <note>original: "quot corpore plumæ, / Tot oculi, totidem linguæ" — Virgil, Aeneid 4.181-182.</note>

Well? Is this not almost a sketch of Eloquence herself, a lifelike image? Her foresight is so sharp-eyed, and the form and appearance of her speech is as varied and manifold as the immense variety of things themselves, which is never bounded by any limits. What of the fact that Eloquence is not only *not* always flowing and overflowing with a great abundance of words, but sometimes, according to the need of the matter and the time, she is plainly mute?

"Mute Eloquence!" someone will perhaps mutter, and will hardly hold back a laugh. Nay indeed, Listeners, it sometimes happens that she falls silent, and achieves more through silence than she could have obtained through a long, composed, and accurate speech. ...which <note>original: "que" — this is the end of the word begun on the previous page, likely "superatque" (and surpasses).</note> he was about to clear away the crimes charged against his father before the ambassadors of the Greek nations; yet he fell silent out of shame and modesty. They did this because they saw that such feelings could be expressed or fashioned by no paintbrush of eloquence. 

And if we pass over the silences of Eurydice in Sophocles, or those of Deianira in the same author—silences crafted with art and sketched after the image of Nature—do we not also see this in nature itself? Whenever we choose to turn our eyes from human affairs back to nature, do we not sometimes encounter in the rivers themselves a certain mute course of water, a silence, as it were? 

Do we not frequently see the Rhône in Europe, the Tigris in Asia, and the Nile in Africa—all vast rivers—hide that very mass of rapid waves? Those twisting whirlpools and rushing columns that were, moments before, breaking through dikes and dealing immense destruction to crops, trees, and farmsteads throughout the fields, are often hidden and withdrawn from our sight, only to burst forth from the earth again after a long distance. Shall we deny that they are still rivers during those times when they subside and are no longer visible to us? And yet, that divine light of the mind, whose sharpness surpasses the sight of the bodily eyes by countless degrees...

Indeed, the forceful brevity of this sentence was preferred over any effuse or redundant oration by two of the most learned and serious writers on the art of Rhetoric, **Aristotle** and **Demetrius of Phalerum** (or rather, the Alexandrian).

Shall we then exclude that concise style of speaking, or the meager and slender one? Yet nothing would be easier for us than to demonstrate—whether by the noble examples of the wisest nations or by the weightiest testimonies and precepts of the most learned men—that this very method of speaking, either briefly or thinly, is not only to be counted among the types of Eloquence, but is often to be preferred in many places and times to that full and grand faculty of speaking which some alone praise.

Let us return again to the nature of springs and rivers, and in their varying sizes, we shall see what is true. Rather, do we not rise in their honor? And do they not, with lowered waters, adore those greater ones as rivers of the greater nations, or even as deities?

What of the fact that even these slender rivers, being closest to their sources, are often extremely clear, pleasant, gold-bearing, and gem-bearing? Even if someone were to scorn these natural gifts (which one might do with a calm mind), certainly for quenching thirst and other necessary uses of human life, nothing is sweeter or more healthful than the bright purity of those translucent springs and streams, which show off schools of fish playing upon the yellow gravel mixed with green herbs.

...nor can mere fluency <term>facundia: the raw ability to speak readily or "the gift of gab," distinguished here from true eloquence</term>, whether it flows from an impure heart or is animated by no vigor of art and reason, or is falsely seasoned, obtain and defend the name of true eloquence. On the other hand, those thin, meager, or shallow streams—provided they are living and rise from natural warmth—whether they are understood literally or applied figuratively to explain the nature of eloquence, are not unbecoming to their kind. And if they are not closest to the highest peak, they are certainly not cast down nor to be despised; instead, they are often placed at such a level of honor and dignity that they either surpass or equal grander styles in their splendor, even those positioned at the very summit of height. 

Therefore, having scattered and cleared away the obstacles that seemed to stand in our way, let us approach the very sources of Eloquence, which we have said spring from the twin heads of talent <term>ingenium: natural wit or innate ability</term> and erudition, flowing together into a single channel.

There was once a famous question among the writers of the art, both among the **Greeks** and the **Latins**: whether nature <note>Latin: *natura*</note> or teaching <note>Latin: *doctrina*</note> contributed more to a perfect eloquence, complete in all its parts. The nearly unanimous opinion of all was that one requires the help of the other, and that when they work together in harmony—joined, as it were, by the bond of marriage—they produce an exceptional and illustrious offspring. The life of this progeny is extended through every age, and by the beauty of its most flawless form, it ravishes spectators into admiration, kindles desire, inflames love, and finally raises and extols those who possess it to the highest peak of glory. 

But this nature, Listeners, is not at our discretion, nor is it a matter within our power. We can provide the teaching, study, labor, and diligence ourselves; but we cannot give ourselves a nature that is skilled and fit for eloquence. That is a heavenly gift, flowing from the fountain of divine kindness. There is, to be sure, a common saying: ***An orator is made, a poet is born*** <note>original: "Oratorem fieri, Poëtam nasci." A famous Classical proverb suggesting that rhetoric is a craft to be learned, while poetry is a divine spark.</note>; but it is less than true, and must be counted among those things that require a gentle interpretation. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of eloquence, specifically moving from the general necessity of combining nature and teaching to a detailed examination of innate human talent. The author argues that since great orators are rare throughout history, eloquence cannot be purely a matter of effort; it requires a specific natural disposition.</meta>

<page-num>341</page-num>
<sig>Y 3</sig>

If our Eloquence could be acquired and prepared by our will or industry alone, the complaints of the most serious men would be vain and foolish when they lament the misfortune of their own ages, in which either no Orator or only a rare one had appeared. Nor would the names of **Demosthenes** and **Cicero**, blooming with perpetual praise, have cast shadows over others by the brilliance of their own fame. To be sure, as it is in the whole nature of things, so too in human talent a certain wonderful variety of disposition shines forth:

> *Here the grain grows more happily, there the grapes;*
> *Elsewhere the fruits of trees and unbidden grasses*
> *Turn green.*
> <note>original: *Hic segetes, illic veniunt felicius uvæ: Arborei fœtus alibi, atque injussa virescunt Gramina.* This is a quote from Virgil's *Georgics* (Book I, 54-56), illustrating that different environments—and by extension, different people—possess different natural strengths.</note>

But it is our duty to know ourselves—that is, to explore our own nature, to track down and distinguish the momentum of our talents, seeing where they most strongly tend and incline. We must see what they can bear, what they can sustain, what they can carry through, and what they can complete. If these talents are discovered to lean toward Eloquence and seem, as it were, "made for it," then we must thereafter employ every doctrine, care, and concern to groom, shape, and adorn them. Therefore, it is worth the effort to recognize what such a nature or talent is, or ought to be. 

When philosophers describe man, they say he consists of soul and body, *one of which, as Sallust says, we share with the Gods, and the other with the beasts.* <note>original: *quorum alterum nobis cum Diis, inquit Sallustius, alterum cum belluis commune est.* A famous line from the Roman historian Sallust's *Bellum Catilinae*.</note> The principal part of this soul is the mind, to which they assign two types of virtues: the innate and the voluntary. They say innate virtues are comprised of teachability <note>Latin: *docilitas*, meaning an aptitude for learning</note> and memory. The voluntary virtues are those four well-known ones: **Prudence**, **Justice**, **Fortitude**, and **Temperance**, since these proceed from the freedom of reason, than which nothing in man is more divine.

Yet this same ***Plato*** affirmed that there are two motions in man: one is external, driven by an outside impulse; the other is his own, which moves by itself and of its own accord. This second motion is more divine than the first and exists only in souls. Because this motion proceeds entirely from heat, the Philosophers called it a "little spark" <note>original: *igniculum*.</note> and a particle of the **divine breath** <note>original: *auræ divinæ*, also implying a "divine air" or "heavenly breeze."</note>—that is, a piece of the ether. They believed that the purer, more mobile, and faster this spark was, the closer it was to its own origin and the more divine it became. 

This is the fire by whose power ***Pericles*** was said to thunder, to flash lightning, and to throw all of Greece into confusion. This is the fire that vibrated as thunderbolts from the gasping mouth of ***Demosthenes*** to strike down kings. This fire, although heavenly, is not always like a lightning bolt; it is not always angry, nor always sounding with a horrific crash. It also shines with a mild splendor, shimmering more gently, and glimmers less frequently. For it has something in common with its kindred ether: which, while it is entirely distinguished and adorned by the shining fires of the stars—the sizes of most of which are immense—it is nevertheless admirable for their numerous diversity no less than for their beauty. Nor indeed, if the sun, illuminating all things with its light, snatches the day away from the rest, or if the golden face of the moon, shining in its full light, claims the night almost for itself alone, do the smaller stars lose their own honor and their own grace for that reason. ...breathes upon it, whether that malice of nature, or some defect, can be corrected and mended by art or study, and whether **talent** <note>The Latin *ingenium* refers to one's innate natural ability, wit, or genius.</note> can in some way be increased, raised up, and amplified? When our soul—clear, pure, and untouched by any stain—immigrated into this body fashioned from an earthly kind of elements as if into a dwelling-place, its vigorous and lively force is blunted, infected, and weakened, according to whether this body is more or less impure and defiled. That agility and speed for which the soul was once known is constrained and hindered by the weight and slowness of the bodily mass, as if by shackles thrown upon it. 

To this contagion of the body is added the various influence of the air and sky under which we are born and live, from which the vital spirit is drawn into the body. Added, too, is the varying quality of the foods by which the body is nourished and raised. Added are the diseases that commonly arise from the body; added are the sicknesses of the soul itself. Added is the crooked education of children, the discipline of living, the method of studies—and from these, the poor shaping of talents. Added are the vices of the age and public morals corrupted by luxury and laziness. Added are the turns of both kinds of fortune <note>Referring to both "good" and "bad" fortune.</note>, and infinite other things by which the human soul is usually cast down from its state of integrity and goodness, and talent is damaged and depraved by evil contagion. 

Therefore, just as streams of leaping waters, choked and obstructed by filthy overflow around their very mouths, can be purged and cleansed of filth and in many ways so assisted and restored that they flow down thereafter in a broader and more generous channel; so also can talent be both freed from many delays and supported by aids, so that it may gather greater strength and, increased in power, grow into the most magnificent greatness.

...weakness. <note>The text likely begins with "infirmitatem" (weakness/infirmity), following from the discussion of physical health on the previous page.</note> The Greeks called our body *soma* <note>original Greek: σῶμα</note>, as if it were a kind of *sema* <note>original Greek: σῆμα</note> for the soul; that is, they called it a tomb. But with how much greater justice shall we assign this name to the body when grief has extinguished every light of talent (*ingenium*), stripped away memory, corrupted judgment, drained the life from greatness, and so thoroughly strangled all the powers of the mind in its embrace—much like ivy—that the very soul itself (which the wisest philosophers and poets have called not only *eternal* but even *a god*) retains nothing but the name, becoming like a tomb? 

Therefore, anyone who desires to come to nature’s aid and to raise and lift up the fallen mind should keep at a distance and expel these lowly emotions—viewing them as the decay and ruin of talent and of the eloquence that bursts forth from it. In their place, one should welcome a gentler and far more kindhearted guest: **joy** (*laetitia*). Joy is inherently rich in speech and is a seeker of all ornament and elegance. 

Why should I go on here to discuss in greater detail the matter of poor education and the other corruptions of talent—some of which I have listed, and others I have left to your conjecture? Therefore, postponing the remaining points for a more opportune time, I shall recall my speech to its proper course and begin to explain which fields of eloquence the praised fountain of talent specifically wanders through.

...is formed, which serves as a sort of fulcrum upon which every part of Eloquence is sustained. It supplies its possessor with such a happy abundance of speech that it can sometimes even lead to surfeit. 

From these riches, and from this inexhaustible storehouse, **Judgment** selects whatever is most fitting and best. Occupying the citadel of reason, as if from a high watchtower, it sends out the lights of the mind across the entire level plain of the subject matter, just like Homer’s Zeus <note>original: "Homerici Jovis"; the author refers to the King of the Gods in the Iliad, who surveys the battlefield from the heights</note>. 

Judgment acts like a general on the battlefield: it does not merely place the spearmen <term>hastati: the first line of a Roman legion</term> in the front line, the chief men <term>principes: the second line of the legion</term> in the middle, and the veterans <term>triarii: the third, most experienced line</term> in the rear. It orders the skirmishers <term>velites: light-armed infantry</term> and light-armed troops to run forward against the enemy and provoke them to battle, and commands the cavalry to move to the right and left wings. 

But Judgment also inspects, examines, and approves every single rank—indeed, every single soldier: the recruits, the veterans, and the recalled volunteers <term>evocati: soldiers who had served their time but enlisted again at the general's invitation</term>. Once they are approved and admitted, Judgment disposes them so that they are intent and ready for every occasion, whether to withstand an enemy rushing in from all sides, to move an opponent from their position, to drive back a retreating foe, or to put a fleeing one to total rout. 

Why need I speak more at length about the dismissal of suspect allies? Why of the removal of the useless crowd of sutlers <note>camp followers who sold provisions</note>, servants, and camp-followers? Why of the trimming away of the massive weight of baggage? We read of more armies being prostrated and crushed by speech than by the sword; and whole cities—why do I say cities?—rather, entire kingdoms and empires have been both saved and subverted by it.

Whence these honors of warfare? Does it not come from the skill of the General’s own talent, the weight of his judgment, and the greatness of his mind? Therefore, give me an Alexander the Great, and I will give you an **Eloquent** man; one whose resources—that is, whose speech—is magnificent, refined, and adorned; and at the same time possesses a vigorous hand, made for every height of the soul: in which there are elements that stand out, that lead the ranks, and that command all others. 

However, we do not require or demand only a single Alexander: let there be Miltiadeses, Themistocleses, Epaminondases, Fabricii, Fabii, Germanicuses, Corbulos, Aëtiuses, and Belisariuses <note>The speaker lists a "who's who" of great Greek and Roman generals spanning from the Persian Wars to the late Roman Empire</note>. Let there even be lesser leaders and generals than these; but let them be powerful in talent, judgment, and sublimity of mind. For in vain will the doors of **Eloquence** be knocked upon if an inept and difficult nature has denied entry. 

The ancients imagined **Eloquence** as a Queen; but what king or what queen exists without ministers or friends to manage admissions? So too, none of you will be admitted to this queen unless **Talent** <term>ingenium: innate mental ability</term> has opened the palace doors, **Judgment** has indicated the proper time for approaching, **Magnificence** <note>likely referring to a "grand style" of speech</note> has given the confidence for addressing her, and **Memory** has supplied the things to be said. Then indeed, with a friendly hand and a charming face, the **Praetorian Prefect** <term>praefecta praetorio: the highest-ranking official in the Roman imperial court</term> will lead you closer and right to the throne of Eloquence itself. She will bring you to the kiss of greeting, and by her recommendation, she will ensure that the Queen counts you among the number of her friends, and gifts you with a golden crown, a purple robe, and a golden belt. Do you ask who this Praetorian Prefect of Eloquence is, Listeners? It is **Erudition** <note>Learning or wide-ranging education</note>, the other...

The fountain of **Eloquence**, though later in order of discussion, is prior in its abundance and dignity. For from this fountain—even more blessedly than from the mere springs of natural talent—bursts forth a richness of both matter and words, from which sacred and profane Eloquence alike form a most ample and beautiful body. Indeed, in both types, **Erudition** <note>The author uses "Eruditio" to mean deep, wide-ranging scholarship and the mastery of various sciences and arts.</note> itself acts as the moderator and governor of talent. 

But sacred Eloquence possesses one thing above the profane: it is occasionally so animated by the divine spirit that it transcends every peak of human talent and learning. Like thunderbolts and lightning flashes sent down from heaven itself, it can in no way be resisted, and no other faculty of speaking can be compared to it in any way. 

From this divine inspiration and breath—which so fills the mind it inhabits that the person appears transformed and nearly possessed by a holy fervor—we shall distinguish this eloquence of ours. Our eloquence, proceeding from natural talent, receives its growth from <term>Erudition</term> <note>original: "eruditione"; the systematic study of literature, history, and philosophy.</note>; and when it has been strengthened by practice and perfected in all its parts, it remains as inferior to that divine inspiration as the foul waters of a muddy swamp are surpassed by the sweetest and most health-giving streams of the Nile. 

Struck with admiration for this, **Augustine** once desired to see—not the previously mentioned **Demosthenes** or **Cicero**—but **Paul** preaching, just as he wished to see Rome in its bloom and **Christ** in the flesh. These were his famous "three wishes," though he knew they were fleeting and vanished like the wind. <note>St. Augustine’s "Three Wishes" (the "tres dotes" or "tria vota") were to have seen Christ in the flesh, Paul in the pulpit, and Rome in its glory.</note>

But just as that divine inspiration is rare, the use of human **Erudition** in sacred Eloquence is frequent, consisting of the knowledge of the sciences and arts. Sacred scripture teaches us that **Moses** was imbued and instructed in the secret wisdom of the Egyptians—surely not without the care and providence of the Supreme Deity—as he was the destined founder of the covenant to be made with his people from their very cradle. 

What of the others? Must we not believe that **Isaiah** was nourished in the best disciplines in the royal court for no other reason than that he might later sing the Gospel of the Christ to be born with an even clearer voice? Was **Paul** brought up at the feet of **Gamaliel** <note>Gamaliel was a celebrated doctor of Jewish Law and a member of the Sanhedrin; Paul cites this education to prove his mastery of tradition.</note> for any other purpose than...

...and that he was likely a man of learning, is it not probable that he would later preach Christ crucified to the nations with such stupendous eloquence? From where came that most eloquent defense of himself before **King Agrippa**? From where came that most flattering introduction, in which he declared himself blessed because he was to have a judge who was an expert in Jewish customs and disputes? From where came those testimonies in his Letters, sought from the best Greek poets—from **Aratus**, **Epimenides**, and **Menander**—if not from that most fertile fountain of **Erudition** which we praise? 

Why say more? Any speech that is sweeter than honey, more turbulent than snowy torrents, and more piercing than a spear, must necessarily possess much natural talent, but even more erudition. For learning provides not only the subject matter that must be spoken, but also the precise words suited for expressing those things.

But [eloquence], having begun from the very elements of letters, syllables, and words, will unfold every refinement and ornament of composed speech. ...on the other hand, the word-arrangement of the unskillful is ridiculous. According to this model, listeners, stands **Eloquence**; though it is a single thing, it is varied into a thousand shapes—from the learned it is a miracle, from the unrefined and unskillful it is a mockery. It is not unlike the tales the poets once told of **Proteus** <note>A shape-shifting sea god from Greek mythology who would change his form to avoid being caught.</note>: that he was accustomed to turn himself into various figures, so that at one moment he was a lion, then a fierce tiger, now a wave, now fire. But those spoke more accurately who handed down the tradition that he was a philosopher-king; that is, one who held the discipline of both acting well and speaking well. To such a man, nothing was easier than to bend, change, and turn his speech, transfiguring it into every kind of form as the subject, the occasion, and the listener seemed to require.

Lest this seem incredible to anyone, consider the letters of the alphabet. Although their true number does not extend beyond sixteen <note>The author likely refers to the "Cadmean letters," the original set of the Greek alphabet before later additions.</note>, yet the painstaking curiosity of certain "little Greeks" <note>original: *Græculorum* — a somewhat dismissive term for Greek scholars who obsessed over technical trifles.</note>, wasting their leisure, discovered that these letters, when variously transposed, produce hundreds of thousands of myriads of syllables. What then shall we say of the manifold transposition of that vast multitude of syllables, from which arises a variety of words as countless and infinite as the multitude of things they were invented to signify and brought into use? To what end is all this? someone will ask. So that you may understand from this, listeners, that he who has joined **Erudition** <note>Deep, comprehensive scholarship.</note> to natural talent has paved the way for himself to every kind of Eloquence.

All posterity has granted the primary place in **Poetic Eloquence** to **Homer**. And from where, I ask, did this come, if not from an infinite knowledge of all things and sciences? It is the mark of a learned man to know and understand Homer’s erudition; nor has anyone ever possessed such a lucky talent that he did not leave behind more things for others to notice in Homer than he himself observed. So inexhaustible is the supply of all-encompassing learning in this poet that, although all poets, philosophers, and orators have drawn innumerable streams from that fountain into their own small gardens, his riches suffer no loss, but sustain themselves with that same abundance.

One can find, therefore, in **Homer** every variety of **Eloquence**: the divine, the human, the civil, the military, the forensic, the public, the private, the natural, the moral; the lofty, the humble, the moderate; the ample, the concise, the harsh, the gentle, the bitter, the sweet, the refined, the rustic, the prudent, the insane, the modest, the impudent, and into whatever other forms the diversity of speech is distinguished.

There was a most abundant harvest of speech here, and a wide-open field of **Eloquence**, if one were free to travel through only the most powerful examples of those excellent men who flourished not in one, but in multiple kinds of speaking. There occur the most diligent interpreters of nature, the Plinys. 

Yet, all these men ingenuously showed that this **Eloquence** of theirs—so full of diversity and variety—flowed from an all-encompassing **Erudition** <note>Deep, wide-ranging learning across many subjects.</note>, built up by the riches of a fertile genius. Therefore, whoever you are that loves a good mind and strives for the path to the perfection of **Eloquence**, add the benefits of learning to the gifts of your natural talent; join them, and let both of these fountains of **Eloquence** flow together into a single channel. 

I deliberately pass over many things here, listeners, because not only would this hour be insufficient, but not even a whole day would suffice for all the things that could be said about this one art of oratory, by which—as if by a mistress—the mind must be formed for **Eloquence**.

Philopoemen <note>A Greek general and statesman of the Achaean League, often called "the last of the Greeks" for his tactical genius.</note> was a most noble General of the Achaeans. When an enemy was lacking, he did not surrender himself to laziness and idleness. Instead, having divided his forces with his lieutenant Lycortas, he would order Lycortas to encounter and attack him as if he were a real enemy—now from the left side, now from the right, now from the front, now from the rear; now in mountainous places, now in the open plains; now at the first light of dawn, now at midday, now late at night; sometimes with only infantry or cavalry, and sometimes with cavalry mixed with the foot-soldiers. He did this so that he would always be most prepared for every true assault by enemy forces. By this art and diligence, he not only proved himself unconquered by his enemies, but also brought it about that—despite not being the leader of the largest nation—he was numbered among the greatest generals of his age. Therefore, just as he acted in war and abroad, so you, in contrast, [must act] at home <margin>at home</margin>...

At home, and in your study rooms, imagine an adversary for yourselves, and do battle with him using your own weapons—that is, the pen <term>stilus: literally the ancient writing tool, used here as a metaphor for the act of writing and composition.</term>. For there is nothing that contributes so much benefit and such great fluency to speaking well as the pen; there is nothing that secures a more ready victory when it comes time for a real battle. 

Why should I excerpt here what Cicero, Fabius <note>The speaker refers to Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, the most influential Roman teacher of rhetoric.</note>, Aulus Gellius, and other excellent authors have collected—those famous and outstanding remarks concerning the frequent use of the pen and tireless practice? Since examples aid the minds of students no less than rules, why should I not instead place before your eyes both the example and the advice of Apelles <note>The most celebrated painter of ancient Greece, active in the 4th century BCE.</note>? For him, no day passed without drawing a line, and he warned his students that no day should be allowed to pass without a line being drawn <note>original: "nulla dies sine linea" — a famous proverb attributed to Apelles, suggesting that mastery requires daily practice.</note>. 

There is also that famous testimony which Cicero gave regarding the diligence of Isocrates <note>A famous Athenian orator (436–338 BCE) who, despite a weak voice and stage fright, became a legendary teacher.</note>: that from his school, as if from the Trojan Horse, only leaders emerged. And yet this great man—who was gifted with such skill in speaking that he was even called the "Father of Eloquence"—shrank from public speaking out of modesty and a certain natural shyness. Nevertheless, he practiced with his pen tirelessly and wrote speeches for others to use on their own behalf in court. And when the Fates extended his life to his ninety-ninth year, in that very extreme old age—specifically in his ninety-fourth year—he composed that outstanding oration titled the *Panathenaicus* <note>A long speech praising the history and achievements of Athens.</note>. 

Devote your time, therefore, to practicing with the pen. And when your hand is weary from writing, let a no less useful exercise take its place: declamation <term>declamation (declamatio): the practice of delivering formal speeches on rhetorical themes to develop one's voice, delivery, and memory.</term>. I think you have heard at some point about Cicero’s students who went on to become consuls. You have read Cicero himself, Seneca, Fabius, Pliny, Petronius, and you have recognized that immense passion the ancients had for declamation. Do you believe this labor was undertaken in vain? Were the frequent public readings and the invited audiences in vain? Were the established contests of Eloquence in vain? For if all those things were once in vain—rather than for preserving and increasing...

...which served as the means for gaining not only a fine but also a ready facility in speaking; let these examples certainly now also rouse your diligence and industry to imitation. But imitate only the best. From this imitation, a habit of the most refined eloquence <term>eloquium: the art of expressive and persuasive speech.</term> will be born, which will accompany you to the pulpits <term>ambones: raised platforms in a church where the Gospel was read or sermons preached.</term> of churches; it will be present at the benches of judges; it will follow you to the chairs of the Academies. And—where the greatest honor lies—when you must eventually speak before the Nobles, the Princes, the Kings, and the Emperors, that eloquence will stand at your side. It will provide such abundance and magnificence of speech that, in their astonishment, they will turn their faces toward yours, and finally, swept away by emotion, they will cry out: *“This, this is the chosen flower of the people, and the very marrow of Persuasion!”* <note>original: "Hic, hic est flos delibatus populi, Suadæque medulla." This is a famous line originally used by the poet Ennius to describe the orator Marcus Cornelius Cethegus; "Suada" is the Roman goddess of persuasion.</note>

You see, most noble young men, that many arguments can be gathered from all sides by which even the most sluggish minds can be spurred toward industry and hard work. If I were to attempt to list them all now, I would not only foolishly abuse the limited time we have, but I would also do an injustice to your own excellent character—which, by its own nature, rises toward every honor of noble praise. 

Therefore, seeing that only one thing remains for me to do, I will turn myself with a brief prayer to God. I will pray to Him, who alone is the most rich Source of all good things, that He might wish this virtuous mindset to be permanent in you, and that He might supply me with the strength of body and soul necessary to continue cultivating, watering, and making it fruitful. Then, indeed, may He deign to bestow with a full hand health upon this most distinguished Assembly, prosperity upon the Academy, and upon the most Serene Princes and the entire Princely family, a happiness that is complete, endless, and undefiled—and may He daily surpass these prayers of mine with an even more generous and overflowing kindness.

# ON THE MOST HAPPY ARRIVAL
## OF THE MOST SERENE
### PRINCES OF CLEVES.

So, the truth is certain: the wandering rumor that filled the towns will no longer mock the people’s devotion, nor torment their hearts as they drift between hope and fear. 

Behold! Even now a thick cloud of dust rises into the air, obscuring the radiant sun’s bright rays and signaling the Duke’s approach. Rise up, you hills of Cleves <note>original: "COLLES Clivosi"; a poetic pun on the name of the Duchy of Cleves (Kleve), which is derived from the German word for cliff or hill.</note>, and hasten to meet the Father of the Fatherland! 

Joyfully fling wide your gates, warlike Wesel <note>original: "VESALIA"; a prominent Hanseatic city in the Duchy of Cleves.</note>, and hurry to drape your doorposts in triumphal laurel. He comes! Behold, the great Duke arrives, and at his side as a companion comes Philip <note>original: "PHILIPPUS"; likely referring to a young prince of the House of Cleves, accompanying his father.</note>, the beloved son of his noble father and the primary joy of his noble mother. 

Now a cheering throng of both nobles and commoners has poured out into the fields. People of every kind rush forward: the elderly, young boys, and unwed maidens. There, the dignified matron forgets her usual reserve, fearing neither the heavy boots nor the bold, wandering hands of the soldiers <note>original: "caligatorum"; literally "the booted ones," a term for common soldiers derived from the *caliga*, the Roman military sandal.</note>. The farm youths cast aside their sickles even as they reap the ripened grain; they abandon their fields—though rich with a bountiful harvest—for the land now seems dull and lowly to them compared to this sight. 

The same passion burns in everyone; their hearts, spurred by devotion, long to press loyal kisses upon the Duke's life-giving hands. Even the River Rhine <note>original: "RHENUS"</note> himself, surrounded by a chosen company of Naiads <note>Water nymphs.</note> and Dryads <note>Tree nymphs.</note>, and those agile spirits who leap with bold feet across the high, wooded ridges, comes forward. He brings with him the Satyrs and the Fauns—the gods of the wild—along with Pan <note>The god of shepherds and the wild.</note>, Pales <note>The Roman goddess of shepherds and livestock.</note>, and powerful Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture and grain.</note>. Bowing low to lick the very footprints of the noble leader, the River welcomes the PRINCE’S ARRIVAL with a voice of thanksgiving.

# CENTENNIAL SONG.

I, my Muse, <note>original: "Camœna." A Latin name for the Muses, goddesses of inspiration.</note> go where I am not permitted to go.

My love, **FREDERICK WILLIAM** <note>Frederick William, the "Great Elector" of Brandenburg (1620–1688).</note>, and the love of the world.
Who, his victorious temples wreathed in thick laurel,
Submitting his own fortune, together with a picked

Walls of **BUDA**, and pours the first <margin>195</margin>
Strength of his men into the city’s shattered fortifications.
Thus, with **SCHÖNING** <note>Hans Adam von Schöning (1641–1696), the Brandenburg general who led the assault on the city.</note> leading and showing the way to others,
**BUDA**, finally recovered by **BRANDENBURG** valor,
Is celebrated in song as subject to the **PALATINE GAMES**. <note>Original: *Palatinis Ludis*; likely referring to courtly celebrations or theatrical displays held in honor of the victory.</note>
Public heraldry of perpetual fame follows <margin>200</margin>
A private collection built into a huge heap, threatening the heavens:
Which, from its own rich wealth, the surpassing
**RETINUE OF THE SACRED PALACE** <note>Original: *Sacri Comitiva Palati*; refers to the office or rank of the Count of the Sacred Palace, a high imperial dignity.</note> provides:
Which, recently drawn from the first origins through old records
By a skillful hand and from ancient <gloss>1</gloss> **MASTERS**, <margin>205</margin>

->Before<-

[Buda], before <note>Original: *Præ-quam*.</note> it was first occupied through trickery by Suleiman <note>Suleiman the Magnificent.</note> in the year 1526, was recovered the following year, soon lost again in the year 1529, and in the same year, and likewise in '99, 1602, 1635, 1669, and 1684, it was besieged in vain; finally in this year, with much groaning from the Turks, it was recovered and returned to its former allegiance.

To Pythagoras: here is the simple <margin>1</margin> UNITY <note>original: "MONAS"; in Pythagorean philosophy, the Monad represents the first, the seed of all numbers, and the source of all things.</note>, here ten times repeated,
And ten times again; so many times is it reported as PERFECT <margin>2</margin>,
And consecrated to the highest Jove. Now, Muses, the THIRD
CENTURY <margin>290</margin> touches you, and you confess your divine power.
Go therefore, and celebrate the joyful day and the solemn feast:
Joined with the crowd of your sisters,
Strengthen the voices of Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of music, poetry, and the sun.</note> with both your presence and your song.
He indeed, having descended to the decorated altars of the temple, <margin>295</margin>
Will receive with calm ears the pious VOWS <margin>3</margin> <note>original: "VOTA"</note> of those praying:
And he will grant many AGES <note>original: "SECLA"</note> of sacred BIRDS <margin>4</margin>,
Surpassing the years: you, report these things MULTIPLIED <margin>5</margin>
TENFOLD: and include the longest lifespans of the Hamadryads <note>Tree nymphs whose lives were tied to the longevity of their trees.</note>
Within the fatal cycle of flowering. <margin>300</margin>

1. The numbers I, X, and C (1, 10, 100) are sacred to Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, and all are contained within the span of a century. *Therefore, the sacred number appears nine times in three centuries.* The Muses, however, first appear in *threes*, then *three times three*. See Ausonius <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius, a 4th-century Roman poet and teacher.</note>.

2. *The number ten [Denarius] was considered perfect by the Pythagoreans, representing God, the Sun, the heavens, an age, and even the ALL.*

3. *In ancient times, solemn vows [vota] were undertaken every five years, and also every ten years, for the health of the Republic and the safety of the Emperors, so that the state might remain in the same condition.*

4. *The birds sacred to Phoebus are the Crow, the Raven, and the Phoenix. Regarding these and their age, there is a poem by Hesiod mentioned in Ausonius.*

5. *Frequently found on ancient coins:* VOWS FOR 10, MULTIPLIED BY 20; VOWS FOR 20, MULTIPLIED BY 30, etc.
